title: Zero-Shot Visualization: Exploring Text Corpora with User-Prompted Axes
summary: We study the application of large language models (LLMs) to the visual exploration of textual corpora. We introduce zero-shot visualization (ZSV), a task in which users specify concepts in natural language and documents are mapped onto the corresponding concept axes for visualization. Building a ZSV system of practical value is non-trivial, as it requires choices at the intersection of feature functions, efficient implementation tradeoffs, and pre/post-processing decisions affecting visualization quality. To that end, we establish a benchmark that compares methods spanning embedding similarity, direct semantic judgments, and conditional likelihood estimation in this setting. Across multiple datasets and use cases we evaluate the properties of different scoring methods and design choices in terms of semantic faithfulness, score fidelity, and computational cost. Our results identify that scoring based on next-token probabilities offers the strongest practical trade-off among the evaluated methods. We further apply this approach to unlabeled corpora to examine its behavior in realistic exploratory settings. These experiments highlight additional design considerations, including the use of graded axes together with binary relevance filtering, and reveal a compositional sentiment bias in off-topic documents. Based on these findings, we provide practical guidelines for constructing end-to-end ZSV baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and benchmarks “zero-shot visualization” (ZSV), a way to use large language models to project documents onto concept axes defined only with natural-language prompts, enabling interactive visual exploration of text corpora without labels or training.
AI.motivation: Existing visual text exploration tools usually need labeled data, predefined features, or task-specific training. With powerful LLMs, we may be able to directly turn natural-language concepts into numerical scores and visualize documents along these axes, but it is unclear how best to do this, which LLM scoring schemes work reliably, and what trade-offs arise between semantic quality and computational cost.
AI.method: They formally define the ZSV task: users give natural-language concept descriptions and documents are mapped to coordinates along these concept axes. They then construct a benchmark that compares alternative LLM-based scoring strategies—embedding similarity, explicit semantic judgments, and conditional likelihood / next-token probabilities—under different implementation and pre/post-processing variants. They evaluate these options on multiple datasets and scenarios by measuring semantic faithfulness (alignment with intended concepts), score fidelity, and computation cost. They also run experiments on unlabeled corpora to simulate realistic exploratory use and probe behaviors like graded axes and relevance filtering.
AI.result: Among the evaluated approaches, scoring based on next-token probabilities (i.e., conditional likelihoods from the LLM) delivers the best overall practical trade-off: relatively strong semantic alignment and score quality at a manageable computational cost. Experiments in unlabeled, exploratory settings show the importance of combining continuous (graded) concept scores with binary filtering for relevance, and they discover a compositional sentiment bias in off-topic documents revealed by the model’s scoring behavior.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can drive zero-shot visualization of text corpora by projecting documents onto user-defined natural-language concept axes. Properly designed next-token–probability scoring is a strong default choice, but achieving good ZSV performance requires careful design of axes, relevance filters, and preprocessing. The paper distills these empirical findings into concrete guidelines for building practical, end-to-end ZSV baselines for visual text exploration.

title: Capacity, Responsiveness and Alignment: What Makes a Latent Structure Actionable
summary: Localizing latent structures in the activation space of language models (LMs) is central to understanding and controlling their behavior. Yet, localized structures can differ substantially in their causal influence, raising the question of what makes a structure actionable. We tackle this question by casting causal influence as a product of three factors and showing empirically that they act as interpretable, distinct constraints: capacity, measuring the sensitivity of the model's output to movement along the structure, responsiveness, capturing how promotable the concept is given the current context, and alignment, reflecting how well the structure aligns with the context-specific representation of the concept. Across 4 LM families and 50 concepts, we observe that causal effectiveness requires all factors to be high; low capacity and responsiveness reduce it by 84% and 95%, respectively, while low alignment can reverse it, suppressing concept expression. Moreover, we find that causality is context-dependent rather than an intrinsic property of the structure, with causally effective directions forming a low-dimensional subspace that varies across contexts. By restricting the training of linear probes to this subspace, we introduce causal probes that achieve 17%-118% improvement in steering across models, with only 3% reduction in concept detection.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when and why latent directions in language model activation space can causally and reliably control model behavior, decomposing causal influence into three measurable factors and using them to design better steering methods.
AI.motivation: Interpretability and controllability methods often identify local directions or structures in a model’s activation space that correlate with high-level concepts, but these directions vary widely in whether they actually let us causally steer the model. The paper is motivated by the need to understand what distinguishes simply correlated features from truly actionable, causal ones, and how this depends on context.
AI.method: The authors formalize causal influence of a latent structure as the product of three factors—capacity, responsiveness, and alignment—and then empirically estimate and validate this decomposition across four language model families and fifty concepts. They analyze how each factor behaves across contexts, how low values in any factor degrade or invert causal control, and they characterize the subspace of directions that remain causally effective in a given context. Finally, they use this insight to constrain the training of linear probes to this low-dimensional causal subspace, creating “causal probes,” and compare their steering and detection performance to standard probes.
AI.result: They find that effective causal control requires high values in all three factors: low capacity and responsiveness reduce causal effectiveness by 84% and 95%, respectively, while poor alignment can even reverse the intended effect and suppress the concept. Causality is shown to be highly context-dependent, with causally effective directions forming a low-dimensional subspace that shifts with the context. Probes trained only within this causal subspace substantially improve steering performance (17%–118% gains across models) while incurring only a minor decrease (~3%) in concept detection accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Causal effectiveness of latent directions in language models is not an intrinsic property of those directions but is jointly determined by capacity, responsiveness, and alignment, all of which are context-dependent. By explicitly modeling and exploiting this structure, one can focus on a low-dimensional, context-specific causal subspace and train causal probes that substantially improve the reliability of steering with minimal loss in interpretive detection power.

title: Tree Navigation Without LLM Summaries: A Matched-Cost Study of Hierarchical Retrieval for Long-Document QA
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds language models in external context, but for long documents flat top-$k$ retrieval can cluster on a single region and miss complementary evidence. RAPTOR-style summary trees address this by recursively clustering chunks and using a language model to summarize each cluster at indexing time, then ranking summary nodes alongside raw chunks at query time. We show the main benefit of summary trees in long-document QA can come from navigation rather than the generated summary content. We introduce NavTree, a leaves-only retriever that builds a deterministic balanced segment tree over chunks (zero language-model calls at indexing) and uses the tree purely as a navigation scaffold: a hybrid lexical-and-dense frontier walk, anchored on top retrieved leaves, descends from the root and emits only leaf chunks to the reader. On a matched-cost evaluation against flat retrievers and an extractive re-implementation of RAPTOR, NavTree is the strongest matched-cost hierarchical retriever in our evaluated grid and ties the strongest flat baseline. On long-document multi-hop QA, it is the only hierarchical method that significantly beats BM25 on a class-vs-class basis, corroborated by a reader-free retrieval-recall check. A matched-reader replication of the published abstractive RAPTOR variant, given strong cluster summaries, still loses to NavTree at every multi-chunk budget, at zero indexing cost. The ranking carries across stronger and open-weight readers, a stronger encoder, and a full factorial that isolates leaves-only emission as the structural lever.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NavTree, a zero-indexing-cost hierarchical retriever for long-document QA that uses a deterministic segment tree for navigation instead of summary nodes, and shows it matches or beats both flat and summary-tree (RAPTOR-style) methods under matched cost, especially on multi-hop tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems for long documents often rely on flat top-k retrieval over chunks, which can over-focus on a single region and miss complementary evidence across the document. RAPTOR-style summary trees attempt to fix this by building hierarchical summaries using language models, but it is unclear whether improvements come from the summaries themselves or from the navigation structure. The paper aims to disentangle these factors and reduce the heavy indexing-time costs associated with LLM-based summarization.
AI.method: The authors propose NavTree, which constructs a deterministic balanced segment tree over document chunks with no language-model calls at indexing time. At query time, NavTree uses a hybrid lexical-and-dense retrieval to identify promising leaf chunks, then performs a frontier walk from the root of the segment tree toward those leaves, using the tree only as a navigation scaffold. The system emits only leaf chunks (no summary nodes) to the reader. They run matched-cost comparisons against flat retrievers and an extractive RAPTOR-style implementation, and also replicate an abstractive RAPTOR variant with strong cluster summaries to isolate the effect of leaves-only emission and navigation structure.
AI.result: Under matched computational cost, NavTree is the strongest hierarchical retriever in their evaluation space and ties the strongest flat baseline. On long-document multi-hop QA, it is the only hierarchical method that significantly outperforms BM25 on a class-vs-class basis, as further validated by a retrieval-recall analysis that does not depend on a reader. The replicated abstractive RAPTOR variant, even with strong summaries, underperforms NavTree across all multi-chunk retrieval budgets while incurring additional indexing cost. These findings generalize across different readers (including stronger and open-weight models), a stronger encoder, and a factorial analysis that points to leaves-only emission as the key structural factor.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical retrieval gains in long-document QA can largely be attributed to better navigation over the document rather than to generated summary content. A simple, deterministic segment-tree structure used purely for navigation, as in NavTree, can match or surpass more complex summary-tree approaches like RAPTOR while incurring zero LLM indexing cost. Leaves-only emission combined with a hybrid lexical-and-dense frontier walk is identified as an effective and efficient structural design for long-document, especially multi-hop, question answering.

title: Component and Dimension Sparsity in Transformer Refusal Mechanisms
summary: Activation steering manipulates large language model behavior by intervening on internal activations, but the mechanistic basis of these interventions remains poorly understood. We decompose refusal steering into component-level interventions across four open-weight models, identifying the sparse subsets of attention and MLP components whose steering suffices to reproduce the full behavioral effect. We find that refusal directions concentrate in sparse component mechanisms comprising 28--48\% of upstream components, retaining 88--101\% of steering effectiveness. Within these mechanisms, effective steering further concentrates in approximately 50\% of residual stream dimensions, retaining 85--98\% of the component-mechanism baseline, consistent with a privileged basis structure. Sparsity thus operates at two levels: which components are steered, and which dimensions within those components carry the signal. Together these findings show that refusal is not diffusely encoded across a transformer but assembled by a structured, identifiable mechanism, providing a foundation for mechanistic understanding of how refusal behaviors are represented and steered. To facilitate reproducibility, we release all code and raw experimental results in https://github.com/wang-research-lab/Refusal_Mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how activation steering causes refusal behavior in large language models, finding that refusal is implemented by sparse, structured mechanisms rather than being diffusely encoded.
AI.motivation: While activation steering can control LLM refusal behavior, we lack a mechanistic understanding of which internal components and representation dimensions actually mediate these effects; the paper aims to open this black box.
AI.method: The authors decompose refusal steering into fine-grained, component-level interventions across four open-weight transformer models, systematically identifying which attention and MLP blocks and which residual stream dimensions are responsible for steering, and measuring how much of the full steering effect each subset retains.
AI.result: They show that effective refusal steering is concentrated in sparse subsets of components—28–48% of relevant upstream attention/MLP blocks can reproduce 88–101% of the full steering effect, and within those blocks, about half of the residual stream dimensions preserve 85–98% of the steering power, indicating a privileged basis-like structure.
AI.conclusion: Refusal behavior in transformers is not distributed uniformly but is implemented by a structured, identifiable and sparse mechanism at both the component and dimensional levels, improving our mechanistic understanding of refusal steering and offering more targeted levers for controlling model behavior; they also release code and experimental data for reproducibility.

title: GAMEGO: Training Game-Dev Agents with Synthetic Trajectories Anchored in Real-World Assets
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in web front-end execution, with browser-based game generation emerging as a particularly prominent frontier. While previous efforts frequently rely on complex multi-turn workflows or focus on static game evaluation benchmarks, this work targets direct end-to-end real-world game synthesis driven by coding agents. However, generating complex games directly from sparse user queries often forces coding agents to make underspecified assumptions, yielding incomplete mechanics, disconnected gameplay flows, and limited visual aesthetics. To resolve this issue, this paper presents GameGo, a scalable framework that systematically transforms brief game seeds into comprehensive Product Requirements Documents grounded in industry game-development practices. To retain core gameplay constraints without restricting design exploration, GameGo uses task-specific dynamic compression to maximize information density while preserving instruction following. Based on this pipeline, GameGoData is constructed with 55,060 development trajectories across 2D, 2.5D, and 3D games, alongside GameGoBench, a benchmark comprising 124 diverse game queries. Training GameGoCoder on GameGoData yields a model that outperforms matched baselines and is comparable to frontier models across gamedev benchmarks. All code, datasets, and models will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GameGo, a framework that expands brief game ideas into detailed game design specs to help coding agents generate complete web games, along with a large dataset, benchmark, and a trained model that achieves strong game development performance.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents can generate browser games, but when users provide short, vague prompts, the agents must guess many details, leading to incomplete mechanics, disjoint gameplay, and poor visuals. Existing work either uses complex multi-step workflows or focuses on static benchmarks instead of realistic end-to-end game creation. There is a need for a scalable way to turn sparse game ideas into structured, industry-style requirements that LLMs can reliably use for high-quality game synthesis.
AI.method: The authors propose GameGo, a framework that converts brief game “seeds” into full Product Requirements Documents (PRDs) modeled after professional game development practice. The system employs task-specific dynamic compression to keep key gameplay constraints while allowing creative freedom, maximizing information density without harming instruction following. Using this pipeline they build GameGoData, a dataset of 55,060 development trajectories covering 2D, 2.5D, and 3D games, and GameGoBench, a benchmark of 124 diverse game queries. They then train GameGoCoder on this data and evaluate it on multiple game development benchmarks.
AI.result: GameGoCoder, trained on GameGoData, outperforms baseline models of similar scale and performs on par with state-of-the-art frontier models across game development benchmarks. The dataset and benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of PRD-style conditioning and dynamic compression for end-to-end web game synthesis from sparse prompts.
AI.conclusion: Structuring vague user game ideas into dense, professionally-inspired requirement documents enables coding agents to generate more complete, coherent, and aesthetically pleasing games. GameGo, together with GameGoData and GameGoBench, provides a scalable pipeline, training corpus, and evaluation suite that significantly improves LLM-based game generation and sets a foundation for future research in real-world, end-to-end game development agents.

title: Stabilizing language models under continual learning via condition-anchored distillation
summary: Continual adaptation of language models can change their output distribution on prompts learned earlier, while retaining every old prompt-answer pair may be undesirable or impossible. We study condition-anchored generative distillation (CAGD): retain a small set of old prompts, use a frozen previous model to reconstruct completions and generation states, and match its predictive distributions while learning the next task. The formulation separates three roles that ordinary replay conflates: conditions select the behavior to protect, teacher generations locate relevant states, and soft targets specify how predictions may change. For autoregressive language generation, teacher-rollout distillation admits an exact chain-rule decomposition of sequence divergence. For masked-diffusion language modeling, our implementation directly controls local denoising drift on teacher-generated completions. In continual adaptation of a 219M masked diffusion language model, CAGD reduces four-task final held-out loss from 2.927 to 1.114 in one task order and from 2.168 to 0.891 in exact reverse. The same soft targets lower final average loss by 0.055 over hard replay when teacher-generated support is held identical. The direction persists on fresh facts and natural instructions across SMDM and Qwen3. On GSM8K, Qwen adaptation preserves answer-format compliance, but exact-match retention is seed-mixed at 0.6B and worsens at 1.7B. These results support condition-anchored functional preservation as a common design principle across the tested language-generation objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes condition-anchored generative distillation (CAGD), a continual learning method for language models that preserves selected old behaviors using a frozen teacher and soft distillation targets, substantially reducing forgetting across multiple language-generation objectives.
AI.motivation: Continual adaptation of language models often changes their behavior on previously learned prompts, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Storing all past data is usually infeasible due to privacy, storage, or legal constraints. Existing replay methods entangle which behaviors to protect, where in the generation those behaviors occur, and how strictly predictions must be preserved. The authors aim to disentangle these aspects and design a principled, sample-efficient way to preserve desired behaviors while still allowing models to adapt to new tasks and information.
AI.method: They introduce condition-anchored generative distillation (CAGD). A small set of past prompts (conditions) is retained. A frozen previous model serves as a teacher that, given each condition, generates completions and intermediate generation states (rollouts). The student model, while learning new tasks, is trained to match the teacher’s predictive distributions at those teacher-visited states via soft distillation targets. The framework explicitly separates: (1) conditions that specify which behaviors to protect; (2) teacher generations that identify the relevant trajectory of hidden states; and (3) soft targets that govern how much the student’s predictions can change. For autoregressive models, they exploit a chain-rule decomposition of sequence divergence for teacher-rollout distillation. For masked-diffusion language models, they implement CAGD by directly controlling the local denoising drift around teacher-generated completions.
AI.result: In continual adaptation experiments with a 219M-parameter masked diffusion language model over four tasks, CAGD substantially reduces final held-out loss compared to baselines. For one task ordering, loss drops from 2.927 to 1.114; for the reverse ordering, from 2.168 to 0.891. When holding the teacher-generated support fixed, using soft targets (CAGD-style) yields a further 0.055 reduction in final average loss relative to hard replay. The beneficial trend carries over to fresh factual knowledge and natural instruction-following tasks using both SMDM and Qwen3 models. On GSM8K with Qwen, adaptation under CAGD keeps answer-format consistency, but exact-match accuracy retention is unstable at 0.6B parameters and degrades at 1.7B, indicating trade-offs at larger scales.
AI.conclusion: Condition-anchored generative distillation is an effective and general approach for preserving selected behaviors of language models during continual adaptation. By decoupling the choice of conditions, the trajectory of teacher states, and the strength/form of distillation targets, CAGD provides a principled way to control functional preservation across different language-generation objectives. The empirical results show strong mitigation of catastrophic forgetting and consistent gains over standard hard replay, though there remain open challenges in fully retaining task accuracy (e.g., on GSM8K) as model scale increases.

title: Text2Dashboard: A Governed Agent Architecture for Natural-Language Dashboard Generation over Enterprise DataBrain
summary:
Text2Dashboard is a DataBrain-specific prototype that turns natural-language analytic requests into inspectable dashboards. An installable Codex plugin and standalone Agent Runtime combine schema-constrained model decisions with typed tools, persistent state, and deterministic Hooks for approval, audit, checkpointing, recovery, and failure handling. The pipeline resolves entities, discovers metadata, enforces read-only SQL, composes dashboards, and applies static checks, dynamic preflight, and browser inspection. The model proposes actions while deterministic software controls execution and records state transitions.
  We evaluate the workflow on frozen real-DataBrain tasks and controlled Hook faults. Strict success was 6/8 on metadata and SQL tasks: metadata selection passed 4/4, all four SQL tasks met semantic criteria, and 2/4 met the exact output-column contract. The final release passed 4/4 single-panel dashboard tasks, one two-panel task, and one existing-dashboard refinement; a parameterised task exceeded its step limit. All ten fault scenarios met their specified outcomes without unapproved external side effects. Model inference accounted for over 97\% of observed runtime in every reported group. These small, DataBrain-specific results do not establish production readiness, general text-to-SQL accuracy, or an efficiency advantage over manual dashboard construction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Text2Dashboard, a prototype that converts natural-language analytics queries into safe, inspectable dashboards for the DataBrain system, combining LLM planning with strictly controlled, auditable execution.
AI.motivation: Analysts and non-technical users increasingly want to query data and build dashboards using natural language, but naive text-to-SQL or text-to-dashboard systems raise issues of safety, auditability, reliability, and operational control. Existing LLM-based agents may generate unsafe queries, modify data, or act opaquely without clear logs or human approval. The authors aim to prototype a constrained, inspectable workflow that keeps models in the role of suggestion engines while deterministic infrastructure enforces read-only behavior, state tracking, error handling, and approvals in the context of DataBrain analytics.
AI.method: The authors build Text2Dashboard, a DataBrain-specific workflow using an installable Codex plugin and a standalone Agent Runtime. The system uses schema-constrained model prompts and typed tools, along with persistent state and deterministic Hooks that gate all side-effecting actions. The pipeline performs entity resolution, metadata discovery, read-only SQL enforcement, and dashboard composition, followed by static checks, dynamic preflight checks, and browser-based inspection before finalizing actions. The LLM proposes structured actions while non-ML software executes them, records state transitions, handles failures, and enforces contracts such as read-only SQL and output-column constraints. They then run the system on a frozen set of real DataBrain tasks plus synthetic fault-injection scenarios in Hooks to evaluate correctness, robustness, and control flow.
AI.result: On eight metadata and SQL tasks, the workflow achieved strict success on 6/8: metadata selection succeeded on all 4 tasks, all 4 SQL tasks were semantically correct, but only 2/4 exactly matched the specified output-column contract. In dashboard construction, the final system passed all 4 single-panel tasks, one two-panel task, and one existing-dashboard refinement, while one parameterized task failed due to exceeding a step limit. In 10 fault-injection scenarios targeting Hooks, every case met its specified outcome with no unapproved external side effects, indicating good containment and failure handling. Across all reported task groups, model inference time dominated runtime, accounting for over 97% of total runtime.
AI.conclusion: Text2Dashboard demonstrates that a tightly scoped, DataBrain-specific integration of LLM planning with deterministic, auditable infrastructure can safely translate some natural-language analytics requests into dashboards, with strong control over side effects and failure modes. However, the authors stress that their results are small-scale and domain-specific and do not prove readiness for production deployment, generalizable text-to-SQL performance, or efficiency gains versus manual dashboard creation. The work is positioned as an initial prototype suggesting that schema-constrained tools, Hooks, and stateful runtime controls are promising ingredients for safer, more inspectable LLM-powered analytics workflows.

title: EMODE: Dynamic Para-Semantic Experts for Emotion-Aware Speech Language Modeling
summary: Large speech language models have demonstrated strong capabilities in unified cross-modal understanding and generation, yet paralinguistic cues, especially emotion, remain difficult to preserve. Existing systems typically rely on entangled acoustic representations, which allow the underlying language model to depend excessively on recovered lexical content instead of grounding its behavior in acoustic-prosodic evidence. We address this limitation with EMODE, an emotion-aware speech language model built around \textbf{Dynamic Para-Semantic Experts (DPSE)}. DPSE decomposes continuous speech features into semantic and paralinguistic pathways, routes them dynamically, and fuses them before integration into the language model. To turn this structural decomposition into functional specialization, EMODE is trained with a three-stage curriculum consisting of semantic warm-up, paralinguistic activation, and joint refinement, guided by Orthogonal Expert Guidance (OEG), Semantic-to-Acoustic Alignment (SAA), and Gating Diversity Regularization (GDR). Experiments on SER test, empathetic response evaluation, and the newly constructed bilingual MEPA benchmark show that EMODE improves the balance between lexical fidelity and emotional sensitivity, strengthens affect-grounded response generation, and exposes the value of explicit para-semantic factorization for robust cross-corpus emotion understanding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EMODE, a speech language model that explicitly separates and leverages semantic and paralinguistic (especially emotional) information to improve emotionally aware speech understanding and generation.
AI.motivation: Large speech language models are good at unified cross-modal understanding and generation but struggle to preserve paralinguistic cues like emotion. Current systems use entangled acoustic representations, causing the language model to over-rely on recovered text and underuse acoustic-prosodic evidence. There is a need for architectures that explicitly factorize semantic and paralinguistic information to better ground emotional understanding and generation in the audio signal.
AI.method: They propose EMODE, centered on Dynamic Para-Semantic Experts (DPSE), which decomposes continuous speech features into separate semantic and paralinguistic pathways, dynamically routes them, then fuses them before feeding into the language model. To enforce this structural decomposition as functional specialization, they design a three-stage training curriculum: (1) semantic warm-up, (2) paralinguistic activation, and (3) joint refinement. Training is guided by three mechanisms: Orthogonal Expert Guidance (OEG) to encourage disentangled experts, Semantic-to-Acoustic Alignment (SAA) to align semantic and acoustic spaces, and Gating Diversity Regularization (GDR) to promote diverse routing behavior across experts.
AI.result: On speech emotion recognition (SER) tests, empathetic response evaluation, and a new bilingual MEPA benchmark, EMODE outperforms baselines in balancing lexical accuracy and emotional sensitivity. It generates responses more grounded in affect and shows better robustness and generalization in cross-corpus emotion understanding tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly factorizing speech into semantic and paralinguistic (para-semantic) pathways via DPSE and training with a targeted curriculum leads to better integration of emotional cues in large speech language models. EMODE demonstrates that such para-semantic decomposition improves both emotion recognition and affect-aware response generation, highlighting the importance of structured treatment of paralinguistic information for robust cross-corpus emotion understanding.

title: FluidPD: In-Place Elasticity for SLO-Aware Prefill-Decode Disaggregated LLM Serving
summary:
Prefill-decode disaggregation is becoming a common architecture for LLM serving because it separates two phases with distinct execution patterns and SLO objectives. Existing systems typically combine a fixed prefill/decode worker ratio with request routing across workers. However, real-world workloads exhibit both short bursts and sustained shifts in the prefill-to-decode demand ratio. As a result, a configuration that is well provisioned at one time may quickly become mismatched, causing latency SLO violations even when idle capacity exists elsewhere. Existing autoscaling mechanisms can add capacity, but they react slowly, require spare GPUs, and do not directly address short-timescale phase imbalance.
  We present FluidPD, a P/D-disaggregated serving system that provides SLO-aware in-place elasticity. FluidPD introduces two complementary mechanisms. FluidToken handles transient imbalance by offloading a bounded portion of prefill computation to decode workers when decode-side slack is available. FluidRole handles sustained imbalance by reassigning running workers between prefill and decode roles in place, avoiding model reload and engine restart. Both mechanisms are guided by lightweight pressure indices that expose prefill and decode-side resource pressure before they appear as SLO violations. Across production Azure trace workloads, FluidPD improves overall SLO attainment over static SGLang by up to 94.6 percentage points, demonstrating that SLO-aware in-place P/D elasticity improves service quality without provisioning additional workers.

AI.tldr: FluidPD is an LLM serving system that elastically balances prefill and decode phases in place to meet latency SLOs without adding workers.
AI.motivation: Prefill-decode disaggregated serving architectures use separate workers for the prefill and decode phases, but real-world workloads show rapidly changing ratios of prefill to decode demand. Fixed prefill/decode worker ratios and slow, capacity-adding autoscalers cannot quickly adapt, leading to SLO violations even when spare capacity exists elsewhere. The paper aims to enable fast, fine-grained balancing of prefill and decode resources to maintain SLOs without overprovisioning GPUs.
AI.method: The paper proposes FluidPD, a serving system with two key mechanisms and SLO-aware control guided by pressure indices. FluidToken temporarily offloads a limited amount of prefill computation to decode workers when those workers have slack, addressing short, transient imbalances. FluidRole supports longer-term adaptation by dynamically reassigning workers between prefill and decode roles in place, avoiding costly model reloads and engine restarts. Both mechanisms rely on lightweight pressure indices that measure prefill and decode resource pressure early, before SLO violations occur, to trigger offloading or role reassignment decisions.
AI.result: On production Azure trace workloads, FluidPD significantly increases SLO attainment compared to a static prefill/decode configuration in SGLang. The paper reports improvements in overall SLO attainment by up to 94.6 percentage points, demonstrating a large reduction in latency SLO violations without requiring additional worker provisioning.
AI.conclusion: SLO-aware in-place elasticity between prefill and decode workers can substantially improve LLM serving quality under dynamic workloads. By combining transient offloading (FluidToken) with in-place role reassignment (FluidRole), FluidPD adapts quickly to both short bursts and sustained shifts in prefill-to-decode demand, achieving much higher SLO attainment than static configurations while using the same number of workers.

title: Verdicts Without Annotated Evidence: Rejection Sampling or Label-Only Post-Training for Evidence Recovery?
summary: In many review workflows the verdict is the only thing retained. The passages behind it are not marked, because that annotation costs far more than recording the decision. We measure how much of that evidence a small language model can recover when it is post-trained on the verdicts alone, with no human evidence labels at any stage. On ContractNLI the human evidence spans are held out until evaluation. Matching the recorded verdict and agreeing with those spans are not the same thing: across six systems the two scores are only weakly related and rank the systems differently, so accuracy is a poor guide when the citations have to be reviewable. Label-only training on the bare verdict reaches accuracy 0.896 and span F1 0.564. Rejection sampling, which keeps a generated trace only when its verdict matches the record and then picks one by an automatic source-grounding score, reaches 0.797 and 0.556, against 0.747 and 0.493 before training. Verbatim citation rises from 0.597 to 0.729 under label-only training and to 0.701 under rejection sampling. One seed on one corpus cannot say which method is better, but both improve the evidence without anyone annotating it.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether a small language model can learn to reconstruct human-like evidence spans in documents when it is trained only on final verdict labels, without any human-annotated evidence, and shows that two simple approaches significantly improve evidence quality and citation behavior.
AI.motivation: In many real-world review and decision-making workflows (e.g., contract review, document classification), only the final verdict labels are saved, while the underlying evidential spans are not annotated due to the high cost. This creates a gap: models can be trained to predict verdicts, but their supporting citations may be poor or unreviewable. The authors want to know how much of the underlying human evidence a model can recover using only the cheap, widely available verdict labels, thereby improving transparency and reviewability without extra annotation cost.
AI.method: Using the ContractNLI dataset, the authors hold out the human-annotated evidence spans and train small language models only on the document-level verdict labels. They evaluate two approaches: (1) label-only supervised training on the verdicts to improve both verdict prediction and inferred evidence spans; and (2) rejection sampling, where the model generates rationale traces, keeps only those whose implied verdict matches the gold verdict, and then selects one trace based on an automatic source-grounding score. They compare systems using standard accuracy for verdict prediction and span F1 for overlap with human evidence spans, also measuring verbatim citation rates.
AI.result: They find that verdict accuracy and evidence span F1 are only weakly correlated across six systems, leading to different rankings, so verdict accuracy alone is not a good proxy for evidence quality. With label-only training, the model achieves accuracy 0.896 and span F1 0.564. Rejection sampling attains accuracy 0.797 and span F1 0.556, compared to a pre-training baseline of 0.747 accuracy and 0.493 span F1. Verbatim citation rates improve from 0.597 to 0.729 with label-only training and to 0.701 with rejection sampling. Both methods yield substantial gains in evidence quality without using human evidence labels during training.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that small language models can recover a substantial fraction of human-like evidence spans using only verdict labels, without explicit evidence supervision. However, verdict accuracy is a poor indicator of evidence quality, so evaluation must explicitly consider evidence spans and citations. Both label-only supervised training and rejection sampling with automatic grounding improve evidence quality and verbatim citation rates over a baseline, though a single corpus and seed are insufficient to declare one method superior. Crucially, these approaches enhance reviewable evidence in settings where only verdict labels are available, avoiding the cost of manual evidence annotation.

title: Anchor Divergence for Semantic Geometry in Contrastive Learning
summary: This paper concerns how semantic context determines geometry in learned vector representations. Similarity is typically measured using cosine similarity, which provides a single fixed geometry. Semantic similarity, however, is inherently context dependent: two images may be similar because they depict the same object, share a visual style, or are relevant to the same clinical finding. We show that contrastive representations naturally encompass a family of geometries that can be specialized to particular semantic structure. The key idea is to use an interplay between contrastive learning, exponential families, and information geometry to establish a correspondence between probability distributions over "anchors" and Bregman geometries on the representation space. We use this correspondence to define "Anchor Divergences", a method for specifying context-specific semantic geometries on fixed representations. Under this correspondence, modeling the anchor distribution models the geometry itself. Experiments on retrieval show that anchor divergences provide an effective and efficient way to specify context-specific semantic similarity.

AI.tldr: They propose a way to define multiple, context-dependent similarity geometries on top of a fixed contrastive representation using ‘Anchor Divergences’.
AI.motivation: Cosine similarity imposes a single, fixed geometry on learned representations, but real semantic similarity is context dependent (e.g., same object vs same style vs same clinical relevance). There is a need to adapt similarity to different semantic contexts without relearning representations.
AI.method: The authors analyze contrastive representations using tools from exponential families and information geometry. They establish a theoretical correspondence between probability distributions over a set of anchor points and Bregman geometries on the representation space. Based on this, they introduce Anchor Divergences, where one specifies or learns a distribution over anchors; this distribution in turn induces a context-specific divergence (geometry) for measuring similarity in the existing representation space.
AI.result: They show empirically on retrieval tasks that using Anchor Divergences to adapt the geometry to a specified context yields better and more efficient context-specific semantic similarity compared to using a single default metric like cosine. Their experiments demonstrate improved retrieval performance in multiple semantic contexts on fixed representations.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive representations inherently support a family of geometries rather than a single one. By modeling distributions over anchors, one can flexibly define context-specific semantic similarity without changing the underlying representation, and Anchor Divergences offer a practical and effective way to do this in retrieval settings.

title: WavePrune: One period is often enough for RoPE
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes token positions by rotating each two-dimensional channel of the query and key vectors at a channel-specific frequency, making the attention logits invariant to a common shift of positions. However, this rotation is periodic, and it leads to position aliasing where relative positions separated by a full rotation period become hard to tell apart. To address this, we propose WavePrune, which restricts each channel to its first rotation period. We show that it removes the distractions in attention maps created by position aliasing and improves overall long-context performance. Specifically, WavePrune raises the HELMET score on four of five models we test without any extra tuning (e.g., 35.7 -> 40.0 on Qwen3-8B). When pretraining models from scratch, WavePrune also achieves lower validation loss at extrapolated lengths than pretraining without it. Because WavePrune restricts each channel to a sliding window, it induces a fine-grained sparsity that our hardware-aligned CUDA kernels exploit for 1.15x prefill and 1.24x decoding speedups over FlashAttention-2 at 32K context. Together, these results show that RoPE's periodic structure, widely regarded as essential, is largely redundant beyond the first rotation period.

AI.tldr: Introduces WavePrune, a modification to RoPE that removes periodic aliasing and yields better long-context performance and speed.
AI.motivation: RoPE’s periodic rotations cause position aliasing, making it difficult for attention to distinguish token pairs whose relative positions differ by a full rotation period, which harms long-context modeling. The authors want to fix this without losing RoPE’s good properties.
AI.method: Constrain each RoPE channel to only its first rotation period, effectively turning each channel into a sliding local positional window. This removes aliasing and induces structured sparsity that can be exploited with custom CUDA kernels. They compare models with and without WavePrune and measure HELMET scores, validation loss at extrapolated lengths, and runtime vs FlashAttention-2 at 32K context.
AI.result: WavePrune reduces distracting attention from aliased positions, improves HELMET scores on four of five tested models (e.g., Qwen3-8B from 35.7 to 40.0) without extra tuning, and yields lower validation loss at long extrapolated context during pretraining. Hardware-aligned kernels leveraging WavePrune’s sparsity get 1.15x prefill and 1.24x decoding speedups vs FlashAttention-2 at 32K.
AI.conclusion: RoPE’s commonly assumed need for full periodic structure is overstated; information beyond the first rotation period is mostly redundant. By pruning rotations to the first period (WavePrune), one can reduce position aliasing, improve long-context performance, and gain inference speedups via induced sparsity.

title: RadOnc-Agent: An LLM-Orchestrated Framework for AI Workflows Across the Radiotherapy Care Pathway
summary: Artificial intelligence has advanced individual radiotherapy tasks, yet these capabilities remain separated across clinical stages, software environments and data modalities. This fragmentation contrasts with the longitudinal radiotherapy workflow from treatment decision-making through follow-up. Here we present RadOnc-Agent, an agentic artificial-intelligence framework that formalizes radiotherapy into four clinical phases and provides 26 callable functions through a conversational interface. A large-language-model controller maps clinical intent to schema-constrained calls, preserves patient and workflow context, and routes requests to specialist services. We evaluated system execution using 2,600 single-function requests (7,800 repeat executions), 200 prespecified synthetic cross-stage scenarios spanning four phases (600 executions), and 120 workflow instances from 60 de-identified patient records (360 clean executions) representing decision-to-planning and planning-to-adaptation. RadOnc-Agent selected the intended function in 98.79% of single-function executions, completed 96.50% of scripted cross-stage workflows, and completed 96.67% of real-patient workflow executions. In comparative ablations, removing longitudinal state reduced cross-stage completion from 96.50% to 84.00%, while disabling schema and identity validation increased mismatched backend dispatch from 0% to 95.28% in a replay/test evaluation. These findings establish the technical feasibility of an LLM-orchestrated architecture for coordinating heterogeneous radiotherapy capabilities and information across longitudinal workflows; they do not establish clinical correctness, clinical utility or prospective benefit.

AI.tldr: RadOnc-Agent is an AI (LLM-based) orchestration framework that connects many specialized radiotherapy tools into a single, conversational, workflow-aware system across the full radiotherapy process.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems for radiotherapy are fragmented: different models and tools handle separate tasks, live in different software systems, and target different stages of care and data types. This does not match the real-world, longitudinal clinical workflow, which requires coordinated use of multiple capabilities from initial decision through treatment planning, adaptation, and follow-up. The authors aim to create and test an architecture that can coordinate these heterogeneous capabilities in a reliable, workflow-aware way.
AI.method: The authors formalize radiotherapy into four clinical phases and implement RadOnc-Agent, an agentic framework with 26 callable functions exposed via a conversational interface. A large language model acts as a controller that interprets clinical intent, maintains patient and workflow context, ensures requests conform to schemas, and routes calls to the correct backend services. They evaluate the system in three settings: (1) 2,600 single-function requests (with 7,800 repeat runs) to test function selection and execution; (2) 200 synthetic multi-step cross-stage scenarios across the four phases (600 executions) to test longitudinal workflows; and (3) 120 workflow instances from 60 de-identified real patient records (360 clean executions) focusing on decision-to-planning and planning-to-adaptation. They also run ablation experiments removing longitudinal state and disabling schema/identity validation to quantify their impact on performance and error rates.
AI.result: RadOnc-Agent correctly selected the intended function in 98.79% of single-function runs, successfully completed 96.50% of scripted cross-stage workflows, and 96.67% of real-patient workflows. In ablation studies, removing longitudinal state reduced cross-stage workflow completion from 96.50% to 84.00%, indicating the importance of context persistence. Disabling schema and identity validation caused the mismatched backend dispatch rate to rise dramatically from 0% to 95.28% in replay/test conditions, showing these safeguards are crucial for reliable routing.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that an LLM-orchestrated, agentic architecture can technically and reliably coordinate multiple specialized radiotherapy tools and data sources across longitudinal clinical workflows. Maintaining longitudinal state and enforcing schema/identity validation are critical to performance and safety. However, the work is positioned as a technical feasibility study only; it does not claim or establish clinical correctness, clinical benefit, or readiness for deployment in patient care without further validation.

title: Calibrated Answers About Randomized Trials From a 4-Billion-Parameter Open Model: A Registered Test and a License-Clean Release
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables. Code, results files and the paper's sources: https://github.com/johann-e-li/fiorillo. Model: https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/10722. Registration: https://osf.io/kaxmn/
summary: Fiorillo v0.5 is an open model that answers typed questions with a probability for each answer. Its main specialist reads a randomized trial's article, cut to 6,144 tokens, and answers whether an intervention significantly increased, significantly decreased or did not significantly change an outcome against a comparator (Evidence Inference 2.0, EI). It is Qwen3-4B-Base with low-rank adapters and a decision head, fine-tuned for EI only on the 1,431 of 2,657 training articles whose own license allows reuse. Four criteria registered on the Open Science Framework before this version's test predictions decided its release, the second bar judged on EI's test split, whose labels are public. On that split (1,218 prompts in 333 articles), the expected calibration error was 0.0168 against a limit of 0.05; log loss was below the prior's by 0.8603 (95 percent interval 0.8104 to 0.9078) and below that of Gemma 4 31B-it, reading the same input, by 0.1829 (0.1164 to 0.2598); and macro-F1 was 0.9248 against 0.8668, so all four criteria passed. Training the same recipe on clean articles alone cost 0.0123 in accuracy (0.0034 to 0.0207; descriptive). With no article, macro-F1 fell to 0.4384; the title alone raised it by 0.0939 (0.0655 to 0.1234), which a title stating the result or recall of the trial could explain; exchanging intervention and comparator reversed 0.6652 of its direction answers. Run as released, the files matched the evaluated predictions within limits set in advance. The release is under the Apache License 2.0 (digital object identifier 10.57967/hf/10722).

AI.tldr: Fiorillo v0.5 is an open-source, probability-calibrated model fine-tuned for evidence inference from clinical trial articles, achieving strong accuracy and calibration versus baselines on a public benchmark.
AI.motivation: Automated evidence inference from randomized trial reports is needed to scale evidence synthesis in medicine, but existing LLMs are often poorly calibrated and limited by licensing of training data. The authors aim to build an open, well-calibrated model that can reliably infer the direction and significance of intervention effects while respecting article licenses and using preregistered evaluation criteria.
AI.method: They start from Qwen3-4B-Base and add low-rank adapters plus a decision head, fine-tuning exclusively on the Evidence Inference 2.0 task: given a clipped trial article, decide whether an intervention significantly increased, decreased, or did not change an outcome versus a comparator. Training uses only the subset of EI training articles whose licenses permit reuse. They preregister four release criteria on OSF (calibration, log-loss improvements over a prior and a strong baseline, and macro-F1 threshold) and evaluate Fiorillo v0.5 on EI’s public test split under these criteria. They also conduct ablations: training with vs without articles deemed unclean, removing the article text, using only titles, and swapping intervention/comparator roles to probe sensitivity. Implementation is released under Apache 2.0 with a DOI.
AI.result: On the EI 2.0 test split (1,218 prompts from 333 articles), Fiorillo v0.5 achieves an expected calibration error of 0.0168 (well below the 0.05 preregistered limit), improves log loss over a simple prior by 0.8603 (95% CI 0.8104–0.9078) and over Gemma 4 31B-it by 0.1829 (0.1164–0.2598), and attains macro-F1 of 0.9248 versus a 0.8668 threshold, thus meeting all four release criteria. Training only on clean articles slightly reduces accuracy by 0.0123 (0.0034–0.0207). Without the article text, macro-F1 drops to 0.4384; using only the title recovers about 0.094 in macro-F1, suggesting titles sometimes leak trial outcomes. Swapping intervention and comparator reverses about two-thirds of direction predictions (0.6652), indicating the model is sensitive to role assignments. The released files reproduce the evaluated predictions within predefined tolerances.
AI.conclusion: Fiorillo v0.5 is a small, open, and well-calibrated model specialized for evidence inference in randomized trial articles, outperforming a much larger Gemma 31B baseline on the EI 2.0 benchmark while respecting licensing constraints. The preregistered evaluation and ablation studies suggest the model meaningfully uses article content (beyond titles) and correctly tracks which arm is the intervention versus comparator. Its Apache 2.0 release and documented performance make it a practical, transparent tool for automated evidence extraction from clinical trials.

title: Metonymic Circuits for Abstract Concept Grounding in Vision Transformers
summary: We study how Vision Transformers ground abstract concepts (e.g., angry) when training data provide limited direct referential evidence. We hypothesize a metonymic grounding mechanism in which abstract predictions are driven by concrete, interpretable anchor concepts (e.g., fire) that bridge visual signals to abstract semantics. By applying Transcoders on CLIP and DINO vision encoders, we recover intermediate features that can be associated with semantic labels for more concrete concepts, and trace their contributions in circuits underlying abstract concept recognition. Experiments on a carefully curated icon dataset reveal structured metonymic circuits, in which perceptual primitives dominate early layers and object-like anchors precede abstract targets. Images containing rendered text instead recruit a distinct perceptual-to-textual route. Causal interventions further validate that metonymic intermediates are functionally involved in grounding abstract concepts.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how Vision Transformers learn and represent abstract visual concepts by relying on concrete intermediate “anchor” concepts, and empirically maps and tests these internal circuits.
AI.motivation: To understand mechanistically how models like CLIP and DINO can recognize abstract concepts (e.g., emotions or qualities) from images despite limited direct supervision, and to uncover whether they rely on more concrete visual proxies rather than directly encoding abstract meaning.
AI.method: They propose a metonymic grounding hypothesis and use Transcoders on pretrained CLIP and DINO vision encoders to decode intermediate features into semantic labels for more concrete concepts. They then analyze the contribution of these decoded units to abstract concept predictions, using a curated icon dataset, circuit tracing across layers, and causal interventions that perturb or remove intermediate units.
AI.result: They find structured metonymic circuits: low-level layers emphasize perceptual primitives (colors, shapes, textures), mid-to-higher layers contain object-like anchor concepts that strongly mediate predictions of abstract targets, and images with rendered text follow a separate perceptual-to-textual pathway. Causal manipulations of these anchor units significantly affect abstract concept recognition performance.
AI.conclusion: Vision Transformers ground abstract concepts via metonymic mechanisms: concrete, interpretable intermediate concepts act as anchors that connect raw visual input to abstract semantics, rather than abstract meaning being encoded in a single step. This grounding is layer-structured and modality-dependent (visual vs text cues), and the identified intermediates are causally involved in abstract concept recognition.

title: Investigating Model Compression for Neural Machine Translation in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Large-scale pretrained transformer models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse machine translation tasks, including multilingual settings. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a sustainable approach for model compression, transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. Similarly, quantization, which reduces the numerical precision of model weights and activations (e.g., from 32-bit to 8-bit representations) is widely used to accelerate inference, enabling models to run several times faster during deployment. However, both techniques face limitations when applied to specialized domain data, particularly under low-resource conditions. In knowledge distillation, the effectiveness of transfer is often constrained by the scarcity of domain-specific parallel data, while quantization can lead to performance degradation as bit precision decreases. In this work, we investigate the combined application of knowledge distillation and quantization for French-to-English biomedical translation, a domain characterized by specialized terminology and limited parallel resources. We develop and compare multiple fine-tuning strategies to adapt compressed student models to this challenging setting. Our experiments demonstrate that a collaboratively distilled and quantized student model achieves a 69% reduction in size, a 98.21% increase in inference speed, and a 98.46% reduction in CO2 emissions compared to the original baseline all without sacrificing translation quality. These results indicate that jointly optimized compression techniques can yield efficient, high-performance models suitable for translation service providers operating under resource constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to jointly use knowledge distillation and quantization to compress a French–English biomedical translation model, achieving major gains in size, speed, and carbon footprint without hurting translation quality.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art multilingual transformer MT models are large and costly to deploy. Knowledge distillation and quantization are popular compression methods, but each has drawbacks on specialized, low-resource domains like biomedical translation: distillation is limited by scarce in-domain parallel data, and aggressive quantization can harm accuracy. There is a need to understand whether combining these techniques, with suitable fine-tuning strategies, can yield compact, fast, environmentally friendly models that still handle domain-specific terminology well.
AI.method: The authors focus on French→English biomedical machine translation. They start from a large pretrained transformer MT model as the teacher, and design smaller student models. They apply knowledge distillation from teacher to students and quantize model weights/activations (e.g., down to 8-bit) under various fine-tuning strategies tailored to the low-resource biomedical domain. They compare different adaptation and compression setups, measuring model size, inference speed, CO2 emissions, and translation quality to identify an effective jointly optimized workflow.
AI.result: One of the collaboratively distilled and quantized student models shrinks model size by 69%, nearly doubles inference speed (98.21% increase), and cuts estimated CO2 emissions by 98.46% relative to the original baseline model. Crucially, these efficiency gains are obtained without observable degradation in translation quality on the biomedical French→English task.
AI.conclusion: Carefully combining knowledge distillation with quantization, plus domain-specific fine-tuning strategies, enables substantial compression and efficiency gains for specialized-domain MT models under low-resource conditions, without sacrificing translation performance. This joint optimization approach is promising for translation providers needing high-quality biomedical MT under tight computational and environmental constraints.

title: Principles that Guide, Actions that Inform: Agent Evolution via Knowledge Abstraction
summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interactive environments, yet their ability to continually evolve from experience remains limited. Although fine-tuning enables adaptation, its dependence on parameter access and high computational costs restrict its flexibility, especially for large-scale and closed-source LLMs. External memory offers an alternative by allowing agents to accumulate experience without modifying model parameters. However, existing methods mainly focus on experience representation and organization, while the acquired knowledge remains tightly coupled with specific tasks and contexts, limiting generalization. A key challenge is how to transform concrete interactions into abstract and reusable knowledge that guides future decisions beyond individual experiences.
  To address this challenge, we propose SAGA (\underline{\textbf{S}}elf-evolving \underline{\textbf{A}}gents through Experience-\underline{\textbf{G}}rounded \underline{\textbf{A}}bstraction), a framework for experience-grounded knowledge abstraction and utilization in LLM agents. SAGA progressively transforms interaction trajectories into episodic descriptions, reusable procedures, and principles with explicit applicability conditions, while maintaining links to execution evidence. Retrieved principles are instantiated into task-specific guidance and used to refine candidate actions through corrective feedback and resampling. This creates an execution--abstraction feedback loop, where accumulated knowledge guides future interactions and new experiences continuously update hierarchical memory. Experiments on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld demonstrate improved task performance, with ablation studies highlighting the importance of contextual instantiation and action regulation for leveraging principle-level knowledge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAGA, a framework that lets LLM agents turn past interaction experiences into abstract, reusable knowledge (principles and procedures) stored in external memory, improving performance in interactive environments without finetuning.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can act well in interactive environments but struggle to continually improve from experience, especially when fine-tuning is impractical due to compute cost and lack of parameter access (e.g., closed-source models). Existing external-memory methods mostly store task-specific experiences that don’t generalize well across tasks. The authors are motivated to find a way to convert concrete experiences into abstract, broadly applicable knowledge that can guide future decisions and enable continual self-improvement.
AI.method: They introduce SAGA, a hierarchical experience-grounded abstraction framework. Agent interaction trajectories are progressively compressed into: (1) episodic descriptions summarizing specific runs, (2) reusable procedures capturing task patterns, and (3) high-level principles annotated with explicit applicability conditions and linked back to supporting execution evidence. During inference, relevant principles are retrieved and instantiated into contextual, task-specific guidance that regulates action selection via corrective feedback and resampling. This forms an execution–abstraction feedback loop: executions generate experiences, experiences are abstracted into memory, and abstracted knowledge shapes future executions.
AI.result: On the ScienceWorld and ALFWorld benchmarks, SAGA-equipped agents achieve higher task performance compared to baselines without such hierarchical abstraction. Ablation studies show that two components—contextual instantiation of principles and their use in regulating candidate actions—are key contributors to the performance gains, indicating that abstraction alone is insufficient without proper grounding into current context and direct influence on action choice.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that experience-grounded abstraction into principles and procedures is an effective alternative to parameter finetuning for enabling continual improvement in LLM agents, particularly when using large or closed-source models. By structuring external memory hierarchically and closing the loop between execution and abstraction, agents can accumulate and reuse knowledge more generally across tasks. The authors suggest this direction as a promising path toward more adaptive, self-evolving LLM agents in complex interactive environments.

title: Turnslide: Scalable Multi-Turn Data Synthesis by Walking a Finite-State Machine
comment: Accepted at the SLM-Agents Workshop, NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Small language models are inexpensive to serve and can run on private infrastructure, but base models are often not good enough at multi-turn tool calling, and fine-tuning them needs per-API data that rarely exists. Existing synthesis methods are too expensive for high-scale fine-tuning, as they often require mock operational environments for different domains and multiple LLM calls per generated conversation turn. We introduce a fully automated, lightweight synthesis framework that models each API as a finite-state machine, representing the system as abstract states that determine when each tool may be called, producing state-valid sequences of tools; sequences are translated into complete examples with a single LLM call. Rather than optimize diversity, we set a target distribution over the number of turns, the tool sequence and task complexity. We measure data quality by fine-tuning SLMs on generated trajectories, showing that our FSM-based generation significantly improves downstream accuracy over an unmutated baseline and, against existing works, reaches 70.7% full accuracy over 63.4% and 53.7% with 3.6-6.6$\times$ fewer tokens.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated, cheap data-synthesis framework for teaching small language models to do multi-turn tool calling via API interactions modeled as finite-state machines.
AI.motivation: Small language models are attractive because they are cheap to run and can be deployed on private infrastructure, but they perform poorly at multi-turn tool use. Improving them via fine-tuning requires large amounts of API-specific interaction data, which is usually unavailable. Existing synthetic data generation approaches are costly, requiring mock environments and many LLM calls per conversation turn, making large-scale fine-tuning impractical.
AI.method: The authors model each API as a finite-state machine (FSM), where abstract system states govern when each tool can be called. They then sample state-valid tool sequences from this FSM under a user-specified target distribution over conversation length (number of turns), tool sequences, and task complexity. Each sampled tool trajectory is converted into a full training example (including natural language context) using a single call to a larger LLM, avoiding heavy simulation or multiple calls per turn.
AI.result: Fine-tuning small language models on the FSM-generated trajectories substantially improves their downstream multi-turn tool-calling accuracy compared to the unmodified base models. Compared with prior synthesis approaches, the method attains 70.7% full-task accuracy versus 63.4% and 53.7%, while using 3.6–6.6 times fewer tokens for data generation.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight, FSM-based data synthesis approach can efficiently generate high-quality training data for multi-turn tool use, enabling small language models to reach significantly higher tool-calling accuracy at a fraction of the token cost and without complex mock environments.

title: AegisFlow: A Multi-Agent Agentic AI Framework for Autonomous Remediation and Self-Healing in Fragile Data Ecosystems
summary: Traditional data pipelines are notoriously brittle, often failing due to upstream schema drift, API contract changes, or website DOM modifications. Present observability tools only raise alerts but for human engineers, resulting in a high Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) and operational fatigue. In this paper we propose AegisFlow (Agentic Engine for Intelligent Self-healing and Graph-driven Operations for Workload remediation), a novel agentic framework that closes the loop between detection and resolution. AegisFlow uses a Watchdog agent to collect runtime telemetry and has a Repair agent to automatically create, test and deploy code patches based on Large Language Models (LLMs). The framework presents the non-intrusive execution model called Parallel Shadow Patching, a non-intrusive execution model based on the Monitor, Analyze, Plan, Execute, Knowledge (MAPE-K) loop to generate and verify patches in digital twin environments. Through experimental testing, we have evaluated AegisFlow across five common failure scenarios, and see 98.1 percent improvement in MTTR (from an average of 170 minutes per patch to 3.2 minutes) and a patch success rate of 92 percent . In particular, the system is successful in dealing with changes in the JSON schema (96 percent ) and punctuation drift (98 percent ), and is least successful in Shadow DOM cases (85 percent ). AegisFlow frees up about 98 percent of data engineering on-call time from firefighting and reallocates it towards innovation. The framework is deployment agnostic consisting of a system that can be deployed in a plugin fashion into an existing pipeline orchestration system with minimal uplift to the existing system.

AI.tldr: AegisFlow is an agent-based, self-healing framework that automatically detects and repairs broken data pipelines using LLM-generated patches validated in a safe, parallel shadow environment, dramatically reducing MTTR and on-call load.
AI.motivation: Data pipelines frequently break due to upstream changes (schemas, APIs, DOMs), and current observability tools only notify human engineers rather than repairing issues, leading to long MTTR, high operational burden, and lost engineering time.
AI.method: The authors design AegisFlow, composed of a Watchdog agent that collects runtime telemetry and detects failures, and a Repair agent that uses LLMs to propose, test, and deploy code patches. They introduce Parallel Shadow Patching, a non-intrusive execution model implementing the MAPE-K loop: monitor pipeline behavior, analyze failures, plan candidate patches, execute them in a digital-twin or shadow environment in parallel with production, and use accumulated knowledge to select and safely roll out successful patches.
AI.result: Across five common pipeline failure scenarios, AegisFlow reduced average MTTR from 170 minutes to 3.2 minutes (98.1% improvement) and achieved an overall patch success rate of 92%. It performed especially well for JSON schema changes (96% success) and punctuation drift (98% success), with lower performance on Shadow DOM issues (85% success).
AI.conclusion: AegisFlow demonstrates that an agentic, LLM-driven, self-healing framework with parallel shadow execution can reliably and safely remediate common data pipeline failures, drastically cutting MTTR and freeing ~98% of on-call data engineering time for higher-value work. The framework is deployment-agnostic and can be plugged into existing orchestration systems with minimal changes.

title: JudgeMoE: Distributional Aggregation for LLM-as-a-Judge
summary: When an LLM judge scores an output, its score distribution retains uncertainty and disagreement information that is lost after scalar compression. We introduce JudgeMoE, a lightweight aggregator that assigns example-specific weights to cached judge score distributions and fuses them before computing a final score. A protocol study shows that score-range choice is unstable across judge--dataset settings and that soft scoring usually outperforms hard decoding. On the original 10-cell benchmark, JudgeMoE improves mean Spearman over uniform log pooling by $+0.079$. Applying the same configuration to six additional cells yields a $+0.0393$ mean gain over the strongest local single judge across 16 cells, with positive differences in 12/16 cells and a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank $p=0.0091$. Validation-based analyses further show that the preferred aggregation method depends on the task and judge pool.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes JudgeMoE, a method for aggregating distributions of scores from LLM judges to better preserve uncertainty and disagreement, improving correlation with ground truth across multiple evaluation settings.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based judges usually compress their full predictive score distributions down to a single scalar score, which discards useful information about uncertainty and inter-judge disagreement. Moreover, the choice of scoring range and decoding strategy appears unstable across different judge models and datasets, leading to suboptimal and inconsistent evaluation quality. There is a need for a principled, data-driven way to aggregate multiple judge outputs that leverages their full distributions rather than hard decisions.
AI.method: The authors introduce JudgeMoE, a lightweight mixture-of-experts style aggregation model operating on cached distributions of scores from multiple LLM judges. For each example, JudgeMoE learns example-specific weights over the available judges, then fuses their soft score distributions into a combined distribution before computing a final scalar score. They perform a protocol study comparing score-range choices (e.g., different scales) and scoring strategies (soft scoring over distributions vs hard decoding to a single label). They evaluate JudgeMoE against baselines such as uniform log pooling and individual judges across multiple benchmark cells.
AI.result: On the original 10-cell benchmark, JudgeMoE improves mean Spearman correlation with ground truth by +0.079 compared to uniform log pooling. When the same JudgeMoE configuration is applied to six additional benchmark cells (for a total of 16 cells), it yields an average Spearman gain of +0.0393 over the strongest local single judge, with improvements in 12 out of 16 cells. A one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives p = 0.0091, indicating that these improvements are statistically significant. The protocol study finds that soft scoring over distributions typically outperforms hard decoding and that score-range choices are unstable across judge–dataset combinations.
AI.conclusion: Preserving and aggregating the full score distributions from LLM judges, rather than compressing them prematurely to scalars, leads to more reliable and accurate evaluation. JudgeMoE, a lightweight per-example weighting and aggregation scheme over judge distributions, consistently improves rank correlation with ground-truth labels across diverse tasks and judge pools. However, the best aggregation strategy is task- and judge-dependent, suggesting that evaluation pipelines should adapt their aggregation method to the specific setting instead of relying on a single fixed protocol.

title: EPOCH: Reliable Discovery through Evidence-Governed Search
summary: AI research agents are increasingly used to search over programs, mathematical constructions, and proofs. However, existing systems typically optimize evaluator feedback without adequately governing how that feedback is interpreted, challenged, and reused. As a result, promising but fragile candidates can be promoted as discoveries, while benchmark improvements, finite certificates, and theorem-level claims are too easily conflated. We introduce EPOCH, an evidence-governed architecture designed to close this gap. EPOCH implements an evidence-governed discovery loop by combining explicit task contracts, typed memory, active falsification, admission checks, and independent replay, so that each candidate is evaluated against the strength and scope of the claim it supports. EPOCH achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance on AlgoTune, substantially exceeding the strongest baseline in mean normalized score (0.65 vs. 0.53), and attains the highest mean score on the internal Math14 suite (0.57). It further shows favorable held-out behavior under official-test replay and leads the descriptive aggregate on AgentHPO. Across ten discovery problems, EPOCH delivers substantial task-specific advances, including improved executable constructions, optimized algorithms, counterexamples, and proof-supported results. These advances demonstrate its ability to convert search into concrete progress across mathematical and computational domains. Together, the results suggest that evidence governance is a necessary step toward AI research agents that produce not only stronger solutions, but also more trustworthy scientific discoveries.
