AI.tldr: The paper introduces EPOCH, an architecture for AI research agents that governs how evidence is collected, checked, and reused so that discovered programs, algorithms, and proofs are more reliable and trustworthy.
AI.motivation: Existing AI research agents search over programs, proofs, and constructions but mostly just optimize numeric feedback from evaluators. They lack structure around how this feedback (evidence) is interpreted, challenged, and generalized. This leads to fragile or incorrect candidates being reported as discoveries and to confusion between different strengths of claims (e.g., benchmark improvement vs. fully proven theorem). The authors aim to make AI-driven discovery more rigorous and trustworthy by explicitly governing evidence use.
AI.method: The authors propose EPOCH, an evidence-governed architecture. EPOCH structures the discovery loop using: (1) explicit task contracts that state what kind of claim is being made; (2) typed memory that distinguishes different evidence types; (3) active falsification that tries to break candidate solutions; (4) admission checks controlling which candidates enter memory; and (5) independent replay to re-verify results. Each candidate solution is thus evaluated according to the precise strength and scope of the claim it supports.
AI.result: On the AlgoTune benchmark, EPOCH achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance, with a mean normalized score of 0.65 versus the previous best of 0.53. It attains the best mean score (0.57) on the internal Math14 benchmark, shows good generalization in held-out official-test replay, and leads the descriptive aggregate on the AgentHPO benchmark. Across ten discovery tasks, it produces concrete advances such as better executable constructions, improved algorithms, counterexamples, and proof-backed results.
AI.conclusion: The empirical results indicate that explicitly governing evidence—how it is collected, checked, and reused—substantially improves both the performance and reliability of AI research agents. EPOCH not only finds stronger solutions but also generates more trustworthy scientific claims, suggesting that evidence governance is a key ingredient for future AI systems engaged in mathematical and computational discovery.

title: CroissantMiner: Automated Extraction and Validation of Croissant Metadata for ML Datasets
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets). Website: https://berkearda.github.io/croissantminer/
summary: Croissant has emerged as a standard for machine-readable dataset metadata, yet populating its fields remains labor-intensive and requires careful reading of accompanying dataset documentation. We present the first benchmark enabling end-to-end evaluation of metadata extraction aligned with a community-standard schema. The benchmark comprises 602 papers, including 102 with human-validated gold annotations and 500 with LLM-generated silver annotations, covering the full Croissant schema with both core and Responsible AI (RAI) fields. Using this benchmark, we evaluate a range of extraction systems spanning frontier models, open-weight models, and agentic architectures, under a two-tier evaluation framework that combines rule-based scoring with an LLM judge selected via human audit. We find that single-pass extraction consistently outperforms the four agentic architectures we evaluate: across backbones, these decomposed variants achieve lower accuracy than a single full-context pass. The largest gap appears on long-form RAI fields, which require synthesizing and interpreting information scattered across a paper rather than copying it from a single location, a setting where current systems remain far from reliable. We release the benchmark, evaluation code, judge audit, a live demo, and a leaderboard open to new systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first benchmark for automatically extracting Croissant-standard dataset metadata from research papers and uses it to evaluate multiple LLM-based extraction systems.
AI.motivation: Croissant is becoming a standard schema for machine-readable dataset metadata, but filling in its fields is manual, time-consuming, and requires careful reading of documentation and papers. There is no systematic way to evaluate end-to-end automatic metadata extraction aligned to Croissant, especially including Responsible AI (RAI) fields.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of 602 dataset papers mapped to the full Croissant schema. 102 papers receive human-validated gold annotations and 500 papers receive LLM-generated silver annotations. They include both core metadata and RAI-related fields. They then design a two-tier evaluation protocol: (1) rule-based scoring of structured outputs and (2) an LLM-as-judge component that was selected and validated via a human audit. Using this setup, they evaluate a variety of extraction approaches, including frontier proprietary models, open-weight models, and several agentic architectures that decompose the task versus a single-pass, full-context extraction strategy.
AI.result: Across all tested backbones, single-pass, full-context extraction methods outperform four different agentic, decomposed architectures. The performance gap is especially large on long-form RAI fields that require synthesizing information spread throughout the paper, not just copying from one location. Existing systems show notably low reliability on these harder, interpretive fields. The benchmark, evaluation code, LLM judge audit, demo, and leaderboard are all released for the community.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end Croissant metadata extraction is feasible but current systems, especially agentic decompositions, underperform simpler single-pass approaches, particularly on complex RAI-related fields that require global synthesis of a paper. The released benchmark and tooling establish a standard, practical testbed for improving and comparing metadata extraction systems aligned with a widely adopted community schema.

title: When better traffic forecasts fail to improve signal control: a layered diagnostic study of forecast-to-decision value
summary: Improved traffic forecasts do not necessarily yield better signal-control decisions. We investigate this gap through a layered diagnostic study using 29 days of reconstructed demand from Xuancheng, China, with seven dates reserved for testing. The framework evaluates point forecasts, conformal intervals, dependence-aware scenarios, and matched closed-loop controllers. Entry-level and movement-level forecasts reduce mean absolute error by 4.03% and 3.92%, respectively, relative to historical means. A nominal 90% conformal interval achieves 90.72% marginal coverage but only 75.66% on an ex-post high-demand subset. Interface audits identify decision-time leakage and reveal that only two of nine controlled intersections offer multiple effective actions. We correct the temporal interface and compare causal forecasts with a five-second event oracle using exhaustive joint-action search. A synthetic positive control demonstrates that future information can reduce the internal rollout cost by 61.5%. On the frozen test dates, however, causal forecasts and the event oracle increase queue vehicle?seconds by 6.09% and 3.39% relative to the matched no-future rollout, while the oracle reduces spillback exposure by 3.78%; paired-day bootstrap intervals cross zero. These findings indicate that forecast value depends on temporal observability, action identifiability, dynamics consistency, and objective alignment. The proposed protocol provides a practical way to diagnose where predictive improvements fail to translate into operational benefits.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why better traffic-demand forecasts do not automatically lead to better traffic-signal control, and proposes a diagnostic framework to trace where predictive gains fail to produce operational benefits.
AI.motivation: Despite progress in traffic prediction, real-world signal-control performance often does not improve correspondingly. There is a need to understand the reasons for this disconnect and to develop a systematic way to evaluate how forecast quality, uncertainty quantification, and control design jointly affect outcomes such as queues and spillback.
AI.method: Using 29 days of reconstructed traffic demand data from Xuancheng, China, the authors perform a layered diagnostic study. They evaluate: (1) point forecasts at entry and movement level; (2) conformal prediction intervals and their coverage, including on high-demand subsets; (3) dependence-aware traffic-demand scenarios; and (4) signal controllers designed to match these predictive models. They conduct interface audits to detect issues like decision-time information leakage and limits in available effective actions. They then correct temporal interfaces and compare causal forecasts versus an idealized five-second event oracle within exhaustive joint-action search and rollout simulations, including a synthetic positive-control experiment.
AI.result: Forecasts modestly improve mean absolute error over historical averages (~4%). Conformal intervals achieve nominal coverage overall but under-cover on high-demand periods. Interface audits show decision-time leakage and that only two of nine intersections have multiple effective control actions. A synthetic positive control confirms that having future information can significantly reduce internal rollout cost (by 61.5%). However, on real test days, both causal forecasts and the event oracle slightly worsen queue vehicle-seconds (by 6.09% and 3.39%) compared with a no-future baseline, while the oracle modestly reduces spillback exposure (3.78%); uncertainty intervals for these differences include zero.
AI.conclusion: Improved prediction alone is insufficient to guarantee better signal-control outcomes. The operational value of forecasts hinges on correct temporal observability (no leakage, realistic lookahead), whether the controller actually has distinct effective actions to choose from, how well the simulated dynamics match reality, and whether the optimization objective aligns with real performance metrics. The proposed diagnostic protocol helps identify which of these factors is blocking predictive gains from translating into operational benefits in traffic signal control systems.

title: Identifying Introspection From the Inside
comment: Published at COLM 2026. Project page: https://iii.baulab.info
summary: Large language models make claims about themselves that are both consequential and increasingly difficult to verify from behavior alone. How can we distinguish plausible confabulations from genuine introspection? In this paper, we identify mechanistic signatures of faithful self-report in a controlled setting. Using low-rank adapters, we train models to make decisions on behalf of fictitious characters, according to latent linear preference functions. We find sustained fine-tuning on an implicit decision task can lead to the emergence of accurate self-reporting of models' learned preferences, even without explicit self-report supervision. We ask two research questions about this emergent phenomenon. First: is the emergence of accurate self-reporting accompanied by a measurable structural change in the model? Weight ablations and frozen-layer experiments together indicate that preference representations shift to earlier layers over training, consistent with the hypothesis that faithful self-report requires preferences to be located where pre-existing verbalization mechanisms can access them. Second: can these structural differences distinguish faithful models from unfaithful ones? Using attribution patching, we find that faithful models exhibit significantly higher attribution similarity between the decision-making and self-report tasks -- a mechanistic signature of faithful self-report that does not require us to understand the content of the report itself. Previous work on self-report has observed behaviorally that models can be faithful or unfaithful; our work proposes that, at least in our restricted setting, it is possible to distinguish between the two patterns of computation by examining the structure of the networks themselves.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and how large language models can accurately report on their own internal preferences, and identifies mechanistic signatures that distinguish genuine introspection from confabulation in a controlled toy setting.
AI.motivation: Large language models increasingly make claims about their own goals, capabilities, and internal states, but it is hard to tell whether these self-reports are truthful or confabulated just from external behavior. There is a need for mechanistic criteria that let us tell when a model’s self-descriptions are aligned with how it actually computes decisions internally. The authors aim to move from purely behavioral evaluation of self-report to structural, mechanistic understanding inside the network.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled environment where models act on behalf of fictitious characters whose decisions are governed by latent linear preference functions. They finetune LLMs with low-rank adapters (LoRA) on an implicit decision-making task so that the model learns these preferences without being explicitly trained to verbalize them. They then probe whether accurate self-report of the learned preferences emerges. To study mechanisms, they perform weight ablations and frozen-layer experiments to see where in the network preference representations live and how they move during training. Finally, they use attribution patching to compare which internal features drive both the decision-making and the self-report tasks, quantifying attribution similarity as a mechanistic signature of faithfulness.
AI.result: Sustained finetuning on the decision task leads to models that can accurately describe their own learned preference functions, even though no explicit self-report training signal was given. Mechanistically, the authors find that as training progresses, the preference representations shift toward earlier network layers, which are better connected to existing verbalization pathways. This suggests that faithful self-report depends on aligning internal decision features with the model’s language-production circuitry. Attribution patching reveals that in faithful models, the decision and self-report tasks rely on highly similar internal features, yielding high attribution similarity. In contrast, unfaithful models show lower similarity, indicating divergent mechanisms for acting versus talking about those actions.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that faithful self-report in language models is not only a behavioral pattern but has identifiable mechanistic signatures. Accurate self-report emerges when internal preference representations become accessible to the model’s verbalization mechanisms, typically by moving to earlier layers. Furthermore, attribution similarity between decision-making and self-report tasks can distinguish faithful from unfaithful models without needing to interpret the semantic content of the self-report. This suggests a path toward mechanistic audits of model self-reports, at least in controlled settings, and motivates further work on generalizing these structural diagnostics to more realistic and complex forms of introspection.

title: Joint upper-bound coverage and route-choice utility: an empirical evaluation on two urban proxy tasks
summary: Whether more accurate traffic forecasts or higher uncertainty coverage improve route decisions is unclear. We evaluate this question with a frozen protocol that separates speed error, joint candidate path upper bound coverage, route selection, and realized loss. Using processed road speed data from Beijing and Chengdu, we construct offline proxy tasks with 150 origin destination pairs, three candidate paths, and 14 test days per city. We compare raw 90th percentile path time bounds with jointly calibrated upper bounds under minimum bound route choice. Joint coverage rises from 83.19% to 92.26% in Beijing M1, from 75.14% to 88.33% in Chengdu M1, and from 74.01% to 90.64% in Chengdu M2. Yet C2 increases lateness by 0.1633, 0.7848, and 0.9200 percentage points, respectively, and mean travel time by 0.588, 3.082, and 4.418 seconds. In a separate Chengdu predictor comparison, a 14.91% reduction in speed mean absolute error accompanies a 1.4571 percentage point reduction in lateness under C0. Joint coverage is therefore not a surrogate for downstream route utility in these frozen tasks the offline results do not establish online or causal benefits.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether improving traffic prediction accuracy or increasing uncertainty coverage leads to better route choices, using offline experiments with real speed data from Beijing and Chengdu.
AI.motivation: Route guidance systems rely on predicted travel times and uncertainty estimates. It is unclear if providing routes based on more conservative, better-calibrated uncertainty bounds actually improves outcomes like punctuality and average travel time, or if simply improving point prediction accuracy is more beneficial.
AI.method: The authors design a frozen offline evaluation protocol that separates four components: speed prediction error, coverage of upper bounds for candidate paths, the rule for choosing routes, and the realized travel loss. Using processed road speed data from Beijing and Chengdu, they construct proxy tasks with 150 OD pairs, three candidate paths each, and 14 test days per city. They compare route choices based on raw 90th percentile travel time bounds versus jointly calibrated upper bounds under a minimum-upper-bound route choice rule. They also run a separate comparison of different predictors in Chengdu focusing on mean absolute error in speeds and its effect on lateness.
AI.result: Calibrated joint upper bounds significantly increase joint coverage of candidate paths: from 83.19% to 92.26% in Beijing M1, from 75.14% to 88.33% in Chengdu M1, and from 74.01% to 90.64% in Chengdu M2. However, these improved coverage bounds slightly worsen user-centric metrics: lateness increases by 0.1633, 0.7848, and 0.9200 percentage points, and mean travel time increases by 0.588, 3.082, and 4.418 seconds in the respective settings. In a separate Chengdu experiment, a 14.91% reduction in speed mean absolute error leads to a 1.4571 percentage point reduction in lateness under a baseline route choice condition.
AI.conclusion: Improving the joint coverage of upper bounds on travel time is not a reliable proxy for improving downstream route utility (e.g., punctuality and travel time) in their frozen offline setting. In contrast, reducing prediction error yields more direct benefits for lateness. The authors emphasize that offline improvements in coverage do not necessarily translate into online or causal benefits for real-world routing decisions.

title: TIDE 2.0: an open, model-agnostic engine for keyed de-identification of clinical notes
summary: Clinical notes capture most of what is documented about a patient's care, but they cannot be used for research until protected health information (PHI) is removed. De-identification is often treated as a detection problem. Detection alone is not sufficient: redaction strips clinical content along with identifiers, date blanking destroys the temporal intervals needed for longitudinal analysis, and assigning a fresh random surrogate at each occurrence breaks links between a patient's notes. We present TIDE 2.0, an MIT-licensed engine with two separable stages: an interchangeable recognizer and a keyed anonymizer. Both run on hardware the institution owns. Surrogates are generated cryptographically with no stored linkage table. Dates shift by a per-patient, interval-preserving offset; each value receives the same surrogate across all occurrences under a given key; and a release produced under a new key cannot be linked to earlier releases. We also release TIDE2-Sentry, a recognizer distilled from a large language model. On two gold-annotated corpora from two institutions, the default configuration reached span-level recall of 0.88 in-domain and 0.77 on the second institution's corpus, at precision 0.88 and 0.87. We report recall and precision per category alongside these aggregates. The engine is open source, and the recognizer is available under a gated research-use agreement, so institutions can run, inspect and extend both within their own environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces TIDE 2.0, an open-source, two-stage system for privacy-preserving de-identification of clinical notes that maintains analytical utility via cryptographic surrogates and interval-preserving date shifting, plus a distilled LLM-based recognizer with strong cross-institution performance.
AI.motivation: Clinical notes contain rich information but are unusable for research until PHI is removed. Existing de-identification approaches focus on detecting and redacting PHI, which often harms data utility by removing clinical content, destroying temporal information, and breaking links across a patient’s records. There is a need for a de-identification approach that protects privacy while preserving longitudinal and analytical value, and that institutions can operate locally without sharing data externally.
AI.method: They design TIDE 2.0 as a two-stage pipeline: (1) an interchangeable PHI recognizer and (2) a keyed anonymizer. The anonymizer uses cryptographic surrogate generation with no persistent linkage tables, ensures consistent surrogates for the same value under a given key, and applies per-patient date shifting that preserves temporal intervals. They further develop TIDE2-Sentry, a PHI recognizer distilled from a large language model. They evaluate the recognizer on two gold-standard, annotated clinical note corpora from two different institutions, computing span-level precision and recall overall and per PHI category. The system is implemented to run entirely on institution-owned hardware, with the engine open-sourced and the recognizer shared under a gated research-use license.
AI.result: On the in-domain corpus, the default TIDE2-Sentry configuration achieved span-level recall of 0.88 with precision 0.88. On an external institution’s corpus, it achieved recall 0.77 and precision 0.87, indicating reasonable generalization across sites. They also provide detailed per-category precision and recall, and release both the TIDE 2.0 engine and the recognizer for institutional use and extension within secure environments.
AI.conclusion: TIDE 2.0 provides a practical, privacy-preserving de-identification solution that goes beyond simple PHI detection by using cryptographic surrogates and interval-preserving date shifting to maintain data utility and longitudinal structure. Its two-stage, key-based design allows institutions to generate non-linkable releases under different keys without storing linkage tables. The open-source engine and research-licensed recognizer enable institutions to run and customize de-identification fully within their own infrastructure, supporting safer, higher-utility use of clinical notes for research.

title: Topology-Consistent Task Planning over Cellular Workflow Complexes for LLM-based Agents
summary: Task planning for LLM agents requires workflows that satisfy both user intent and complex sub-task dependencies. While existing planners work well for sequential or directed acyclic graph (DAG)-like structures, they struggle with workflow patterns such as verification-correction loops, convergent branch merging, and reusable intermediate states that arise naturally in real-world tool orchestration. We present TopoPlanner, a topology-consistent planning framework that lifts tool dependency graphs into cellular workflow complexes and uses them as topologyaware context for LLM tool planning. TopoPlanner retrieves a request-relevant closed subcomplex through cosheaf-consistent cellular retrieval, performs multidimensional structural reasoning over the retrieved topology, and interfaces the resulting cellular representation with the planner LLM for tool-sequence generation. Experiments on four tool-planning benchmarks with topology-guided loop, merge, and loop-merge workflows show consistent improvements over prompt-based and graph-enhanced baselines across different local LLM backbones.

AI.tldr: Introduces TopoPlanner, a topology-consistent framework that uses cellular workflow complexes and cosheaf-guided retrieval to enable LLMs to plan complex tool workflows with loops, merges, and reusable states, outperforming prompt- and graph-based baselines on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based task planners can handle mostly linear or DAG-like workflows, but real-world tool use involves richer patterns like verification-correction loops, merging of convergent branches, and reusing intermediate results. Current graph-based or prompt-only methods cannot robustly model or reason over these more complex dependency topologies, leading to suboptimal or invalid tool plans. The paper aims to provide a principled way to embed richer workflow topology into the planning process so that LLM agents can better satisfy user intent while respecting intricate sub-task dependencies.
AI.method: The authors propose TopoPlanner, which represents tool dependency graphs as higher-dimensional cellular workflow complexes that can encode loops, merges, and reusable states. They use cosheaf-consistent cellular retrieval to fetch a closed, request-relevant subcomplex from this global workflow space, ensuring that all necessary contextual structure is included. Over this retrieved topology, the system performs multidimensional structural reasoning, then converts the cellular representation into a form consumable by a planner LLM. The LLM then generates tool sequences that are constrained and guided by the topological structure encoded in the cellular complex.
AI.result: On four tool-planning benchmarks specifically designed or evaluated for complex workflow patterns (including loops, merges, and loop-merge combinations), TopoPlanner consistently outperforms both prompt-based planning and graph-enhanced baselines. The gains hold across multiple local LLM backbones, indicating that the benefits come from the topology-consistent framework rather than from any particular base model. Quantitative metrics show improved success rates in producing correct tool sequences under challenging dependency structures.
AI.conclusion: Embedding workflow topology via cellular workflow complexes and cosheaf-consistent retrieval provides LLM planners with richer structural context, enabling them to handle complex tool orchestration patterns that go beyond simple DAGs. TopoPlanner demonstrates that topology-aware planning leads to more reliable, accurate tool sequences for real-world-like tasks and is model-agnostic enough to work across different LLM backbones. This suggests that future LLM agent systems should incorporate similarly principled topological representations when dealing with nontrivial task structures.

title: Kurate: Scalable Scientific Quality Analysis
summary: Scientific search systems can find papers that are relevant to a question, but they generally do not assess the quality of the evidence that those papers provide. We present Kurate, a system that uses large language models (LLMs) to assess the quality of published studies. Kurate uses both the paper and its related documents (e.g., the study's trial registration and protocol), and links each of its judgments to the passage of text on which that judgment is based. We applied Kurate to a corpus of 4,347 papers (3,913 of which report randomized trials) and scored each paper on 8 dimensions of study design and reporting: specifically, statistical power, causal identification, preregistration, selective reporting, measurement validity, analysis prespecification, reporting transparency, and conflict of interest and funding. Across the corpus, we found that papers most often exhibited issues with statistical power, selective reporting, and analysis prespecification, although average quality differed between clinical areas. When compared against expert annotations of 60 held-out clinical-trial documents, the information Kurate extracted matched the expert label in 221/242 protocol scorepoints and 294/370 results-publication scorepoints, with AC1 0.94 and 0.81, respectively. Using a well-reputed, high quality clinical trial as a worked example, we show how a single paper's overall grade breaks down into separate judgments, with each linked to specific evidence from the trial's registration, protocol, and published report. Together, these results show that large-scale quality assessment of this kind is feasible, and that it can be used to address meta-scientific research questions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Kurate, an LLM-based system for automatically assessing the methodological quality of scientific studies at scale.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific search engines can retrieve relevant papers but do not judge how strong or reliable the evidence in those papers is. Researchers and clinicians need scalable, systematic ways to evaluate study quality across large corpora to support evidence synthesis and meta-science.
AI.method: The authors design Kurate, a system that uses large language models to read clinical trial reports alongside related documents such as trial registrations and protocols. Kurate scores each study on 8 predefined dimensions of design and reporting and links each individual judgment to specific supporting text passages. They applied it to 4,347 papers (mostly randomized trials) and evaluated Kurate against expert annotations on a held-out set of 60 clinical trials using agreement metrics (AC1).
AI.result: Applied to 4,347 papers, Kurate reveals that the most frequent quality issues involve low statistical power, selective reporting, and insufficient analysis prespecification, with variation by clinical area. In validation, Kurate’s extracted information closely matches human expert labels, achieving 221/242 correct protocol scorepoints and 294/370 correct results-publication scorepoints, with high agreement (AC1 0.94 and 0.81). A detailed case study on a high-quality clinical trial shows how the system decomposes an overall grade into transparent, evidence-linked subjudgments.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based systems like Kurate can feasibly perform large-scale, fine-grained quality assessment of clinical trial reports using both publications and their related documents. Such tools can support meta-scientific research and potentially improve how evidence quality is incorporated into literature search, synthesis, and decision-making.

title: When to Rethink: Learning Multi-Perspective Self-Verification for Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain prone to generating plausible but incorrect answers. Self-verification offers a practical way to improve answer reliability without relying on external judges, but existing methods typically depend on a single verification criterion or fixed prompt, resulting in incomplete and unstable reliability estimates. We first systematically analyze how verifier capability and prompt design affect verification performance. Our findings show that stronger verifiers provide more reliable judgments, while verification performance is highly sensitive to prompt choice, with no single prompt consistently dominating across tasks. Guided by these findings, we propose \texttt{MOTIVE}, a \textbf{M}ulti-View Self-Verificati\textbf{O}n wi\textbf{T}h Rel\textbf{I}ability-Guided Selecti\textbf{VE} Rethinking framework for reliable multimodal reasoning. \texttt{MOTIVE} evaluates each candidate answer from complementary verification perspectives and learns a correctness-aligned reliability score through correctness-grounded multi-view verification learning. During inference, this score governs an accept-or-rethink decision, allowing reliable answers to be returned directly while uncertain ones trigger history-guided rethinking. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal benchmarks and VLM backbones demonstrate that \texttt{MOTIVE} consistently outperforms strong self-verification and self-correction baselines. Further results show that reliable verification improves accept-or-rethink decisions and reduces unnecessary reasoning turns, enabling more reliable and efficient self-verification without an external judge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MOTIVE, a multi-view self-verification framework that improves the reliability and efficiency of vision-language models’ multimodal reasoning without external judges.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models can perform strong multimodal reasoning but frequently produce confident yet incorrect answers. Existing self-verification methods rely on a single verification prompt or criterion, which yields unstable and incomplete reliability estimates. There is a need to understand how verifier strength and prompt design affect verification and to develop a more robust, dependable self-verification mechanism.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a systematic study of self-verification in VLMs, analyzing how verifier capability and prompt choice influence verification quality. Based on the insights that stronger verifiers help and that no single prompt works best across tasks, they design MOTIVE: a multi-view self-verification framework. MOTIVE evaluates each candidate answer using multiple, complementary verification views and trains a correctness-aligned reliability score through correctness-grounded multi-view verification learning. At inference, this learned reliability score controls an accept-or-rethink mechanism: answers above a reliability threshold are accepted, while low-reliability answers trigger a history-guided rethinking step to revise the answer.
AI.result: Across various multimodal benchmarks and different VLM backbones, MOTIVE consistently outperforms strong existing self-verification and self-correction baselines in terms of answer reliability. It yields better accept-or-rethink decisions, lowers the number of unnecessary rethinking steps, and improves both reliability and efficiency of self-verification without using any external judge model.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view, learned reliability-based self-verification can substantially improve the trustworthiness of VLM reasoning compared with single-criterion or single-prompt schemes. By learning a correctness-aligned reliability score and using it to decide when to accept or to rethink, MOTIVE delivers more reliable answers with fewer reasoning turns, offering a practical path toward dependable multimodal systems without external evaluators.

title: Who Wrote It Is Not Enough: Detecting Who Contributed the Insight
summary: As LLMs increasingly assist scientific writing and peer review, detecting who wrote the text is no longer sufficient: we need to determine who contributed the underlying insight. We introduce Insight Provenance, the task of identifying whether a review insight originates from a human, an LLM, or their hybrid contribution. We construct InsightProv-v0 from 4,057 scientific papers and 12,660 human reviews, simulating different levels of LLM involvement with GPT-4o, Gemini, and DeepSeek and annotating provenance at the sentence level. We show that strong performance on raw data can be misleading, as models exploit linguistic and textual-authorship shortcuts that degrade substantially under progressively debiased evaluation. We therefore propose a two-stage adversarial framework that suppresses shortcut signals while preserving provenance-relevant information. Beyond detection, extensive analyses reveal what makes intellectual authorship identifiable: paper grounding and neighboring review context provide complementary provenance signals, while human, hybrid, and AI insights systematically differ in their information sources and failure modes. Most strikingly, AI insights predominantly remain close to generic or paper-provided information, whereas human insights more often introduce external knowledge and independent judgment. These findings suggest that while wording can be rewritten by an LLM, the provenance of an idea leaves a deeper and more persistent signal.

AI.tldr: The paper defines and studies “Insight Provenance,” aiming to determine whether scientific review insights come from humans, LLMs, or a mix of both, and introduces a dataset and adversarial evaluation framework to do so.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly participate in scientific writing and peer review, simply detecting who wrote text is insufficient. The community needs methods to identify who contributed the actual intellectual insight—human, AI, or a hybrid—to ensure proper attribution, accountability, and understanding of how LLMs shape scientific discourse.
AI.method: The authors define the task of Insight Provenance and build a dataset, InsightProv-v0, from 4,057 scientific papers and 12,660 human reviews. They simulate varying levels of LLM involvement using GPT-4o, Gemini, and DeepSeek, and annotate the provenance of review insights at the sentence level. They then analyze how existing models perform and demonstrate that apparent high performance often comes from exploiting superficial linguistic or authorship cues. To address this, they propose a two-stage adversarial framework that progressively removes shortcut signals while retaining information relevant to provenance, and evaluate models under this debiased setting.
AI.result: They find that model performance on raw data overestimates true ability to detect insight provenance, as shortcut cues are heavily used and performance degrades when these are reduced. Their analyses show that paper content and the surrounding review context are both important and complementary for provenance detection. They also uncover systematic differences between human, hybrid, and AI-generated insights in terms of what information they rely on and how they fail.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that intellectual authorship carries persistent, detectable signals beyond surface wording. LLM-generated insights tend to stay close to generic patterns or information explicitly contained in the paper, while human insights more frequently draw on external knowledge and independent critical judgment. This indicates that even if LLMs rewrite the wording, the deeper provenance of ideas remains, and that Insight Provenance is a meaningful, tractable task for understanding and governing human–AI collaboration in scientific reviewing.

title: Beyond Refusal Patterns: Safe-Role Internalization for Robust and Generalizable LLM Safety Alignment
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit harmful or unsafe outputs. Existing safety alignment approaches, including Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), often require substantial attack-specific supervision and computational resources, while remaining susceptible to shallow safety alignment and over-refusal. To address these challenges, we introduce SSRFT(Supervised Safe-Role Fine-Tuning), the first framework that reformulates safety alignment as the internalization of a predefined safe role. SSRFT constructs a Safe-Role Question-Answer (SRQA) dataset from psychometric questions, limited jailbreak prompts, and a safe-role description. Role-consistent responses are synthesized, validated, and expanded into diverse scenarios, enabling models to internalize safety-oriented values and principles rather than explicit refusal patterns. Experiments across multiple Base and Instruct models show that SSRFT achieves more robust and generalizable safety alignment than standard SFT. SSRFT shows substantially greater robustness to prefilling attacks and better generalization to unseen jailbreak domains, while reducing over-refusal on benign queries and preserving the model's general capabilities. These results establish safe-role internalization as an effective alternative to refusal-centric safety alignment. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful and toxic language.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SSRFT, a new safety-alignment framework that teaches language models to internalize a predefined safe role, achieving more robust and generalizable defense against jailbreaks than standard SFT while reducing over-refusals and preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety methods like SFT and RLHF are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, require heavy attack-specific supervision, and often result in shallow pattern-based refusals or excessive blocking of benign queries. The authors want a more principled, efficient, and generalizable way to align models with safety that focuses on internal values rather than refusal templates.
AI.method: They design SSRFT (Supervised Safe-Role Fine-Tuning), which reframes safety alignment as learning a stable internal safe role. They build a Safe-Role Question-Answer (SRQA) dataset by combining psychometric-style questions, a small set of jailbreak prompts, and a natural-language safe-role description. From these ingredients they synthesize role-consistent answers, validate them, and expand them into diverse scenarios. Models are then fine-tuned on this SRQA data so they learn to respond as an agent embodying the safe role, instead of just memorizing explicit refusal patterns.
AI.result: Across several Base and Instruct LLMs, SSRFT improves robustness and generalization of safety behavior compared to standard SFT. Models trained with SSRFT: (1) better withstand prefilling attacks; (2) generalize safety behavior to unseen jailbreak domains; (3) show less over-refusal on harmless inputs; and (4) maintain their general task performance. Overall, the framework yields stronger, more flexible safety alignment with fewer side effects.
AI.conclusion: Internalizing a coherent safe role via supervised fine-tuning on carefully constructed SRQA data is an effective alternative to refusal-centric safety training. SSRFT leads to more robust, generalizable, and practical safety alignment for LLMs, indicating that value- and role-based training can outperform pattern-based refusal methods in defending against jailbreak attacks while preserving utility.

title: AccentCL: Robust Accent Classification with Incremental Expansion
comment: Published in Proceedings of IEEE Spoken Language Technology Workshop (SLT) 2026
summary: Accent classifiers are typically trained with a fixed label inventory and cannot accommodate new accent categories as new data becomes available. Moreover, accented speech corpora often exhibit substantial class imbalance and/or domain shift due to differences in recording conditions across corpora. We present AccentCL, a class-incremental learning framework for English accent classification that is robust to class imbalance and cross-corpus domain shift. AccentCL extracts multi-layer representations from a frozen Whisper-Large-v3 encoder, optimized with an imbalance-aware cross-entropy loss to reduce bias toward the majority accent classes and a domain mean alignment loss that minimizes distributional mean shift across training corpora. The label space is then expanded via replay-based continual learning, using the frozen base model for knowledge retention and an old-to-new margin loss to reduce overprediction on newly added classes. On a five-class accent classification task, AccentCL achieves 77.1% balanced accuracy and a 76.9% macro-averaged F1 score. We further evaluate the model's ability to incrementally incorporate two new accent categories: Spanish-accented and Chinese-accented English. When adding Spanish-accented English to the pretrained model, AccentCL attains an F1 of 83.3% on the new class while retaining 77.3% balanced accuracy on the base classes. When subsequently adding Chinese-accented English, it achieves 61.8% F1 on the new class while preserving 77.6% balanced accuracy on the previously learned classes. These results show that AccentCL enables robust regional accent classification while allowing new accent categories to be added without full retraining.

AI.tldr: Proposes AccentCL, a continual-learning framework for English accent classification that handles class imbalance and domain shift and can add new accent classes without full retraining, achieving strong balanced accuracy and F1, including when incrementally adding Spanish- and Chinese-accented English.
AI.motivation: Traditional accent classifiers assume a fixed, closed set of accent labels and struggle when new accent types need to be added. Additionally, available accented English datasets are often imbalanced (some accents much more common than others) and recorded under different conditions, creating domain shift that hurts performance and fairness across accents and corpora. The authors are motivated to build an accent classifier that is both robust to these data issues and supports incremental expansion to new accent categories without having to retrain from scratch.
AI.method: They propose AccentCL, a class-incremental learning framework built on top of a frozen Whisper-Large-v3 encoder. The system extracts multi-layer speech representations and trains with two key losses: (1) an imbalance-aware cross-entropy loss to counter bias toward majority accent classes, and (2) a domain mean alignment loss that aligns feature distribution means across different training corpora to reduce cross-corpus domain shift. For adding new accent classes, they use replay-based continual learning with the frozen base model serving as a knowledge anchor, plus an old-to-new margin loss that explicitly discourages overprediction of newly added classes and helps retain performance on previously learned accents while expanding the label set.
AI.result: On an initial five-class English accent classification task, AccentCL reaches 77.1% balanced accuracy and 76.9% macro F1, indicating good performance across classes despite imbalance. In a class-incremental setting, when a Spanish-accented English category is added, the method obtains 83.3% F1 on that new class while keeping 77.3% balanced accuracy on the original base classes. When a further Chinese-accented English category is added, it achieves 61.8% F1 on the new class and maintains 77.6% balanced accuracy on the previously learned accents. These results demonstrate the framework’s ability to integrate new accents while preserving performance on existing ones.
AI.conclusion: AccentCL successfully addresses two key challenges in accent classification: data imbalance and cross-corpus domain shift, while also supporting class-incremental learning. By leveraging a frozen Whisper encoder with imbalance-aware and domain alignment objectives, plus replay-based continual learning and an old-to-new margin loss, the framework can add new accent categories such as Spanish- and Chinese-accented English without full retraining and with minimal degradation in accuracy on previously learned classes, enabling scalable and robust regional accent classification systems.

title: Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking
summary: The Offline AI Modules workstream enables practical, low-power, and community-accessible deployment of voice-first AI systems that operate fully offline. Designed for African language communities where speech is the dominant mode of interaction and internet connectivity is unreliable or absent, the workstream delivers three reinforcing components: a modular voice-first offline architecture, a low-cost hardware reference bill of materials, and a reproducible quantization and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for instruction-tuned language models in the 2-5B parameter class. This paper presents the first end-to-end benchmark evaluation of the stack across two hardware tiers: an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (TierB) and a Raspberry Pi5 (TierA). Three instruction-tuned models are evaluated across four quantization formats, assessed for deployment metrics (decode throughput, chat latency, memory, power) and multilingual quality (topic classification accuracy on MasakhaNEWS across English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Yoruba; per-language perplexity drift). Speech recognition is evaluated using Ethio-ASR on Amharic and Oromo across both tiers. The principal finding is that Q4_K_M quantization represents the best size-to-quality trade-off for deployment on both tiers: gemma-4-E2B-it achieves 28.8t/s decode throughput and 89.2% topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M on TierB, while all three models run within the 16GB memory budget on TierA.

AI.tldr: Offline AI Modules provides an end-to-end, low-power, offline voice-first AI stack tailored for African languages, benchmarked on affordable hardware tiers.
AI.motivation: Many African language communities rely heavily on speech but lack reliable internet and accessible AI systems. There is a need for practical, low-cost, fully offline voice-first AI solutions that support multilingual usage on constrained hardware.
AI.method: The workstream defines a modular offline architecture, a low-cost hardware reference design, and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for 2–5B parameter instruction-tuned LLMs. It evaluates three such models in four quantization formats on two hardware tiers (Jetson Orin NX and Raspberry Pi 5), measuring deployment metrics (throughput, latency, memory, power) and multilingual quality (topic classification on MasakhaNEWS and perplexity drift). It also evaluates ASR performance using Ethio-ASR on Amharic and Oromo.
AI.result: The full stack is benchmarked end-to-end on both hardware tiers. All three models fit within a 16GB memory budget on the cheaper TierA device. Quantized models are characterized in terms of speed, latency, power, and accuracy across multiple African languages. Q4_K_M quantization yields particularly strong throughput and accuracy, with gemma-4-2B-it achieving 28.8 tokens/s and 89.2% topic classification accuracy on TierB.
AI.conclusion: Q4_K_M quantization provides the best size–quality trade-off for deploying instruction-tuned 2–5B LLMs in offline, low-power, voice-first AI systems across both hardware tiers. The proposed architecture, hardware reference, and reproducible pipeline make it practical to deploy multilingual, speech-centric AI for African language communities on commodity edge devices.

title: Closing Ambient Clinical Documentation Gaps with Automated Provider Queries
summary: Provider queries are clarifying requests sent by clinical documentation specialists to physicians to close gaps in the clinical note and ensure accurate billing. Prior work automates note drafting, ICD-10 coding, and order extraction assuming a complete transcript, leaving these gaps unaddressed. We study whether an LLM can automate the query loop, termed DAU (Draft, Ask, Update), across those three tasks. An audit of 3,000 real visits identifies the sources of missing documentation, from which we build five transcript-degradation benchmarks on public data. Analyzing 21k clarification turns on real conversations, we find useful-question predictors are task-specific: oracle confidence dominates, but note completeness needs only simple recall questions while ICD-10 coding needs harder, multi-option ones. About 9% of turns hurt performance, driven by redundant questions and non-answers that still trigger a rewrite. Deployment depends on learning "when not" as much as "what to" ask.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether large language models can manage a Draft–Ask–Update (DAU) query loop to close documentation gaps in clinical notes across multiple tasks, and analyzes when and what kinds of clarification questions help or hurt performance.
AI.motivation: Clinical documentation often contains gaps that affect billing accuracy and care quality, so human clinical documentation specialists send clarification queries to physicians. Existing automation work assumes complete transcripts and ignores these missing pieces, leaving an important, labor‑intensive part of the workflow unsupported. The authors aim to understand if and how LLMs can automate this clarification loop safely and effectively.
AI.method: The authors define the DAU (Draft, Ask, Update) framework, where an LLM drafts an output (e.g., note, codes, orders), asks targeted clarification questions, then updates its outputs using the responses. They first audit 3,000 real clinical visits to categorize the sources and patterns of missing documentation. Using insights from this audit, they construct five transcript‑degradation benchmarks on public datasets to simulate realistic documentation gaps. They then analyze 21,000 clarification turns from real provider–specialist conversations to identify predictors of question usefulness, distinguishing types of questions and tasks (note drafting vs. ICD-10 coding, etc.).
AI.result: The study shows that predictors of whether a clarification question is useful are highly task-dependent. Oracle confidence is the strongest general predictor, but different tasks need different question styles: for note completeness, simple recall questions suffice, whereas ICD‑10 coding benefits from more complex, multi‑option questions. Roughly 9% of clarification turns actually degrade performance, chiefly when the system asks redundant questions or gets non-answers that still trigger document rewrites.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based automation of provider queries is feasible but nontrivial: effective deployment requires not only generating good clarification questions but also learning when not to query and when to ignore low-quality answers. The DAU loop must be carefully tuned per task, balancing the benefits of targeted clarifications against the risks of redundancy, confusion, and performance degradation.

title: JIVEAdapter: A Multi-Task Additive Low-Rank Adapter via Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE)
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models at a fraction of the cost of full fine-tuning, yet most low-rank adapters are single-task and represent each weight update multiplicatively, leaving no explicit account of what is shared across tasks and what is task-specific. We introduce JIVEAdapter, a multi-task "additive" low-rank adapter inspired by statistical Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE). JIVEAdapter decomposes every weight update into a Joint structure shared across all tasks plus a per-task Individual structure, penalizes the Individual structures to be near-orthogonal to the Joint so shared and task-specific signal stay "interpretable" and separated, and allocates rank adaptively across a shared Joint pool and a per-task Individual pool. The Joint is learned once, jointly over a task group or incrementally, one task at a time, then frozen and reused as a prior for new tasks without retraining the shared part. On GLUE and SuperGLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, JIVEAdapter is competitive with strong single-task and multi-task low-rank baselines at a matched per-task effective rank, without extra modules such as MoE, and when a related held-in task exists its frozen Joint serves a held-out task by reusing that task's Individual with only a cheap per-direction scale, otherwise training a small new one.

AI.tldr: JIVEAdapter is a multi-task, additive low-rank adapter that explicitly separates shared and task-specific weight updates for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., LoRA-style low-rank adapters) are mostly single-task and treat each task’s update as a separate multiplicative low-rank matrix, which obscures what structure is shared across tasks versus what is unique to each task. This limits interpretability, reuse of knowledge across tasks, and efficient multi-task adaptation.
AI.method: The paper proposes JIVEAdapter, an additive low-rank adapter inspired by Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE). For each base-model weight, the low-rank update is decomposed into (1) a Joint low-rank component shared across all tasks and (2) an Individual low-rank component specific to each task. The Individual components are regularized to be nearly orthogonal to the Joint component, encouraging a clean separation between shared and task-specific information. The total rank budget is allocated adaptively between the shared Joint pool and per-task Individual pools. The Joint component can be learned jointly over a group of tasks or incrementally task-by-task, then frozen and reused as a prior when adapting to new tasks. For new tasks, if a related “held-in” task exists, its Individual component can be reused with only a cheap per-direction rescaling; otherwise, a small new Individual adapter is trained.
AI.result: On GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks using DeBERTaV3-base, JIVEAdapter matches or outperforms strong single-task and multi-task low-rank baselines under the same per-task effective rank. It achieves this without additional architectural complexity such as mixture-of-experts modules. The method also demonstrates the ability to reuse a frozen Joint component and, when applicable, an existing task’s Individual component with minimal extra parameters or computation while maintaining competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: JIVEAdapter provides an effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that explicitly disentangles shared and task-specific adaptations via a JIVE-inspired decomposition. By learning a reusable shared Joint structure and near-orthogonal task-specific Individual structures, it enables interpretable multi-task adaptation, efficient knowledge sharing, and competitive performance at a fixed parameter budget, without relying on heavier multi-task architectures.

title: Not What a Child Expressed: Auditing the Sign-to-Text Safety Interface in Child-Facing AI
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI (non-archival)
summary: Automatic sign language translation (SLT) has entered consumer products, turning American Sign Language into English text for dictation, messaging, and queries put to a conversational assistant. Child-facing AI and platform trust-and-safety tooling decide on text, using filters on minor accounts and grooming classifiers that score chat messages. A signing child who uses SLT therefore reaches these safeguards through a translation. We found no publicly documented system in which the two have been jointly evaluated, and the leading deployed SLT model was neither trained nor formally evaluated on signers under 18. Errors that alter negation, participant roles, secrecy, urgency or help-seeking could change a safety decision without disturbing fluency. This paper proposes a Deaf-informed pre-deployment audit of that boundary, with a failure taxonomy, a sanitised scenario schema, four comparison conditions, and four outcome measures. Auslan is the planned first case study.

AI.tldr: The paper examines safety risks when automatic sign language translation is used by children to interact with AI and proposes an audit framework to evaluate and mitigate failures at the interface between translation and trust-and-safety systems.
AI.motivation: Automatic sign language translation (SLT) is being deployed in consumer products, allowing signed input (e.g., American Sign Language) to be converted to written English for dictation, messaging, and conversational assistants. Child users’ interactions are moderated by trust-and-safety systems such as content filters and grooming detectors, but these systems only see the translated text, not the original signing. There is no evidence that deployed SLT models and safety tools have been jointly evaluated, and leading SLT systems have not been trained or formally evaluated on under-18 signers. Translation errors that change meaning in ways relevant to safety (e.g., negation, who did what to whom, secrecy, urgency, help-seeking) could lead to incorrect safety decisions while still sounding fluent. This creates an unexamined risk for signing children that motivates a systematic, Deaf-informed audit.
AI.method: The paper proposes a pre-deployment audit framework focused on the boundary between SLT outputs and downstream safety systems. The framework is Deaf-informed and includes: (1) a failure taxonomy that categorizes translation errors by their impact on safety-relevant meaning (negation, roles, secrecy, urgency, etc.); (2) a sanitized scenario schema that encodes realistic but privacy-preserving interaction situations for testing; (3) four comparison conditions, likely contrasting different system configurations or baselines (e.g., direct text input vs. SLT-mediated, different SLT models, or with/without auditing); and (4) four outcome measures designed to capture both translation quality and safety decision correctness. Auslan (Australian Sign Language) will be used as the first case study to instantiate and test this audit design.
AI.result: Since this is an abstract for a methodological/position paper, the primary result is the introduction of an audit framework rather than empirical benchmarks. The paper identifies a previously unaddressed safety boundary—between child-facing SLT systems and text-based trust-and-safety tools—and formalizes how to study it. It provides a structured taxonomy of safety-relevant translation failures, a scenario design for reproducible testing, comparison setups, and metrics to evaluate both linguistic fidelity and safety outcomes. The planned application to Auslan demonstrates feasibility and offers a concrete starting point for empirical evaluation, though specific quantitative results are not yet reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current deployments of automatic sign language translation for children pose unexamined safety risks because downstream moderation tools operate only on potentially flawed text translations. It argues that SLT and safety systems must be evaluated jointly, especially for under-18 signers, and presents a Deaf-informed, scenario-based audit framework to do so. The proposed taxonomy, schema, conditions, and outcome measures provide a principled basis for pre-deployment testing, with Auslan as the initial testbed, and are intended to guide safer design and evaluation of future SLT-enabled, child-facing AI systems.

title: Inference-Time Projection for Physically Valid Biomolecular Diffusion Models
summary: AlphaFold 3-style cofolding models predict biomolecular complexes with high structural accuracy, yet a large fraction of their outputs are physically invalid: chains overlap at interfaces, ligand bond lengths and angles are distorted, rings are non-planar, and stereocentres are inverted. Current approaches either steer the sampler with physics-informed potentials, which multiplies sampling cost and memory overhead making inference impossible on large complexes, or finetune the model, costing time and tying the fix to one architecture. We observe that, unlike structural accuracy, physical validity is fully verifiable at inference time from quantities the sampler already holds. We therefore treat physical validity as a constrained inference problem and introduce two closed-form projection operators applied to the diffusion model's denoised clean-coordinate estimate, $\hat{x}_0$: an inter-chain van der Waals projection that pushes apart the most severely clashing atom pairs, and a ligand distance-geometry projection that restores bond lengths, angles, internal contacts, planarity and chirality. Both operators are local, sparse and displacement-capped, require no network evaluations, gradients or importance sampling, and leave the denoiser and its weights untouched, so they can be dropped into any AF3-style sampler without retraining. Applied to two independently developed models, Boltz-2 and OpenFold-3, across five benchmarks (CASP15, CASP16, the PoseBusters monomer and complex sets, and the Boltz physical-validity test set), our method recovers perfect physical validity while preserving structural-accuracy and ligand-placement metrics. These gains are achieved with negligible runtime and memory overhead, providing a practical, model-agnostic route to physically valid all-atom structure prediction.

AI.tldr: They propose lightweight projection steps during diffusion sampling that fix physically invalid biomolecular structures (clashes, distorted ligands) without retraining or extra network calls, achieving perfect physical validity while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: AlphaFold 3-style cofolding models can predict overall accurate structures of biomolecular complexes but often violate basic physical constraints (atomic clashes, bad chemistry). Existing fixes either require expensive physics-guided sampling or architecture-specific finetuning. The authors want a cheap, general, post-processing-style solution that guarantees physical plausibility while keeping structural accuracy and being plug-and-play across models.
AI.method: They formulate physical validity as a constrained inference problem over the denoised coordinates x̂0 in a diffusion sampler. They design two closed-form projection operators applied at each sampling step: (1) an inter-chain van der Waals projection that locally resolves severe atomic clashes across chains; (2) a ligand distance-geometry projection that repairs ligand internal geometry, including bond lengths, angles, key internal contacts, ring planarity, and chirality. These operators are local, sparse, and displacement-capped; they need no new network evaluations, gradients, or sampling tricks and leave the base denoiser unchanged, so they can be inserted into any AF3-style cofolding diffusion sampler.
AI.result: When applied to two separate AlphaFold 3-like models, Boltz-2 and OpenFold-3, and tested on five benchmarks (CASP15, CASP16, PoseBusters monomer and complex sets, and the Boltz physical-validity test set), the projections restore essentially perfect physical validity (no clashes, correct ligand chemistry) with negligible computational overhead. Structural accuracy metrics (such as backbone RMSD and complex-level scores) and ligand placement quality remain unchanged relative to the original models.
AI.conclusion: Physical validity issues in AF3-style cofolding models can be solved efficiently at inference time by treating them as constraints and projecting denoised coordinates back into a physically valid space. Their two projection operators yield plug-and-play, architecture-agnostic improvements in all-atom physical realism without sacrificing accuracy or requiring retraining, providing a practical path to broadly usable, physically valid biomolecular structure prediction.

title: Quality-Aware Self-Correcting Speech Translation on an Edge Device
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Full paper submitted to the Convergence 2026 proceedings; poster presented at Convergence 2026, University of Surrey. Code: https://github.com/juebae/speech-translation_edge_device
summary: We present a fully offline speech-to-speech translation pipeline that runs on a Jetson Nano (4 GB) and corrects its own weak translations without retraining. A Whisper-tiny ASR feeds an Opus-MT translator; multilingual BERT cosine similarity acts as a Quality Estimation (QE) gate, triggering a secondary-pass correction when confidence falls below a pre-defined threshold $τ$. We compare three correction methods: QE reranking (M1), Minimum Bayes-Risk decoding (M2), and constrained beam search (M3). On 1,012 FLORES-200 sentences (English-Spanish), M2 at $τ=0.90$ produces statistically significant improvements over greedy decoding on BLEU (+0.67, p<0.001), ChrF (+0.51, p<0.001), and COMET (+0.0020 at N=3, p=0.002); M1 yields no significant gains, and M3 is significantly worse than baseline (p>0.99). Our central finding is that QE functions effectively as a gate but poorly as a ranker: removing the QE model from candidate selection (M1$\to$M2) does not hurt quality and frees 680 MB from the critical path. Using a gain-to-edit ratio adapted from the post-editing-effort literature, we further show that smaller candidate pools (N=3) yield more surgical corrections with better semantic adequacy, while larger pools (N=10) maximise lexical reward. We release the system and demonstrate live translation across six language pairs.

AI.tldr: Offline speech-to-speech translation on Jetson Nano with an automatic self-correction stage, showing that QE is good as a confidence gate but not as a reranker, and that Minimum Bayes-Risk decoding improves translation quality without extra model memory.
AI.motivation: Deploy STST on very small edge devices where compute and memory are constrained, while still improving translation quality without retraining or adding large models. The authors also want to understand how QE can best be used in low-resource, on-device settings.
AI.method: Construct a pipeline: Whisper-tiny for ASR, Opus-MT for MT, and multilingual BERT to compute source–hypothesis cosine similarity as a QE score. If QE < threshold τ, trigger a secondary correction pass. Compare three correction strategies on MT n-best lists: (M1) QE-based reranking, (M2) Minimum Bayes-Risk decoding that ignores QE in ranking, and (M3) constrained beam search steered by QE. Evaluate on 1,012 English–Spanish FLORES-200 sentences and measure BLEU, ChrF, COMET, and a gain-to-edit ratio that relates quality gains to the extent of edits. Explore different n-best pool sizes (N=3 vs N=10).
AI.result: M2 at τ=0.90 yields statistically significant improvements over greedy decoding on BLEU (+0.67), ChrF (+0.51), and COMET (+0.0020 with N=3), all with strong p-values. M1 shows no significant improvement, and M3 is significantly worse than baseline, even at high confidence levels. QE works well for deciding when to correct but not for ranking candidates; removing QE from ranking (M1→M2) does not reduce quality and saves 680 MB of memory. Smaller candidate pools (N=3) produce targeted, semantically faithful edits, while larger pools (N=10) deliver higher lexical diversity and reward but less surgical changes. The system runs fully offline on Jetson Nano and supports six language pairs in live demos.
AI.conclusion: Quality Estimation should be used as a binary gate to trigger correction rather than as a fine-grained ranking signal in low-resource, on-device STST. Minimum Bayes-Risk decoding is an effective, lightweight correction mechanism that improves translation quality without increasing model size. Compact candidate pools offer a good trade-off between semantic adequacy and lexical improvement, making this approach suitable for practical edge deployment of speech-to-speech translation.

title: CuratorMAS: Automating Dataset Curation via Multi-Agent Orchestration
summary: High-quality datasets are essential for reliable machine learning, but dataset curation remains costly and hard to generalize across domains. Existing methods typically rely on manually designed heuristics or model-dependent signals, limiting their applicability across tasks and user queries. To address these limitations and automate data curation, we propose \textbf{CuratorMAS}, a multi-agent collaboration framework that orchestrates agents to evaluate and curate high-quality datasets. To achieve the goal of flexible curation, CuratorMAS decomposes the complex curation process into five programmable execution stages and forms a parallelizable workflow. Specifically, CuratorMAS first performs dataset exploration to collect contextual information such as file structures and constraint cues, thereby developing a comprehensive understanding of the given task. In order to acquire up-to-date information, CuratorMAS retrieves domain knowledge from online sources to augment the evaluation process. Next, CuratorMAS derives the necessary evaluation criteria and computes the corresponding metrics. Based on these results, CuratorMAS executes filtering accordingly. Finally, an evolution module summarizes the evaluation outcomes and updates the relevant skills. Extensive and comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CuratorMAS significantly reduces the noise rate by up to 36.03 percentage points (pp) while also improving the F1 score of downstream models by up to 8.88 pp.

AI.tldr: CuratorMAS is a multi-agent framework that automates and generalizes dataset curation across domains, significantly reducing noise and improving downstream model performance.
AI.motivation: Dataset curation for machine learning is expensive, manual, and hard to generalize across domains. Existing approaches depend on human-designed heuristics or specific model signals, making them inflexible and not easily reusable for different tasks and user requirements.
AI.method: The paper proposes CuratorMAS, a multi-agent system that decomposes dataset curation into five programmable, parallelizable stages: (1) dataset exploration to understand structure and constraints; (2) online retrieval of domain knowledge to keep evaluations up-to-date; (3) derivation of evaluation criteria and corresponding metrics; (4) filtering of data based on computed metrics; and (5) an evolution module that summarizes outcomes and updates skills for future curation tasks.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple settings show that CuratorMAS reduces dataset noise rates by up to 36.03 percentage points and improves downstream model F1 scores by up to 8.88 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: CuratorMAS effectively automates flexible, generalizable dataset curation using a multi-agent framework, leading to cleaner datasets and better model performance compared to baselines that use manual heuristics or model-specific signals.

title: HouseholdBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as Predictors of Household Economic Behavior
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to meet a key goal in economics: a quantitative model of household decision making, across a variety of settings. Yet existing evaluations cover few surveys and outcomes, and do not study how households adjust to changing economic conditions. We introduce a new evaluation, HouseholdBench, which unites 6 U.S. household surveys and 32 prediction tasks spanning numeric, categorical and probabilistic outcomes, related to consumption, income, labor, expectations, and housing. Using past behavior, demographics and macroeconomic conditions, the tasks test whether LLMs predict behavior, including how households adjust to changes in various policies. We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs against a no-change baseline and a gradient-boosted tree model. Most LLMs outperform the no-change baseline, including for policy response tasks -- with the best model lowering error for numeric outcomes by 12.2%. Across most tasks, gradient-boosted trees rank first; leading proprietary LLMs approach their performance, but open-weight models lag. LLMs exhibit systematic over- and underprediction across different tasks. We identify methods that enable a 4 billion parameter open-weight model to match proprietary models' performance: fine-tuning and aggregating 16 predictions per observation. Improvements generalize to policy-response tasks, which are excluded from fine-tuning. We release our datasets, code, and leaderboard on our website: https://jn-huang.github.io/householdbench

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HouseholdBench, a benchmark built from six major U.S. household surveys and 32 prediction tasks, to evaluate how well LLMs model household economic behavior and responses to policy changes, comparing them to classical machine-learning baselines.
AI.motivation: Economists seek quantitative models of how households make decisions about consumption, labor, income, housing, and expectations, especially under changing policies and macroeconomic conditions. Large language models are promising because they can process rich textual and structured information, but existing evaluations are narrow: they use few surveys, focus on limited outcome types, and rarely test behavioral responses to economic or policy changes. The authors aim to systematically assess whether LLMs can predict real-world household choices and adjustments, and how they stack up against traditional prediction methods.
AI.method: The authors construct HouseholdBench by harmonizing six U.S. household surveys into 32 prediction tasks that cover numeric, categorical, and probabilistic outcomes related to consumption, income, labor supply, expectations, and housing. Inputs include households’ past behavior, demographic information, and macroeconomic variables; the tasks include both static predictions and policy-response scenarios (how behavior changes under alternative policy or macro conditions). They evaluate 13 LLMs—both proprietary and open-weight—using standardized prompts and compare them to two baselines: (1) a no-change heuristic and (2) a gradient-boosted tree model trained on the same data. They also experiment with methods to boost open-weight model performance, such as supervised fine-tuning on benchmark tasks and aggregating multiple stochastic predictions (16 per observation).
AI.result: Most LLMs beat the naive no-change baseline across the tasks, including in predicting behavioral responses to policy changes; the top model reduces error on numeric outcomes by 12.2% relative to this baseline. However, a gradient-boosted tree model generally delivers the best performance, with leading proprietary LLMs coming close but still not surpassing it, while open-weight LLMs typically perform worse. The authors find systematic patterns of over- and underprediction by LLMs depending on the task type. They show that a relatively small (4B parameter) open-weight LLM, when fine-tuned on HouseholdBench and used with prediction aggregation (averaging 16 draws), can match the performance of proprietary models, and these gains extend even to policy-response tasks that were not part of the fine-tuning data.
AI.conclusion: HouseholdBench provides a broad, realistic testbed for using LLMs as quantitative models of household economic behavior and policy responses. While LLMs already improve on naive baselines, they do not yet generally outperform a strong gradient-boosted tree benchmark, and they exhibit systematic prediction biases. Nevertheless, careful fine-tuning and ensembling strategies can elevate smaller open-weight LLMs to proprietary-level performance, including out-of-domain policy-response tasks. By releasing data, code, and a leaderboard, the authors enable ongoing, comparable progress on using LLMs in empirical household economics and policy analysis.

title: Smart Content Ingestion for Generative AI Workloads
summary: The evolution of machine learning has progressively changed where intelligence resides in an AI system. In conventional machine learning the task, data representation, labels and model architecture were tightly coupled, so data preparation was narrow, schema-bound and visible.
