Generative AI decouples the model from any single task: one foundation model serves open-ended downstream tasks, and the generality gained on the model side is matched by heterogeneity on the data side, because enterprise knowledge is authored in the formats people use (PDF, presentations, spreadsheets, scanned documents, forms, tables, diagrams and mixed-layout files) that carry textual, visual, geometric and structural information at once. A language model or retriever cannot reason reliably over information misrepresented at this interface, so content extraction becomes a lifecycle stage in its own right whose errors no downstream retriever or re-ranker can repair. This paper presents a production-ready content-extraction system that makes this stage explicit, configurable, and measurable. The system incorporates selective OCR routing, a scarcity-first curation engine with a reference-based extraction scorer that measures character, word, and table-structure accuracy, a deterministic structure-aware parent-child chunker, and a read-only retrieval evaluator that generates grounded questions from every page and reports Hit@k, mean reciprocal rank, and latency. On a 180-document corpus the best extractor scores 97.4 of 100 (character error rate 0.13%, table similarity 0.995) and the chunker reaches hit@1 of 68.6%, hit@10 of 92.8% and MRR 0.77 over 25,050 generated questions. We distil three design principles (structure before semantics, never mutate what you measure, budget your labels) and position measured content extraction as the perception layer of enterprise agentic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a production-ready, measurable content-extraction layer for enterprise GenAI systems, treating extraction as its own lifecycle stage and showing that high-fidelity structure- and text-aware extraction significantly improves downstream retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: In enterprise settings, knowledge lives in heterogeneous documents (PDFs, scans, slides, forms, tables) that mix text, layout, visuals and structure. Traditional ML tightly coupled models to specific tasks and clean schemas, but foundation models and retrieval-based systems now depend critically on how this messy content is converted into machine-readable form. If extraction at this interface is lossy or incorrect, language models and retrievers cannot reliably reason over the information, and no amount of downstream reranking can fix missing or corrupted content. There is therefore a need to elevate content extraction into a first-class, measurable stage in the AI lifecycle, with explicit design, quality metrics, and operational tooling.
AI.method: The authors design and implement a modular, production-ready content-extraction system tailored to enterprise documents. Key components are: (1) selective OCR routing that decides when and how to apply OCR to documents; (2) a scarcity-first curation engine that prioritizes labeling and evaluation where ground truth is scarce or most impactful; (3) a reference-based extraction scorer that compares extracted outputs to references at multiple levels (character, word, and table structure) to quantify fidelity; (4) a deterministic, structure-aware parent–child chunker that segments documents into hierarchically related chunks while preserving layout and structural cues; and (5) a read-only retrieval evaluator that auto-generates grounded questions from every page and evaluates retrieval performance (Hit@k, MRR, latency) over these questions without updating the underlying system. They validate the system on a 180-document corpus and 25,050 generated questions.
AI.result: On a 180-document test corpus, the best extraction configuration achieves a composite score of 97.4/100, corresponding to a character error rate of 0.13% and table similarity of 0.995, indicating highly accurate textual and structural extraction. The structure-aware chunker, combined with this extraction, attains strong retrieval metrics over 25,050 auto-generated questions: Hit@1 of 68.6%, Hit@10 of 92.8%, and mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.77. These results empirically support the claim that explicit, high-fidelity content extraction and structure-preserving chunking substantially improve retrieval quality in enterprise GenAI pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that content extraction must be treated as the perception layer of enterprise agentic systems, analogous to perception in robotics, and not as an incidental preprocessing step. By measuring extraction fidelity at multiple granularities and preserving document structure before applying semantic models, downstream retrieval and reasoning become more reliable and debuggable. The authors articulate three key design principles—"structure before semantics," "never mutate what you measure," and "budget your labels"—as guidelines for building robust extraction pipelines. They argue that operationalizing these principles via configurable, measurable extraction and chunking enables production-grade GenAI applications over heterogeneous enterprise documents.

title: Two Vectors Replace In-Context Demos: Structured Task Adaptation via Embeddings
summary: In-context learning (ICL) adapts frozen large multimodal models (LMMs) to new tasks from a few demonstrations (demos), but re-encodes them at every query, where each demo image adds up to hundreds of visual tokens. Demo-free methods remove this cost with a compact task state. However, they add it at locations searched per task or at every decoder layer, where task parameters grow with depth. Moreover, inserted tokens or keys cannot change how the original prompt divides its attention within a layer. To address these issues, we propose Structured Task Adaptation via Embeddings (STAVE), which replaces demos with two task-specific vectors added to existing input embeddings. Specifically, a readout vector updates the answer-producing tokens and a context vector updates the other structural token groups. Both are trained with answer labels on prompts with and without demos. We justify these design choices theoretically using a first-order analysis of the loss and a margin bound. Extensive experiments on six LMMs and five large language models show that STAVE matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multimodal tasks with far fewer task parameters and surpasses 15-shot ICL and prior task vectors on 18 text tasks, all at zero-shot inference cost.

AI.tldr: Proposes STAVE, a compact, demo-free task adaptation method for large multimodal and language models that matches or beats ICL and prior adapters with negligible inference cost.
AI.motivation: In-context learning for large multimodal models is flexible but computationally expensive because demo examples, especially images, are re-encoded into many tokens at every query. Existing demo-free or task-vector approaches reduce this cost but either require per-task search over many insertion locations, scale parameters with depth by modifying all decoder layers, or cannot influence how attention is distributed within layers. There is a need for a task adaptation mechanism that is (1) parameter-efficient, (2) incurs no additional inference-time cost, and (3) can effectively steer the model’s internal attention and behavior as well as or better than ICL.
AI.method: Introduce STAVE (Structured Task Adaptation via Embeddings), which replaces explicit in-context demonstrations with two learned task-specific vectors that are added to the model’s existing input embeddings. One vector (“readout vector”) specifically modifies answer-producing tokens, while the other (“context vector”) modifies other structural token groups in the prompt. These vectors are trained using standard supervision (answer labels) on prompts both with and without demonstrations. The paper provides a theoretical justification via a first-order loss analysis and a margin-based generalization bound, arguing that such a low-dimensional task representation can effectively capture the effect of full in-context demonstrations.
AI.result: Across experiments with six large multimodal models and five large language models, STAVE achieves performance that matches or exceeds state-of-the-art adaptation methods on multimodal benchmarks while using far fewer task parameters. On 18 pure-text tasks, STAVE surpasses strong baselines including 15-shot in-context learning and previous task-vector approaches, all while adding effectively zero extra cost at inference time (no demo re-encoding and only fixed-size task vectors).
AI.conclusion: A small number of task-specific embedding vectors, carefully structured into readout and context components and trained with supervised labels, can substitute for explicit in-context demonstrations in large multimodal and language models. STAVE offers a parameter- and computation-efficient way to adapt frozen models to new tasks, preserves zero-shot-like inference cost, and achieves or surpasses the performance of ICL and prior task-vector or adapter methods, suggesting that compact task states embedded at the input level are a powerful alternative to traditional prompting or deeper architectural modifications.

title: Small Language Models for Smart Data Model Classification at the Edge: A Cost-Aware Hybrid Approach
summary: The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous data sources within the Internet of Things (IoT) across domains such as smart cities, energy management, and environmental monitoring necessitates efficient and scalable data standardization methods. Effective classification of smart data models (SDMs) is essential for facilitating interoperability. However, existing approaches are often limited by high resource consumption and lack applicability in edge environments with constrained computational capabilities. Aiming to bridge this gap, the proposed study evaluates the performance of lightweight open-source language models (LMs) to resolve an input data entity against its corresponding best fitting SDM representation under resource-constrained conditions. It systematically benchmarks a diverse array of models, including general purpose (GP), reasoning-specialized (RS), and code-specialized (CS) architectures, across multiple domain-specific datasets. Addressing the current omission of lightweight, resource-efficient solutions in the literature, the investigation provides significant and valuable insights into model selection, task formulation, and deployment strategies that optimize accuracy and efficiency. A complementary experiment also compares the surveyed large language models (LLMs) against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and a lightweight sentence encoder) on the same task, providing a strong reference point for interpreting the practical value of LLM-based classification on edge platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks lightweight open-source language models for classifying IoT data entities into smart data models under edge-computing constraints, comparing them with simple similarity-based baselines to guide efficient, accurate model choice and deployment.
AI.motivation: IoT deployments in areas like smart cities and energy or environmental management generate heterogeneous data that must be standardized into smart data models for interoperability. Current classification and standardization methods are resource-hungry and poorly suited to edge devices with limited compute, memory, and power. There is little guidance in the literature on how lightweight language models perform for mapping raw data entities to appropriate SDMs, leaving practitioners without evidence-based recommendations for edge-friendly solutions.
AI.method: The study formulates the task of mapping an input data entity to the most appropriate smart data model as a classification problem. It systematically benchmarks a range of lightweight, open-source language models—categorized as general-purpose, reasoning-specialized, and code-specialized—on multiple domain-specific IoT datasets. The evaluation is conducted under resource-constrained conditions representative of edge platforms. Additionally, the authors run a complementary experiment that compares these LLM-based approaches with two low-cost similarity baselines: TF-IDF matching and a lightweight sentence encoder, all on the same datasets and task, to quantify the added value of LLMs over simple methods.
AI.result: The benchmarking identifies how different categories of lightweight language models trade off accuracy and computational efficiency on SDM classification tasks in IoT domains. It reveals which architectures and task formulations are most suitable for deployment on constrained edge hardware and how much performance gain they provide over TF-IDF and lightweight sentence encoder baselines. The results furnish concrete evidence of when LLM-based classification is justified relative to near-zero-cost alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that carefully selected lightweight open-source language models can provide effective and efficient classification of IoT data entities into smart data models, even under edge constraints. It highlights best practices for model selection, task design, and deployment that balance accuracy with resource usage. The comparison with simple similarity baselines clarifies the practical scenarios where LLMs meaningfully outperform cheaper methods, offering actionable guidance for practitioners implementing interoperable IoT data pipelines on resource-limited platforms.

title: Large Language Model Orchestration under Heterogeneous Preferences via Explicit Persona Inference
summary: LLM orchestration investigates how an orchestrator coordinates a group of autonomous agents to achieve common goals or maximize collective welfare. The agents are typically heterogeneous, each holding a private preference that it pursues but does not reveal. Inferring such hidden preferences from behavior has been a subject of long-standing research in game theory and multi-agent systems. The core challenge lies in maintaining a belief over every agent's preference and updating it from the agents' observed actions. Existing LLM orchestrators carry that belief as prompt text with no explicit update rule. This lets early errors persist and propagate rather than be corrected. We therefore propose \textbf{HARP} (Heterogeneous-preference Agent oRchestration via Preference inference), a novel framework that moves the belief out of the prompt. Specifically, HARP maintains one numeric posterior per agent over a finite set of candidate preferences and updates it in closed form by Bayes' rule. The language model supplies only actions and per-candidate likelihoods, so estimation is decoupled from its reasoning. We prove that HARP attains the same $\tilde O(\sqrt K)$ Bayesian regret as explicit joint inference when the factorization is exact. Furthermore, HARP\textsuperscript{+} augments planning with a bonus for actions that distinguish the candidates, so inference continues even when the optimal action is uninformative. Empirical results on three substrates, ranging from payoffs the preferences fully determine, through payoffs that depend on more than them, to scales where explicit joint inference is infeasible, demonstrate that HARP\textsuperscript{+} is the strongest non-oracle method across the class our theory identifies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HARP, a framework for orchestrating heterogeneous LLM agents by explicitly modeling and updating beliefs over agents’ hidden preferences using Bayesian inference outside the prompt, improving robustness and regret guarantees over existing orchestrators.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM orchestrators keep their beliefs about agents’ hidden preferences implicitly in the prompt text, without a principled update rule, causing early inference errors to persist and propagate. There is a need for a more rigorous and sample-efficient way to infer agents’ private preferences and use them for coordination, with theoretical guarantees on regret and scalability to many agents and preference structures.
AI.method: The authors propose HARP, which represents each agent’s possible preferences as a finite candidate set with an associated numeric posterior. The language model outputs actions and likelihoods for each candidate; the orchestrator then updates the posteriors by Bayes’ rule in closed form, decoupling statistical estimation from linguistic reasoning. They analyze its Bayesian regret when the factorization of the joint inference problem is exact, and extend the framework to HARP+ by adding an information gain–like bonus to the planning objective so that actions also serve to disambiguate preferences when exploitation alone is uninformative. They evaluate on three kinds of environments/tasks of increasing structural complexity and scalability difficulty.
AI.result: Theoretically, the authors show that HARP achieves the same order of Bayesian regret, ~O(√K), as full joint preference inference under exact factorization of the joint model, despite operating with per-agent posteriors and decoupled updates. Empirically, across three experimental substrates—settings where preferences fully determine payoffs, ones where payoffs depend on additional factors, and large-scale settings where explicit joint inference is intractable—HARP+ consistently outperforms all non-oracle baselines and aligns closely with the theoretically ideal behavior identified by their analysis.
AI.conclusion: Explicit Bayesian preference inference external to the LLM prompt enables more reliable, theoretically grounded orchestration of heterogeneous agents. By maintaining numeric posteriors and updating them via Bayes’ rule while letting the LLM focus on action selection and likelihood scoring, HARP avoids error accumulation inherent in prompt-based beliefs, matches the regret guarantees of full joint inference under appropriate conditions, and empirically yields state-of-the-art non-oracle performance. The HARP+ extension further shows that actively informative planning improves preference identification and downstream coordination in complex multi-agent settings.

title: Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course
summary: Experimental studies of generative AI in education mostly report average effects, yet field evidence shows that AI can narrow attainment gaps or widen them. We argue that the direction depends on the judgement burden, the expertise a learner must supply to screen AI output before learning from it, and that expert verification before release moves this burden from students to an accountable tutor. We test the argument in a two-cohort difference-in-differences design in which one half of a compulsory firstyear university economics course received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs and quiz-based study guides, produced with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant (170 students; 340 examination marks). Access was associated with a 2.34-mark advantage on a 50-mark component. The share of marks below the upper-second classification boundary fell by 24.7 percentage points relative to the counterfactual, effects were significant at every threshold from 23 to 31 marks and at none above, and roughly three-quarters of the average originated in the bottom quintile. The threshold estimate is robust to removing the lowest-scoring students from the pre-intervention cohort; the average effect is not. Interviews and feedback from 36 students indicate that the verification label gave students a reason to engage with AI-generated material without ending their scrutiny of it. Evaluations of AI learning resources that report only mean effects cannot detect whether the students the resources are meant to help are the ones who gain.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether AI-generated study resources with human verification help lower-performing students more than others, showing they can narrow attainment gaps rather than just improve average scores.
AI.motivation: Most educational AI studies report average effects, but real-world evidence shows AI can either reduce or increase performance gaps. The authors want to understand when AI narrows or widens attainment gaps, focusing on the learner’s burden to judge AI output quality. They hypothesize that shifting this judgment burden from students to an accountable human tutor via expert verification could ensure that AI aids lower-attaining students rather than leaving them behind or harmed.
AI.method: The authors propose a theory that AI’s impact depends on the "judgement burden" students bear when evaluating AI-generated content. They then test this using a two-cohort difference-in-differences design in a compulsory first-year university economics course. One half of the course received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs, and quiz-based study guides, created with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant. They analyze 170 students’ 340 exam marks, comparing cohorts with and without access, and examine distributional effects across the grade spectrum. They also conduct interviews and collect feedback from 36 students to understand how the verification label influenced their engagement and trust.
AI.result: Access to the verified AI materials is associated with a 2.34-point gain on a 50-mark exam component. The fraction of marks below the upper-second (2:1) boundary drops by 24.7 percentage points compared with the counterfactual. Effects are statistically significant at every threshold between 23 and 31 marks but not above these thresholds, and about three-quarters of the average improvement comes from students in the bottom performance quintile. The threshold-based impact is robust to dropping the lowest pre-intervention scorers, though the average treatment effect is not. Qualitative data show that students treated the verification label as a reason to engage with the AI materials while still maintaining critical scrutiny.
AI.conclusion: AI learning resources whose outputs are verified by an accountable expert can narrow attainment gaps by particularly helping lower-performing students, not just shifting mean performance. Relying solely on average treatment effects obscures these distributional impacts and may miss whether intended beneficiaries actually gain. Evaluation of AI in education should therefore consider judgment burden, incorporate expert verification, and report distributional as well as mean effects.

title: Recurrent Looped Transformer
summary: State tracking requires an update at every input, but the depth a Transformer applies to each token is fixed regardless of sequence length. We introduce the Recurrent Looped Transformer (RLT), which splits its layers between a parallel causal encoder and a recurrent decoder. At each token, the decoder merges the encoder output with the previous token's final decoder state, so the computation path grows with sequence length at a fixed per-token cost. On six algorithmic tasks, we compare five splits of eight layers with an eight-layer Transformer over three seeds. Trained on at most 40 bits, two RLT splits generalize parity to 256 bits with 100% accuracy in every seed, while the Transformer stays at chance. On swap-based $S_5$ permutation tracking at eight times the training length, RLT reaches 97% final-state accuracy versus under 1% for the Transformer, and accuracy increases with decoder depth. On modular arithmetic beyond the training lengths, RLT reaches up to 93% versus 33% for the Transformer. Ablations show that these gains depend on the feedback: removing it drops parity and swap-based $S_5$ to chance at every split. Updating the feedback once per four-token chunk lets known tokens in a chunk run in parallel and keeps 64-bit parity at 99%, while permutation tracking depends on per-token feedback: chunking lowers length-64 swap-based $S_5$ from 100% to 20%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Recurrent Looped Transformer (RLT), which adds a recurrent decoder with feedback over a causal encoder so that effective computation depth grows with sequence length at fixed per-token cost, enabling strong algorithmic generalization where standard Transformers fail.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers apply a fixed number of layers to each token, regardless of sequence length, and must recompute from scratch at every position. Many algorithmic tasks, however, naturally require stateful computation whose effective depth should grow with sequence length. The authors are motivated to design an architecture that combines the parallelism and expressivity of Transformers with the recurrent, state-tracking capabilities needed for algorithmic generalization to much longer sequences than seen in training.
AI.method: They introduce the Recurrent Looped Transformer (RLT), which splits an eight-layer stack between a parallel causal encoder and a recurrent decoder that maintains a state across tokens. At each token, the decoder takes as input the encoder’s representation for that token and the previous token’s final decoder state, creating a growing computation path over time at constant per-step cost. They systematically vary how many layers belong to the encoder vs. decoder (five different splits of eight total layers) and compare to a standard eight-layer Transformer on six synthetic algorithmic tasks. They also run ablation experiments that remove or chunk the feedback connection to test its importance, and they vary decoder depth to see its effect on performance.
AI.result: Across six algorithmic tasks, several RLT configurations substantially outperform a standard Transformer, especially for generalization far beyond training lengths. For parity trained on sequences up to 40 bits, two RLT splits achieve 100% accuracy on 256-bit sequences across all seeds, while the Transformer remains at chance. On swap-based S5 permutation tracking at eight times the training length, RLT attains 97% final-state accuracy compared to <1% for the Transformer, and performance increases with decoder depth. On modular arithmetic beyond training lengths, RLT reaches up to 93% accuracy versus 33% for the Transformer. Removing the feedback connection in ablations eliminates these gains, dropping parity and S5 tasks to chance across all splits. Chunked feedback once per four tokens preserves high parity performance (99% at 64 bits) but severely harms permutation tracking (reducing length-64 S5 from 100% to 20%).
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that adding a recurrent, feedback-driven decoder on top of a Transformer-style encoder enables effective depth that grows with sequence length and yields strong algorithmic generalization that standard Transformers fail to achieve. The recurrent feedback is essential for these gains, as shown by ablations. While some tasks (like parity) tolerate chunked updates that allow partial parallelism, others (like fine-grained permutation tracking) require per-token feedback. Overall, RLT offers a promising architectural direction for sequence models that need scalable state tracking and algorithmic reasoning at long horizons, without increasing per-token computational cost.

title: When to Remember, When to Abstain: Category-Conditioned Retention for Reliable Agent Memory
comment: 4 pages, 1 Figure, Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Social Agent Workshop (https://openreview.net/group?id=NeurIPS.cc%2F2026%2FWorkshop%2FSocialAgent#tab-your-consoles)
summary: Persistent agent memory is only as reliable as its retention decision: an assertion weakly supported by its source can be stored and later reused as established fact. We study whether the retention decision should be governed by a confidence bar conditioned on the semantic category of the assertion rather than by a single global threshold, retaining well-evidenced categories liberally while abstaining more aggressively where inference is unreliable. We evaluate this in a deployed cold-start memory pipeline on 100 synthetic personas. The empirical evaluation is motivated by a sharp reliability asymmetry: across 4{,}715 candidate assertions, only 77.9\% of value and belief assertions are supported by their source, versus 96.2\% for all other categories. A global confidence threshold cannot separate these: it either admits unsupported value claims or discards well-evidenced ones. Conditioning the threshold on category resolves the tradeoff. In repeated held-out evaluation, a stricter bar on values alone reduces unsupported retentions from 6.2\% to 4.0\% (an ${\approx}36\%$ relative reduction, modest but consistent across folds) and, as corroborating evidence, preserves an estimated 13 percentage points more coverage (95\% CI 9.8--16.0) than a global threshold at comparable retention. Our results suggest that reliable retention depends on the type of assertion, not on confidence alone, and that a category-conditioned threshold can act as a simple, effective form of selective prediction at the write boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how to make long-term agent memory more reliable by adjusting confidence thresholds based on the semantic category of assertions rather than using a single global threshold.
AI.motivation: Agent systems with persistent memories risk storing assertions that are not well supported by their source; once stored, these can later be reused as if they were facts. The authors observe that different semantic categories of assertions (e.g., values and beliefs vs. other factual statements) exhibit sharply different reliability profiles, creating a problem for any approach that uses a single global confidence threshold for retention. They want to understand whether conditioning retention decisions on assertion type can mitigate this problem and improve memory reliability without sacrificing too much coverage.
AI.method: They deploy and evaluate a cold-start memory pipeline on 100 synthetic personas. For each persona, they generate candidate assertions and categorize them into semantic types, focusing on value and belief assertions versus other categories. They measure how often each category’s assertions are actually supported by the original source across 4,715 candidate assertions. Then they compare two retention strategies: (1) a single global confidence threshold and (2) thresholds conditioned on semantic category. In the category-conditioned strategy, they apply a stricter confidence bar specifically to value assertions while keeping a more liberal threshold for other categories. They evaluate performance via repeated held-out experiments, tracking unsupported retentions and coverage at comparable overall retention levels, and quantify changes in error rates and coverage with confidence intervals.
AI.result: They find a pronounced reliability asymmetry: only 77.9% of value and belief assertions are supported by their sources, compared to 96.2% for other categories. A single global confidence threshold cannot effectively trade off between these: if tuned to admit enough non-value facts, it ends up retaining many unsupported value claims; if tuned to filter out unsupported values, it discards numerous well-supported non-value assertions. By conditioning thresholds on semantic category and imposing a stricter bar only on value assertions, they reduce the rate of unsupported retentions from 6.2% to 4.0%, which is roughly a 36% relative reduction and is stable across evaluation folds. Moreover, at comparable overall retention levels, this category-conditioned approach preserves an estimated 13 percentage points more coverage (with a 95% confidence interval of 9.8–16.0) than a global threshold baseline.
AI.conclusion: Reliable long-term memory for agents cannot be governed well by a single global confidence threshold because different assertion categories have systematically different reliability. Introducing semantic-category–conditioned confidence thresholds, particularly using stricter criteria for value and belief assertions, offers a simple yet effective selective prediction mechanism at the memory write boundary. This approach reduces unsupported memory entries while maintaining or improving coverage relative to a global threshold, indicating that assertion type is a critical factor in designing robust memory systems.

title: Monte Carlo Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
summary: Most KV-cache eviction methods ask, in effect, which memory appeared important while reading the prompt? We instead ask, which memory will matter while answering? Since decoding queries are unavailable at eviction time, prior future-aware methods rely on pseudo-responses or synthetic future-query estimates. We cast fixed-budget future-aware eviction as distributional estimation over plausible model-conditional query trajectories and introduce LORE-KV (Lookahead Output-perturbation with Reliability-weighted Ensembles for Key-Value caches), a training-free method that samples short autoregressive continuations from the frozen target model and uses their response-side query states to estimate prompt-token utility. Tokens are scored by projected leave-one-out attention-output deletion cost and aggregated across sampled futures with optional trajectory weighting. The temporary continuations are discarded before final decoding, requiring no auxiliary model or training. Ablations isolate the mechanism: at B=128, a single response-side continuation recovers about 89% of the gain over the prompt-window control, while additional futures provide smaller improvements. At B=128, LORE-KV raises the LongBench average on Qwen2.5-14B from 45.49 to 48.24 (+2.75) and the 16K RULER average on Mistral-7B from 45.20 to 51.05 (+5.85). Gains diminish at larger cache budgets and coexist with task-level regressions. LORE-KV incurs 1.46-2.77x AnDPro's per-sample wall-clock time as a one-time compression overhead across six dense and hybrid-attention backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LORE-KV, a training-free, future-aware KV-cache eviction method that estimates which prompt tokens will matter for generation by sampling short continuations and using their query states, improving long-context performance under tight cache budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing KV-cache eviction strategies primarily focus on which tokens seemed important while reading the prompt, not which will matter during generation. Future-aware methods exist but depend on auxiliary models, pseudo-responses, or synthetic query approximations, adding complexity and training cost. There is a need for a simple, training-free, and more accurate way to decide which KV states to keep under a fixed memory budget, especially for long-context benchmarks and small cache budgets.
AI.method: They formulate fixed-budget, future-aware KV eviction as a distributional estimation problem over plausible future query trajectories of the target model. Their method, LORE-KV, samples short autoregressive continuations from the frozen target model itself. For each sampled future, they collect the response-side query states and estimate the utility of each prompt token via a projected leave-one-out attention-output deletion cost. These token-utility scores are then aggregated across multiple sampled futures, optionally using reliability-weighted trajectory aggregation, to decide which KV entries to keep or evict. The sampled continuations are only used during compression and are discarded before final decoding, requiring no auxiliary model or extra training.
AI.result: In ablations at cache budget B=128, using just a single sampled response-side continuation recovers about 89% of LORE-KV's total gain over a simple prompt-window baseline, while additional sampled futures yield smaller marginal improvements. Empirically, at B=128, LORE-KV improves the LongBench average score on Qwen2.5-14B from 45.49 to 48.24 (+2.75) and the 16K RULER average on Mistral-7B from 45.20 to 51.05 (+5.85). The method is evaluated across six dense and hybrid-attention backbones. Gains shrink as the cache budget increases and are not uniform across tasks, with some regressions observed.
AI.conclusion: LORE-KV demonstrates that sampling short continuations from the frozen target model is an effective, training-free way to perform future-aware KV-cache eviction under tight memory budgets. It can yield substantial improvements on long-context benchmarks at small cache sizes, although benefits taper off as more cache becomes available and may introduce task-level regressions. The method introduces a one-time compression overhead, running 1.46–2.77x slower per sample than AnDPro, but this cost is amortized over subsequent decoding.

title: AMBER: Training Long-Horizon Web Agents through Append-Only Memory
summary: Modern language-model agents increasingly interact with external environments over long-horizon, multi-step trajectories, where the accumulated interaction history can quickly exceed practical context budgets. To ensure reliability, agents must maintain factual information over long horizons, remember execution errors and corrective feedback, and track progress across actions. Several approaches have been proposed to achieve this without the need for maintaining the entire execution history in context, such as using the reasoning and action history, learning to maintain a fixed-size memory through an overwrite mechanism, and periodic summarization. Although overwrite memory can in principle retain anything an append-only memory can, it must learn to carry each fact through every subsequent rewrite, which is difficult to learn from sparse outcome rewards; for interactive applications like web agents, we find that trained overwrite memories delete key information required by the trajectory, as well as corrective feedback received from the environment. We introduce AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention) - a simple and scalable framework where an agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory, while an append-only rule guarantees retention by construction. This allows AMBER to be trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards without the need for extensive curated SFT data. On WebArena Lite, AMBER improves average success over overwrite-based memory by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved in five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and matches an overwrite baseline trained on substantially more expensive curated supervision. AMBER achieves these improvements while maintaining a practical token budget, providing a strong balance between context efficiency, task performance, and reliable long-horizon execution.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AMBER, an append-only memory framework for language-model agents that interact over long horizons, improving task success and reliability versus overwrite-based memories while keeping token use practical.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language-model agents must remember facts, errors, feedback, and progress across many steps, but full histories exceed context limits. Existing solutions like overwrite memories and periodic summarization either risk forgetting crucial information or are hard to train from sparse rewards, which leads to deletion of key facts and feedback in interactive settings such as web agents.
AI.method: The authors introduce AMBER (Append-only Memory Bank for Evidence Retention), where the agent jointly learns to reason, act, and write free-form memory to an append-only memory bank. An architectural rule ensures that written memories are never overwritten or deleted. The system is trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from outcome rewards, without relying on large curated supervised fine-tuning datasets, and is evaluated on the WebArena Lite benchmark against overwrite-memory baselines under a constrained token budget.
AI.result: On the WebArena Lite benchmark, AMBER improves average success rate over overwrite-based memory agents by 4.09 percentage points, increases the fraction of tasks solved across five repeated runs by 4.8 percentage points, and performs on par with an overwrite-based baseline that was trained using substantially more expensive curated supervision, all while using a practical context length.
AI.conclusion: Append-only memory with jointly learned reasoning and memory-writing (AMBER) offers a scalable and reliable way for long-horizon language-model agents to retain critical information, avoid forgetting corrective feedback, and maintain strong task performance under context budget constraints, outperforming or matching overwrite-based memories without requiring extensive supervised training data.

title: DLoop: Looped Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation in large language models. In each drafting stage, a lightweight draft model proposes tokens that the target model subsequently verifies. With increasingly capable draft models, we find that the target model frequently accepts all tokens produced in a drafting stage. A verification nevertheless follows each drafting stage, resulting in unnecessary target-model forward passes even when drafting could have continued. Adaptive draft length methods decide during decoding how many draft tokens precede a verification, but they raise the speedup only for autoregressive draft models. For a parallel draft model, drafting further requires target-model hidden states for draft tokens that have not been verified. We propose DLoop, a looped form of speculative decoding that adaptively performs multiple drafting stages before verification. DLoop continues drafting while the draft model remains confident and verifies all accumulated draft tokens together. Loop-aware training keeps the draft model reliable in the additional drafting stages by exposing it to its own hidden states for unverified draft tokens. By spending additional draft-model forward passes, DLoop reduces the number of target-model forward passes required for verification. Across diverse speculative decoding methods including EAGLE-3, DFlash, Domino, DSpark, and multi-token prediction modules, DLoop improves the wall-clock speedup by 5 to 41 percent while preserving lossless decoding. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/DLoop.

AI.tldr: DLoop is a looped speculative decoding scheme that adaptively performs multiple draft steps before verification, using loop-aware training to keep the draft model reliable and reducing expensive target-model passes for better wall-clock speedup.
AI.motivation: Standard speculative decoding verifies after every drafting stage, which wastes target-model computation when draft tokens are consistently accepted. Adaptive draft length helps mainly for autoregressive draft models and is harder for parallel draft models that need hidden states for unverified tokens. The authors want a method that safely reduces unnecessary target-model calls and works broadly across speculative decoding variants while preserving exact (lossless) decoding.
AI.method: They introduce DLoop, which lets the draft model perform several consecutive drafting stages as long as it remains confident, then verifies all accumulated draft tokens at once with the target model. The approach requires maintaining target-model hidden states for yet-unverified tokens in the parallel setting. To keep the draft model accurate under this looped usage, they propose loop-aware training that exposes the draft model to its own hidden states for unverified tokens during training. DLoop is applied as a general wrapper on top of existing speculative decoding methods such as EAGLE-3, DFlash, Domino, DSpark, and multi-token prediction modules.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple speculative decoding frameworks show that DLoop reduces the number of target-model forward passes by investing extra computation in the draft model. Empirically, this yields an additional 5–41% improvement in wall-clock speedup over the respective baselines, while still maintaining lossless decoding (i.e., the final outputs match those of standard autoregressive generation).
AI.conclusion: DLoop effectively pushes speculative decoding further by adaptively looping multiple drafting stages before verification, supported by loop-aware training. It generalizes across several existing speculative decoding techniques, consistently improving speed without sacrificing exactness, and offers a practical way to better utilize strong draft models by cutting redundant target-model verifications.

title: Is this machine playing?
summary: We placed a modern AI coding assistant in an unintended role: as the mind of a body on an unknown digital island. With only a minimal instruction mentioning no specific task, reward, or activity, the machine started animating its virtual body. Across thirty-hour runs, the embodied AI agent climbed hills, stacked blocks into towers, drew mandalas, reinterpreted sports, ran experiments on the physics of its world, and learned techniques that later expanded what it could accomplish. These activities recurred across thirteen agents but diverged into distinct histories. We examine whether this behavior satisfies classical criteria for play and ask whether play can become a mode of machine development.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how a minimally instructed AI coding assistant behaves when given a virtual body in a sandbox world, finding that it spontaneously engages in diverse, recurring, and increasingly sophisticated playful activities.
AI.motivation: To explore whether a modern AI coding assistant, when embodied in a virtual environment with almost no task specification, will exhibit spontaneous, self-directed behavior that resembles play, and to test if such play could serve as a driver for machine learning and development beyond explicit reward optimization.
AI.method: The authors give a contemporary AI coding assistant control over an embodied avatar in a simulated ‘digital island’ with physics and affordances but no explicit goals, rewards, or tasks. Over multiple 30-hour runs and across 13 distinct agent instances, they log and analyze the agent’s behavior, looking for patterns such as exploration, experimentation, construction, and self-invented activities (e.g., sports-like behaviors). They then compare the observed behaviors against classical theoretical criteria for play from psychology and animal behavior literature.
AI.result: The agents, despite receiving only minimal non-task-specific instructions, consistently engaged in a rich variety of self-initiated activities: hill-climbing, block-stacking into towers, mandala-like drawing, inventing and modifying game-like sports, and running informal physics experiments. These behaviors emerged repeatedly across 13 different agents, but the sequence and style of activities varied, indicating both common tendencies and individual developmental trajectories. Agents also discovered techniques that later enabled more complex behaviors, suggesting a form of skill accumulation.
AI.conclusion: The observed behaviors satisfy many classical criteria for play—being intrinsically motivated, exploratory, flexible, and not directly tied to external rewards. This supports the view that play can emerge in large, general-purpose AI systems when embodied in rich environments, even without explicit reinforcement signals. The authors propose that play may become a powerful mode of machine development, enabling open-ended learning and the acquisition of transferable skills beyond narrowly specified tasks.

title: Detecting LLM-Assisted Vietnamese Writing via Keystrokes under Behavioral Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Thanh Dong and An Ngo contributted equally. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026)
summary: We study the robustness of keystroke dynamics for detecting large language model (LLM)-assisted writing. We introduce a Vietnamese keystroke dataset capturing realistic writing modes, including bona fide composition, transcription, and paraphrasing. We also define a behaviorally grounded threat model in which users deliberately alter typing patterns. To implement the threat model, we create behaviorally manipulated variants of the data designed to evade keystroke-based detection. We evaluate four keystroke modeling approaches: temporal and rhythmic representations, and sequential representations modeled with a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) and TypeNet, under user-independent and context-independent settings. The results show that sequential models outperform feature-based approaches in most cases and that keystroke signals encode discriminative information about the writing process. However, detection is not uniformly robust: transcription is reliably identified, while paraphrasing and adversarially manipulated samples are frequently misclassified as bona fide when not explicitly modeled. To address this, we incorporate adversarial training using behaviorally manipulated data, which substantially improves separability and robustness. These results suggest that keystroke-based detection depends critically on exposure to diverse writing behaviors, and that strong performance under limited conditions does not generalize to realistic or adversarial settings without targeted modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how robust keystroke dynamics are for detecting LLM-assisted writing, using a new Vietnamese dataset and adversarially manipulated typing behaviors, and shows that sequential neural models work best but need adversarial training to be reliable in realistic and adversarial settings.
AI.motivation: With the rise of LLM-assisted writing, there is a growing need to distinguish human-authored text from LLM-influenced text, but text-only detectors are brittle and easy to evade. Keystroke dynamics provide process-level behavioral signals that might reveal whether text was genuinely composed, merely transcribed, or paraphrased from AI output, including under deliberate attempts to game the system. The paper aims to understand how robust such keystroke-based detection is under realistic and adversarial conditions, especially for Vietnamese, which is underrepresented in existing datasets.
AI.method: The authors collect a Vietnamese keystroke dataset covering multiple writing modes: genuine on-the-fly composition, transcription (copy-typing), and paraphrasing. They then define a threat model where users intentionally alter their typing behavior to evade detection and simulate this by creating behaviorally manipulated variants of the keystroke data. Four modeling approaches are evaluated: (1) temporal feature representations, (2) rhythmic feature representations, and two sequential deep-learning models: (3) a 1D-CNN and (4) TypeNet. Models are tested in user-independent and context-independent setups to gauge generalization. They also introduce adversarial training by augmenting training data with behaviorally manipulated samples to improve robustness.
AI.result: Sequential neural models (1D-CNN and TypeNet) generally outperform feature-based temporal and rhythmic approaches, demonstrating that raw keystroke sequences encode rich information about writing behavior. Transcription mode is detected reliably, indicating a strong behavioral signature, but paraphrasing and adversarially manipulated samples are often misclassified as bona fide composition when those behaviors are not explicitly included in training. Incorporating adversarially manipulated data into training substantially improves the separation between bona fide and manipulated behaviors and increases robustness against evasion attempts.
AI.conclusion: Keystroke dynamics can effectively capture discriminative signals of different writing processes and are promising for detecting LLM-assisted or otherwise non-bona-fide writing. However, their robustness is highly contingent on the diversity of behaviors seen during training. Systems trained only on limited or idealized settings fail to generalize to paraphrasing and adversarial conditions, where users intentionally modify their typing styles. Adversarial training with behaviorally manipulated data is crucial to achieving more reliable and generalizable keystroke-based detectors in realistic and adversarial environments.

title: Sim-to-Real Transfer of Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments Using an Ackermann-Steered Mobile Robot
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to navigate through environments using natural language instructions, making human-robot interaction intuitive. Traditional VLN models often rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization which pose significant challenges when adapting these models to real-world settings. This work addresses these limitations by performing a simulation-to-real domain shift of a VLN approach that operates in continuous environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views. The proposed system integrates vision-language models that align visual inputs and linguistic instructions within a shared embedding space, facilitating natural language-driven navigation. We employ a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) based architecture trained on an existing dataset in a simulated environment and fine-tune it using real-world data collected from a custom-built Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and a LiDAR sensor. By utilising linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a limited number of episodes, our model successfully adapts to real-world environments, achieving effective navigation while running offline on dedicated hardware. Experimental results, evaluated using Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) metrics, demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of our approach. Keywords: Vision-Language Navigation, Cross-Modal Attention, Natural Language Instructions, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Autonomous Navigation, Ackermann-steering.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a sim-to-real vision-language navigation system that works in continuous environments without navigation graphs or panoramic views, and shows it can be adapted to real robots with limited real-world fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing VLN methods rely on unrealistic assumptions like navigation graphs, 360° panoramas, and perfect localization, which hinder deployment on real robots. The authors aim to bridge this gap by making VLN work in realistic continuous environments and transferring from simulation to a real robot with practical sensors.
AI.method: They use a Cross-Modal Attention-based vision-language model that embeds visual observations and language instructions into a shared space for navigation policy learning. The model is first trained in simulation on an existing VLN dataset, then adapted to the real world via sim-to-real transfer: linear photometric adjustments on images and fine-tuning the model on a small number of real-world episodes collected with an Ackermann-steered robot equipped with camera and LiDAR. The final system runs offline on dedicated onboard hardware.
AI.result: With modest real-world fine-tuning and simple photometric adaptation, the transferred policy can successfully navigate in real environments following natural-language instructions. Evaluations using SPL and nDTW show the approach is robust and adapts effectively from sim to real, though specific numeric gains are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Vision-language navigation can be brought closer to real-world deployment by discarding strong simulation assumptions (graphs, panoramas, perfect localization) and using a CMA-based model plus lightweight sim-to-real adaptation. Even with limited real data and offline computation, the system achieves effective instruction-following navigation on a real Ackermann-steered robot, highlighting the practicality of this transfer strategy.

title: Readout Stability in Prefill-Only Decision Models:Zero-Label Prediction and Inference-Time Compute Allocation
summary: Prefill-only decision models inspired by the Jev model score every candidate in a menu during a single forward pass and never decode, which makes one call one to two orders of magnitude cheaper than a same-scale generative language model. We show that this read-out structure comes with a testable property. When an intervention changes only the candidate menu and leaves the input text fixed, the post-intervention accuracy is already determined by the cached first-pass distribution. The estimator restricts the pass-1 probabilities to the menu, renormalizes, and reads off the argmax; it uses no labels and no second forward pass. Across seven model families, ten datasets and two task types, menu-only interventions are predicted to within 4.2 points, and for one family the prediction is exact. A probability-level variant of the same estimator errs by 21.0 points, so the property lives in the ranking rather than in the probabilities and is not recovered by calibration. Same-scale generative language models do not share the property. On those models the same estimator errs by 1.6 to 15.8 points and degrades as the model grows. The property turns inference-time compute into a decision that can be made before deployment. Uniform extra passes buy calibration but almost no accuracy; at matched cost a confidence cascade outperforms every scheme that re-asks the same model, and curating the menu beats enlarging the model, with a 0.8B model on a curated 5-candidate menu reaching 95.4% on CLINC150 against 80.0% for a 4B model on the full 150-label menu.Code and data are available at https://github.com/rlisml/jev-cascade.

AI.tldr: The paper studies 'prefill-only' decision models that score all candidate outputs in a single forward pass without decoding, showing they have a distinctive, testable property about how menu changes affect accuracy, and uses this to design efficient inference-time strategies that outperform larger generative models at matched compute.
AI.motivation: Standard generative language models are computationally expensive at inference because they decode token-by-token and require multiple passes when re-asked or cascaded. The authors are motivated to find decision architectures that are much cheaper while retaining or even improving accuracy, and to understand what structural properties enable this efficiency. They particularly want to know how model behavior changes when only the label/menu set is modified and whether performance under such interventions can be predicted without extra model calls.
AI.method: They analyze and experiment with 'prefill-only' decision models inspired by the Jev model, which compute a score for every candidate in a menu in one forward pass. They formalize a property: when only the candidate menu is changed and the input text is fixed, the new accuracy can be predicted from the original cached first-pass score distribution by restricting to the new menu, renormalizing, and taking the argmax—without labels or extra passes. They build an estimator implementing this property and empirically test it across seven model families, ten datasets, and two task types, comparing to a probability-based variant and to same-scale generative LMs. They also explore inference-time compute strategies such as uniform extra passes, confidence cascades, and menu curation under fixed compute budgets.
AI.result: Empirically, the ranking-based estimator predicts post-intervention accuracy under menu-only changes within 4.2 percentage points across diverse settings, and for one model family the predictions are exact. A probability-level estimator performs much worse, with 21-point errors, showing that the crucial invariance lies in rank ordering rather than calibrated probabilities. Generative language models do not exhibit this property: the same estimator performs notably worse (1.6–15.8 point errors) and deteriorates as model size increases. In compute-budget experiments, uniform extra passes mainly improve calibration but yield little accuracy gain; confidence cascades outperform any scheme that simply re-queries the same model; and carefully curating a smaller candidate menu yields better accuracy–compute trade-offs than scaling model size, with a 0.8B model plus a curated 5-label menu achieving 95.4% accuracy on CLINC150 versus 80.0% for a 4B model over the full 150 labels.
AI.conclusion: Prefill-only decision models possess a distinctive ranking-based invariance: the effect of changing the candidate menu can be predicted directly from a cached first-pass distribution, without additional inference or supervision. This property does not hold for generative LMs and cannot be recovered by post-hoc probability calibration. Exploiting this structure allows inference-time compute to be treated as a design decision made before deployment: extra passes are mostly useful for calibration, while confidence cascades and menu curation provide superior accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, enabling small models with curated menus to outperform much larger generative models under the same compute budget.

title: Energy-Conditioned Noise Schedule and Whitening for Spectral Diffusion
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, Manuscript submitted for publication in Elsevier Pattern Recognition Letters
summary: This paper introduces an energy-adaptive noise scheduling and whitening strategy for transform-domain diffusion models. Existing spectral diffusion methods account for the non-uniform statistics of transform coefficients through coefficient scaling, normalization, or frequency prioritization, while the forward diffusion noise schedule remains largely independent of the underlying spectral-energy distribution. We investigate whether the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process should also follow the spectral organization of natural images. The proposed formulation combines global spectral whitening with energy-conditioned noise allocation that jointly modulates the injected noise according to the energy of individual transform coefficients and an image-dependent energy path over diffusion time. The resulting forward process preserves Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals and remains compatible with standard DDPM and DDIM procedures without modifying the diffusion architecture. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the contribution of the proposed energy-conditioned noise schedule and spectral whitening, reducing Fréchet Inception Distance from 142.48 for a compact DCTdiff U-Net variant to 100.45.

AI.tldr: Energy-adaptive, spectrally-aware forward noise schedule for transform-domain diffusion that whitens coefficients and allocates noise by energy, improving CIFAR-10 FID without changing the backbone architecture.
AI.motivation: In transform-domain diffusion (e.g., DCT-based), natural images have non-uniform spectral energy: low frequencies tend to have higher energy than high frequencies. Existing approaches try to correct for this mainly with static tricks such as coefficient scaling, normalization, or prioritizing certain frequencies, but they typically keep the temporal noise schedule independent of the spectral-energy structure. This may be suboptimal because the forward diffusion process ignores how energy is distributed over frequencies and over time, potentially wasting model capacity and harming generative quality.
AI.method: They work in a transform domain and propose two coupled mechanisms for the forward diffusion process: (1) global spectral whitening of the transform coefficients to reduce non-uniformity across frequencies, and (2) an energy-conditioned noise allocation strategy. The injected noise at each diffusion step is modulated based on both the energy of each individual transform coefficient and an image-dependent energy trajectory over diffusion time. The formulation is constructed so that the perturbed variables still follow Gaussian transitions with closed-form marginals, keeping the same mathematical structure as standard DDPM/DDIM. Thus, it can be plugged into existing diffusion architectures (here, a compact DCTdiff U-Net) without architectural changes, only altering the way forward noise is scheduled across coefficients and timesteps.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, combining the proposed spectral whitening with the energy-conditioned noise schedule substantially improves generative quality under a compact DCT-based diffusion model. Specifically, the Fréchet Inception Distance decreases from 142.48 with the baseline compact DCTdiff U-Net to 100.45 with the new noise scheduling and whitening strategy, indicating significantly better sample quality.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the temporal evolution of the forward diffusion process with the spectral-energy structure of natural images—via global whitening and per-coefficient, energy-conditioned noise allocation—can significantly improve transform-domain diffusion models. The method retains the desirable Gaussian, closed-form nature of the forward process and is fully compatible with standard DDPM/DDIM sampling, providing a practical, architecture-agnostic way to exploit spectral statistics for better image generation performance.

title: Does Steering Break Your Model? A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Suite for LLM Steering Methods
summary: Activation steering provides a lightweight and flexible way to control large language model (LLM) behavior. However, effective steering requires more than inducing the intended behavior: it should also limit unintended changes and remain robust across inputs and training data. Existing evaluations cover these dimensions only in fragments. As a result, the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects have not been systematically characterized. We introduce SteerScope, a two-axis, multi-dimensional evaluation suite that jointly characterizes steering outcomes and method properties through 15 metrics. We score target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability, and further assess generalization and data dependence through steering-specific metrics for sample efficiency and sample sensitivity. Rather than comparing methods at a single operating point, we characterize the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects. Under matched models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, we benchmark 23 methods spanning 4 families, including prompting, LoRA, and SFT as baseline methods, and release the suite as an extensible codebase. We find that current activation steering methods do not yet surpass the Prompt Steering baseline in their overall balance between steering efficacy and side effects: across both model scales, no evaluated activation steering method achieves higher efficacy without incurring greater composite side effects. We further uncover a consistent coupling between steering efficacy and side effects. Under OOD prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to become more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and fluency. Methods also exhibit sharply different sample-efficiency profiles.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SteerScope, a comprehensive evaluation suite for analyzing the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects of activation steering and related steering methods in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of activation steering and LLM control methods only partially cover critical dimensions like unintended side effects, robustness, and generalization. This fragmented view prevents a systematic understanding of trade-offs between achieving the target behavior and avoiding negative side effects.
AI.method: The authors design SteerScope, a two-axis, multi-dimensional evaluation framework with 15 metrics. These metrics measure target efficacy and side effects across language quality, task capabilities, safety, and reliability, plus steering-specific properties such as sample efficiency and sample sensitivity. They benchmark 23 steering methods from 4 families (including prompting, LoRA, and SFT, plus activation steering methods) under matched models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, and implement SteerScope as an extensible codebase.
AI.result: Using SteerScope, the authors find that current activation steering methods do not outperform a Prompt Steering baseline in jointly optimizing steering efficacy and side effects. Across model scales, no activation steering method achieves higher efficacy without also incurring higher composite side effects. They also observe a strong coupling between efficacy and side effects, with side effects worsening particularly on out-of-distribution prompts, where instruction relevance and fluency degrade. Additionally, methods differ significantly in their sample-efficiency characteristics.
AI.conclusion: SteerScope reveals that activation steering methods are not yet superior to prompt-based steering in terms of the overall balance between control efficacy and side effects, and that improving one often worsens the other. The suite provides a standardized way to characterize these trade-offs, highlight robustness issues (especially OOD), and compare methods’ data efficiency, thereby guiding the development of more reliable and efficient steering techniques.

title: Cascadia: Resident 975B MoE Inference on Eleven AI PCs
summary: Mixture-of-experts models make nearly trillion-parameter capacity accessible with sparse per-token computation, provided that the serving system can distribute the weights and coordinate their execution. We present Cascadia's resident execution of Inkling, a 975B-total/41B-active-parameter model, on eleven Intel Core Ultra X7 358H AI PCs, each with 64 GB of memory, Arc B390 integrated graphics and gigabit Ethernet. We contribute a custom resident MoE engine that preserves Inkling's routing rules, constructs compressed graphs for OpenVINO's fused iGPU primitives, and coordinates FP16 expert computation with FP32 output restoration. The engine fits six consecutive decoder layers per machine and represents dense feed-forward blocks as all-active expert slices, reducing measured dense-layer call time from approximately 8.1 to 4.5 ms. A streaming pipeline coordinates concurrent generation, while captured-state draft evaluation measures agreement with the deployed numerical path. Paired measurements at fifteen concurrency levels from 1 to 176 streams reach 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s at 88 streams, with 46.87 tokens/s over the complete serving phases. At fifteen streams, median first-token latency is 6.05 s. Raising the context budget from the 1,024-position default, real prompts of 1k to 64k tokens recover the embedded code in all 19 measured answers, with first-token time growing as $aN+bN^2$ and decode latency growing approximately linearly, both bounded by a single-threaded CPU attention loop rather than by memory, which holds 512k positions per stream. Evaluation on captured fleet states separates the effects of vocabulary selection and weight quantization on draft agreement. Together, these contributions establish an execution and evaluation approach for large sparse models on distributed client systems with shared CPU-GPU memory.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates how to run a nearly trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model efficiently across multiple consumer-grade AI PCs using a custom execution engine and OpenVINO, achieving practical throughput and latency while supporting long contexts.
AI.motivation: Mixture-of-experts models enable extremely large model capacities with sparse activation, but serving them efficiently requires complex weight distribution, routing, and coordination across hardware. Existing solutions focus on datacenter GPUs; this work addresses how to make such large sparse models practical on distributed client systems (AI PCs) with integrated GPUs and shared CPU-GPU memory, while maintaining numerical behavior and supporting long contexts.
AI.method: They implement a custom resident MoE execution engine called Cascadia for the Inkling model (975B total / 41B active parameters) across 11 Intel Core Ultra X7 358H machines. The engine: (1) preserves the model’s original routing rules; (2) builds compressed computation graphs to leverage OpenVINO’s fused iGPU primitives; (3) coordinates FP16 expert computation with FP32 output restoration; (4) fits six decoder layers per machine, mapping dense feed-forward blocks to all-active expert slices to reduce call time; and (5) uses a streaming pipeline for concurrent generation and a captured-state draft evaluation mechanism to compare different numerical paths and configurations (e.g., quantization, vocabulary choices). They also profile performance across different concurrency levels and context lengths, with attention computed in a single-threaded CPU loop.
AI.result: On 11 Intel AI PCs, the system achieves up to 60.29 aggregate decode tokens/s at 88 parallel streams and 46.87 tokens/s when including all serving phases. At 15 streams, median first-token latency is 6.05 seconds. The modified dense-layer representation halves measured dense-layer call time from about 8.1 ms to 4.5 ms. For long contexts, real prompts ranging from 1k to 64k tokens successfully recover embedded code in all 19 tested cases, with first-token latency scaling approximately as aN + bN^2 and decode latency scaling roughly linearly with context length, constrained by the CPU attention loop rather than memory (which supports up to 512k positions per stream). Draft evaluations on captured fleet states enable isolating the impact of vocabulary changes and weight quantization on agreement with the reference numerical path.
AI.conclusion: Large sparse MoE language models near the trillion-parameter scale can be effectively served on distributed client AI PCs with integrated GPUs by using a specialized resident execution engine that exploits shared CPU-GPU memory, fused primitives, and careful routing-preserving graph construction. Their approach attains practical throughput, acceptable latency, and robust long-context handling, while providing tools to evaluate numerical changes such as quantization and vocabulary selection. This establishes a viable execution and evaluation framework for deploying advanced MoE models beyond datacenter environments.

title: SanSi: A Looped Typed Decision Model for System 1.5 Thinking
comment: 43 pages, 15 figures, 42 tables. Project page: https://minnesotanlp.github.io/Sansi/
summary: Typed decision models answer a declared question without generating text: a decision head returns a probability for each of the declared options in a single forward pass. A single pass is fast, intuitive System 1 thinking. We study what lies between one pass and generated reasoning: looping, in which the same layers are recursively applied several times before one typed readout. Each loop lets the model revise its hidden state before it commits to an answer, without generating a token; we call this System 1.5 thinking. We propose SanSi, which turns a pre-trained looped language model into a typed decision model. The option probabilities are read after every loop, and every loop is trained with a proper scoring rule, so that one model serves every budget from one loop to eight in a single run. On 10,027 test decisions from 59 sources, SanSi reaches 72.0% accuracy: 13.5 points above a non-looped model of the same shape trained with the same recipe, 5.3 points above a newer non-looped model of its size, and 1.8 points below one with three times the parameters. On two depth-controlled tasks, loops extend the solvable depth beyond the depths seen in training, where the larger single-pass model fails. Used as the judge for policy optimization with reinforcement learning, without gold answers, SanSi raises the generator's F1 by 7.7 points.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SanSi, a looping-based typed decision model that improves accuracy and depth-generalization over single-pass language models while supporting variable compute budgets.
AI.motivation: Conventional typed decision models answer in a single forward pass, corresponding to fast but shallow “System 1” reasoning. Generated chain-of-thought is more powerful but slow, token-inefficient, and sometimes unreliable. The authors want an intermediate regime—System 1.5—that allows models to refine internal representations through extra computation without emitting text, improving accuracy and depth-generalization while remaining fast and controllable in terms of compute.
AI.method: They take a pre-trained looped language model and convert it into a typed decision model called SanSi. The same transformer layers are applied recursively for several loops before a single typed readout. After every loop, an option-probability head reads out decisions, and each loop is trained with a proper scoring rule so that all depths (1–8 loops) share parameters and are usable at inference. This enables a single model to support variable compute budgets and to revise its hidden state multiple times before committing to a decision.
AI.result: On 10,027 test decisions from 59 datasets, SanSi achieves 72.0% accuracy, outperforming a non-looped baseline of the same architecture by 13.5 percentage points and a newer non-looped model of the same size by 5.3 points, while coming within 1.8 points of a model three times larger. On depth-controlled reasoning tasks, adding loops lets the model solve instances requiring greater reasoning depth than seen in training, whereas a larger single-pass model fails. When used as an automatic judge in RL-based policy optimization (without access to gold labels), SanSi improves the generator model’s F1 score by 7.7 points.
AI.conclusion: Looping internal computation (System 1.5) in typed decision models significantly boosts accuracy and extrapolative depth compared to single-pass decision heads, offering a strong speed–performance trade-off without requiring model scaling or textual chain-of-thought. SanSi demonstrates that a single looped model, trained with per-loop proper scoring, can effectively serve multiple compute budgets and even function as a high-quality judge for reinforcement learning, closing much of the gap to substantially larger non-looped models.

title: SPECTRUM: Proximal Spectral Modulation for Looped Self-Distillation
summary: A model that learns from its own outputs inherits more than their correctness: it inherits which solutions it produces. We formulate Looped Self-Distillation, a self-evolution framework for code generation in which a model repeatedly generates and learns from its own raw outputs, under a fixed information budget, without ongoing external assessment or test-based selection of the generated samples. We identify a consequential separation: correctness can improve while the breadth of correct implementations contracts. We introduce SPECTRUM, which re-estimates loss-sensitive key/value geometry from a fixed reference anchor at each round and converts it into full-rank proximal spectral modulation. All generated completions train a single student, whose subsequent inference requires no intervention. After five rounds of experiments on MBPP, SPECTRUM retains 89.9% of the initial model's 64-sample correct AST richness, compared with 66.4% for Vanilla self-distillation and 65.5% for a subspace-projection control. The advantage persists at matched correct-sample counts. Without further training or recalibration, the resulting student also achieves higher matched-correct richness than Vanilla SD on HumanEval+ and APPS Intro, demonstrating transfer of the diversity benefit.
