These findings establish correct-solution retention as a complementary objective of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and show that generation-time intervention can improve the solution repertoire retained by subsequent students.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how models that train on their own code outputs risk losing diversity of correct solutions, and proposes SPECTRUM, a spectral modulation method that maintains solution diversity during looped self-distillation.
AI.motivation: In recursive self-improvement and self-distillation for code generation, models typically learn from their own outputs. While this can increase the overall correctness of generated programs, it may inadvertently narrow the range of distinct correct implementations the model can produce, which is problematic for robustness, generalization, and creativity. The authors want to formally study this tradeoff and design a method that preserves the breadth of correct solutions during self-training without relying on external test-based selection or human labeling.
AI.method: They define Looped Self-Distillation: repeatedly generating raw code completions from a model and then training a new student model on these completions under a fixed information budget, with no ongoing external evaluation of samples. They introduce SPECTRUM, which at each self-distillation round re-estimates a loss-sensitive key/value geometry from a fixed reference anchor and transforms it into a full-rank proximal spectral modulation of the model. All generated completions (not just filtered correct ones) are used to train a single student model, whose inference requires no special intervention afterward. They compare SPECTRUM against vanilla self-distillation and a subspace-projection control, controlling for budget and sample counts.
AI.result: On the MBPP benchmark after five self-distillation rounds, SPECTRUM retains 89.9% of the original model's correct AST diversity when using 64 samples, whereas vanilla self-distillation retains only 66.4% and the subspace-projection control 65.5%. This diversity advantage holds even when matching the number of correct samples. Additionally, without any extra training or calibration, the SPECTRUM-trained student transfers this higher diversity to other code benchmarks (HumanEval+ and APPS Intro), outperforming vanilla self-distillation on matched-correct-sample diversity there as well.
AI.conclusion: The paper shows that in recursive self-improvement for code generation, it is important not only to maximize correctness but also to retain a diverse repertoire of correct solutions. Standard self-distillation can erode this diversity, but SPECTRUM, a spectral modulation approach applied during generation, substantially mitigates that loss. Generation-time intervention can thus shape what kinds of correct solutions are preserved in later students, and correct-solution retention should be treated as an explicit, complementary objective in self-evolving code models.

title: From Evidence to Action: How Tool-Using Agents Fail
summary: Tool-using agents make consequential changes to external state, yet correct outcomes do not guarantee that their actions were supported by evidence established beforehand. We study where this evidence-to-action chain breaks as agents move from deciding whether to act to executing single actions and dependent workflows. Across ten model-harness configurations, strong static action assessment can coexist with much weaker interactive execution. Failures often begin before execution: agents stop with incomplete investigation or act before required evidence is established. Once required evidence is obtained, single-action execution is usually reliable, while multi-action workflows additionally expose unresolved prerequisites and incomplete execution. For this analysis, we introduce SafeActBench, comprising 656 cases across six operational domains and five protocols that progress from static action judgment and investigated non-action to single- and multi-action workflows. A provenance-bound Evidence Ledger and deterministic trajectory evaluator track what information was established, when actions occurred, and whether downstream dependencies were satisfied. These results show that failures arise not only from missing information, but also from how agents use established evidence when deciding and executing actions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SafeActBench to evaluate how well AI agents connect evidence gathering to safe and correct tool-using actions, revealing that strong static judgment often breaks down during interactive, multi-step execution.
AI.motivation: AI tool-using agents can produce correct final outcomes while still acting unsafely or without adequate prior evidence. Existing evaluations mostly test static decision quality or final results, not the full chain from evidence gathering to action execution. The authors want to understand where this evidence-to-action pipeline fails and to provide a benchmark for systematically probing those failure modes across realistic operational domains.
AI.method: The authors build SafeActBench, a benchmark of 656 scenarios in six operational domains, each framed under five protocols that range from static action judgment to interactive investigation, single-tool actions, and multi-step workflows. They add an Evidence Ledger to log what information the agent has established and when, and a deterministic trajectory evaluator that checks whether actions are taken only after required evidence is available and whether dependencies across steps are satisfied. They run ten different model-harness configurations to compare static assessment capabilities with interactive execution performance and analyze failure patterns.
AI.result: They find a significant gap between models’ strong static action assessment (deciding in principle what should be done) and their weaker performance during interactive execution. Many failures occur before tools are actually run: agents either terminate prematurely with incomplete investigation or proceed to act without having gathered the required evidence. Once the necessary evidence is available, single actions tend to be executed reliably. In contrast, multi-step workflows reveal additional errors, such as missing prerequisite steps and partially completed plans.
AI.conclusion: SafeActBench shows that safe, evidence-grounded tool use cannot be assessed only by static questions or final outcomes. Failures commonly stem from how agents collect and apply evidence over time—especially during investigation and in coordinating multi-step workflows. The benchmark and its Evidence Ledger provide a structured way to diagnose these temporal and dependency-related weaknesses, suggesting that improving agent design and training must focus on evidence-aware decision processes and workflow management, not just on better static judgment.

title: Can Semantic Geometry Teach an AI Judgement?
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Four bounded studies of semantic measurements for pre-action judgment; consequence-graph hypothesis remains untested
summary:
How can an AI agent determine what rules to follow? One rule permits an action. Another imposes a condition, exception, or conflicting obligation. Deterministic systems can resolve those relationships when they have been specified. When they remain implicit in language, an agent can follow one rule while missing another that should stop it. Refusing every unresolved action avoids that risk, but also blocks permissible actions.
  We wanted the agent to make the distinction and still act. Our initial hypothesis was that geometric measurements could supply a basis for judgment. We represented actions and policies as vectors, then tested whether their geometry could identify governing policies and interpret the action's relation to them.
  Across four studies, the tested approaches did not establish reliable pre-action judgment. In the final synthetic study, a lexical router recovered every governing and blocking policy while reducing median policy checks by 97.7%. The composed pipeline nevertheless escalated all 2,304 test actions, including those it should have allowed. Supplying every policy to the same downstream mechanism changed no decision. Finding the policies had not solved the problem of interpreting them.
  This result led us to revise our hypothesis: judgment in AI agents requires developing a consequence graph. Such a graph would connect the actor and authority to policy conditions, exceptions, and the changes an action would produce. Follow-on studies will ask whether making those relationships explicit helps the agent distinguish when to act, stop, or seek review.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how AI agents can decide which rules or policies govern a proposed action, finds that geometric and lexical routing methods fail to deliver reliable pre-action judgment, and argues that agents instead need explicit consequence graphs linking actions, authorities, and policy conditions.
AI.motivation: AI agents operating under multiple overlapping rules or policies risk either violating constraints (by missing applicable rules) or becoming overly conservative (by refusing any action with unresolved policy conflicts). Existing deterministic approaches work only when rule relationships are explicitly encoded, while many real-world policies are stated in natural language and contain implicit conditions, exceptions, and conflicts. The authors aim to enable agents to distinguish when they may act versus when they must stop or escalate, without defaulting to blanket refusal.
AI.method: The authors hypothesized that geometric representations could help an AI agent judge which policies govern a proposed action. They embedded actions and policies as vectors and explored whether geometric relationships (e.g., similarity, proximity, or other spatial relations) could identify the governing and blocking policies and characterize an action's relation to them. Across four studies, including a final synthetic experiment, they compared geometric approaches with a lexical routing method that attempted to efficiently retrieve relevant policies before a decision step.
AI.result: The geometric approaches failed to support reliable pre-action judgment: they could not consistently identify governing and blocking policies or correctly interpret how an action related to them. In a final synthetic study, a lexical router successfully retrieved every governing and blocking policy and reduced median policy checks by 97.7%. However, when these retrieved policies were passed to the downstream decision mechanism, the system escalated all 2,304 test actions, including ones that should have been allowed. Even when all policies were provided to the same mechanism, the decisions did not change. Thus, better policy retrieval did not translate into better rule interpretation or nuanced action decisions.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that identifying relevant policies is insufficient for enabling AI agents to make sound pre-action judgments. Their findings falsify the initial hypothesis that geometric policy representations would be enough and suggest that the core difficulty lies in interpreting policy interactions and consequences. They propose a revised hypothesis: agents require an explicit consequence graph that connects actors and authorities to policy conditions, exceptions, and the concrete state changes an action would cause. Future work will investigate whether constructing such graphs helps agents determine when to proceed, halt, or seek human review under complex, overlapping rule sets.

title: No Transformer Beats Six Covariates: Long-Horizon Prediction of Depressive Symptoms from Childhood Essays
summary: Natural language processing (NLP) models can detect depression-related language in text written near the time symptoms are measured, but whether pretrained transformers can predict depressive symptoms from text written twelve years earlier is largely untested. In the National Child Development Study, a British birth cohort, we predict probable depressive symptoms at age 23 from essays the same people wrote at age 11. Our baseline, a logistic regression on six childhood covariates, outperforms every text model that sees only the essay: seven fine-tuned transformers, a bag-of-words model, frozen embeddings and four zero-shot large language models. Its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) is 0.737 against 0.670 for the best transformer on the primary seed, and no added text score detectably raises the baseline's AUC-ROC. None of the five domain-pretrained transformers detectably beats its general-domain control after Bonferroni correction. For long-horizon prediction, the baseline remains the model to beat.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether modern NLP models can predict depressive symptoms in adulthood from childhood essays written 12 years earlier, finding that simple demographic/childhood covariates outperform all tested text-based models.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows NLP can detect depression from text written close in time to symptom measurement, but it is unclear whether such models can forecast long-term mental health outcomes many years in advance using childhood language, which matters for early identification and intervention.
AI.method: Using data from the National Child Development Study, the authors predict probable depressive symptoms at age 23 from essays written at age 11. They compare a baseline logistic regression model using six childhood covariates against multiple text-only models: seven fine-tuned transformer models, a bag-of-words model, models using frozen embeddings, and four zero-shot large language models. They evaluate performance using AUC-ROC, conduct significance testing, and apply Bonferroni correction when comparing domain-pretrained transformers to general-domain controls.
AI.result: The logistic regression baseline using six childhood covariates achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.737, outperforming all text-only models; the best transformer reaches only 0.670 on the primary seed. Adding essay-based text scores to the baseline does not significantly improve its AUC-ROC. None of the five domain-pretrained transformers significantly outperforms its general-domain counterpart after Bonferroni correction.
AI.conclusion: For predicting depressive symptoms 12 years into the future, simple models based on a small set of childhood covariates remain superior to a wide range of modern NLP text models. Long-horizon prediction of depression from childhood essays appears difficult for current pretrained transformers, and specialized domain pretraining does not yield clear gains over general-domain models in this setting.

title: Internalizing Agent Experience into Diffusion Model Weights via On-Policy Context Distillation
summary: Wrapping an image generation model in an agentic harness can effectively boost Text-to-Image task performance: the harness can leverage memory, skills, workflow orchestration, result verification, and iterative refinement to continually construct and revise prompts, thereby eliciting better images. These gains, however, remain external to the diffusion model and are realized only while the full harness runs. We propose Diffusion On-Policy Context Distillation (D-OPCD), which treats the agent-improved prompt as privileged context and distills the knowledge encoded in the agent harness into the weights of the diffusion model, so that the model retains part of the harness's benefit when conditioned on the original query alone. Using a Text-to-Image agent equipped with our proposed Auto Skill Evolver (ASE), we show that D-OPCD can internalize harness capabilities into the generator's weights, raising the average direct-generation score from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks. With this knowledge absorbed into the weights, the harness can shed its saturated skills and resume evolving: a second ASE round on the updated generator improves on a skill-free harness by additional 1.83 points, pointing toward text-to-image systems in which harness and model keep improving each other through continual co-evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces D-OPCD, a method to distill the capabilities of an agentic harness for text-to-image generation directly into a diffusion model’s weights, improving baseline generation quality without needing the full harness at inference time.
AI.motivation: Agentic harnesses around diffusion models (with memory, skills, workflows, and refinement loops) significantly improve text-to-image results but are expensive and must run at inference time; their benefits are not internalized in the model. The authors want a way to capture and retain these improvements directly in the diffusion model so that it performs better even with only the raw user prompt.
AI.method: They propose Diffusion On-Policy Context Distillation (D-OPCD), which treats the agent-refined prompts as privileged context and distills them into the diffusion model’s parameters. Using an agentic text-to-image system equipped with a new Auto Skill Evolver (ASE), they generate improved prompts and images, then train the diffusion model such that, when conditioned only on the original query, it reproduces the quality obtained with the improved prompts. ASE is used to automatically discover and refine the agent’s skills, and D-OPCD periodically retrains the generator on these agent-produced trajectories.
AI.result: D-OPCD enables the diffusion model to internalize some of the harness’s abilities, raising average direct-generation scores from 60.52 to 65.09 across four benchmarks when using only the original prompts. After updating the generator with D-OPCD, running ASE again on top of the improved model yields a further 1.83-point gain over a harness that starts from a non-distilled, skill-free model, showing that the harness and model can iteratively boost each other.
AI.conclusion: Distilling the agentic harness’s prompt-engineering and workflow knowledge into the diffusion model via D-OPCD leads to lasting improvements in text-to-image generation quality, even without running the full harness at inference time. Moreover, by alternating between harness skill evolution (ASE) and model distillation, the system can achieve continual co-evolution where both the generator and the harness progressively improve.

title: Reading, Not Manipulating: Leveraging Router Logits for Multimodal Safety in MoE Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) face compositional safety risks where harmful intent emerges from the interaction between visual and textual inputs. As mixture-of-experts (MoE) VLMs become increasingly common, recent work has explored various safety interventions, including prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and routing-based expert steering. However, these methods show inconsistent improvements across models and evaluation distributions, and the intervention into model behavior or internal states introduce safety-utility tradeoffs by over-refusal. Rather than manipulating internal states to steer model behavior, we instead ask whether routing states can serve as diagnostic signals for multimodal safety. We find that router logits indeed provide highly predictive signals of whether a multimodal input is safe or not. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a lightweight router-logit safety detector that reads out routing signals during prompt prefill and identifies unsafe requests before generation, without modifying model parameters or expert routing. Across Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL, the proposed detector substantially reduces safety errors on the HoliSafe benchmark and resoundingly generalizes to out-of-distribution safety benchmarks featuring different safety patterns, including MISHard and MM-SafetyBench. The success of the proposed router-logit detector also suggests a broader perspective on model internals: rather than focusing only on manipulating internal components to steer behavior, simply reading naturally emerging signals and linking them to an external safety mechanism can provide a simple, effective, and non-intrusive complement to existing safety interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using router logits in mixture-of-experts vision-language models as a non-intrusive safety detector that predicts whether a multimodal input is safe, achieving strong and robust safety performance without modifying the model or its routing.
AI.motivation: Existing safety interventions for MoE vision-language models—such as prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and routing-based expert steering—yield inconsistent improvements and can cause over-refusal, harming model utility. The authors want a safety method that is effective, robust across benchmarks, and does not require manipulating internal states or retraining the model.
AI.method: The authors analyze the routing logits (router outputs that determine which experts are used) in MoE vision-language models to see if they correlate with input safety. Finding strong predictive signals, they build a lightweight safety detector that reads router logits during the prompt prefill phase, before generation starts. This detector classifies multimodal inputs as safe or unsafe using these routing features, without changing model parameters or routing behavior. They evaluate it on multiple models (Qwen3-VL, Kimi-VL) and safety benchmarks (HoliSafe, MISHard, MM-SafetyBench).
AI.result: Router logits are shown to be highly predictive of whether an input is safe. The proposed router-logit safety detector significantly reduces safety errors on HoliSafe for both Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL and generalizes well to out-of-distribution safety benchmarks like MISHard and MM-SafetyBench, which involve different safety patterns. This demonstrates that internal routing states can be effectively used as diagnostic signals for safety without behavioral steering.
AI.conclusion: Router states in MoE VLMs naturally encode strong signals about input safety. Instead of steering or modifying internal components, simply reading these routing signals and connecting them to an external safety detector can yield a simple, effective, and non-intrusive safety mechanism. This approach complements existing safety interventions and suggests a broader perspective: model internals can be exploited as diagnostic signals, not only as control levers.

title: MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents
summary: Developers increasingly run a fleet of coding agents side by side on one workstation. The tools they reach for, terminal multiplexers like tmux and a new generation of agent managers, were built to arrange windows, not to govern memory. When ten agents each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, no standard tool can say how much memory belongs to which agent, confirm that a terminated agent's descendants are gone, notice a child that has escaped its agent, or keep the machine off the swap cliff when an OOM kill would silently discard uncommitted work. We treat these as runtime-verification problems: an agent-hosting substrate should continuously emit observable signals an operator or auditor can check while agents run. We present MemMux, a local runtime that turns resource governance into checkable signals (per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead), with a claims-disciplined benchmark against tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads. Under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, MemMux keeps the fleet under budget (7.5 GiB) with zero swap by admitting a subset and reclaiming under pressure, while the ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at its RAM ceiling (2x over budget), and spill about 2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree where the raw baseline strands half of it, and it alone surfaces escaped children (10 of 10 detected). We report the cost: the 1 Hz attribution scan runs near 0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten, above our 2% target. Running the harness on real Claude Code sessions shows 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees. We release the engine, benchmark, and a one-command reproducer.

AI.tldr: MemMux is a local runtime that governs memory for multiple concurrent coding agents by turning resource usage into verifiable signals, enabling safe admission, attribution, and reclamation of processes under a fixed memory budget.
AI.motivation: Existing tools like tmux and current agent managers focus on arranging and orchestrating agents and windows, not on robust memory governance. When many agents run simultaneously, they each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, leading to complex process trees where memory usage is hard to attribute to specific agents. Current tools cannot reliably measure per-agent memory, ensure full cleanup after termination, detect processes that escape their agent context, or prevent the system from hitting swap and silently losing work due to OOM kills. The authors aim to treat these operational concerns as runtime-verification problems and provide a substrate that makes memory governance observable and auditable in real time.
AI.method: The authors design and implement MemMux, a local runtime for hosting coding agents that instruments and governs process trees. MemMux continuously emits checkable signals about each agent’s resource usage, including per-agent memory attribution, completeness of reclamation after termination, detection of escaped child processes, adherence to a bounded memory footprint under overcommit conditions, and its own monitoring overhead. They build a claims-disciplined benchmark that compares MemMux to tmux, a specialized agent multiplexer, and a raw-process baseline while running identical agent workloads. The system uses a periodic attribution scan (1 Hz) to measure memory and enforce a global budget, admitting only a subset of agents and reclaiming resources under pressure.
AI.result: On a Linux host with a strict memory budget of 7.5 GiB, MemMux successfully keeps the total fleet within budget with zero swap usage by selectively admitting agents and reclaiming memory under pressure. In contrast, ungoverned tools (tmux, a purpose-built agent multiplexer, and raw processes) run all agents simultaneously, drive memory to 2x the budget, and cause about 2 GiB to spill into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of the processes in a terminated agent’s subtree, whereas the raw-process baseline leaves about half of these processes running. MemMux is also the only system that reliably surfaces escaped child processes, detecting all 10 out of 10 injected escapes. The attribution scan costs approximately 0.6% CPU at one agent and 2.7% at ten agents, slightly exceeding the 2% overhead target at higher concurrency. Experiments on real Claude Code sessions show that full attribution and low overhead generalize to real-world agent trees.
AI.conclusion: MemMux demonstrates that memory governance for fleets of coding agents can be treated as a runtime-verification problem, with the runtime emitting auditable signals about per-agent memory, reclamation, and escaped processes. Compared to existing tools, MemMux enforces a strict memory budget without swapping, fully cleans up terminated agents, and exposes otherwise hidden escaped children, albeit at a modest CPU overhead that slightly exceeds the authors’ target at higher agent counts. The system and its benchmarking harness are released, along with a one-command reproducer, suggesting practical applicability and enabling independent verification of the claims.

title: APEX: Speculate smarter, not deeper
summary: Speculative decoding reduces large language model inference latency by drafting multiple tokens before target-model verification, but its effectiveness depends on both the proposal mechanism and draft depth. Fixed configurations cannot respond to changes in predictability, repetition, and acceptance during generation, so deeper drafting can increase wasted computation without proportional speedup. We introduce APEX, a learned controller that balances decoding speed and draft-token waste through request-level expert selection and block-level depth adaptation. APEX-Router selects among EAGLE-3, n-gram, and draft-model speculation for each request, while APEX-Depth adjusts draft length at each verification block using causal decoding signals and recent verifier feedback. APEX models accepted draft length as censored survival feedback, learning position-wise rejection hazards, block execution costs, and an action utility that balances throughput, accepted progress, and wasted tokens. This allows the controller to adapt speculation while retaining the target model's verification procedure. We integrate APEX into vLLM and evaluate it with Qwen3-8B across six workloads, achieving up to 5.24X speedup over autoregressive decoding. Across the aggregate evaluation, APEX-S achieves 4.27X speedup, while APEX-B achieves 3.27X speedup with a 41.0% relative reduction in wasted-token percentage compared with fixed n-gram speculation at k=16, providing distinct operating points for balancing acceleration and draft-token utilization.

AI.tldr: APEX is a learned controller that dynamically chooses speculative decoding strategies and draft depths to speed up LLM inference while reducing wasted draft tokens, achieving over 4x speedups versus standard decoding.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding can accelerate LLM inference by drafting multiple tokens, but fixed draft mechanisms and depths fail to adapt to changing token predictability and acceptance rates, leading to wasted computation and suboptimal speedup. There is a need for an adaptive system that chooses both the speculation method and draft length based on runtime signals to better balance latency and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors design APEX, a two-level controller for speculative decoding: (1) APEX-Router performs request-level expert selection among EAGLE-3, n-gram, and draft-model speculation; (2) APEX-Depth performs block-level draft-depth adaptation during generation using causal decoding signals and recent verifier feedback. They formulate accepted draft length as censored survival feedback, learning position-wise rejection hazards, block execution costs, and a utility function that trades off throughput, accepted token progress, and wasted draft tokens. The controller is integrated into the vLLM framework with Qwen3-8B and tested on multiple workloads.
AI.result: Integrated with vLLM and Qwen3-8B, APEX achieves up to 5.24x speedup over standard autoregressive decoding on six workloads. On aggregate, the APEX-S variant attains 4.27x speedup, and the APEX-B variant attains 3.27x speedup while reducing wasted-token percentage by 41.0% relative to fixed n-gram speculation with k=16. These results demonstrate that adaptive expert selection and depth control improve both speed and draft-token utilization compared to fixed speculative decoding baselines.
AI.conclusion: A learned, adaptive controller for speculative decoding can significantly accelerate LLM inference while reducing wasted draft computation. By modeling accepted draft lengths via survival analysis and jointly optimizing for speed and utilization, APEX flexibly adjusts both the speculation strategy and draft depth without modifying the target model’s verification procedure, offering practical operating points that balance latency and efficiency across diverse workloads.

title: Verifying Coordination in Parallel Coding Agents: NP-Bench and a Scheduling Planner
summary: A team of coding agents can look fine agent by agent yet fail as a team: each passes its own tests while the merged result is broken, and single-agent evaluation never catches it. As teams run several LLM coding agents in parallel on one codebase, the agents collide: two rewrite the same function, one codes against a contract a teammate just changed, and integration fails after the work is done. Most coordination tools react (watch for a conflict, then warn), but at agent speed the warning arrives after the wasted edit. We recast the problem as scheduling: take each work item's declared scope, partition the work into disjoint scopes, and order merges along the producer->consumer graph, all up front. We build this planner into Nerveplane and evaluate it with NP-Bench, an environment-grounded three-arm benchmark (no coordination; reactive detection; proactive planning) that verifies integration off a real git merge, both in a deterministic simulation and with live agents. The planner lifts clean-integration from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios and cuts merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with a gap that grows in the number of agents. On a live breaking contract change it rescues an outcome both baselines miss on every seed: the clean-integration rate rises from 0 (no coordination and reactive detection) to 1.0 on a frontier model and 0.6 on a small one, while agents respect assigned scopes (0/5 leakage). A cross-session memory drops the repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00 on strong and weak models alike. We also report a negative result: routing facts to agents does not rescue long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales; its value is cost and capacity, not attention. Across two capability tiers and two vendors, the benefit did not shrink as models got stronger, because it comes from how work is allocated, not model reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a proactive scheduling-based coordination system for multi-agent LLM coding, showing it dramatically improves integration success and reduces conflicts compared to no or reactive coordination, with benefits persisting across model sizes and vendors.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM coding teams often fail at integration even when each agent’s code passes its own tests, because agents independently edit overlapping code, change contracts others depend on, and only discover conflicts after work is done. Existing coordination tools are mostly reactive, warning after conflicts occur, which is too late at agent speeds and leads to wasted computation and brittle systems. The authors aim to provide a principled way to coordinate agents so that parallelism is preserved while integration remains reliable and predictable.
AI.method: They reframe coordination as a scheduling and planning problem: given work items annotated with their codebase scopes and dependencies, partition them into disjoint scopes and impose an execution and merge order that respects a producer–consumer graph. This planner is implemented in a system called Nerveplane. They design NP-Bench, a three-arm benchmark with (1) no coordination, (2) reactive conflict detection, and (3) proactive planning, and evaluate on realistic coding workflows using real git merges. Experiments are run both in a deterministic simulation and with live LLM coding agents across different model strengths and vendors. They also test a cross-session memory for avoiding repeated mistakes and study whether routing relevant facts to specific agents can mitigate long-context issues.
AI.result: The proactive planner raises the number of scenarios with clean integration from 1/9 under baselines to 9/9, and reduces merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with gains increasing as more agents are added. In a difficult setting involving a live breaking contract change, both baselines fail on every random seed, while the planner enables perfect integration with a strong model (rate 1.0) and 0.6 with a smaller model, with no scope leakage (0/5). Cross-session memory eliminates repeated mistakes, dropping their rate from 1.00 to 0.00 across strong and weak models. A negative finding is that routing facts to specific agents does not fix long-context degradation when the context fits in the window; the benefit is in cost and capacity, not better attention. The performance gains are consistent across capability tiers and vendors, and do not diminish for stronger models.
AI.conclusion: Proactive scheduling of work scopes and merge order is a highly effective way to coordinate LLM coding agents, transforming fragile parallel edits into reliably integrating workflows while avoiding merge conflicts. The improvements stem from structuring and allocating work, not from improved reasoning in individual models, and they hold across different model strengths and providers. Cross-session memory is crucial to prevent repeated failures, while information-routing alone cannot overcome intrinsic long-context limitations at current context sizes. Overall, planning-based coordination is a key ingredient for scalable, robust multi-agent LLM coding systems.

title: One Step at a Time: Trading LLM Autonomy for Process Predictability
summary: Organizations automating operational processes need more than a correct outcome: they need to predict how a process will run, know which one actually ran, and inspect it step by step. When an agent is the executor that predictability is normally lost: the prescribed procedure goes into the system prompt, and only a final answer comes back. We deliver the procedure step by step over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) instead: a server releases one step at a time, the agent executes it, and each step returns a structured step_output. This trades autonomy for predictability, and two properties then follow by construction, independent of the executor. The execution path is prescribed before the run, so the process is predictable in advance rather than reconstructed afterwards; and the completed step records form a machine-readable execution log that downstream tooling can audit and optimize step by step. Evaluating 15,475 trials across 13 SOP-Bench domains and four open-weight executors from frontier (Kimi K2.5) to lightweight (Ministral 3 8B), we find step-level delivery makes the executed process predictable and inspectable for every executor, and additionally raises accuracy when the executor is small. Across all four, process adherence rises significantly (76-95% to 95-99%) and ungrounded answers (correct outputs produced without executing the SOP) near-vanish, falling from 2.1-4.5% to 0.2-0.3% of trials (all 95% CIs exclude zero); under prompt-based delivery, 31-49% of correct answers on know_your_business bypass the SOP entirely, even for the frontier executor. Accuracy is where the executor's capability enters: the lightweight executor gains +6.5pp grounded accuracy because supplying the process externally removes a reconstruction burden it cannot carry, while capable ones trade a small raw-accuracy decrement for a predictable, auditable process.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes delivering standard operating procedures (SOPs) to AI agents step by step over MCP to make automated processes predictable and auditable, improving process adherence and sometimes accuracy, especially for smaller models.
AI.motivation: In operational automation, organizations need not just correct outcomes but also predictability, traceability, and stepwise inspectability of how processes are executed. When AI agents run procedures via a big system prompt and only return a final answer, the actual execution path is opaque and may diverge from the intended SOP, making it hard to audit, trust, and optimize processes. The authors aim to restore predictability and observability without depending on any particular model’s internals.
AI.method: The authors introduce a protocol where the SOP is delivered one step at a time over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A server prescribes the full execution path in advance, then sequentially releases each step for the agent to execute; the agent returns a structured step_output for every step, forming a machine-readable execution trace. They evaluate this step-level delivery against traditional prompt-based delivery on SOP-Bench, spanning 13 domains and 15,475 trials, using four open-weight executors of varying capability (from frontier-scale Kimi K2.5 to small models like Ministral 3 8B). They measure process adherence, occurrence of ungrounded answers, and task accuracy.
AI.result: Step-level delivery makes process execution predictable and inspectable for all tested executors, independent of model capability. Process adherence improves markedly from 76–95% to 95–99%. Ungrounded answers—cases where correct outputs are produced without following the SOP—drop sharply from 2.1–4.5% to 0.2–0.3% of trials, with confidence intervals ruling out no effect. For the know_your_business domain, 31–49% of correct answers under prompt-based delivery come from bypassing the SOP, even for strong models. For a lightweight executor, grounded accuracy rises by 6.5 percentage points, indicating that externalizing the process alleviates its burden of reconstructing the SOP; for more capable models, raw accuracy decreases slightly but is exchanged for a predictable, auditable process.
AI.conclusion: Delivering SOPs stepwise over MCP, rather than embedding the entire procedure in the prompt, structurally enforces process predictability and inspectability while improving adherence and greatly reducing ungrounded reasoning. This architecture decouples process control from model capability: any executor that can follow step instructions can participate in predictable, auditable workflows. Smaller models particularly benefit in grounded accuracy, while larger ones trade a minor raw-accuracy loss for stronger guarantees that business processes are actually followed and can be audited and optimized step by step.

title: Does the Model Use the Feature? Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs
summary: Internal features in LLMs are often interpreted as mechanisms when they track a concept and their manipulation changes a related behavior. Yet steering can push a feature far outside its natural range, where its effects need not reflect the model's own computation. We examine this inference and propose an empirical contract whose tests evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs. One test copies a feature's value from an input that shows a behavior into a matched input that does not (installation) or the reverse (removal); the other restores the feature after an upstream edit (downstream rescue). Installation measures how far the feature suffices for the behavior; removal and downstream rescue measure how much the model uses it. Applied to three kinds of representations, the two strengths separate sharply. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values from either published latent into matched prompts transfers only a small fraction of the natural known--unknown abstention contrast. Dense known--unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in Gemma and Llama, and how fully a released subject--verb agreement feature set reproduces and restores the behavior depends on how its values are written into the model. Tracking a concept and steering a behavior therefore do not by themselves show that the model uses a feature, and each conclusion holds only for the intervention tested.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques standard interpretations of internal LLM features based on steering and proposes stricter tests for whether models actually use these features.
AI.motivation: Researchers often treat internal features that correlate with concepts and can steer model behavior as mechanistic explanations, but this can be misleading because interventions may push features far beyond their natural ranges, misrepresenting the model’s real computations.
AI.method: The authors define an empirical “contract” for mechanism claims and introduce two tests performed only at naturally observed feature values: (1) installation/removal, where a feature’s value is copied from an input that exhibits a behavior into a matched input that does not (or vice versa), and (2) downstream rescue, where the feature is restored after an upstream edit to see if it recovers the original behavior. They apply these tests to three kinds of representations in LLMs, including known published latents and dense directions, across different models like Gemma and Llama.
AI.result: They find that features previously thought to mechanistically drive behaviors often do not fully suffice for or are not fully used by the model. For example, an unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention when dialed, but installing its natural values transfers only a small part of the natural abstention contrast. Dense known–unknown directions show differing asymmetries between installation and removal across Gemma and Llama. For a subject–verb agreement feature set, the extent to which it reproduces and restores the behavior depends sensitively on how its values are written into the model.
AI.conclusion: Tracking a concept and being able to steer a behavior are not sufficient to claim that a model uses a feature mechanistically. Mechanistic claims are valid only relative to specific, carefully designed interventions at natural activation ranges, and stronger tests like installation/removal and downstream rescue are needed to substantiate such claims.

title: Nucleus Speculative Decoding: Plausibility-Aware Verification Beyond Exact Distribution
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by using a lightweight draft model to propose multiple tokens that are verified by a target model in parallel. However, the standard acceptance rule focuses on exact distribution correction and rejects tokens that remain highly plausible under the target model when the draft model assigns excess probability. This conservative verification limits the number of draft tokens retained after each verification forward pass. We introduce Nucleus Speculative Decoding (NSD), a relaxed verification method that incorporates target-model plausibility into speculative decoding. NSD accepts a draft token if it satisfies the standard acceptance rule or belongs to the target model's nucleus. We theoretically characterize the distributional deviation introduced by our method and show that the single-step error is exactly determined by the draft model's excess probability within the target nucleus. We further derive sequence-level fidelity bounds that quantify how local deviations accumulate over autoregressive decoding. Experiments across multiple target models and proposal mechanisms demonstrate that NSD consistently improves speculative decoding efficiency while maintaining competitive task performance. Our method achieves throughput speedups of up to $5.16\times$ over autoregressive decoding and up to $3.15\times$ over standard speculative decoding. These improvements coincide with longer accepted lengths, allowing more output tokens to share the cost of each target verification pass. Analysis shows that plausibility-aware verification provides an effective approach for relaxed verification and speculative decoding efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Nucleus-Speculative-Decoding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Nucleus Speculative Decoding (NSD), a relaxed speculative decoding scheme that accepts draft tokens either under the standard rule or if they lie in the target model’s nucleus, trading exact distribution matching for higher decoding speed with bounded error.
AI.motivation: Standard speculative decoding is overly conservative: it rejects many tokens that are still highly plausible under the target model whenever the draft model overestimates their probabilities, which limits speedups. The authors want a principled way to relax verification so more draft tokens can be accepted, improving throughput while keeping model outputs faithful to the target model.
AI.method: They modify the verification stage of speculative decoding. A draft token is accepted if (1) it satisfies the usual acceptance rule (which enforces exact distribution correction) or (2) it is inside the nucleus (top-p set) of the target model’s next-token distribution. They analyze the resulting sampling distribution, proving that the one-step error is governed by the draft model’s excess probability mass inside the nucleus and derive sequence-level bounds on divergence accumulated over autoregressive steps. They then empirically test NSD across several target LMs and proposal schemes.
AI.result: NSD increases the average length of consecutively accepted draft tokens per verification pass, leading to higher throughput. Across diverse models and proposal mechanisms, it yields up to 5.16× speedup over plain autoregressive decoding and up to 3.15× over standard speculative decoding, while maintaining similar task performance metrics, demonstrating that the relaxed plausibility-aware rule does not significantly degrade output quality.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing speculative decoding verification to be plausibility-aware via a nucleus-based rule is an effective way to boost decoding efficiency. NSD provides a controlled trade-off between exact distributional fidelity and speed, with theoretical bounds on deviation and strong empirical speedups, suggesting that such relaxed verification schemes are promising for faster large language model inference.

title: A Trust Layer for Agent Evaluation
summary: Deterministic benchmark scores show that an agent received credit, but not whether that credit was earned, reported honestly, or would hold on a second run. We introduce a Trust Layer for Agent Evaluation, an additive post-hoc framework that reports, beside each recorded score, whether it should be believed. It verifies four properties: whether the result is supported by the benchmark's own grading logic, whether a passing answer was earned through traceable computation, whether the agent's completion claim matches what occurred, and whether the result is stable under repeated execution. The first three use only saved artifacts; the fourth re-runs the agent. Model judgments only label evidence under majority voting; all verdicts follow deterministic rules and never modify the recorded score. Applied to five agent configurations on 108 tasks from Agents' Last Exam, every model shows passing runs with no traceable computation (at rates varying tenfold), confirmed false completion claims, and unstable results: 18-46% of tasks do not stay in one score band over five runs. Only 22.6% of recorded passes clear all four checks (95% CI 15.0-32.6, n=84). Measuring what an agent can do and verifying that it did it are different problems, and current benchmarks address only the first.

AI.tldr: They propose a “trust layer” that sits on top of existing agent benchmarks to tell you whether each reported score should actually be believed.
AI.motivation: Current deterministic benchmark scores for agents say what score was recorded, but not whether it was honestly earned, reproducible, or supported by evidence. Agents can appear competent via fragile, untraceable, or misreported successes, so there is a need to distinguish between what an agent can in principle do and what it reliably and verifiably did on a run.
AI.method: They design an additive, post-hoc evaluation framework (Trust Layer) that, for each benchmark run, checks four properties using saved run artifacts and controlled re-runs: (1) whether the outcome is consistent with the benchmark’s own grading logic, (2) whether a passing answer is backed by traceable computation in the agent’s trajectory, (3) whether the agent’s self-reported completion status matches what actually happened, and (4) whether the score is stable across repeated executions. Judgments by models are confined to labeling evidence, while final verdicts are deterministic and never alter the original score.
AI.result: Applying this framework to five different agent configurations on 108 tasks from the Agents’ Last Exam benchmark, they find systematic reliability issues: successful runs often lack traceable computation, there are confirmed cases where agents’ completion claims are false, and performance is unstable, with 18–46% of tasks changing score band across five runs. Only 22.6% of recorded passes satisfy all four trust checks (95% CI 15.0–32.6, n=84).
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy evaluation of agents requires more than just recording benchmark scores; it also requires verifying that successes were properly earned, honestly reported, and reproducible. Existing benchmarks largely ignore this second problem, so the authors argue for adopting a Trust Layer-style approach to separate measurement of potential capability from verification of realized, reliable behavior.

title: OMIT the Action: Measuring Framing-Invariant Omission Bias under Philosophical Disagreement
summary: As LLMs increasingly assist in moral reasoning, omission bias, the tendency to prefer inaction even when equivalent framings reverse substantive outcomes, poses a significant risk of skewed decision-making. Yet omission bias remains underexplored in LLM evaluation, with the few existing studies limited in scale and focused largely on utilitarian-deontological conflicts. To address this gap, we introduce OMIT, a benchmark consisting of 218 paired-frame scenarios across 10 conflict types, constructed by leveraging disagreement patterns from an LLM-based, five-perspective philosophical persona panel (utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics, care ethics, and contractualism). Evaluating eight LLMs, we find that omission bias is pervasive but inversely correlates with model size within families. We further evaluate four inference-time interventions and find that interventions encouraging models to consider moral principles before committing to a yes/no answer reduce omission bias and increase frame-consistent responses, although lower omission bias rates can also coincide with shifts toward action-biased responses. Ultimately, this work contributes not only the OMIT benchmark, but also a methodology for using diverse philosophical disagreement signals to evaluate framing-sensitive inaction preferences and the distributional effects of mitigation attempts in LLMs under complex moral conflicts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OMIT, a benchmark to measure omission bias in LLMs and study how model size and inference-time interventions affect this bias in complex moral scenarios.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for moral reasoning, but they may show omission bias: preferring inaction even when different but equivalent framings flip what counts as harmful or preferable. Existing evaluations of LLM moral behavior rarely focus on omission bias and are narrow in scale and moral perspectives, often centered only on utilitarian vs. deontological tradeoffs. This leaves a gap in systematically understanding how LLMs respond to action vs. inaction under varied moral conflicts and framings, and how to mitigate any undesirable bias.
AI.method: The authors build OMIT, a dataset of 218 moral scenarios presented in paired framings (e.g., action vs. omission) spanning 10 conflict types. They create these scenarios by first running an LLM-based panel of five philosophical personas (utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics, care ethics, contractualism) and leveraging their disagreement patterns to identify morally contested cases. They then evaluate eight different LLMs on these scenarios to quantify omission bias and frame-consistency. Finally, they test four inference-time prompting interventions that prompt models to reflect on moral principles or reasoning steps before giving a binary yes/no answer, to see how these change omission bias and response distributions.
AI.result: Across the eight evaluated models, omission bias is widespread, but its strength tends to decrease as model size increases within the same model family. Interventions that explicitly encourage principled moral reflection before answering reduce omission bias and make responses more consistent with the framing of the scenario. However, lowering omission bias sometimes results in a shift toward favoring action over inaction, indicating that mitigation strategies can change not just bias levels but also the overall action/inaction balance of the model’s moral choices.
AI.conclusion: The work provides (1) OMIT, a new benchmark specifically designed to probe omission bias in LLMs across diverse moral conflict types, and (2) a general methodology that uses disagreement signals from multiple philosophical perspectives to construct framing-sensitive moral evaluation datasets. The findings show that omission bias is common but modulated by model size, and that inference-time moral-reflection interventions can meaningfully alter omission bias and frame-consistency, though with important distributional side effects (e.g., increased action bias). This framework can be used to study and tune how LLMs handle inaction vs. action preferences in complex moral contexts.

title: The Right Memory in the Wrong Context: Verifying Retrieval Admissibility in Long-Term Agent Memory
comment: 26 pages. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development". Code: https://github.com/ziwang11112/right-memory-wrong-context
summary: Long-term-memory agents can retrieve relevant information that is inadmissible for the current request because it belongs to another principal, violates policy, or reflects an incompatible lifecycle state. Recall and final-answer accuracy do not reveal this: a route can appear safe by missing required evidence, while a correct answer may follow inadmissible prompt exposure. We introduce a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that assigns each memory-query pair one of three statuses (admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved), compares routes at matched required-evidence recall with bounds for unresolved cases, and tracks memory IDs through prompt exposure while linking exposure to target-level disclosure. We evaluate its stages on separate, non-pooled populations. A post-hoc top-20 reanalysis of frozen rankings from two public long-term-memory benchmarks, RHELM and MemOps, covers 3,767 queries. All released anchors lie within trusted query namespaces; with within-namespace scores unchanged, off-namespace filtering cannot lower their ranks. Top-20 anchor recall increases from 0.432 to 0.533, 80% recall feasibility from 0.237 to 0.311, and exact similarity evaluations decrease by 98.3%. In a frozen 72-case development diagnostic, a released-metadata reference preserves required evidence, whereas neither text-only verifier detects violations under the 1% required-anchor false-denial limit. Across 1,523 paired benchmark-native cases, namespace routing is associated with judged-accuracy gains of 0.053-0.068 across three readers; recall also changes, so this comparison is observational. In 16 controlled exposure scenarios, only one of four reader-specific 95% confidence intervals excludes zero for relevant-inadmissible literal disclosure (+0.156, 95% CI [0.031, 0.312]). Results motivate separate verification of candidate support, admissibility, prompt exposure, and answer disclosure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a framework to verify whether information retrieved by long-term-memory agents is admissible with respect to principals, policies, and lifecycle states, separating correctness from policy-compliant evidence use.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term-memory agents are evaluated mostly on recall and final-answer accuracy, which cannot reveal whether correct answers rely on inadmissible information (e.g., data from a different user, policy-violating content, or outdated lifecycle states). This creates hidden safety, privacy, and compliance risks: a route can look safe by missing required evidence, and correct answers can be produced only because inadmissible memories were exposed in prompts. Current benchmarks and verifiers do not adequately measure these dimensions.
AI.method: The authors introduce a retrieval-admissibility verification framework that labels each memory–query pair as admissible, inadmissible, or unresolved. It (1) compares different retrieval routes at matched levels of required-evidence recall while propagating bounds due to unresolved cases, (2) tracks memory identifiers through the model’s prompt exposure, and (3) links which exposed memories actually cause target-level disclosure in answers. They evaluate each stage of the framework on separate, non-pooled data populations and perform a post-hoc top-20 analysis on frozen rankings from two public long-term-memory benchmarks (RHELM and MemOps). They also run a 72-case development diagnostic to test verifiers under a strict false-denial limit, examine 1,523 paired native-benchmark cases to study namespace routing effects on judged accuracy, and construct 16 controlled exposure scenarios to assess how often inadmissible content leads to literal disclosure.
AI.result: In the top-20 reanalysis of 3,767 queries, constraining to trusted query namespaces while filtering off-namespace memories never reduces the rank of released anchors, yielding improved metrics: top-20 anchor recall rises from 0.432 to 0.533, 80% recall feasibility from 0.237 to 0.311, and the need for exact similarity assessments drops by 98.3%. In a 72-case diagnostic, a verifier that uses released metadata preserves required evidence, whereas two text-only verifiers fail to detect violations once a 1% false-denial cap for required anchors is imposed. On 1,523 paired cases, adopting namespace routing correlates with judged-accuracy gains of 0.053–0.068 across three human readers, though this is observational because recall also changes. In 16 controlled exposure scenarios, only one of four reader-specific 95% confidence intervals for relevant-inadmissible literal disclosure is significantly above zero (+0.156, 95% CI [0.031, 0.312]).
AI.conclusion: Correctness and recall alone are insufficient to assess the safety and compliance of long-term-memory agents, because they can obscure the use of inadmissible evidence. The proposed framework shows that retrieval admissibility, prompt exposure, and answer disclosure can and should be evaluated as distinct steps. Namespace-constrained routing can improve both recall and judged accuracy without hurting benchmark anchors, and metadata-aware verification is more reliable than text-only checks under strict false-denial constraints. Overall, systems should separately verify candidate support, admissibility, prompt exposure, and final-answer disclosure to better manage privacy, policy, and lifecycle risks in memory-augmented AI agents.

title: Dynamic Positional Attention Modulation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become a standard approach for adapting large language models to downstream tasks. However, most existing PEFT methods rely on uniform and static adaptations, without accounting for the structured heterogeneity of attention across dimensions, heads, layers, and input tokens. In practice, attention representations exhibit non-uniform behavior, and positional encoding mechanisms such as rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) induce dimension-dependent positional structure, making uniform adaptation suboptimal. In this work, we propose DyPAM (Dynamic Positional Attention Modulation), a PEFT method that adapts how positional information contributes to attention by operating directly on the query and key representations. DyPAM combines input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation with head-wise and layer-wise structural modulation, performing fine-grained adaptation of positional attention aligned with the RoPE-induced structure without modifying the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks across multiple backbone models demonstrate that DyPAM consistently outperforms existing strong PEFT baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes DyPAM, a PEFT method that dynamically modulates positional contributions in attention to better align with RoPE structure, improving reasoning performance over prior PEFT baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods treat adaptations uniformly across dimensions, heads, layers, and tokens, ignoring structured heterogeneity in how attention and RoPE-based positional information behave. This uniformity leads to suboptimal adaptation for tasks, especially where positional structure matters, like reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce DyPAM (Dynamic Positional Attention Modulation), which operates directly on query and key representations to adjust how positional information affects attention. It performs input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation plus structural modulation across heads and layers, all aligned with RoPE’s dimension-dependent positional structure, while keeping the original backbone weights frozen.
AI.result: Across multiple backbone LLMs and on mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, DyPAM yields consistent performance gains and surpasses strong existing PEFT baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, structure-aware modulation of positional attention—rather than uniform, static PEFT—is an effective and parameter-efficient way to adapt RoPE-based LLMs, particularly for reasoning tasks, without altering the pretrained backbone.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Inference-Time Overreliance Using Agentic Memory
summary: Agentic memory allows LLM agents to reuse past experience, yet retrieved memories can also distort inference even when they are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved. We study this failure mode, which we call memory over-reliance. Across benchmarks and memory architectures, we find that memory is useful when past experience transfers to the current task, but can become misleading when only part of the evidence transfers. Failures are strongest under partial query-memory overlap, a pattern further confirmed by controlled experiments thatvary the amount of overlapping evidence. Motivated by this finding, we propose MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls its reuse at read time. MEMTRIM removes repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information, requires no retraining, and applies to both embedding-based and structured memory systems.Experiments show that MEMTRIM reduces memory overreliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory across models and memory settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language model agents can become overly dependent on their memory of past experiences, and introduces MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that filters memory content to reduce misleading influence while keeping useful information.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM systems increasingly rely on memory to reuse past experience, but even correct and relevantly retrieved memories can distort current reasoning. There is a need to systematically characterize this failure mode and to design mechanisms that keep the benefits of memory without inducing harmful over-reliance.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze LLM agents with different memory architectures and benchmarks to identify when memory helps versus hurts, focusing on scenarios with partial overlap between current queries and stored memories. They run controlled experiments that vary the amount of overlapping evidence to isolate the effect. Based on these insights, they design MEMTRIM, which indexes evidence at write time and selectively filters or controls its use at read time to remove repeated or conflicting information while preserving memory-specific details, without retraining the underlying models and supporting both embedding-based and structured memory systems.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrate that memory is beneficial when past experiences fully transfer to the current task but becomes misleading when only part of the evidence transfers, with the most severe failures under partial query-memory overlap. Applying MEMTRIM across different models and memory setups significantly reduces such memory over-reliance while largely maintaining the performance gains that memory provides when it is actually useful.
AI.conclusion: Memory over-reliance is a distinct and important failure mode for LLM agents that arises especially under partial overlap between queries and stored experiences. MEMTRIM offers an effective, training-free, and architecture-agnostic way to manage memory by trimming redundant or conflicting evidence, thereby mitigating over-reliance while preserving the advantages of agentic memory.

title: ReFold: Training-Free Reversible Inter-Turn Context Folding for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents act on an append-only interaction history that is re-sent to the model at every step, so the context and its cost grow with steps until the sessions exceed the context window. Existing methods manage the context through context requirement prediction, relying on additional model calls, heuristic rules, or trained policies. However, these predictive approaches introduce runtime overhead, invalidate prefix caches, and permanently discard content with no guarantee of recovery. To overcome these limitations, we introduce ReFold: a training-free rendering layer that preserves the underlying interaction history while compressing only the model's rendered context. It removes two kinds of inter-turn redundancy without an auxiliary predictor: content an earlier turn already displayed, replaced by a stub, and turns the agent itself reports finished, folded into a one-line note. Both operators use chunked rendering, rewriting the cached prefix once every few steps rather than at every step. Every removal is strictly reversible, a wrong removal costs one restore from the history rather than permanent content loss. Because it operates at the rendering layer, ReFold is plug-and-play across standard ReAct-style harnesses. Evaluations across five long-horizon benchmarks and two frontier LLMs demonstrate that ReFold reduces token consumption by up to 2.5x and halves the KV-cache memory per session without degrading task success rates. Under capped context budgets, it avoids up to 92% of forced compactions. Under concurrent serving workloads, it reduces request queuing delays by up to 100%, accelerating inference by up to 1.7x, while cutting inference costs by up to 3.4x.

AI.tldr: ReFold is a training-free rendering layer for long-horizon LLM agents that compresses only the rendered context, not the underlying history, achieving ~2.5x token savings and large speed/memory gains without hurting success rates.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents currently re-send an ever-growing append-only interaction history each step, causing context and cost to grow linearly and eventually exceed the context window. Existing context management methods rely on predictive mechanisms (extra calls, heuristics, or policies) that add runtime overhead, break prefix caching, and irreversibly discard content, risking performance and recoverability. There is a need for a context management approach that is cheap, reversible, and compatible with existing agent frameworks while preserving full history fidelity.
AI.method: The authors propose ReFold, a training-free rendering layer that sits between the full interaction history and the model’s visible context. Instead of modifying or deleting the underlying history, ReFold only compresses the rendered context by (1) replacing content that has already been displayed in earlier turns with short stubs, and (2) folding turns that the agent has explicitly marked as finished into single-line summaries. Both operations are done via chunked rendering, so the cached prefix is rewritten only every few steps instead of each step. All removals are strictly reversible by restoring from the full history. ReFold integrates plug-and-play with standard ReAct-style agent harnesses and does not require auxiliary predictors or model retraining.
AI.result: On five long-horizon benchmarks and two strong LLMs, ReFold achieves up to 2.5x reduction in token consumption and halves KV-cache memory per session while maintaining task success rates. Under fixed context budgets, it avoids up to 92% of forced compactions. In concurrent serving scenarios, it reduces request queuing delays by up to 100%, yields up to 1.7x faster inference, and cuts total inference costs by up to 3.4x.
AI.conclusion: ReFold provides an efficient, prediction-free, and reversible mechanism for managing context in long-horizon LLM agents by operating at the rendering layer. It preserves the full interaction history while substantially reducing effective context length, improving memory usage, latency, and cost without sacrificing success rates, and can be used as a plug-and-play component in existing ReAct-style systems.

title: Rule-Based Languages for Neurosymbolic AI
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of Rules and Reasoning - 10th International Joint Conference, RuleML+RR 2026, Vilnius, Lithuania
summary: Logic programming is increasingly used as the symbolic component of neurosymbolic AI systems. We survey the main rule-based languages in this setting, namely Datalog, answer set, and probabilistic logic programs, along four axes: semantics, expressiveness, neural integration, and evaluation mechanism. We analyse over 50 recent systems and applications, comparing formalism usage across four research areas: databases and programming languages, machine learning, vision, and robotics. We provide a decision matrix mapping application scenarios to required features and close by outlining open problems.

AI.tldr: Survey of logic programming formalisms in neurosymbolic AI, comparing languages, integrations, and applications, and outlining open challenges.
AI.motivation: Logic programming is becoming central as the symbolic part of neurosymbolic AI, but the landscape of available rule-based languages, their semantic differences, and how they integrate with neural components is fragmented and not systematically compared.
AI.method: The authors survey more than 50 recent neurosymbolic systems and applications using rule-based languages such as Datalog, answer set programming, and probabilistic logic programming, and analyse them along four dimensions: semantics, expressiveness, neural integration style, and evaluation mechanisms. They also categorize usage patterns across four research domains: databases & programming languages, machine learning, vision, and robotics.
AI.result: They produce a comparative analysis of different rule-based formalisms in neurosymbolic AI, including a decision matrix that maps various application scenarios to the logical features and evaluation properties they require, and a cross-domain overview of which formalisms are used where.
AI.conclusion: The paper clarifies how Datalog, answer set programming, and probabilistic logic programming are currently used as symbolic components in neurosymbolic AI, helps practitioners choose suitable formalisms for specific scenarios via a decision matrix, and identifies open research problems and gaps in existing languages and integration mechanisms.

title: Visual Abstention in Unified Multimodal Models
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Project page: https://visual-abstention.github.io
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) integrate understanding and generation, yet their generative behavior is rarely governed by what they understand about the task. We formalize visual abstention: when a requested visual transformation is impossible under the task's rules, the model should recognize that no valid solution exists, state this, and decline to generate. We introduce Draw-or-Decline (DoD), a benchmark of 1,050 feasible-infeasible request pairs across 7 task categories that jointly measures editing success and the refusal of infeasible requests. Evaluating 8 UMMs, we find that editing ability and abstention are distinct capabilities: even the strongest editor, at 68.4% editing accuracy, refuses only 0.4% of infeasible requests under ordinary instructions. Their reasoning shows why: the models rarely notice the conflict, and instead plan the edit as if the request were possible, often describing objects that are not in the image, or quietly change the request into one they can complete. Explicitly prompting these UMMs to report infeasibility increases textual refusals but reduces editing accuracy. We propose VisTA (Visual Transformation and Abstention), a training method that pairs feasible and infeasible examples so that a model judges feasibility before deciding whether to generate. We train VisTA-BAGEL to perform feasible edits and decline infeasible requests. Without any reminder, it refuses 93.0% of infeasible requests, up from 0.4% for the strongest editor, while falsely refusing only 0.8% of feasible ones. Unlike a reminder, this does not cost editing accuracy: VisTA-BAGEL completes 74.3% of feasible edits, more than any of the 8 evaluated UMMs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how unified multimodal models should sometimes refuse to generate images when a user’s requested edit is impossible, and proposes a benchmark and training method to make models reliably abstain from such infeasible visual transformations without hurting editing quality.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal models can both understand and generate images, but in practice they often try to satisfy any request, even when the requested visual change contradicts the image or task rules. This leads to unrealistic edits, hallucinations, and user confusion. The authors want models whose generative behavior is constrained by their understanding of what is possible, including the ability to explicitly say “no valid solution exists” when a request is infeasible. There was no standardized way to measure or train this kind of visual abstention, so the work fills that gap.
AI.method: 1) They formalize the notion of visual abstention: for impossible visual transformation requests, the model should detect infeasibility, explain it, and refuse to generate. 2) They build Draw-or-Decline (DoD), a benchmark of 1,050 paired feasible and infeasible visual editing requests across 7 task types, designed to measure both successful edits and correct refusals. 3) They evaluate 8 existing unified multimodal models under normal and refusal-reminder prompts, analyzing their editing accuracy, refusal rates, and reasoning traces. 4) They propose VisTA (Visual Transformation and Abstention), a training strategy that uses paired feasible/infeasible examples and an explicit feasibility-judgment step before generation, and train a model called VisTA-BAGEL with this procedure.
AI.result: On the DoD benchmark, current UMMs show that editing and abstention are largely independent capacities: even the best editor reaches 68.4% accuracy on feasible edits but refuses only 0.4% of infeasible ones under ordinary instructions. When prompted to consider infeasibility explicitly, these models refuse more often in text but their editing performance drops. The newly trained VisTA-BAGEL model, in contrast, automatically refuses 93.0% of infeasible requests without reminders, while incorrectly refusing only 0.8% of feasible ones, and improves feasible edit success to 74.3%, surpassing all 8 evaluated baselines.
