They also construct a “claim-check table” mapping six common industry claims to required evidence types, grounded in NIST, IETF, and OWASP draft standards, and illustrate the approach via a detailed case study that tracks one claim across five possible evidence states.
AI.result: The paper delivers: (1) a precise definition of “auditable claim” for AI agents; (2) theoretical results showing that, under their model, omitting any of the three additional agent conditions makes it impossible to properly support claims; (3) an extension of the Policy Checkability dimension in their Auditable Agents framework from individual actions to broader claims; (4) a practical claim-check table for six common assurance claims, aligned with emerging standards; and (5) a worked example demonstrating how evidence quality and availability influence the assessment of a claim over time.
AI.conclusion: To make organizational claims about AI agents meaningfully checkable, they must be formulated as auditable claims that specify policy, scope, evidence, responsibility, and decision rules in advance, and rely on records that satisfy independence, authorization binding, and completeness. Without these conditions, claims cannot be robustly supported or audited under the authors’ formal model. The authors argue that operators, purchasers, auditors, and standard-setting bodies should adopt this structure for claims, use tools like claim-check tables, and integrate explicit evidence requirements into practice and standards to make compliance and assurance around AI agents more rigorous and reliable.

title: DirectSpeech2LLM: A Simple End-to-End Framework to Mitigate Prompt Overfitting in Speech-LLMs
summary: Speech-LLMs often exhibit prompt overfitting, where models solely trained on automatic speech recognition (ASR) instruction fail to generalize to new instructions such as speech translation and continue to behave primarily as ASR system. We propose DirectSpeech2LLM, a simple end-to-end framework that preserves the instruction-following ability of the LLM on unseen tasks when conditioned on speech. It computes distance-based CTC loss over the frozen LLM embedding matrix and uses greedy CTC labels to derive geometrically and temporally aligned speech embeddings respectively as an input to the LLM. Trained solely on 960 hours of LibriSpeech ASR data, DirectSpeech2LLM outperforms the cascaded system on ASR (seen task) and generalizes zero-shot to speech translation and emotion recognition (two unseen tasks), closely matching the cascaded system upper bound on these two new instructions despite seeing neither during training. We also find that geometric alignment strength plays a smaller role than previously assumed, as our modified CTC loss is shown to provide sufficient implicit geometric grounding without requiring an explicit regression loss. Results are consistent across two LLM families and scale with both more training data and model capacity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DirectSpeech2LLM, an end-to-end framework that aligns speech directly to a frozen LLM’s embedding space via a modified CTC loss, preserving the LLM’s instruction-following abilities and enabling zero-shot generalization from ASR-only training to unseen speech tasks like translation and emotion recognition.
AI.motivation: Existing Speech-LLMs trained mainly on ASR-style instructions suffer from prompt overfitting: they tend to behave as ASR systems and fail to follow new instructions such as speech translation or emotion recognition. There is a need for a simple, data-efficient method that connects speech to LLMs without destroying their general instruction-following and enabling zero-shot transfer to new speech tasks using only ASR supervision.
AI.method: The authors propose DirectSpeech2LLM, an end-to-end framework that maps speech into the embedding space of a frozen LLM. They introduce a distance-based CTC loss computed over the LLM’s embedding matrix and use greedy CTC decoding to obtain labels that are both geometrically (in embedding space) and temporally aligned to the LLM tokens. These speech-derived embeddings are then directly fed into the frozen LLM. The method avoids explicit regression losses for geometric alignment and trains only on LibriSpeech ASR data, keeping the LLM itself fixed while learning the speech front-end.
AI.result: Trained solely on 960 hours of LibriSpeech ASR data, DirectSpeech2LLM outperforms a standard cascaded speech-to-text plus LLM system on the seen ASR task. More importantly, it generalizes in a zero-shot fashion to two unseen tasks—speech translation and speech emotion recognition—achieving performance close to the cascaded system’s upper bound despite never seeing these instructions during training. The authors also show that the implicit geometric grounding provided by their modified CTC loss is sufficient, and that explicit regression-based alignment brings limited additional benefit. Performance trends hold across two different LLM families and improve with larger datasets and model scales.
AI.conclusion: DirectSpeech2LLM provides a simple, effective way to connect speech encoders directly to frozen LLMs using a modified CTC loss over the LLM embedding space. This design preserves the LLM’s instruction-following ability and mitigates prompt overfitting, enabling robust zero-shot generalization from pure ASR training to unseen speech tasks like translation and emotion recognition. The findings further suggest that strong explicit geometric alignment is less critical than previously thought, as implicit grounding from the CTC formulation suffices, and that the approach scales well with data and model size.

title: COMPASS: Finding Where Reasoning Lives in Language Models
summary: Explicitly eliciting reasoning substantially improves LLM performance. Existing approaches require a predefined characterization of reasoning, whether through CoT prompt design, contrastive CoT directions, or via SAE derived reasoning features. For mathematical reasoning with verifiable answers, we show that a much simpler signal suffices, which is the correctness of the model's own direct answer attempts. This signal yields a latent direction that elicits reasoning. This direction is decodable within the activations of most attention heads, but only a small subset of them can be effectively intervened. We introduce COMPASS, an inference-time steering method that identifies these heads using a logit-space attribution score and steers their activations along the correctness direction, requiring only per-head activation statistics. Across three model families and multiple math benchmarks, COMPASS outperforms the activation-steering baselines we compare against, improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average, and approaches CoT accuracy with 20-70\% fewer generated tokens. Interventions transfer without re-fitting to unseen benchmarks, and ablations show that both the correctness direction and the small set of heads carrying it are necessary, with the effect concentrated in remarkably few heads.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes COMPASS, an inference-time steering method that uses a latent correctness direction—derived solely from whether a model’s own direct math answers are correct—to elicit better reasoning in LLMs, achieving large math accuracy gains with fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought (CoT) style prompting substantially improves reasoning in LLMs but typically requires explicit, hand-designed reasoning signals or features (e.g., CoT prompts, contrastive directions, or sparse autoencoder-derived features). These are costly to design, not always generalizable, and may depend heavily on supervision. The authors aim to find a simpler, more automatic way to induce reasoning in LLMs, especially for math tasks where correctness is easily verifiable, and to do so through activation steering without retraining models or requiring elaborate annotations.
AI.method: The authors exploit the binary signal of whether an LLM’s direct, non-CoT answer to a math question is correct or incorrect. They aggregate model activations conditioned on this correctness signal to estimate a latent "correctness direction" in activation space. They then analyze which attention heads encode this direction and define a logit-space attribution score to identify heads where intervening is effective. The proposed method, COMPASS, steers the activations of only this small, high-attribution subset of heads along the correctness direction during inference, using per-head activation statistics and without changing the model weights or requiring CoT supervision.
AI.result: COMPASS consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across three different LLM families and multiple math benchmarks. On GSM8K, it yields an average accuracy improvement of about 16 percentage points over the base model and outperforms other activation-steering baselines. It reaches accuracy close to that of CoT prompting while generating 20–70% fewer tokens. The learned interventions generalize to unseen math benchmarks without re-fitting. Analysis shows that the correctness direction is widely decodable across attention heads, but only a small subset of heads can be effectively steered, and that both the correctness direction and this specific subset of heads are necessary for the observed gains, with effects concentrated in remarkably few heads.
AI.conclusion: A simple correctness-based signal is sufficient to uncover a latent direction in LLM activations that elicits more effective mathematical reasoning. By focusing on a small, carefully selected set of attention heads and steering them along this correctness direction at inference time, COMPASS delivers substantial accuracy improvements comparable to CoT prompting, while being more token-efficient and requiring no explicit reasoning annotations. The findings suggest that reasoning-relevant features are already present and localized in a small number of attention heads, and that targeted activation steering can unlock them using minimal supervision.

title: SAGE: Semantic Anchor-Guided Evolution for Grounded Medical QA Data Synthesis
summary: Developing reliable models for clinical tasks, such as Medical Question Answering (QA), is severely constrained by the limited availability of high-quality, expert-annotated training data. This challenge is exacerbated by stringent privacy requirements and the impracticality of utilizing large open-source corpora or proprietary cloud APIs within resource-limited clinical settings. To address these obstacles, we introduce SAGE (\textit{Semantic Anchor-Guided Evolution}), a novel data synthesis framework that enables small, locally deployed models to generate high-quality medical training data. SAGE leverages lightweight, publicly available taxonomies such as MeSH as semantic anchors, imposing a structured prior to effectively guide and ground the data generation process. At its core, SAGE iteratively interleaves atomic (individual concept-based) and associative (relation-based) synthesis, bootstrapping training data from minimal seeds. This approach eliminates the need for large collections of medical documents or reliance on external APIs, providing a practical solution for on-premises data creation. Extensive experiments across multiple medical question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that models fine-tuned with SAGE-synthesized data consistently outperform those trained using self-derived or conventional document-based paradigms, highlighting tangible improvements in data efficiency and resource utilization for medical LLM development. Code is available at https://github.com/DIaacKr/SAGE.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a framework for synthesizing high-quality medical QA training data using small, local models guided by semantic taxonomies instead of large corpora or external APIs.
AI.motivation: High-quality, expert-annotated medical QA data is scarce due to cost, privacy, and deployment constraints, and many institutions cannot use large web corpora or cloud LLM APIs. There is a need for a way to create useful medical training data locally with limited resources while maintaining reliability and privacy.
AI.method: SAGE (Semantic Anchor-Guided Evolution) uses lightweight medical taxonomies (e.g., MeSH) as semantic anchors to structure and constrain synthetic data generation. It runs on small, locally hosted models that iteratively generate QA data in two modes: atomic synthesis, which focuses on individual medical concepts, and associative synthesis, which captures relations between concepts. The framework bootstraps from a minimal set of seed examples and alternates between these two modes to expand a synthetic dataset, without relying on large document collections or external APIs.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple medical QA benchmarks show that models fine-tuned on SAGE-generated data perform better than models trained on self-generated data or on data made with traditional document-based synthesis techniques. These improvements are seen in both performance and data efficiency, demonstrating that SAGE can effectively create useful training data under resource and privacy constraints.
AI.conclusion: SAGE offers a practical, on-premise method for generating high-quality medical QA training data by grounding small local models with semantic taxonomies. This taxonomy-guided, iterative synthesis strategy improves downstream medical QA performance and resource utilization, providing a viable alternative to document-heavy or cloud-dependent data creation approaches.

title: PsyCIDRA: A Dual-Agent Framework for Psychiatric Interviewing and Diagnostic Reasoning
summary: Large language models show promise in clinical reasoning, but psychiatric interviewing requires guiding an evolving conversation. Their ability to carry out this interactive assessment remains less studied. We present PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent framework linking free-form psychiatric interviewing with diagnostic reasoning for expert review. Its interviewer agent uses tools to maintain working notes, load expert-written skills, and retrieve ICD-11 references to guide inquiry. Its diagnostic reasoning agent then receives the completed interview transcript and reports hypotheses alongside supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, withholding a final hypothesis when none is sufficiently supported. Using patient profiles generated with PsyCPG, we first evaluate PsyCIDRA in simulation. Across four models on 53 evaluation cases, it achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, rank-1 accuracy is 60.5% versus 51.9%. In a blinded study of 101 human participants in separate arms, PsyCIDRA agrees with psychologists on whether to propose a diagnostic hypothesis in 79.6% of cases, compared with 65.4% for direct prompting. Together, these findings support the potential of LLM agents to assist psychiatric assessment through free-form dialogue. By examining diagnostic reasoning, interview quality, and safety together, this study contributes to understanding the capabilities and limitations of psychiatric interview agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent LLM framework for psychiatric interviewing and diagnostic reasoning, showing it outperforms direct prompting in simulated and human-evaluated settings.
AI.motivation: While LLMs show promise in clinical reasoning, psychiatric assessment requires interactive, evolving interviews rather than static Q&A, and it is unclear how well LLMs can manage this process safely and effectively.
AI.method: The authors design PsyCIDRA with two agents: an interviewer agent that conducts free-form psychiatric interviews using tools (working notes, expert skill modules, ICD-11 retrieval) and a diagnostic reasoning agent that processes completed transcripts to generate hypotheses with supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence, and may withhold a final diagnosis. They evaluate performance using simulated patient profiles from PsyCPG across four LLMs and then run a blinded human study with 101 participants comparing PsyCIDRA to direct prompting.
AI.result: In simulation across 53 cases, PsyCIDRA achieves higher diagnostic agreement than direct prompting; on 81 held-out cases, rank-1 diagnostic accuracy improves from 51.9% to 60.5%. In a blinded study with 101 human participants, PsyCIDRA’s decisions about whether to propose a diagnosis agree with psychologists 79.6% of the time, versus 65.4% for direct prompting.
AI.conclusion: PsyCIDRA demonstrates that structured, dual-agent LLM frameworks can better support psychiatric interviewing and diagnostic reasoning than simple direct prompting, suggesting LLM agents may meaningfully assist psychiatric assessment via free-form dialogue while highlighting the importance of jointly considering reasoning quality, interview quality, and safety.

title: Penalty-Framed No-Valid-Option MCQA: Analyzing LLM Abstention under Invalid Choices
comment: Accepted to AACL-IJCNLP 2026 Main Conference (Short Paper)
summary: Multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) is commonly used to evaluate large language models under the assumption that one of the provided options is correct, typically using answer-selection accuracy. However, in real deployments, users or retrieval systems may provide invalid option sets in which none of the listed choices is correct, and selecting one of them may incur downstream cost. We study this setting as penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA. Using the mathematics subset of MMLU-Pro, we remove the labeled correct option, allow models to either choose a remaining option or output ABSTAIN, and penalize invalid forced-choice responses. We further introduce correct-conditioned analysis, evaluating abstention only on instances that the model originally answered correctly. Experiments show that high MCQA accuracy does not fully guarantee abstention reliability: even under explicit no-valid-option-aware instructions and penalty-based scoring, models still produce invalid forced-choice responses for a subset of originally correct instances. These results show that penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA reveals an aspect of model reliability not captured by standard answer-selection accuracy.

AI.tldr: They modify standard multiple-choice QA evaluation by removing the correct answer and allowing models to abstain, showing that normal accuracy hides important reliability failures when no valid option is present.
AI.motivation: Standard multiple-choice QA assumes one displayed option is correct and evaluates only answer-selection accuracy, but real-world use includes cases where none of the options is correct; in such cases, blindly forcing a choice can be harmful and we need to measure how reliably models can abstain instead of guessing.
AI.method: Using the mathematics subset of MMLU-Pro, they construct a no-valid-option setting by removing the labeled correct answer from each question’s options, add an ABSTAIN option, and apply a penalty for choosing any remaining incorrect option; they also propose a correct-conditioned analysis that focuses on questions the model answered correctly in the original setting and then evaluates abstention behavior on those when the correct choice is removed.
AI.result: They find that models with high standard MCQA accuracy still frequently choose an incorrect option instead of abstaining when the correct answer has been removed, even when given explicit instructions about the no-valid-option setting and penalty-based scoring; this shows a gap between traditional accuracy and abstention behavior.
AI.conclusion: Penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA exposes a distinct reliability dimension: models can appear strong under standard accuracy metrics yet still systematically fail to abstain when no valid choice is available, so future evaluation and deployment should account for abstention reliability rather than relying solely on answer-selection accuracy.

title: In With the Old: Enhancing 'Classical' Document Automation with Generative AI
comment: 10 pages. AI for Access to Justice Workshop at ICAIL 2025
summary: Software-based legal assistance systems have leveraged many different forms of knowledge representation and reasoning. This article explores how document automation services rooted in expert system style and other symbolic approaches can usefully enhance and be enhanced by current generative AI approaches. We discuss the possible benefits and challenges, and report on preliminary experiments in using large language models to identify and fix issues in texts written by laypeople.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how traditional rule-based document automation systems in law can interact synergistically with modern generative AI, backed by early experiments on LLMs correcting layperson-written legal texts.
AI.motivation: Legal tech has long used symbolic, expert-system-like tools for document automation, but generative AI has recently shown strong capabilities with natural language. The authors want to understand how these older, structured approaches and newer LLM-based approaches can complement each other rather than exist in isolation, especially for helping non-lawyers create better legal documents.
AI.method: The paper conceptually analyzes integration patterns between expert system-style document automation and generative AI, outlining benefits and challenges. It then conducts preliminary experiments where large language models are tasked with detecting and correcting problems in legal texts drafted by laypeople, observing performance and practical issues.
AI.result: Preliminary experiments show that large language models can meaningfully identify and fix some issues in layperson-written legal documents, though with limitations and potential risks. The conceptual analysis highlights concrete ways symbolic document automation can provide structure, constraints, and checks that improve LLM reliability, and how LLMs can enhance flexibility and usability of existing systems.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic document automation and generative AI are not competing paradigms but can reinforce each other. Expert-system-based structures and rules can guide and validate LLM outputs, while LLMs can make systems more adaptive and user-friendly. However, realizing this synergy requires careful handling of accuracy, explainability, and risk in legal contexts, and more extensive empirical study beyond the preliminary experiments reported.

title: Making COMET Comparable Across Scripts: Diagnosis and Correction of Tokeniser-Induced Script Bias in Indic MT Evaluation
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. Camera-ready version, accepted at WMT 2026. Code and data: https://github.com/John-salvin/script-bias-comet-normalisation
summary: COMET reports translation quality as a single number, and that number is routinely compared across target languages written in different scripts. Such a comparison assumes Script Invariance: the score should not depend on the writing system that carries the target. We test it on IndicMT Eval by re-encoding the target into Latin script, which changes orthographic form while holding content and human ratings fixed. Script identity then accounts for 22.9% of native-script COMET variance, and agreement with annotators falls in all five languages studied. We trace the effect to the tokeniser and measure it with three label-free diagnostics. The bias is two faults, not one. Scores from different scripts occupy incompatible ranges, and within a single script the metric orders translations less accurately. No order-preserving transform of the score can repair the second fault. The first is removed exactly by COMET-QN, which maps the score distribution of each (language, script) pair onto a shared reference. Pooled agreement with annotators rises from 0.300 to 0.399, which is what makes scores from different scripts safe to place on one axis, and every within-language ordering is provably preserved. A regressor over parity features recovers a further 17.1% of the lost sensitivity. The remainder belongs to the encoder, and no post-processing can reach it. We therefore recommend publishing the normalised score, the three diagnostics, and the identity of the tokeniser they were computed against, so that a reader can tell how much of a score reflects translation quality and how much reflects the writing system.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that COMET translation scores are biased by the target script and proposes normalization and diagnostics to make cross-script comparisons safer.
AI.motivation: COMET is widely used to evaluate machine translation using a single quality score, often compared across languages that use different writing systems. This implicitly assumes that the metric is invariant to script, but this assumption had not been rigorously tested. If script affects COMET scores, then cross-language comparisons and system rankings may be misleading, motivating a systematic investigation and mitigation methods.
AI.method: The authors test Script Invariance by using IndicMT Eval, re-encoding human-rated translation targets from native Indic scripts into Latin script while keeping content and human judgments fixed. They measure how much COMET variance is explained by script identity and how script affects agreement with human annotators across five languages. They then trace the source of bias to the tokenizer and design three label-free diagnostics to quantify it. They analyze two distinct faults: incompatible score ranges across scripts and degraded within-script ordering. To address range differences, they introduce COMET-QN, which normalizes score distributions per (language, script) pair against a shared reference while provably preserving within-language orderings. They also train a regressor on parity features to recover additional sensitivity beyond the normalization.
AI.result: Script identity explains 22.9% of the variance in COMET scores on IndicMT Eval, and cross-script tokenization differences reduce COMET’s agreement with human annotators in all five languages. The authors show that no monotonic transformation of raw COMET scores can fix the within-script ordering degradation caused by the tokenizer. Their COMET-QN normalization fully removes the cross-script range incompatibility and raises pooled human agreement from 0.300 to 0.399 while preserving all within-language rankings. A parity-feature regressor further recovers 17.1% of the sensitivity loss attributable to tokenization effects. Residual insensitivity remains in the encoder and is not recoverable by post-processing.
AI.conclusion: COMET is not script-invariant: target writing systems substantially affect its scores and their agreement with human judgments. This bias arises mainly from tokenization and manifests both as incompatible score ranges across scripts and as worse ordering within a script. Range differences can be corrected exactly with COMET-QN, which enables safe cross-script score comparison while preserving rankings, and a parity-feature regressor can partially restore lost sensitivity. However, biases rooted in the encoder remain irreparable via post-processing. The authors recommend that practitioners always report normalized scores, the three diagnostics, and the tokenizer identity so that users can disentangle translation quality from script effects when interpreting COMET-based evaluations.

title: Does Muon Need Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping?
summary:
Muon combines current and past gradients into matrix momentum. For $M=UΣV^\top$, the idealized polar update $Q=UV^\top$ gives every singular direction the same weight. We refer to this as the flat profile. Several recent optimizers replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that give each direction its own gain. We ask how much of this spectral detail a Muon update needs. Our spectral diagnostics show that approximately $94$--$97\%$ of measured singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with a reference gradient.
  We introduce BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants. The latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko--Pastur reference edge for Muon's Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from the spikes above it. Both variants increase the bulk's relative weight through one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix's unreweighted direction. For a fixed partition, our theory gives the first-order condition under which moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss. It also quantifies the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate, over all per-mode reallocations, that two bands can capture. Across 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia-14M to 410M and six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with the fine-grained power-law profile of Freon and outperforms Spectra. Measured against Muon's flat profile, Freon reduces final loss by $0.022\%$ of the pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of $0.073$--$0.147\%$. These observations suggest that useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BulkBoost, a simple two-band spectral reweighting scheme for the Muon optimizer that shifts weight from spike to bulk singular modes and achieves similar or better gains than more complex fine-grained spectral optimizers.
AI.motivation: Recent matrix-momentum optimizers like Muon traditionally use a flat spectral profile, giving equal weight to all singular directions, while newer methods introduce complex, finely-tuned spectral gains per singular mode. It is unclear how much of this detailed spectral shaping is actually necessary to improve optimization, especially given that most singular modes appear to lie in a noisy bulk yet still align positively with the true gradient. The authors aim to understand whether simpler, low-dimensional spectral modifications can capture most of the benefits of these sophisticated optimizers.
AI.method: The authors first perform spectral diagnostics on Muon’s Nesterov input, estimating a noise edge using random matrix theory (Marchenko–Pastur law) and split-minibatch gradient differences. They show that 94–97% of singular modes fall into a noisy bulk below this edge but still align positively with a reference gradient. They then propose BulkBoost, a two-band reweighting scheme that partitions singular values into bulk (below the edge) and spikes (above it). Both fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants are considered. In each update, BulkBoost increases the relative gain on the bulk via a single bulk-to-spike gain parameter, while preserving the Frobenius norm of the matrix’s unreweighted direction. Theoretical analysis derives a first-order condition under which reallocating weight toward the bulk reduces the loss and quantifies how much of the optimal first-order improvement a two-band scheme can capture compared to arbitrary per-mode reallocations.
AI.result: Empirically, BulkBoost is evaluated in 30 continued-pretraining setups on language models ranging from Pythia-14M to 410M parameters across six corpora. The two-band reweighting variants consistently match or surpass the performance of more complex optimizers such as Freon, which uses a fine-grained power-law spectral profile, and Spectra. Relative to Muon’s flat spectral profile, Freon achieves an average reduction of 0.022% of the pre-adaptation loss, whereas BulkBoost’s two-band variants achieve larger improvements of 0.073–0.147%. These results indicate that a simple two-band spectral reweighting can obtain or exceed the benefits of more detailed spectral shaping.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that effective deviations from Muon’s flat spectral profile are surprisingly low dimensional. Despite most singular modes being in a noisy bulk, boosting this bulk via a single bulk-to-spike gain is both theoretically justified and empirically powerful. A simple two-band spectral reweighting like BulkBoost captures at least as much optimization benefit as finely tuned, per-mode spectral profiles, suggesting that practical matrix-momentum optimizers do not require high-resolution spectral control to achieve strong performance gains.

title: STRUCTURALCOST: A controlled reading time dataset for modeling human sentence processing difficulty
summary: We introduce STRUCTURALCOST, a self-paced reading dataset of 475 participants and 40,800 observations isolating the processing cost of long-distance subject-verb dependency resolution. We replicate a low-powered psycholinguistic finding at NLP scale, namely that human reading times at the main verb increase with dependency length, driven by syntactic embedding beyond linear distance. Different language models -- spanning n-gram models, SSMs, and transformers -- partially mirror this graded difficulty profile, yet underestimate the integration cost humans incur, with a gap that persists across architectures and model sizes. This suggests these models capture the predictive component of human processing but not the full integration cost that working memory imposes. STRUCTURALCOST provides data needed to drive progress toward evaluating the cognitive plausibility of language models.

AI.tldr: The paper presents STRUCTURALCOST, a large self-paced reading dataset for studying how humans process long-distance subject-verb dependencies, and uses it to compare human behavior with various language models.
AI.motivation: Psycholinguistics has shown that longer subject-verb dependencies increase processing difficulty, but prior experiments were low-powered and small-scale. At the same time, NLP language models are increasingly evaluated for cognitive plausibility, yet we lack large, focused datasets that isolate specific processing costs (like long-distance agreement). The authors aim to create a robust, high-powered dataset to (1) validate classic findings about structural integration costs and (2) systematically test whether modern language models exhibit similar graded difficulty patterns as humans.
AI.method: They collect a self-paced reading corpus, STRUCTURALCOST, with 475 human participants and 40,800 reading-time observations targeted at long-distance subject-verb dependencies. The stimuli are designed so that linear distance and structural embedding can be disentangled, letting them isolate the cost of syntactic embedding on main-verb reading times. They then evaluate a range of language models—n-gram models, state-space models (SSMs), and transformers—on the same materials, and derive model-based difficulty measures (e.g., surprisal) to compare with human reading times as dependency length and syntactic embedding vary.
AI.result: Human data replicate a previous psycholinguistic effect: reading times at the main verb increase as subject-verb dependency length grows, and this increase is mainly driven by structural embedding, not just linear distance. Language models show a qualitatively similar graded difficulty pattern, indicating some sensitivity to long-distance dependencies, but they systematically underestimate the magnitude of the integration cost that humans display, and this underestimation remains across different architectures and model sizes.
AI.conclusion: STRUCTURALCOST enables stronger, large-scale testing of theories about the processing costs of long-distance dependencies and provides a benchmark for evaluating the cognitive plausibility of language models. The persistent gap between human and model difficulty profiles suggests that current language models capture predictive aspects of processing but lack mechanisms for the full working-memory-based integration costs humans experience, indicating directions for both cognitive modeling and LM architecture development.

title: MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation
summary: Long-history recommenders often compress each user's history into a compact, candidate-independent memory that is cached and reused to score large candidate pools. We show that real user histories exhibit multi-scale semantic structure, with short-lived intent, medium-term interests, and long-term preferences coexisting in one sequence, and that monolithic cached memories preserve these scales unevenly: linear probes recover recent and mid-range content far worse than long-range content. We call this failure mode \textit{temporal aliasing}. We propose \textbf{MARS}, a multi-resolution user memory that writes the full history into recurrent state tracks anchored to different half-lives, and a sparse routing reader that materializes compact seed memories by selecting the relevant temporal resolutions for each seed, preserving fixed-size candidate scoring. MARS outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains that grow with history length. Component-matched ablations with paired tests show that temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond what hard-window memories or added capacity provide. The advantage of MARS over its interface-matched baseline also widens after within-user behavioral shifts, at about $1.02\times$ that baseline's warm-cache serving latency for $1{,}000$ candidates per user.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a failure mode called temporal aliasing in long-history recommenders and proposes MARS, a multi-resolution user memory that better captures multi-scale user interests for improved recommendation quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing long-history recommender systems compress user histories into a single cached memory, which is then reused to score many candidates. However, real user behavior includes short-term intent, medium-term interests, and long-term preferences, all mixed in one sequence. The authors observe that monolithic cached memories do not preserve these temporal scales evenly, especially failing to represent recent and mid-range content compared to long-range content. This mismatch limits recommendation quality, particularly after behavioral shifts or when user histories are very long.
AI.method: The authors propose MARS, a multi-resolution user memory architecture. It writes the full user history into multiple recurrent state tracks, each anchored to a different temporal half-life, thereby explicitly modeling multiple temporal resolutions. A sparse routing reader then selects which temporal resolutions are most relevant for a given seed (e.g., a query or context) and combines them into a compact, fixed-size seed memory. This allows the system to retain fixed-size candidate scoring while adapting which temporal scales are emphasized per seed. The authors also perform component-matched ablations and paired tests to isolate the impact of temporal diversity and selective routing versus simpler designs like hard temporal windows or merely increasing capacity.
AI.result: Across three public datasets, MARS outperforms strong baseline recommenders, with improvements that become more pronounced as user history length grows. Empirical analyses using linear probes show that monolithic memories suffer from temporal aliasing by underrepresenting recent and mid-range content compared to long-range content, whereas MARS alleviates this. Ablation experiments demonstrate that both temporal diversity (multi-resolution tracks) and selective routing each add value beyond hard-window memories or simply adding more parameters. The benefits of MARS over an interface-matched baseline increase especially after within-user behavioral shifts. The method maintains practical serving performance, achieving these gains at roughly 1.02× the baseline’s warm-cache latency when scoring 1,000 candidates per user.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that temporal aliasing is a significant and previously under-recognized issue in long-history recommender architectures that rely on monolithic cached memories. By explicitly modeling user histories at multiple temporal resolutions and adaptively routing read operations to the most relevant temporal scales, MARS can better preserve and exploit the multi-scale structure of user behavior. This leads to higher recommendation quality, particularly for users with long histories or recent behavioral changes, while maintaining near-baseline serving latency and fixed-size candidate scoring interfaces.

title: Memory Depth and Reconstructed Context Width: A Controlled Evaluation of Hierarchical Retrieval
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the PALM Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Long-term conversational memory is becoming an integral component of modern LLM systems. Proposed architectures group records by topics and events, construct hierarchies and graphs, and connect facts through causal and temporal relations. We experimentally study the interaction between two memory parameters: structural depth and the width of context supplied to the answer model. Using EverMemBench, we evaluate depths D1-D4, core budgets of 1,024/2,048/4,096 tokens, and additional Production and Oracle conditions up to the full archive. Increasing width from 1K to 4K improves Accuracy by 10.11-17.98 percentage points, whereas increasing depth provides no monotonic gain. Beyond 8-16K, Production performance reaches a plateau while tokens per correct answer continue to increase; Oracle preserves quality on full archives of 68-71K tokens. These results motivate further investigation of large, coherent context blocks instead of progressively deeper memory structures.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically analyzes how long-term conversational memory works in LLM systems, focusing on how much structured depth vs. raw context width actually helps question-answering over large archives.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM applications increasingly rely on long-term conversational memory, and many proposed systems add complex structures such as topic hierarchies, event graphs, and causal-temporal links. However, it is unclear how much benefit this growing structural depth provides compared to simply giving the model wider, more contiguous context windows. The authors want to disentangle the impact of memory structural depth from the impact of the size of the context given to the answer model.
AI.method: They use EverMemBench, a benchmark for long-term conversational memory, to systematically vary two parameters: (1) structural depth of the memory architecture (D1–D4) and (2) the width of the context or core budget given to the LLM for answering (1,024 / 2,048 / 4,096 tokens), plus additional Production and Oracle conditions that can extend to the full archive. They then measure accuracy and efficiency (tokens per correct answer) across these settings.
AI.result: Expanding context width from 1K to 4K tokens yields substantial accuracy gains (10.11–17.98 percentage points). In contrast, increasing structural depth does not yield consistent, monotonic improvements. In Production-like settings, performance plateaus once the context window reaches about 8–16K tokens, even though the number of tokens consumed per correct answer continues to grow. Under Oracle conditions, quality can be maintained even when the full archive of 68–71K tokens is supplied.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that simply providing larger, coherent blocks of context is more beneficial than constructing increasingly deep and complex memory structures. Beyond a certain point, deeper structural organization does not translate into better performance, while wider context does—up to a plateau. This motivates reorienting memory system design toward optimizing large-context retrieval and coherence rather than emphasizing hierarchical depth.

title: On Open-Ended Information Seeking for Information Elicitation Agents
summary: Information elicitation is an open-ended information-seeking problem in which an interaction can unfold in many potentially valuable directions, requiring an elicitor to continually determine which information to pursue as new information emerges. In agentic elicitation, these decisions may be delegated to a foundation model, yet how model choice shapes the resulting information-seeking behavior remains understudied. We study how judgments about information value vary across LLMs and how these differences shape sequential information seeking. We first examine these judgments across 11 LLMs spanning multiple model families and parameter scales, using a shared set of information and elicitation objectives. We then develop a controlled elicitation simulation in which different models encounter the same information space and use the same selection rule, isolating these judgments from question generation and respondent behavior. Using this setting, we characterize the breadth-depth behavior that emerges from model-specific information-seeking preferences over the course of elicitation. We further examine how interaction history changes the evaluation and subsequent selection of prospective information. We test the robustness and boundaries of these findings through sensitivity analyses and ablations over the opportunities available to the elicitor, the response labels used to operationalize information-seeking preferences, the presence of interaction history, and whether redundancy is explicitly relevant to the assessment. The project code, data, and trajectory files are available at https://github.com/infosenselab/open-elicitation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different large language models (LLMs) evaluate the value of information and how this shapes their step‑by‑step questioning strategy in open‑ended information elicitation tasks.
AI.motivation: In open‑ended information elicitation, an agent (human or AI) must continually decide what to ask next as new information appears. When this role is delegated to LLMs (agentic elicitation), the specific model used may systematically influence which information is pursued, but these differences and their consequences for sequential questioning are not well understood. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors compare information‑value judgments across 11 LLMs from different families and sizes on a common set of information items and elicitation goals. They then construct a controlled elicitation simulation where all models face the same information space and identical selection rules, so that only their judgments of information value differ. Within this environment, they analyze breadth‑versus‑depth questioning behaviors, how interaction history modifies value assessments, and run sensitivity analyses and ablations that vary: (1) the choice set of information opportunities, (2) the response labels used to encode information‑seeking preferences, (3) whether interaction history is included, and (4) whether redundancy is explicitly part of the evaluation criterion.
AI.result: Different LLMs exhibit systematically different preferences over which pieces of information are valuable, which in turn lead to distinct breadth‑depth elicitation trajectories under the same selection policy. Interaction history changes how models evaluate and prioritize future information. These effects are robust across multiple experimental manipulations, though their strength and form vary depending on the available opportunities, labeling schemes, history usage, and whether redundancy is salient in the task definition.
AI.conclusion: Model choice materially shapes information‑seeking behavior in agentic elicitation: even when models operate under the same rules and environment, their internal valuations of information lead to different questioning strategies over time. Understanding and characterizing these model‑specific information preferences is therefore crucial for designing and controlling LLM‑driven elicitation systems. The authors release code, data, and trajectory logs to support further study.

title: Language Unalignability: Why Some Concepts Resist Cross-Cultural Benchmark Evaluation
comment: Position paper. 32 pages (10 pages main text), 6 figures, 12 tables
summary: Current evaluation of multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) rests on an implicit Translation-Isomorphism Assumption (TIA): that semantic structures across languages are congruent and mutually mappable without loss of information. We argue that this assumption is not merely violated in practice, but ill-posed in principle for a typologically identifiable class of concepts, including pragmatic markers, honorifics, and diachronically stratified terms. We formalize this failure using a usage-cloud framework, representing concepts as point sets of contextualized embeddings. We define $α$-unalignability as the impossibility of any mapping that simultaneously preserves lexical faithfulness (centroid correspondence) and structural faithfulness (local neighborhood topology). We provide three layers of evidence. Behaviorally, we show that FLORES-200 translation failures are predicted by language family and resource class but not by script, and that LOBSTER reasoning scores vary by family. Mechanistically, we report a Representation-Intervention Gap (RIG) in a nine-model case study on Yami: the models' activations encode a regularity along which Yami groups with other low-resource and Austronesian languages, yet interventions on language-specific neurons show no demonstrated advantage over random masks: the regularity is visible but not usable by this intervention. Finally, we operationalize these findings into a multidimensional diagnostic profile: Cycle-Consistency, Pragmatic-Load Disagreement, Manifold-Curvature Mismatch, and RIG. We argue that collapsing cultural competence into a single scalar incentivizes "probabilistic flattening," and that recognizing the unalignable class is a precondition for AI that respects, rather than erases, cultural divergence. This suggests that multilingual alignment is not a single well-defined objective, but a set of mutually incompatible projections.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that standard ways of evaluating multilingual LLMs rely on a flawed assumption that meanings are perfectly translatable across languages, and shows both theoretically and empirically that some culturally grounded concepts are fundamentally unalignable, proposing new diagnostics and a multidimensional view of multilingual alignment.
AI.motivation: Most multilingual LLM evaluation benchmarks and alignment schemes assume that all languages encode the same underlying semantic structures such that they can be mapped to each other without loss. The authors believe this Translation-Isomorphism Assumption fails for many real-world linguistic phenomena (e.g., pragmatics, honorifics, culture-specific concepts), which leads to misleading evaluations and encourages models that wash out cultural differences. They want to formalize and empirically demonstrate these failures, and propose a more realistic framework for assessing multilingual and cultural competence in LLMs.
AI.method: Concepts are modeled as usage-clouds: sets of contextualized embedding points that capture how words are used in context. Within this framework, the authors define α-unalignability: the impossibility of constructing a mapping between languages that simultaneously preserves lexical faithfulness (alignment of concept centroids) and structural faithfulness (conservation of local neighborhood topology). They then provide three empirical lines of evidence. (1) Behavioral analyses: they examine FLORES-200 translation errors and LOBSTER multilingual reasoning scores, correlating performance with language family, resource level, and script. (2) Mechanistic analyses: a nine-model case study on Yami (a low-resource Austronesian language), where they inspect internal activations and perform neuron-level interventions to test whether encoded cross-language regularities are causally usable. (3) They aggregate findings into a practical diagnostic profile with dimensions like Cycle-Consistency, Pragmatic-Load Disagreement, Manifold-Curvature Mismatch, and the Representation-Intervention Gap.
AI.result: They show theoretically that a class of typologically identifiable concepts—such as pragmatic markers, honorifics, and historically layered lexical strata—cannot be made mutually isomorphic across languages under a single mapping that preserves both lexical and structural faithfulness; these are α-unalignable. Empirically, they find: (1) FLORES-200 translation failures correlate with language family and resource class, but not with script, and LOBSTER reasoning performance also varies systematically by language family. (2) In Yami, model activations consistently group Yami with other low-resource and Austronesian languages along a latent dimension, indicating that these regularities are represented; however, neuron-level interventions based on language specificity do not improve performance over random interventions, revealing a Representation-Intervention Gap. (3) The proposed multidimensional diagnostic metrics reveal that multilingual performance and cultural competence decompose into distinct, sometimes conflicting, factors, rather than a single scalar of alignment quality.
AI.conclusion: The Translation-Isomorphism Assumption underpinning many multilingual LLM evaluations is conceptually ill-posed for an important class of culturally and typologically grounded concepts. Because some semantic structures are α-unalignable, multilingual alignment cannot be reduced to a single objective or score; attempts to do so promote "probabilistic flattening" that erases meaningful cultural divergences. The authors argue for treating multilingual competence as a vector of partially incompatible projections, measured via a multidimensional diagnostic profile (including cycle-consistency, pragmatic-load disagreement, manifold-curvature mismatch, and RIG), as a prerequisite to building AI systems that acknowledge and preserve, rather than homogenize, cross-linguistic and cultural diversity.

title: From Local Evidence to Safety Verdicts: Causal Tracing in Vision-Language Models
summary: A vision-language model may need to combine an image with a prompt to recognize a safety risk that neither reveals alone. Where does this joint safety judgment become accessible inside the model? We introduce SSU-Bench, a dataset of matched safe and unsafe image-text combinations constructed using single-item prompt edits or image edits with annotated intended regions. Using three vision-language models, we transfer internal states between paired inputs and measure the resulting change in the safety verdict. Across models and both types of counterfactual, interventions at the changed input positions are effective in earlier decoder layers, while interventions at the final input token become effective later. Directions estimated from other examples produce similar late-layer effects. A linear readout of the final-token state also predicts the model's own verdict, including incorrect judgments, and cross-model comparisons reveal similarities in the patterns of counterfactual change. These findings identify a recurring transition in where interventions can influence a joint safety verdict and distinguish a readable model decision from a correct safety judgment.

AI.tldr: The paper probes where and how multimodal safety judgments (over image + text) arise inside vision-language models, using a new benchmark and causal interventions on internal activations.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models can miss safety risks that only appear when combining an image with a prompt. To improve safety and interpretability, we need to know where in the network this joint safety judgment is formed, and whether it is linearly readable, transferable, and manipulable via internal interventions.
AI.method: They build SSU-Bench: pairs of safe/unsafe image-text inputs differing by minimal edits in the text or image, with annotated regions. Using three vision-language models, they perform activation steering / causal tracing by transferring internal states between the paired safe/unsafe inputs at specific tokens or visual positions and at different layers. They then measure how the model’s safety verdict changes. They also estimate shared “safety directions” from other examples and train a linear probe on final-token states to predict the model’s own verdict, and compare effects across models.
AI.result: Intervening on activations at the edited positions affects safety judgments mainly in early decoder layers, whereas intervening at the final input token becomes effective later in the network. Safety directions estimated from other data also influence verdicts, but primarily in late layers. A linear readout from the final token reliably predicts the model’s safety decision, including when that decision is wrong. Different models show similar structural patterns in how counterfactual activations change the verdict.
AI.conclusion: Joint image-text safety judgments emerge via a characteristic transition: localized edits matter early, while global, final-token representations control the verdict later. The final-token state contains a linearly decodable representation of the model’s decision, but this “readable” decision need not match the correct safety label. This clarifies where safety-relevant information resides in vision-language models and separates interpretability of the decision from its normative correctness.

title: Foresight-over-Graph: Reasoning Beyond Local Horizons for Knowledge Base Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in question answering, yet they still frequently suffer from hallucinations on knowledge-intensive tasks. Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide LLMs with structured, interpretable, and updatable factual grounding, making them a promising external knowledge source for reliable reasoning. However, existing LLM-guided graph reasoning methods typically rely on hop-wise greedy or beam-style pruning during evidence retrieval. Such local decision processes are inherently myopic: evidence that appears weak near the source may become crucial only after deeper graph context is explored, causing answer-critical branches to be discarded prematurely and making the reasoning chain difficult to recover. To address this limitation, we propose Foresight-over-Graph (FoG), a foresight-aware evidence retrieval framework for knowledge base question answering (KBQA). FoG iteratively constructs a question-relevant evidence subgraph and uses far-to-near feedback to guide path exploration, and maintains a compact memory subgraph to support continued exploration. Extensive experiments on widely used KBQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG achieves state-of-the-art performance, with a particularly large improvement of 16.58% in Hit on CWQ, while also reducing LLM calls and token usage. Our code is available at https://github.com/yhong7/FoG .

AI.tldr: FoG is a foresight-aware evidence retrieval framework that lets LLMs reason over knowledge graphs more accurately and efficiently, avoiding myopic pruning and achieving state-of-the-art KBQA performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs hallucinate on knowledge-intensive tasks because they lack reliable factual grounding and existing LLM-guided graph reasoning methods rely on locally greedy or beam-style hop-wise pruning. This myopic retrieval discards potentially crucial evidence paths early, harming answer accuracy and making reasoning chains hard to recover. The authors aim to design a KG-based retrieval method that can look ahead in the graph and retain globally important evidence while keeping reasoning efficient and interpretable.
AI.method: The authors propose Foresight-over-Graph (FoG), a foresight-aware evidence retrieval framework for knowledge base question answering. FoG iteratively builds a question-relevant evidence subgraph rather than following only locally promising paths. It introduces a far-to-near feedback mechanism: information gleaned from deeper or more distant parts of the graph is propagated back to guide earlier path selection, reducing myopic pruning. FoG also maintains a compact memory subgraph to store and organize explored evidence so that the LLM can continue exploration efficiently with fewer calls and tokens. The overall pipeline alternates between subgraph expansion and feedback-guided refinement to construct a high-quality reasoning subgraph for the final answer prediction.
AI.result: On multiple standard KBQA benchmarks, FoG achieves state-of-the-art results. In particular, it obtains a substantial improvement of 16.58% in Hit on the CWQ dataset compared with prior methods. At the same time, FoG lowers the number of LLM calls and total token usage, indicating that its foresight-guided retrieval is not only more accurate but also more resource-efficient.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating foresight into KG-based evidence retrieval helps LLMs avoid myopic reasoning, preserve globally important paths, and improve KBQA performance. FoG’s iterative evidence subgraph construction with far-to-near feedback and a compact memory subgraph yields state-of-the-art accuracy while reducing computational cost, suggesting that foresight-aware graph exploration is an effective direction for reliable and efficient LLM reasoning over knowledge graphs.

title: Grounding What Shapes the Plan: Rethinking Groundedness for Physical Intelligence in Autonomous Driving
summary: Driving models increasingly ground reasoning in causal relations, spatial structure, perceptual evidence, and predicted futures. These advances make reasoning more faithful to the driving scene, but leave a fundamental question unresolved: what should groundedness mean when the model ultimately outputs an action? Correctly grounded reasoning does not, by itself, ensure desirable driving outcomes. We introduce GroundAct, which starts from a simple premise: driving unfolds through physical entities and their interactions. Entities therefore become the unit of grounding; a lightweight reference token keeps each selected entity's continuous state addressable through symbolic reasoning; and only the referenced entities' interactions with the evolving proposal correct the plan. The result is an explicit path from what reasoning grounds to what the plan does, which we call grounded planning. To assess its practical value, we evaluate GroundAct in both open- and closed-loop settings. GroundAct shows strong open-loop planning across normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical scenarios, with closed-loop results extending this evidence to driving in simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GroundAct, a grounded planning framework for autonomous driving that links reasoning about entities in the scene directly to action selection, improving performance in both simulated and open-loop evaluations, including safety-critical and out-of-distribution scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing driving models have become better at grounding their reasoning in causal relations, spatial structure, perception, and future predictions, but there is a gap between such internal reasoning and the final driving actions. Correct reasoning about a scene does not necessarily translate into safe or desirable driving behavior. The authors aim to define and implement a notion of groundedness that extends all the way to the actual plan and executed actions.
AI.method: The authors introduce GroundAct, which treats physical entities in the driving scene (e.g., vehicles, pedestrians, obstacles) as the core units of grounding. For each selected entity, a lightweight reference token is maintained so that its continuous state (position, velocity, etc.) remains accessible for symbolic reasoning. The planning process only allows the referenced entities and their interactions with the evolving proposal to modify or correct the current action plan. This creates an explicit link from the entities used in reasoning to the concrete driving actions (grounded planning).
AI.result: GroundAct is evaluated in both open-loop (plan generation without controlling the full system) and closed-loop (controlling a simulated vehicle over time) settings. It demonstrates strong open-loop planning performance under normal driving conditions, out-of-distribution situations, and safety-critical scenarios. Closed-loop experiments in simulation further validate that the benefits of GroundAct’s grounded planning translate into effective, desirable driving behavior over time.
AI.conclusion: By making entities and their interactions the explicit basis of grounding, GroundAct provides a clear pathway from scene understanding and reasoning to actual driving plans. This grounded planning framework not only clarifies what it means for actions to be grounded but also yields strong empirical performance in challenging driving scenarios, suggesting it is a promising direction for more reliable autonomous driving systems.

title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Cross-Domain and Multi-Turn Generalization of Latent Underspecification Signals
summary: Large language models routinely answer questions that cannot be answered from the information given, and in dialogue they answer before enough has been said. Unanswerability is linearly decodable from hidden states, but it is unclear which of its forms share a representation and whether the signal is useful in dialogue. We contribute a turn-labeled multi-turn benchmark (423 conversations, 1,661 labeled turn-states) and an evaluation harness with a simulated user who answers clarifying questions, and use them with six datasets and six open-weight LLMs to test how far probes for unanswerability carry. Probes transfer robustly between datasets that share a ground of unanswerability: missing information in math (AUROC 0.77-0.97) and in a passage (SQuAD 2.0<->MuSiQue, 0.77-0.90). Probes for epistemic "known-unknowns" transfer poorly to math, but this separation weakens under lexical controls and changes with layer and coordinate system, so it remains unresolved. Single-turn probes fail zero-shot to detect when a conversation becomes answerable; in-structure probes recover it, but no better than a bag-of-words classifier. A gate on the calibrated probe, with no model fine-tuning, fires on underspecified turns far more precisely than chance, and its end-task success comes within 0.08 of a gate given the true labels. Yet across four models it does not reliably beat vanilla generation or prompted consolidation. The remaining gap lies mostly in how models use a clarification, not in detection.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether large language models internally represent when a question is unanswerable, how that generalizes across tasks, and whether that signal can be used in dialogue to avoid hallucinations.
AI.motivation: LLMs often answer questions even when necessary information is missing, leading to hallucinations and premature answers in dialogue. Prior work showed that unanswerability is linearly decodable from hidden states in some settings, but it is unknown which kinds of unanswerability share representations, how robust these signals are across tasks, and whether they help models decide when to ask clarifying questions instead of answering.
AI.method: The authors build a turn-labeled multi-turn benchmark of 423 conversations with 1,661 labeled turn-states indicating answerability vs. unanswerability. They create an evaluation harness with a simulated user who responds to clarifying questions. Using six datasets and six open-weight LLMs, they train linear probes on model hidden states to predict unanswerability and test transfer across tasks involving different grounds for unanswerability (e.g., missing math info, missing passage info, epistemic unknowns). They compare single-turn vs. structure-aware probes, examine effects of layer and representation basis, and evaluate gating strategies that use calibrated probe scores to decide whether the model should answer or ask for clarification, without fine-tuning the base LLM.
AI.result: Probes trained on one dataset transfer well to others when the underlying cause of unanswerability is similar (e.g., missing problem information in math tasks with AUROC 0.77-0.97; missing passage information between SQuAD 2.0 and MuSiQue with AUROC 0.77-0.90). Probes that target epistemic known-unknowns do not transfer well to math tasks, though this distinction becomes blurrier when controlling for lexical cues and varies across layers and coordinate systems. Single-turn probes cannot zero-shot detect when a multi-turn conversation has become answerable, but probes that incorporate conversation structure can, performing comparably to a bag-of-words baseline. A calibrated probe-based gating mechanism identifies underspecified turns far better than chance and achieves task performance within 0.08 of an oracle gate that uses ground-truth labels, but across four models this does not consistently outperform standard generation or prompted consolidation baselines. The main limitation appears to be in how models use clarifications, not in detecting unanswerability.
AI.conclusion: LLMs contain decodable internal signals about question unanswerability that generalize across tasks sharing a similar type of missing information. These signals can support reasonably accurate gating to detect underspecified dialogue turns without fine-tuning. However, distinctions between different kinds of unanswerability remain murky, and leveraging the signal in practice is limited by models’ poor use of clarification information rather than by detection quality itself. Improving how models integrate clarifications may be more impactful than further refining unanswerability probes alone.

title: A Systematic Investigation of Bias in Large Language Models for Advertising Relevance
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to judge how well an advertisement matches a query, but the fairness of these judgments has received limited attention. We conduct a systematic study of fairness in relevance judgments made by LLMs for queries and advertisements. Our counterfactual framework examines the effects of advertiser identity and possible popularity, input language, and demographic wording. We study GPT-4o as a categorical relevance judge and a Qwen-7B model trained specifically for relevance prediction. The advertiser and language experiments use query and advertisement pairs sampled from real advertising logs. Controlled synthetic queries are used to study demographic associations in employment, housing, and credit. For both models, changing the advertiser identity or input language can alter the relevance assessment. Selected demographic comparisons also show patterns consistent with common stereotypes, particularly those involving gender and occupation. We further study mitigation during model inference and training. The results indicate that its effectiveness depends on whether advertiser information is relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are distributed in the training data. These findings can help advertising practitioners identify fairness risks and develop suitable mitigation methods for LLM relevance systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes fairness in how large language models judge the relevance of ads to queries, showing that judgments can change with advertiser identity, language, and demographic wording, and evaluating mitigation strategies.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed to automatically judge how well ads match user queries, their potential unfairness or bias can systematically disadvantage certain advertisers or demographic groups, yet this fairness aspect has been understudied. The authors aim to fill this gap and provide guidance for safer use of LLM-based relevance systems in advertising.
AI.method: The authors design a counterfactual evaluation framework where they vary factors such as advertiser identity and popularity proxies, input language, and demographic wording while holding the underlying information need constant. They test two models: GPT-4o used as a categorical relevance judge and a specialized Qwen-7B model fine-tuned for relevance prediction. Real-world ad log data is used to analyze advertiser and language effects, while controlled synthetic queries in domains like employment, housing, and credit probe demographic associations and stereotypes. They then explore mitigation strategies applied both at inference time and during model training, and analyze how effectiveness depends on the relevance of advertiser information and its distribution in the training data.
AI.result: The study finds that both GPT-4o and the fine-tuned Qwen-7B model exhibit variability in relevance judgments when only advertiser identity or the input language is changed, even when the actual query–ad content is equivalent. Demographic wording experiments reveal patterns consistent with known stereotypes, especially related to gender and occupation. Mitigation techniques can reduce some unfair patterns, but their success is contingent on whether advertiser information is actually relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are represented in training data; in some cases, mitigation may be limited or uneven.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based ad relevance systems are vulnerable to fairness issues driven by advertiser identity, language, and demographic wording, which can manifest as biased or stereotype-consistent relevance scores. While mitigation strategies at inference and training time can help, they are not universally effective and depend on data distributions and task structure. The authors conclude that practitioners should explicitly evaluate fairness when deploying LLM relevance judges and carefully design mitigation approaches tailored to their specific ad ecosystems.

title: Rethinking Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation: From Alignment Coverage to Supervision Reliability
summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations using teacher feedback. With different tokenizers, comparing teacher and student predictions requires alignment at both sequence and vocabulary levels. In this paper, we examine whether expanding this alignment coverage improves learning. Across three heterogeneous teacher--student pairs on mathematical reasoning and code generation, strict 1:1 groups already cover most student-generated tokens despite substantial vocabulary mismatch. On responses sampled from the students before distillation, the shared vocabulary retains nearly all teacher and student probability mass at strictly aligned positions on average. Restricting reverse KL to a student-selected top-16 subset of the shared vocabulary at each strict position achieves accuracy comparable to full shared-vocabulary OPD, outperforming the evaluated cross-tokenizer baselines. Adding mean squared error supervision on span log-probabilities in mismatch groups gives complete supervision coverage, yet reduces accuracy. At checkpoints from training with only the strict loss, the span gradients show weak or negative directional agreement with the strict gradients and grow in magnitude relative to them. These diagnostics may help explain the accuracy drop from adding span supervision. Our findings motivate a shift from maximizing alignment coverage to prioritizing supervision reliability: compact supervision at strict positions can be more effective than broader coverage that introduces weakly aligned or conflicting training signals.

AI.tldr: The paper studies cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) and finds that small, strictly aligned supervision over shared tokens is often sufficient and more reliable than attempting full coverage via looser span-based alignment, which can hurt performance.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation lets a student model learn from a teacher’s feedback on the student’s own outputs, but when teacher and student use different tokenizers, it is unclear how best to align their predictions. Prior work aimed to maximize coverage across vocabularies and spans, assuming more alignment is better. The authors question this assumption and investigate whether broad but noisy alignment or compact but reliable alignment is more effective for learning in settings like math reasoning and code generation.
AI.method: They study three heterogeneous teacher–student LLM pairs with different tokenizers on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. They analyze token-level coverage of strictly aligned 1:1 token groups between teacher and student vocabularies on student-generated responses. They then implement OPD with reverse KL restricted to: (1) the full shared vocabulary at strictly aligned positions, and (2) a student-selected top-16 subset of the shared vocabulary at those positions. They compare these to baselines requiring cross-tokenizer handling. To increase coverage, they additionally introduce a mean squared error loss on span log-probabilities for mismatched-token groups and inspect the resulting gradient directions and magnitudes relative to the strict-loss gradients over the course of training.
AI.result: They find that despite significant tokenizer differences, strict 1:1 token groups already cover most tokens produced by the student, and at these positions the shared vocabulary captures almost all probability mass for both teacher and student. Limiting reverse KL to a top-16 subset of shared-vocabulary tokens at strictly aligned positions yields accuracy comparable to using the full shared vocabulary and better than evaluated cross-tokenizer baselines. Introducing span-level MSE supervision on mismatched-token groups achieves full coverage but consistently reduces task accuracy. Gradient analysis at checkpoints shows that span-loss gradients have weak or even negative alignment with the strict-loss gradients and grow larger in norm, suggesting the additional supervision introduces conflicting or noisy signals.
AI.conclusion: Maximizing alignment coverage across different tokenizers in OPD is not necessarily beneficial. High-quality, compact supervision on strictly aligned shared-vocabulary tokens is often sufficient and can outperform methods that pursue full coverage through looser span-based alignment. Added span-level supervision, while covering more tokens, can introduce misaligned gradients and harm accuracy. The authors argue that future work on cross-tokenizer distillation should prioritize the reliability and alignment of supervision signals rather than simply increasing the fraction of tokens or spans covered.

title: Decoupled Multi-Agent Orchestration
summary: Learned orchestration can automatically construct effective language-model multi-agent systems, but existing approaches couple planning to fixed worker pools and train decomposition and collaboration from the same terminal outcome, limiting transfer and obscuring credit assignment. We introduce DeOrch, which separates worker-agnostic planning from concrete worker selection. Its two-stage planner first decomposes the task without worker information, then chooses collaboration operations using compact, worker-identity-free matchability feedback from the pool, enabling conditional credit assignment to decomposition and collaboration decisions. A lightweight matcher estimates worker suitability from behavior on a fixed probe set and adapts online with a contextual bandit, allowing new workers to be incorporated without retraining the planner or matcher.
