Across diverse in- and out-of-distribution tasks, DeOrch outperforms prior automatic MAS orchestration methods with fewer worker calls than competing learned orchestrators, remains effective when transferred to an entirely unseen worker pool without retraining, and shows consistent gains from both components.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DeOrch, a two-stage, worker-agnostic orchestration framework for language-model multi-agent systems that separates task decomposition from worker selection and generalizes to new worker pools with fewer calls and better performance than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing learned orchestration approaches for language-model multi-agent systems tightly couple planning to a specific, fixed pool of workers. They also learn both task decomposition and collaboration behavior only from final task outcomes. This coupling limits the ability to transfer a planner across different worker pools and makes it difficult to assign credit separately to decomposition quality and collaboration choices, hindering robustness and scalability.
AI.method: DeOrch introduces a two-stage, worker-agnostic planner. In the first stage, the planner decomposes the task without using any information about specific workers. In the second stage, it selects collaboration operations (e.g., which workers to involve and how) based on compact, worker-identity-free matchability feedback from the worker pool. A lightweight matcher module estimates each worker’s suitability by observing behavior on a fixed probe set and updates online via a contextual bandit algorithm. This design allows the planner to remain independent of concrete worker identities and enables conditional credit assignment to the separate decomposition and collaboration decisions.
AI.result: On a variety of both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, DeOrch surpasses previous automatic multi-agent orchestration systems. It achieves higher performance while using fewer worker calls than competing learned orchestrators. Furthermore, DeOrch maintains strong effectiveness when transferred to completely unseen worker pools without any retraining, and ablation-style evidence indicates that both the worker-agnostic decomposition and the adaptive matcher components contribute consistently to these gains.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling task decomposition from worker-specific collaboration and representing worker suitability through identity-free matchability signals enables robust, transferable orchestration of language-model multi-agent systems. DeOrch demonstrates that a worker-agnostic two-stage planner combined with a lightweight, online-adapting matcher can reduce resource usage, improve performance, and generalize across different worker pools, addressing key limitations of prior orchestration methods.

title: Agentic AutoRAG: RAG Pipeline Optimization through Reasoning-Driven Agents
comment: Accepted at the Second Workshop for REsearch on Agent Language Models (REALM) at EMNLP 2026 and at the Machine Learning for Systems Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 9 pages plus references and appendix (16 pages total), 4 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/Agentic-Systems-Lab/Agentic-AutoRAG
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a widely used approach for grounding large language models (LLMs) in external knowledge. However, configuring a pipeline is an expensive hyperparameter optimization problem over many interacting choices, from chunking and embedding model to reranking and generation. Existing optimizers, from greedy search to Bayesian optimization, reduce each trial to an aggregate score and search without modeling why a configuration performed as it did, even though the retrieved chunks already provide evidence about whether each failure occurred during retrieval or after it. We introduce Agentic AutoRAG, an LLM-agent optimizer for multi-objective RAG hyperparameter optimization with retrieval-versus-generation failure attribution. It proposes configurations scored on a frozen exam from the corpus: after each trial a Diagnoser attributes each failed question to retrieval or generation, and a Proposer, grounded in a knowledge base of model rankings and pricing, selects the next configuration, weighing accuracy against cost to trace a Pareto frontier. On three multi-hop QA benchmarks it reaches higher LLM-judge accuracy than every baseline we compare, and within its first 10 trials it matches or beats the statistical baselines' full 30-trial judge accuracy. In its cost-aware mode on a real-world healthcare corpus it reaches a median exam accuracy of 77%, above the strongest baseline's 71.5%, at about 58% of that baseline's cost per query, and it matches that 71.5% at about 22% of the cost.

AI.tldr: Agentic AutoRAG uses an LLM-based agent to automatically tune and reason about RAG pipelines, outperforming standard hyperparameter search in both accuracy and cost-efficiency.
AI.motivation: Building an effective RAG pipeline requires tuning many interdependent choices (chunking, retriever, reranker, generator, etc.), which is expensive and typically treated as a black-box optimization problem. Existing methods optimize only an aggregate score and do not explicitly separate retrieval errors from generation errors, even though the retrieved chunks already contain clues about what went wrong. There is also a practical need to jointly optimize for both accuracy and cost in real-world deployments.
AI.method: The authors design Agentic AutoRAG, an LLM-agent-based optimizer for RAG hyperparameters. The system runs over a fixed exam-style evaluation set built from the target corpus. For each configuration trial, the pipeline is executed and a Diagnoser LLM examines failed questions, classifying each failure as caused by retrieval or generation. A Proposer LLM then uses this diagnostic feedback, along with a knowledge base containing prior rankings and prices of models and components, to suggest the next RAG configuration. The search is explicitly multi-objective, balancing accuracy against query cost to approximate the Pareto frontier of configurations.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks, Agentic AutoRAG achieves higher LLM-judge accuracy than all compared baselines, including greedy and Bayesian optimization approaches. It reaches or surpasses the baselines’ 30-trial accuracy within only 10 trials. In a cost-sensitive setting on a real healthcare corpus, it attains a median exam accuracy of 77%, outperforming the best baseline’s 71.5%, while incurring only about 58% of that baseline’s per-query cost. When constrained to match the baseline accuracy of 71.5%, it can do so at roughly 22% of the baseline cost.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning-driven, agentic optimization of RAG—explicitly attributing failures to retrieval vs. generation and jointly considering accuracy and monetary cost—can discover better, more efficient configurations than standard black-box hyperparameter search. Agentic AutoRAG shows that LLMs themselves can be used as optimization agents over complex RAG design spaces, rapidly approaching the Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. cost in both benchmark and real-world domains.

title: Navigating Route Latent Space for Synthesizable Molecular Design
summary: Goal-directed molecular design has advanced rapidly, yet a substantial proportion of designed molecules remain difficult to synthesize in practice, limiting their real-world utility. Prior synthesizability-aware methods either project generated molecules back to synthesizable analogs that deviate from the intended target, or optimize directly in discrete synthesis spaces that lack a continuous landscape for efficient search. We argue that this limitation mainly comes from the search space rather than the optimizer. To address this, we propose RouteFlow, a framework that reformulates synthesizable molecular design as a search over a continuous route latent space, where each latent maps back to a complete synthesis route and synthesizability is inherently preserved. To navigate this space, we adopt reward-guided flow matching as an efficient sampler that steers toward high-property regions. Since reward optimization may push latents off the manifold of real synthesis routes, where decoding becomes unreliable, we further introduce a cycle-consistency mechanism to stabilize fine-tuning. Across 16 optimization tasks from Therapeutic Data Commons, RouteFlow achieves the best sample efficiency among synthesizability-aware baselines, with the best synthetic accessibility and the highest retrosynthesis success rate. Our results also confirm that the proposed cycle-consistency reliably keeps optimization on-manifold while improving target properties, supporting effective synthesizable molecular discovery.

AI.tldr: RouteFlow introduces a continuous latent space over synthesis routes and uses reward-guided flow matching plus cycle-consistency to efficiently design molecules that are both high-performing and synthesizable.
AI.motivation: Many goal-directed molecular design methods propose molecules that are hard or impossible to synthesize, which limits their practical value. Existing synthesizability-aware approaches either alter designed molecules into nearby synthesizable analogs—losing fidelity to the original design—or perform optimization directly in discrete synthesis spaces, which are combinatorial and lack smooth structure for efficient search. The authors argue the main bottleneck is the search space formulation rather than the optimization algorithm itself, motivating a new representation that is continuous yet always decodes to valid synthesis routes.
AI.method: The authors introduce RouteFlow, which represents synthesizable molecular design as optimization in a continuous latent space of synthesis routes. Each latent corresponds to a full synthetic route that can be decoded, so synthesizability is built in. They employ reward-guided flow matching as the generative mechanism, steering sampling toward regions in latent space associated with high target properties (e.g., biological activity). Since aggressive reward optimization can push latent points off the manifold where decoding corresponds to realistic routes, they add a cycle-consistency mechanism: latents are decoded to routes and then re-encoded, enforcing consistency to keep them on-manifold and stabilize fine-tuning.
AI.result: On 16 molecular optimization benchmarks from the Therapeutic Data Commons, RouteFlow outperforms synthesizability-aware baselines in sample efficiency, achieves better synthetic accessibility scores, and attains the highest retrosynthesis success rate. Empirical results also show that the cycle-consistency mechanism effectively constrains optimization to remain close to the manifold of valid synthesis routes while still improving task-specific molecular properties.
AI.conclusion: RouteFlow provides a new continuous search space over synthesis routes that inherently guarantees synthesizability, and combines it with reward-guided flow matching and cycle-consistency to efficiently discover high-quality, synthesizable molecules. The framework addresses the limitations of discrete synthesis optimization and post-hoc projection methods, and demonstrates superior performance across multiple realistic drug discovery tasks, indicating its promise for practical synthesizable molecular design.

title: UNREAL: Unifying Retrieval and Long-Context with a Single Model
summary: Long-context inference and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) handle evidence selection at vastly different scales, from a single long prompt to an entire corpus. We ask whether a single model-internal mechanism can select evidence across this range. We introduce UNifying REtrieval And Long-Context with a Single Model (UNREAL), a model-native evidence selection framework to span corpus retrieval and long-context inference. UNREAL encodes chunks and derives retrieval queries directly from the frozen LLM's internal representations. It adds fewer than 500K trainable parameters and leaves the backbone unchanged. On a 3B-token, 21M-chunk Wikipedia index, all four dense and hybrid UNREAL backbones outperform state-of-the-art retriever-reranker systems. The best model raises recall from 49.1% to 73.2% on HotpotQA, from 31.7% to 60.1% on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and from 8.8% to 14.4% on MuSiQue. Applied to long-context tasks, the same selection mechanism removes distractors before generation, raising NoLiMa accuracy from 1.0% to 24.83% at its maximum context length of 128K tokens, and LV-Eval's F1 score from 49.97% to 54.66% at 256K. UNREAL also reduces FLOPs and time-to-first-token relative to full-context inference from roughly 32K tokens onward, with larger gains as context grows. Together, these results establish model-internal evidence selection as a common foundation for corpus retrieval and evidence-sparse long-context inference.

AI.tldr: UNREAL is a lightweight, model-internal evidence selection mechanism that unifies corpus-scale retrieval and long-context filtering, improving recall, long-context accuracy, and efficiency without changing the base LLM.
AI.motivation: Existing systems treat corpus retrieval (RAG) and long-context inference as separate problems, even though both require selecting relevant evidence from large input spaces. Traditional retrievers are external to the LLM and long-context models often waste computation on irrelevant tokens, especially at extreme context lengths. The authors aim to create a single, LLM-native mechanism that can select evidence both from huge document corpora and from very long prompts, improving effectiveness and efficiency while minimally modifying the base model.
AI.method: They propose UNREAL, a model-native framework that uses the frozen LLM’s internal representations to both encode document chunks and derive retrieval queries. A small set of additional parameters (fewer than 500K) is trained while keeping the backbone LLM fixed. The same mechanism is used in two regimes: (1) corpus retrieval, where it indexes and retrieves from a large Wikipedia corpus (3B tokens, 21M chunks) in dense or hybrid configurations; and (2) long-context inference, where it scores and filters context chunks to remove distractors before feeding the reduced context to the generator. They evaluate on multi-hop QA benchmarks and long-context benchmarks, while also measuring compute efficiency (FLOPs and latency).
AI.result: On corpus retrieval, all UNREAL-based dense and hybrid retrievers outperform state-of-the-art retriever–reranker pipelines on a large Wikipedia index. The best UNREAL variant dramatically boosts retrieval recall: from 49.1% to 73.2% on HotpotQA, 31.7% to 60.1% on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and 8.8% to 14.4% on MuSiQue. On long-context benchmarks, using the same selection mechanism to prune distractors before generation significantly improves performance: NoLiMa accuracy increases from 1.0% to 24.83% at 128K tokens, and LV-Eval F1 rises from 49.97% to 54.66% at 256K tokens. UNREAL also reduces FLOPs and time-to-first-token once contexts exceed roughly 32K tokens, with larger savings for longer contexts.
AI.conclusion: A single, lightweight evidence selection mechanism embedded in the LLM can effectively unify corpus-scale retrieval and long-context input filtering. By leveraging internal representations of a frozen backbone and training fewer than 500K additional parameters, UNREAL achieves superior retrieval quality and better long-context task performance while improving computational efficiency at large context lengths. This supports the view that model-internal evidence selection can serve as a common foundation for both RAG and evidence-scarce long-context inference, reducing the need for separate specialized components.

title: Unanimously Wrong: Certified Abstention from How Medical LLM Consensus Forms
comment: Accepted at the GenAI4Health Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: In clinical practice, agreement among independent experts is treated as evidence of reliability, and multi-round consensus has become a core mechanism of agentic medical question-answering systems. When such a system must decide whether to trust its own answer, the prevailing signal is again agreement, now among the sampled answers. But agreement is a fragile proxy for correctness. A system can be unanimously wrong, returning the same incorrect answer on every sample, and on these questions agreement-based signals carry no information. The cause is that these signals read only the final state of the consensus and discard how it was reached. Agreement that was reached by resolving disagreement with evidence looks identical, at the end, to agreement that was present from the first sample because every sample shares one misconception. ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework that bases the abstention decision on how the consensus formed. Process features trace agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation. For unanimous votes, rationale semantic entropy checks whether the reasons behind the vote cohere, and an active probe retrieves counter-evidence and measures whether the consensus survives. A stratified Learn-then-Test calibration then converts these scores into a distribution-free bound on selective risk. We evaluate ProbeGuard on three medical QA benchmarks and a hard-frontier reference, with a published multi-round agentic RAG substrate, against six abstention baselines. On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong, and no agreement-based signal can flag them. Process signals raise the discrimination of correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers six in ten unanimous-layer questions at an observed selective risk of 9.0%, and nine in ten once in-domain calibration data accumulate.

AI.tldr: ProbeGuard is a framework that decides when a medical QA system should abstain by analyzing how expert-like consensus is formed, not just whether answers agree, and provides certified risk bounds for those abstentions.
AI.motivation: In medical QA, systems often rely on agreement among multiple agents or samples as a proxy for correctness. However, agreement can be misleading because a system can be confidently and unanimously wrong, especially when all samples share the same misconception. Existing abstention or confidence methods that only look at final agreement cannot distinguish between robustly justified consensus and uniform error. There is a need for a method that looks at the process by which consensus forms and can provide formal guarantees on the risk of the answers it chooses not to abstain on.
AI.method: The paper introduces ProbeGuard, a certified abstention framework. Instead of only using final agreement, ProbeGuard extracts process features that capture how consensus evolves across multiple rounds: agreement trajectories, persistence of minority opinions, and retrieval saturation in a multi-round agentic RAG setting. For cases with unanimous votes, it measures rationale semantic entropy to assess whether the underlying reasons are coherent. It also runs an active probe step that retrieves potential counter-evidence and tests whether the consensus survives this challenge. These scores are then fed into a stratified Learn-then-Test calibration procedure that produces a distribution-free upper bound on the selective risk (error rate on non-abstained predictions).
AI.result: On three medical QA benchmarks and a hard-frontier reference dataset, using an existing multi-round agentic RAG system as the base, ProbeGuard is compared to six abstention baselines. On MedQA, the authors find that 13.4% of unanimously agreed answers are in fact wrong, and that purely agreement-based signals cannot identify them. Incorporating process features raises the AUROC for distinguishing correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696. The certified abstention rule can answer about 60% of questions that reach unanimous consensus while keeping the observed selective risk at 9.0%, and with more in-domain calibration data it can answer about 90% of such questions under the certified risk control.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing the dynamics of consensus formation, rather than just final agreement, substantially improves the reliability of abstention decisions in medical QA systems. ProbeGuard uses process-aware signals and active probing to detect unanimously wrong consensus and, through Learn-then-Test calibration, provides distribution-free guarantees on the error rate of accepted answers. This leads to safer, more trustworthy deployment of agentic medical QA, especially in high-stakes settings where agreement alone is an unreliable proxy for correctness.

title: Language-model ratings of depression reflect the rater more than the patient
summary: Depression has no diagnostic blood test. Language models promise tireless, consistent assessment, but can accurate raters disagree about individuals? We pre-registered 880 language-model raters, crossing 11 open models with prompting and scoring choices, and applied them to 189 interviews against the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire. Model choice explained 30.0% of summed-symptom score variance, stable participant differences 10.5%. Two randomly drawn raters with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) >= 0.70 disagreed on screening decisions for 40% of participants, on average. Average over-rating governed how many were flagged, yet equal-capacity raters chose differently for about one participant in five. A locked analysis of 86 new interviews reproduced the main pre-registered findings. Exploratory recalibration with 40 labelled participants raised accuracy from about 60% to 75% and halved disagreement, leaving one participant in five decided differently. Calibration repaired much of the rater dependence without securing agreement about individuals.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how consistently large language models (LLMs) can rate depression severity from interview transcripts and finds substantial disagreement between equally accurate models, even after calibration.
AI.motivation: Depression lacks an objective diagnostic blood test, so assessment relies heavily on subjective questionnaires and clinician judgment. With the rise of LLMs, there is interest in using them as scalable, consistent raters of mental health from text. However, it is unclear whether different LLMs – even when similarly accurate at the group level – make the same decisions for individual patients. This matters for clinical deployment and fairness: two equally ‘good’ automated raters should not sharply disagree on who screens positive for depression.
AI.method: The authors pre-registered a large panel of 880 LLM-based raters, created by crossing 11 open-weight language models with different prompting and scoring strategies. These raters assessed 189 depression-related interviews that also had ground-truth scores from the 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8). They quantified how much of the variability in symptom scores was due to model choice versus stable participant differences, and measured disagreement in binary screening decisions (depressed / not depressed) among raters that achieved AUC ≥ 0.70. A locked follow-up analysis on 86 new interviews tested reproducibility. Exploratory recalibration used labels from 40 participants to adjust each rater’s outputs and examine changes in accuracy and disagreement.
AI.result: Model identity accounted for about 30% of the variance in predicted summed symptom scores, compared with 10.5% attributable to stable differences between participants, indicating strong rater dependence. Among raters with AUC ≥ 0.70, two randomly selected raters disagreed on depression screening decisions for roughly 40% of participants on average. The proportion of participants flagged as positive was largely driven by each model’s overall rating bias (over‑ or under‑rating), yet even among raters with similar average behavior and similar overall accuracy, about one in five participants received different screening decisions. The confirmatory analysis on 86 new interviews reproduced these main findings. With recalibration using labels from 40 participants, mean accuracy improved from around 60% to 75% and disagreement between raters was roughly halved, but disagreement for about 20% of individuals persisted.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based depression raters, even when reasonably accurate in aggregate, can disagree substantially on individual screening decisions, and a significant fraction of prediction variance is driven by which model is used rather than by patients’ true differences. Simple calibration with small labelled samples can improve accuracy and reduce, but not eliminate, rater dependence. These findings caution against uncritical clinical use of LLM raters and highlight the need to treat model choice and calibration as central design decisions, especially when outcomes hinge on individual-level classifications.

title: Cooperating with Future Collaborators: Multi-Agent RL under Staggered Participation
summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents are often trained under concurrent participation, while in many tasks some agents act earlier and leave task-relevant information that becomes useful to agents participating later. We study this setting as staggered participation (SP), which introduces a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency because an early action may affect the return through the information it provides and the later policy that uses it. Learning under SP therefore requires both identifying what information is useful for future decisions and learning how later agents should use it. We propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that addresses these two parts with prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents. We evaluate SPL across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns. Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average difference of 14.1%. The gains also extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab, providing evidence across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time method for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning where some agents act earlier and leave information for later agents, improving performance across diverse environments and backbones.
AI.motivation: In many real-world cooperative MARL tasks, agents do not all act concurrently: some operate earlier, leave behind task-relevant information, and others join later and must exploit that information. Standard MARL training typically assumes simultaneous participation and does not explicitly handle the cross-time, cross-agent dependency where early actions affect future returns partly by shaping what later agents can observe and how they act. There is thus a need for methods that explicitly learn what information early agents should produce for future teammates and how later agents should use it.
AI.method: The authors formalize the setting as Staggered Participation (SP), where agent participation is temporally offset, creating cross-time, cross-agent learning dependencies. They propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation applicable to policy-based MARL backbones. SPL decomposes learning into two parts: (1) prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents, which guides them to acquire and leave information that will be useful for future decisions; and (2) outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents, which trains them to interpret and exploit that inherited information based on task outcomes. SPL is integrated into existing MARL algorithms as an additional supervision mechanism rather than a new architecture.
AI.result: SPL is evaluated on multiple policy-based MARL backbones and environments under various staggered-participation patterns, including MPE (Multi-Agent Particle Environments), RWARE (a warehouse environment), teams of up to eight agents, and a physics-based UAV-UGV setting in Isaac Lab. Across 60 different MPE/RWARE backbone comparisons, SPL consistently achieves higher mean task completion, with an average improvement of 14.1% over baselines. The performance gains persist across different temporal structures of participation and more complex embodied robotic environments.
AI.conclusion: Staggered Participation Learning effectively addresses the challenges of cooperative MARL with temporally staggered agents by explicitly training early agents to produce useful information and later agents to exploit it. The method is a general training-time augmentation that improves task completion across diverse algorithms, participation schedules, and simulated/embodied environments, suggesting its broad applicability to real-world multi-agent systems with non-simultaneous participation.

title: Wiki-Talkie: Multilingual Benchmarking of Persona-Based Agents on Real-World Discussions
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in social environments, making it critical to study their ability to faithfully simulate human interactions. Central to this is grounding agents in realistic user personas, yet existing datasets rely on fictional personas and are limited to a handful of languages, lacking the empirical grounding necessary to evaluate behavioral fidelity across diverse populations. We introduce Wiki-Talkie, a multilingual dataset of real-world conversations from Wikipedia Talk pages across five languages spanning two language families: Germanic (German, English) and Romance (Spanish, French, Italian), paired with personas derived from real user communities and encompassing sociodemographic attributes, self-descriptions, and behaviorally grounded interaction traits. Using Wiki-Talkie, we evaluate agent interactional behavior on a next-turn generation task across various persona conditioning strategies. Our evaluation assesses whether agents collectively reproduce the distributional behavioral patterns observed in human discussions. Results show that user's comment history exemplifying interaction behavior consistently outperforms explicit persona information. In addition, models systematically underproduce negative or extreme sentiments, while over producing references and suggestions, revealing biases toward agreeableness and positivity. Crucially, these patterns hold robustly across languages, with small cross-lingual differences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Wiki-Talkie, a multilingual dataset of real Wikipedia Talk page discussions with real user personas, and uses it to evaluate how well LLM agents reproduce human-like interaction behaviors across languages under different persona-conditioning strategies.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used as autonomous agents in social settings, it is important to know whether they can realistically simulate human interactions. Existing persona-based benchmarks mostly use artificial, fictional personas and are limited in language coverage, so they lack empirical grounding and diversity. The authors want a way to study behavioral fidelity of LLM agents using real interaction data and real user personas across multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors construct Wiki-Talkie, a dataset of real conversations from Wikipedia Talk pages in five languages (English, German, Spanish, French, Italian). They derive personas for users that include sociodemographic information, self-descriptions, and interaction traits based on behavior. They then frame a next-turn generation task where LLM agents are conditioned using different persona strategies (e.g., explicit persona info vs. comment history exemplifying behavior). They evaluate whether model-generated interactions collectively reproduce observed human distributional behavioral patterns (e.g., sentiment, use of references, suggestions) across languages.
AI.result: Across conditions, conditioning models on a user’s comment history that showcases their interaction style leads to better reproduction of human-like behavioral patterns than using explicit persona descriptions. Models tend to systematically underproduce negative or extreme sentiments and overproduce content such as references and suggestions, reflecting a tendency towards agreeableness and positivity. These behavioral biases appear consistently across all five languages, with only minor cross-lingual variation.
AI.conclusion: Behaviorally grounded, history-based persona information is more effective than explicit persona descriptions for making LLM agents mimic human interaction behaviors. However, current LLMs exhibit systematic, cross-lingual biases toward positive, agreeable communication and away from negativity or extremity, meaning they fail to fully replicate the true behavioral distribution of human online discussions. Wiki-Talkie provides a multilingual, empirically grounded benchmark to study and quantify these effects.

title: LOGIC: An LLM Benchmark for Intent-Grounded Change Impact in Aerospace Electrical Systems
summary: Aerospace electrical-design revisions can contain multiple genuine changes, although an engineering request may authorize only a subset. Propagating every detected difference can therefore produce overly broad impact reports. We present LOGIC, a controlled benchmark and evaluation framework in which locally deployable language models ground a request in a deterministic candidate-change inventory before selected changes are propagated through a typed electrical traceability graph. This separation permits candidate-selection errors to be distinguished from downstream propagation errors. LOGIC contains 168 scenarios, including 144 selection and 24 abstention cases. We evaluate three 7--8B models against intent-agnostic, lexical, and structured-evidence methods, with an oracle-root upper bound. On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases, gate-only structured evidence achieves candidate F1 of 1.0000, compared with 0.9677 for token-lexical matching. On 12 relational-paraphrase cases, token-lexical F1 is 0.1772 and gate-only F1 is 0.0000, compared with 0.5000--0.6400 for the large language models. Model grounding degrades as candidate inventories grow from 4 to 64 changes, while affected-element and typed-path accuracy remain comparatively stable when frozen selections are replayed over graphs of approximately 1K to 100K nodes. Strict evidence gating suppresses false positives but can remove correct semantic selections. An exploratory evidence-empty abstention policy raises strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 for all three models and reduces unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, while decreasing answerable-case coverage by 16.0--27.1 percentage points. Four of six conflicting requests remain unsafe for each model. These findings support combining literal evidence and language-model reasoning with engineering review when intent cannot be established reliably.

AI.tldr: LOGIC is a benchmark and framework for using locally deployed language models to select and propagate authorized electrical-design changes in aerospace systems, separating errors in change selection from errors in downstream impact analysis.
AI.motivation: In aerospace electrical design, a single design revision can include many actual changes, but an engineering request may only authorize some of them. Existing automated diff/propagation methods tend to treat all detected differences as relevant, leading to overly broad and potentially unsafe impact reports. There is a need for a controlled setting to study how language models can be grounded in explicit change inventories and traceability graphs, and to disentangle where errors occur in the process: in mapping a natural-language request to concrete changes, or in propagating those changes through complex system models.
AI.method: The authors introduce LOGIC, a benchmark and evaluation framework where: (1) a deterministic inventory of candidate design changes is constructed; (2) locally deployable language models must select which candidates are authorized by a given engineering request; and then (3) the selected changes are propagated through a typed electrical traceability graph to assess impact. The framework partitions cases into selection and abstention scenarios, and evaluates three 7–8B parameter language models against several baselines: intent-agnostic selection, lexical token matching, and structured-evidence (gate-only) methods. They vary the size of candidate inventories and the scale of the traceability graphs to probe scalability and robustness. They also test abstention policies based on the presence or absence of explicit evidence and examine performance on conflicting requests.
AI.result: On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases, a structured gate-only evidence method perfectly matches candidates (F1=1.0000), slightly outperforming token-based lexical matching (F1=0.9677). However, on 12 relational-paraphrase cases that require deeper semantic understanding, lexical matching achieves low F1 (0.1772) and gate-only evidence fails (F1=0.0000), while the language models perform substantially better (F1 between 0.5000 and 0.6400). Model grounding quality declines as the number of candidate changes grows from 4 to 64, but when the selected changes are fixed, the accuracy of affected-element and typed-path predictions is relatively stable even as graph size scales from about 1K to 100K nodes. Strict evidence gating sharply reduces false positives but also filters out many correct semantic matches. An abstention strategy that triggers when no supporting evidence is found improves strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 across all models and lowers unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, at the cost of a 16.0–27.1 percentage point drop in coverage on answerable cases. Despite these mitigations, four out of six conflicting-request scenarios remain unsafe for each model tested.
AI.conclusion: Grounding language models in deterministic change inventories and typed traceability graphs makes it possible to separate and analyze selection versus propagation errors in aerospace electrical-design impact analysis. Literal, strictly gated evidence methods are highly reliable on explicitly stated requests but fail on semantic or paraphrased instructions, where language models add clear value. However, as candidate inventories grow, model grounding degrades, and even with conservative evidence-based abstention policies, some conflicting or ambiguous requests still yield unsafe reports. The study indicates that the most effective and safe approach is to combine literal evidence methods, language-model semantic reasoning, and human engineering review, particularly when the underlying intent of a request cannot be established with high confidence.

title: How High Is 0.6? Floors, Ceilings, and Headroom in Interpretability Probing
summary: Probes are the workhorse of interpretability. If a model's hidden states predict a variable, the model is said to represent it. But a probe score has no fixed meaning. An $R^2$ of 0.6 may only reflect what the input already gives away, and the same score can mean different things on different data. We propose reading every probe score against two reference points: a floor, what a declared set of simple inputs already predicts, and a ceiling, what the full input can predict. The gap between them, the headroom, is the range in which a probe can show that a model computes something beyond the simple inputs. We prove that headroom vanishes in two ways: the target stops depending on a hidden variable the model must infer, or the input stops revealing it. We test this on transformers trained for in-context meta-analysis, which must infer the hidden heterogeneity between studies to weight them correctly, and where both reference points are known. Under distribution shift, probe scores fall and prediction error rises $12$--$15\times$, yet the model recovers a similar share of the headroom, indicating that the data lost information, not the representation. We then analyze the real models. The single-cell foundation model scGPT encodes biological variability only partially. We also revisit four influential LLM probing studies, which claim that models represent geography, the state of an Othello board, truth, and the demographics of their users. Against a floor computed from the input text alone, some of these claims hold, while others are largely explained by the text itself.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that raw probe scores used in interpretability (like R^2) are hard to interpret in isolation, and proposes evaluating them relative to a floor (what simple input features can predict) and a ceiling (what the full input can predict), focusing on the remaining “headroom” as evidence that a model truly computes additional information.
AI.motivation: In interpretability research, probing classifiers are widely used to claim that models “represent” certain variables when their hidden states can predict them. However, probe performance is tricky to interpret: the same score can mean very different things across tasks or datasets, and high performance may simply reflect information already present in the surface input rather than genuine internal computation. The authors want a principled way to distinguish between (i) information trivially available from inputs, (ii) information that could in principle be extracted from the full input, and (iii) genuine added value from the model’s internal representations.
AI.method: They introduce a comparative framework for probe evaluation with two reference points: (1) a floor, defined as the performance of a probe that only has access to deliberately simple or restricted input features; and (2) a ceiling, defined as the performance achievable when a probe has access to the full input that defines the task. The difference (ceiling – floor) is called headroom and represents the maximal possible evidence that the model’s internal states encode nontrivial information beyond the simple inputs. They provide theoretical results showing two scenarios where headroom disappears: when the target no longer depends on a hidden variable to be inferred, or when the input no longer carries information about that variable. Empirically, they apply this framework to transformers trained for in-context meta-analysis (where ground-truth floor and ceiling are known), to the single-cell model scGPT, and to four existing LLM probing studies, recomputing results against the new floor and ceiling baselines.
AI.result: On in-context meta-analysis transformers, they observe that under distribution shift, probe performance drops and prediction error increases by 12–15×. However, the fraction of headroom captured by probes stays similar, implying that the data themselves lost information but the internal representations maintained a comparable share of what was in principle extractable. For scGPT, they find that the model’s representations only partially encode underlying biological variability. In reanalyses of four prominent LLM probing works (on geography, Othello board state, truth, and user demographics), some original claims remain robust when judged against the floor baseline, but others are largely accounted for by information directly available in the input text, diminishing the evidence that models learned deeper internal representations of those variables.
AI.conclusion: Probe scores alone are not reliable evidence that a model truly represents a target variable. Instead, they should be evaluated relative to a floor (simple-input baseline) and a ceiling (full-input upper bound), focusing on the share of headroom a model captures. This framework both clarifies what probe results actually show and prevents over-interpreting correlations that may be explained by surface-level input features. Applied to practical cases, it reveals that some celebrated probing findings do reflect genuine internal computation, while others mostly track information already explicit in the text or lost due to data limitations.

title: Representation Bias, Correction Transfer, and Resolution Sensitivity in Three-Dimensional Mitochondrial Morphometry
summary: Quantitative imaging pipelines can produce precise but systematically different measurements of the same object. We present an empirical reliability assessment of three-dimensional mitochondrial morphometry that connects representation bias, a controlled processing intervention, correction transfer, and resolution sensitivity. Using 2,720 development objects from the 3D Mitochondria Shape Library for Optical Microscopy, we find that occupancy-derived volumes exceed reference mesh volumes by 3.665% on average despite an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.994. Boundary analysis identifies an outward label displacement of 0.00304 normalized units. In a controlled label-pipeline reimplementation, removing the depth offset reduces volume error in all 55 analyzed objects by a mean of 1.57 percentage points, approximately 45% of mean reproduced inflation; the source of the remainder is not isolated. A frozen regression using occupancy-derived features reduces median absolute percentage error from 3.481% to 0.664% in 2,728 previously unused objects from the same resource. However, its calibrated error bound covers only 92.1% overall and 49.2% in a low-occupancy subgroup, demonstrating that accuracy and uncertainty transfer must be evaluated separately. In 550 rat-cortex objects from the MitoEM resource, coarsening in-plane spacing from 8 to 24 nanometers changes median surface area by minus 10.60% and sphericity by plus 11.76%, despite a rank correlation of 0.994. These results provide quantitative checks for distinguishing processing-induced descriptor changes from candidate biological differences, without establishing biological invariance or cross-source correction transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how reliable 3D mitochondrial shape measurements are across different imaging and processing settings, quantifying systematic biases and how well corrections and uncertainties transfer.
AI.motivation: Quantitative 3D imaging of mitochondria is widely used to infer biological differences, but different imaging and processing pipelines can give systematically different measurements even for the same objects. Researchers need to know how big these biases are, where they come from, and whether corrections and uncertainty estimates learned in one setting can safely be applied to others.
AI.method: The authors use large public datasets of segmented 3D mitochondria (3D Mitochondria Shape Library and MitoEM) to empirically compare different morphometric pipelines. They quantify biases between occupancy-based and mesh-based volume estimates, analyze boundary displacements, reimplement a label-processing pipeline with and without a depth offset, and test a frozen regression model trained on biased features. They then study how changes in voxel spacing (image resolution) affect surface area, sphericity, and rank correlations of descriptors.
AI.result: They observe that occupancy-derived volumes systematically overestimate mesh-based ground truth volumes by about 3.7% on average, despite an extremely high intraclass correlation (0.994). Boundary analysis attributes a small but consistent outward displacement of labels. Removing the depth offset in a controlled pipeline reduces volume inflation by about 1.6 percentage points (≈45% of the reproduced bias), but does not eliminate all error. A regression model trained on biased features substantially improves volume prediction accuracy on new objects from the same resource, but its uncertainty estimates fail to cover as many cases as intended, particularly in a low-occupancy subgroup. Changing in-plane resolution in a different dataset (MitoEM) leads to large changes in surface area (−10.6%) and sphericity (+11.8%) while still preserving very high rank correlation (0.994).
AI.conclusion: Even when shape descriptors and volumes from different 3D imaging pipelines show excellent correlations, they can have non-negligible systematic biases that are sensitive to label placement, processing details, and resolution. Corrections for bias and associated uncertainty estimates do not automatically transfer across subgroups or datasets. The proposed quantitative checks help distinguish processing-induced changes from potential biological differences, but they do not guarantee biological invariance or cross-dataset correction validity.

title: Latent space bias directions in LLMs capture confidence, not fairness
summary: Activation steering has gained popularity as a lightweight inference-time debiasing technique for large language models. However, prior work reports that steering vectors generalise poorly, with unintended effects on model performance and limited transfer to new datasets. Our work analyses what the debiasing direction used for activation steering actually encodes, in order to shed light on its inconsistent performance. We study the linear debiasing direction obtained by contrasting the activations of anti-biased and biased prompts, and evaluate it as a steering intervention across bias and general knowledge benchmarks. We find that this direction is dominated by model confidence, pointing from regions of high to low-probability tokens in activation space rather than encoding a meaningful representation of model bias. Steering along it does reduce measured bias, but this is a consequence of reducing model confidence: on QA benchmarks we find that this steering drives the model to abstain from answering, with a side effect of improving fairness metrics. Our experiments show that model confidence is the dominant separating factor between biased and anti-biased prompts in hidden space, indicating that isolating a linear representation of bias which is disentangled from model confidence is difficult and steering-based debiasing results should be interpreted with care. In short, steering appears to reduce bias, not by correcting the model's underlying preferences, but by making it less confident, even on tasks unrelated to bias.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that current activation steering debiasing mostly lowers model confidence instead of truly removing bias, so reduced bias scores may be misleading.
AI.motivation: To understand why activation steering as an inference-time debiasing method often generalizes poorly, affects unrelated capabilities, and behaves inconsistently across datasets and tasks.
AI.method: Compute a linear debiasing direction in activation space by contrasting hidden activations from biased vs anti-biased prompts; apply steering along this direction during inference and systematically evaluate its effects on bias benchmarks and general QA/knowledge tasks.
AI.result: The learned “debiasing” direction mainly captures model confidence, pointing from high-probability to low-probability token regions, rather than an interpretable bias dimension. Steering along it lowers measured bias but primarily by pushing the model to be less confident or abstain from answering, even on non-bias-related tasks.
AI.conclusion: A clean linear representation of bias disentangled from model confidence is hard to isolate; activation-steering-based debiasing may give the illusion of fairness improvements while actually just suppressing model confidence, so such methods and metrics should be interpreted with caution.

title: Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation with Cross-Platform User History
summary: Modern recommendation is shifting from platform-centric personalization toward user-governed personalization, where a personal LLM agent can act on the user's behalf across services. We formalize this emerging paradigm as Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation: a platform recommender ranks a candidate set using platform-local information, and a personal agent uses user-authorized cross-platform history to mediate the resulting ranking and produce the final top-K slate. Such mediation is nontrivial: the platform ranking can encode strong population evidence that the personal agent cannot observe, so effective mediation must therefore balance beneficial rescues against harmful overrides. To study this trade-off, we introduce MediateRec, a benchmark that includes scalable proxy cross-platform environments and a real cross-platform test under a controlled platform-agent information boundary. To train the agent to use cross-platform history effectively, we further propose Personal Attribution Mediation Optimization (PAMO), which counterfactually masks that history to estimate personal mediation support and reallocates rank-aware advantage mass under a platform-relative value floor. We theoretically prove that PAMO preserves cutoff-level advantage mass and is locally optimal among first-order reallocations that preserve this mass without lowering average platform-relative value. Experiments on MediateRec show that personal-agent mediation enables meaningful platform corrections, yet even strong proprietary LLMs introduce non-negligible harmful overrides. PAMO consistently improves over matched outcome-only RL across seen and unseen target platforms and on the real cross-platform test, while achieving a better rescue-harm balance.

AI.tldr: They propose and study a new recommendation paradigm where a user’s personal LLM agent re-ranks platform recommendations using cross-platform history, introduce a benchmark (MediateRec), and an optimization method (PAMO) to balance helpful corrections vs harmful overrides, showing PAMO outperforms standard RL.
AI.motivation: Recommendation is moving toward user-governed personalization, where a single personal agent can act across platforms. Existing recommenders are platform-centric and cannot easily use rich cross-platform user history that only the user or their agent can access. When a personal agent re-ranks a platform’s recommendations, it may sometimes correct platform errors (rescues) but may also override good platform choices with worse ones (harmful overrides). There is no clear framework, benchmark, or training method that captures this mediation problem and the trade-off between rescue and harm under strict information boundaries between platform and agent.
AI.method:
1) Formalize “Personal-Agent Mediated Recommendation,” where a platform recommender produces an initial ranked list and a user-owned agent, informed by cross-platform history, mediates this list to produce the final slate.
2) Build MediateRec, a benchmark with scalable simulated cross-platform environments plus a real cross-platform test scenario, designed to respect an information boundary: the platform only sees its own data, the agent sees user-authorized cross-platform history.
3) Propose PAMO (Personal Attribution Mediation Optimization), a training objective for the agent that:
   - Uses counterfactual masking of cross-platform history to estimate how much each recommendation is supported by personal (cross-platform) evidence.
   - Reallocates a rank-aware “advantage mass” to recommendations, but only in ways that respect a platform-relative value floor (i.e., avoid making items too much worse than what the platform would choose).
   - Enforces that the total advantage mass above cutoff is preserved while trying to maximize mediated performance.
4) Provide a theoretical analysis proving that PAMO preserves cutoff-level advantage mass and is locally optimal among all small reallocations that preserve this mass and do not reduce average platform-relative value.
5) Evaluate various agents (including strong proprietary LLMs) and training schemes on MediateRec, comparing PAMO to outcome-only RL baselines in terms of rescues vs harmful overrides across multiple platforms.
AI.result:
1) MediateRec demonstrates that having a personal agent with cross-platform history can significantly improve recommendation outcomes by correcting platform mistakes.
2) However, even powerful LLM-based agents introduce a substantial number of harmful overrides, indicating that naive or outcome-only RL training is insufficient and can degrade user experience.
3) PAMO-trained agents consistently outperform outcome-only RL baselines across both simulated and real cross-platform settings, including previously unseen target platforms.
4) PAMO yields a more favorable trade-off between beneficial rescues and harmful overrides, improving overall mediated recommendation quality without excessively sacrificing the implicit information encoded in the platform’s original ranking.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes personal-agent mediated recommendation as a distinct and important problem for future recommender systems in a world of user-governed personalization. It shows that mediation must carefully respect platform evidence while leveraging cross-platform user history, and that naive approaches can cause harmful overrides. Their MediateRec benchmark and PAMO training objective provide practical tools and theoretically grounded methods to train personal agents that better balance rescues against harms. This suggests that carefully designed mediation algorithms, rather than generic LLM re-ranking or standard RL, are key to making personal LLM agents effective and safe intermediaries in recommendation.

title: Incidental information contaminates patient notes and disrupts clinical reasoning in large language models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly relied upon to support ambient documentation and clinical reasoning. Here we examine the impact of a failure mode shared between these two applications by assessing their sensitivity to information incidental to the patient encounter. In 576 patient-clinician dialogues, we found that frontier models inserted small-talk exchanges into 35% of notes, while mean quality scores changed by at most 0.20 points on five-point scales. In 3.7% of frontier notes, models misattributed the asides or used them clinically. In 57 mock recorded consultations, background speech from a separate patient encounter at -10 dB leaked into 48.2% of transcripts, with contamination detected in 5.3% of downstream notes generated by four open-weight models. We propose a dual encoding hypothesis of clinical reasoning and distraction in LLMs, with preliminary evidence that LLM components associated with disruption by incidental information also support clinical reasoning. These findings support evaluating resistance to incidental information before clinical use, with safeguards that prevent contamination while preserving clinical reasoning.

AI.tldr: Study analyzes how incidental small-talk and background speech affect LLM-generated clinical notes and reasoning, finding frequent inclusion but limited average impact on note quality, with rare but important misuses and transcript contamination.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly embedded in clinical documentation and decision support, it is critical to understand how non-clinical, incidental information (e.g., small-talk, background conversations) can distract models, contaminate documentation, or distort clinical reasoning, potentially creating safety and privacy risks.
AI.method: The authors evaluated multiple frontier and open-weight LLMs on 576 real or simulated patient–clinician dialogues to see how often small-talk appeared in generated notes and whether it was misused clinically, measuring note quality on five-point scales; they also ran 57 mock recorded consultations where background speech from a separate patient at -10 dB was mixed in, measuring how often it leaked into ASR transcripts and then into downstream notes. They advanced and tested a “dual encoding” hypothesis by examining associations between model components that are sensitive to incidental information and those used for clinical reasoning.
AI.result: Frontier models included small-talk segments in 35% of generated notes, but mean note quality changed by ≤0.20 on 5-point scales, suggesting limited average impact on perceived quality; however, in 3.7% of cases, models misattributed small-talk or used it in clinical reasoning, indicating safety concerns. In the audio experiments, -10 dB background conversations from other patients contaminated 48.2% of ASR transcripts and appeared in 5.3% of clinical notes produced by four open-weight LLMs. Model analyses provided preliminary support for the dual encoding hypothesis: components that were most disrupted by incidental information also seemed to contribute to clinical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: LLMs used for clinical documentation and reasoning are meaningfully susceptible to incidental information such as small-talk and background speech, producing rare but concerning misattributions and privacy or safety risks. The dual encoding hypothesis suggests that the same internal mechanisms that enable strong clinical reasoning may also make models vulnerable to distraction. The authors argue that any clinical deployment should assess robustness to incidental information and include safeguards—such as better filtering, separation of speech sources, or model designs that minimize contamination risk without impairing reasoning ability.

title: LSC-DPO: Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a standard reward-model-free approach for aligning language models with preference data. However, as the scaled preference margin grows during training, the logistic DPO loss becomes progressively less sensitive to further changes. We study DPO from a loss-level geometric perspective and identify the sigmoid factor as a learning signal that characterizes the local sensitivity of the objective. Based on this view, we propose Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization (LSC-DPO), which dynamically regulates the learning signal near a target regime. A log-space analysis establishes conditions for stable tracking of the target learning-signal regime. Experiments on AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH show that LSC-DPO consistently improves over DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines. We further find that different coefficient initializations induce distinct transient learning-signal trajectories even when their later signal levels become similar. Based on this observation, we derive a signal-budget compensation rule that adjusts the target learning signal to compensate for these transient differences. The resulting compensation substantially reduces performance variation across coefficient initializations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Learning-Signal-Controlled DPO (LSC-DPO), a modification of Direct Preference Optimization that explicitly controls the effective learning signal, yielding more stable and stronger preference optimization.
AI.motivation: Standard DPO uses a logistic loss whose gradient (learning signal) shrinks as the preference margin grows, making the objective increasingly insensitive and potentially limiting further alignment improvements. The authors want to understand this behavior geometrically and design a method that maintains an appropriate learning signal throughout training to improve stability and final performance.
AI.method: They analyze DPO from a loss geometry perspective and identify the sigmoid term as the key learning signal governing local sensitivity. They define a target regime for this signal and introduce Learning-Signal-Controlled DPO (LSC-DPO), which dynamically adjusts training to keep the learning signal near this target. Using a log-space analysis, they derive conditions ensuring stable tracking of the target signal. They also study how different coefficient initializations lead to different transient signal trajectories and propose a signal-budget compensation rule that adjusts the target signal according to these trajectories.
AI.result: On benchmarks including AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH, LSC-DPO consistently outperforms standard DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines. They further show that applying the signal-budget compensation rule significantly reduces performance variability that previously arose from different coefficient initializations.
AI.conclusion: Actively controlling the effective learning signal in preference optimization—rather than passively inheriting it from the logistic loss—leads to more stable and effective alignment. LSC-DPO provides a principled way to maintain the learning signal in a desired regime and to compensate for transient differences due to initialization, improving both average performance and robustness across runs.

title: Generative AI translations in high-stakes emergency messaging
summary: Emergency messaging such as extreme-weather reports and earthquake instructions can involve high stakes, to the extent that translation errors can lead to tragic consequences. The use of machine translation or generative artificial intelligence might therefore not be recommended. On the other hand, time savings in the initial translation can allow greater investments of resources in revision and authorization processes, as well as a wider range of target languages. An experiment with generative AI translations of an earthquake instruction text from English into Chinese and Spanish shows that use of discourse-specific prompts can considerably improve understandability and actionability, although the translations may still not be trusted by translators. Human revision is still required, not only to detect errors but also because of the ethical need for someone to take responsibility for any errors or delays in such messaging.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether generative AI can safely and effectively assist in translating high‑stakes emergency messages, finding that tailored prompts improve output quality but cannot replace human oversight and responsibility.
AI.motivation: Emergency messages (e.g., extreme-weather alerts, earthquake instructions) are high stakes; translation errors can cause severe harm. While machine translation and generative AI are fast and cheap, their reliability in such contexts is questionable. The authors want to evaluate whether and how generative AI can be used without compromising safety, and if its speed gains can free human resources for better revision, authorization, and multilingual coverage.
AI.method: The authors conduct an experiment translating an earthquake instruction text from English into Chinese and Spanish using generative AI. They compare default outputs with versions produced using discourse-specific prompts designed for emergency instructions, and assess understandability, actionability, and perceived trustworthiness from translators, with a focus on whether AI output can enter professional workflows.
AI.result: Discourse-specific prompts substantially improve the understandability and actionability of AI-generated translations of earthquake instructions into Chinese and Spanish. However, despite these improvements, professional translators still do not fully trust the AI-generated translations for high‑stakes use.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI can help in the initial translation of emergency messages, especially when guided by carefully crafted, discourse-specific prompts, and this can yield time savings and support wider language coverage. Nonetheless, AI output must be followed by human revision and formal authorization because of persistent error risks and the ethical requirement that a human be accountable for any harmful consequences of incorrect or delayed information.

title: Beyond Scalar IoU: Structured Verification from Rollout Groups for Video Temporal Grounding
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides a natural framework for adapting pretrained models to video temporal grounding, where generated temporal intervals can be scored directly against ground truth intervals. Yet existing overlap verifiers typically score each rollout independently, leaving the joint structure of the rollout group unused. We introduce SUTURE, which conditions verification on the rollout group and exploits its structure at two complementary scales: disagreement across rollouts controls how strongly the target is reweighted, while coverage at each position determines where reward mass is redistributed. We show that the resulting verifier admits an exact decomposition into the standard IoU term and a covariance correction determined by the rollout group. A local gradient diagnostic finds a preference for responses covering relatively less supported target regions in the analyzed groups. Across five temporal grounding benchmarks, SUTURE improves grounding performance at every reported IoU threshold. Its trained policy also shows less video-start anchoring in reasoning traces: for later events, the first temporal mention more often overlaps the annotated target. Together, these results show that the joint structure of a rollout group can support a more informative temporal verifier.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes SUTURE, a new verifier for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) applied to video temporal grounding, leveraging structure across multiple rollouts.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR overlap verifiers for temporal grounding evaluate each rollout independently against ground truth, ignoring joint information across a group of rollouts, which may limit reward informativeness and learning efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce SUTURE, a verifier that conditions its scoring on the entire rollout group and exploits two scales of structure: (1) disagreement across rollouts to modulate how strongly the target is reweighted, and (2) coverage at each temporal position to redistribute reward mass. The verifier is analytically decomposed into a standard IoU term plus a covariance-based correction derived from the rollout group. A local gradient diagnostic is used to analyze verifier preferences.
AI.result: On five temporal grounding benchmarks, SUTURE consistently improves grounding performance at all reported IoU thresholds compared to baselines. The trained policy exhibits reduced video-start anchoring, particularly for later events, where the first predicted temporal span more often overlaps the annotated target.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the joint structure of rollout groups in RLVR leads to a more informative temporal verifier, improving video temporal grounding performance and altering model behavior to rely less on early-video anchors, demonstrating the value of group-conditioned verification.

title: InterCorrect: Intersection-Aware Correction of Demographic Model Merging for Fair ASR
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems often show uneven performance across demographic groups, and errors can be especially difficult to address for speakers belonging to multiple demographic groups. This work studies demographic-aware model merging for fair Speech-LLM-based ASR. Starting from a SLAM-ASR-based model, we fine-tune only the connector on demographic-specific subsets and merge the resulting subgroup-adapted connectors into a global model. We then identify critical cross-axis demographic pairs using subgroup WER and task-vector conflict, and apply intersection-specific correction vectors to the global merged model. Experiments on Fair-Speech show that global demographic merging improves overall WER over the base model, while intersection correction provides additional gains for several merging strategies. In particular, TIES with WER-based correction achieves the best overall WER, reducing it from 7.38\% to 5.13\%. Subgroup and disparity analyses further show that the proposed approach improves performance across demographic axes, while highlighting that lower average WER does not always imply reduced subgroup disparity.

AI.tldr: They propose a demographic-aware model-merging strategy for Speech-LLM ASR that fine-tunes and merges demographic-specific connectors, then adds intersection-specific corrections to improve fairness and overall WER.
AI.motivation: ASR systems perform unevenly across demographic groups, and performance can be particularly poor and hard to fix for speakers who lie at the intersection of multiple demographics (e.g., age × gender × accent). Existing approaches may improve average WER but still leave or even worsen disparities for certain groups. The paper is motivated by the need for ASR methods that explicitly handle multi-axis demographic fairness while maintaining or improving overall accuracy.
AI.method: Starting from a SLAM-ASR-based Speech-LLM model, they freeze the main model and fine-tune only the connector module on different demographic-specific data subsets to obtain subgroup-adapted connectors. These adapted connectors are then merged into a single global connector via different model-merging strategies (e.g., TIES and others). Next, they analyze subgroup word error rates (WER) and the conflict between demographic task vectors to identify high-risk cross-axis demographic pairs. For those intersectional pairs, they learn small intersection-specific correction vectors, which are added on top of the globally merged connector. They evaluate on the Fair-Speech benchmark and perform subgroup and disparity analyses across demographic axes.
AI.result: On the Fair-Speech dataset, demographic-aware merging of subgroup-adapted connectors already improves overall WER compared to the base SLAM-ASR model. Adding intersection-specific correction vectors yields further gains for multiple merging schemes. The best configuration—TIES merging with WER-based intersection correction—reduces overall WER from 7.38% to 5.13%. Subgroup-level and disparity analyses indicate that many demographic groups benefit from the proposed method, though improvements in average WER do not systematically translate into lower disparity across all subgroups.
AI.conclusion: Demographic-aware model merging with intersection-specific corrections is an effective way to improve the performance of Speech-LLM-based ASR while explicitly accounting for multi-axis demographic fairness. The approach significantly reduces overall WER and benefits numerous demographic groups, but the analysis underscores that optimizing average performance alone is insufficient to guarantee reduced demographic disparity. Fairness-sensitive ASR evaluation should therefore include detailed subgroup and intersectional analyses beyond global metrics.

title: VALSE: Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficient Inference in Large Language Models
summary: This paper establishes a theoretical framework for vertical adaptive layer skipping, proving three foundational results: (i) an Expected FLOPs formula (theorem 2) giving a closed-form expression for the computational cost of arbitrary per-sample skip schedules as a function of layer-wise skip probabilities; (ii) function-space superset (theorem 10) and strict inclusion (theorem 11) theorems showing that skip-layer models are strictly contained in---yet meaningfully approximate---the full-layer function space, with an explicit separating example; and (iii) a structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (proposition 6), positioning vertical depth-wise sparsity as the orthogonal counterpart to horizontal width-wise sparsity. Building on this theory, we propose VALSE (Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficiency), a per-sample, non-contiguous layer skipping method: a lightweight difficulty estimator scores each input from the first few layers, and per-layer gates selectively skip redundant layers---including arbitrary middle layers while retaining deeper ones---so that only the necessary depth is activated for each input, whose feasibility is preliminarily assessed at prototype scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a theoretical and practical framework (VALSE) for per-sample vertical adaptive layer skipping in deep networks, providing FLOPs analysis, function-space characterization, and a link to Mixture-of-Experts, then demonstrating a prototype system that skips arbitrary middle layers based on input difficulty.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks often waste computation by using the same full depth for all inputs, even though many samples could be processed accurately with fewer layers. Existing efficiency methods like pruning or width-wise sparsity (e.g., Mixture-of-Experts) do not fully exploit per-sample, depth-wise adaptability, especially for non-contiguous skipping of middle layers. A theoretical understanding of such vertical adaptive skipping and its computational tradeoffs is missing, making it hard to design principled and efficient architectures.
AI.method: 1) Develop a theoretical framework for vertical adaptive layer skipping, including: (a) a closed-form formula for Expected FLOPs under arbitrary per-layer skip probabilities; (b) function-space analysis showing that the hypothesis class of skip-layer models is strictly contained in, but can approximate, that of full-depth models, with a concrete separating example; (c) a structural duality result connecting vertical sparsity (VALSE) to horizontal sparsity in Mixture-of-Experts. 2) Based on this theory, design VALSE: a per-sample, non-contiguous layer-skipping scheme where an initial lightweight difficulty estimator uses early-layer features to assign scores, and subsequent per-layer gates decide which later layers (including arbitrary middle layers) to skip or execute for each input. 3) Implement and preliminarily evaluate a prototype to show the feasibility and efficiency gains of the approach.
AI.result: Theoretically, the paper derives: (i) a closed-form Expected FLOPs expression for arbitrary skip schedules; (ii) proofs that the function space of skip-layer models is a strict subset of that of full-layer models, yet can approximate it well, with an explicit example separating the two; and (iii) a structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, formally relating vertical depth-wise sparsity to horizontal width-wise sparsity. Empirically (at prototype scale), it demonstrates that VALSE can selectively skip redundant middle layers on a per-sample basis, activating only the necessary depth and thereby reducing computational cost while retaining performance, though the abstract emphasizes feasibility rather than large-scale benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Vertical adaptive layer skipping can be rigorously analyzed and systematically designed. The proposed VALSE framework offers a principled way to achieve per-sample, depth-wise computational savings by skipping arbitrary layers, with solid theoretical backing on FLOPs, function space, and connections to Mixture-of-Experts. Initial prototype experiments indicate that such non-contiguous, input-dependent layer skipping is practical and can improve efficiency without fully sacrificing representational power, motivating further scaling and empirical exploration.

title: Towards In-Parameter Memory Augmentation for Large Language Models
summary: Recently Large Language Models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents increasingly need to incorporate knowledge acquired after pretraining, e.g., domain facts, user preferences, documents, and interaction experience.
