In-context learning (ICL) and ICL-based agent harness remain flexible, but they consume context capacity and incur repeated discretized encoding cost that grows with context length. \textbf{In-parameter memory} offers a complementary substrate: reusable memory information is represented in model parameters, adapters, or other parameter-like objects that are composed into the forward pass at inference time. This survey focuses on methods that augment LLMs with such parametric memory at deployment: a memory-bearing parameter object is plugged into the forward pass during inference, whether it is acquired before or during deployment. We organize the landscape with two orthogonal axes: \textbf{Parameter Placement}, which includes Embedding, Attention, FFN layers, or Hybrid when two or more layers are used; and \textbf{Parameter Acquisition Time}, which distinguishes methods whose memory object is acquired during deployment (online) from those acquired before it (offline). We clarify boundaries, conduct comparisons, and discuss open directions in interference, safety, co-design with ICL, and recursive self-improvement.

AI.tldr: Survey of methods that store reusable knowledge directly in LLM parameters at deployment time, instead of (or in addition to) in-context prompts.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly must use new knowledge after pretraining—like domain facts, user preferences, documents, and interaction histories. Pure in-context learning can be expensive, as it uses up limited context window and requires re-encoding the same information every time. There is a need for more efficient, reusable memory that doesn’t rely solely on long prompts.
AI.method: Conceptual survey and taxonomy. The authors define and focus on “in-parameter memory”: memory encoded in parameters, adapters, or similar modules that can be plugged into the model at inference. They categorize methods along two axes: (1) where in the network the memory-bearing parameters are placed (embeddings, attention layers, FFN layers, or hybrid combinations), and (2) when these parameters are acquired (online during deployment vs. offline before deployment). They then compare approaches and analyze limitations and opportunities.
AI.result: The paper systematizes a fragmented space of techniques for augmenting LLMs with parametric memory at inference time, clarifies what counts as in-parameter memory vs. other forms (like context-only methods), and maps existing methods into the proposed taxonomy. It highlights patterns and trade-offs across parameter placement and acquisition time and identifies common themes in how memory modules are trained and used.
AI.conclusion: In-parameter memory is a powerful complement to in-context learning for making LLMs more efficient and adaptable at deployment, enabling reusable knowledge without constant prompt overhead. Different parameter placements and acquisition times involve distinct trade-offs in capacity, interference, and practicality. The authors point to open challenges in controlling interference, ensuring safety, coordinating in-parameter memory with ICL-based methods, and enabling forms of recursive self-improvement where models refine their own memory modules over time.

title: BioStudyBench: Evaluating Agents on Post-Cutoff Biomedical Studies
summary: We evaluate whether AI agents can match the reported findings of published biomedical studies using public data. Existing evaluations do not consistently separate analysis from prior knowledge or retrieval of the published answer. We introduce BioStudyBench, a benchmark of 25 long-horizon analysis tasks drawn from studies first published between July and September 2026, after the developer-reported knowledge cutoffs of the models we evaluate, semi-automatically filtered down from 404,019 PubMed records. In each task, the agent receives a neutral research question but no data files, so it must find and download the relevant public data, search the literature through tools that return only records dated before its cutoff, and report findings through data analysis. To measure gains over prior knowledge, we run every task both with and without access to data and tools. Across eight models, access to data and tools raises the pass rate by 47 percentage points on average over the no-data baseline. Open-weight models across sizes trail closed-weight models, with the best open-weight model passing 81.3% of tasks against 94.7% for the best closed-weight model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BioStudyBench to test if AI agents can independently reproduce findings of recent biomedical studies using only public data and pre-cutoff literature tools, showing that access to data and tools substantially boosts performance, with closed-weight models outperforming open-weight ones.
AI.motivation: To rigorously assess whether AI agents can truly perform end-to-end biomedical data analysis—locating data, analyzing it, and reproducing study findings—rather than merely recalling or retrieving known answers from prior training or post-cutoff literature.
AI.method: The authors construct BioStudyBench, a benchmark of 25 long-horizon analysis tasks derived from biomedical studies first published between July and September 2026, ensuring they postdate model knowledge cutoffs. Tasks provide a neutral research question without data files, forcing agents to: (1) discover and download relevant public datasets, (2) search the literature via tools restricted to pre-cutoff records, and (3) conduct data analysis to generate findings. They evaluate eight AI models in two settings: with and without access to data and tools, comparing pass rates to isolate the benefit of actual analysis capabilities over prior knowledge.
AI.result: Access to data and tools increases the average pass rate across the eight evaluated models by 47 percentage points compared with a no-data baseline. Closed-weight models outperform open-weight ones: the best open-weight model passes 81.3% of tasks, while the best closed-weight model passes 94.7% of tasks.
AI.conclusion: BioStudyBench demonstrates that modern AI agents can often reproduce findings of recent biomedical studies when allowed to discover and analyze public data, but there remains a notable performance gap between open- and closed-weight models. The benchmark provides a way to disentangle genuine analytic capability from memorized knowledge or direct answer retrieval, and highlights both progress and remaining limitations in AI-driven biomedical research automation.

title: Evidence-Bound Reasoning: Neuro-Semantic Verification of Biomedical AI in Glioblastoma Radiogenomics
summary: Background: Biomedical AI can generate plausible explanations without reliably verifying whether each statement is supported by patient-specific evidence. We developed a neuro-semantic verification framework that converts radiomic measurements into addressable evidence records and machine-checkable claims. Methods: UPenn-GBM radiomics were aligned with de novo CaPTk extraction from standardized MRI and expert-validated segmentations in an independent multicenter cohort. The shared space comprised 1,728 features from T1, T1GD, T2, and FLAIR MRI across three tumor regions. Reference-defined semantic states were derived from 611 UPenn cases. We evaluated cross-cohort transportability, model-linked provenance, deterministic verification, controlled predictive degradation, and an LLM claim-extraction pilot; MGMT prediction served only as a transport stress test. Results: Median semantic-state agreement was 0.786 (weighted kappa 0.709), ranging from 0.918 for morphologic to 0.252 for intensity features. The external evidence ledger contained 1,655 model-linked records for 331 patients. The verifier achieved 100% exact-set accuracy in a 6,620-claim corruption benchmark. In a 24-case pilot, GPT-5.6 Sol reproduced 72/72 prespecified atomic claims, and the frozen verifier recovered 24/24 expected conditions. During controlled degradation, ROC AUC declined from 0.899 to 0.500 while verification accuracy remained 1.000. External MGMT discrimination was weak (ROC AUC 0.543). Conclusions: Verifiability can be engineered and evaluated independently of predictive performance. LLMs may structure explanations, while final evidence-consistency checking remains deterministic.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a neuro-semantic verification framework that translates radiomic features into explicit, machine-checkable evidence records and claims, enabling deterministic verification of AI-generated biomedical explanations independent of predictive performance.
AI.motivation: Current biomedical AI systems, including LLM-based explanation tools, can generate plausible but potentially unsubstantiated narratives that are not tightly linked to patient-specific evidence. This hallucination risk is critical in clinical settings, where every explanatory statement should be traceable to validated measurements. The authors aim to create a framework in which model explanations can be rigorously checked against a structured evidence base of radiomic features, with clear provenance, to ensure that explanatory claims remain consistent with underlying data, even when predictive performance varies or degrades.
AI.method: The authors align radiomics from the UPenn-GBM dataset with de novo feature extraction using CaPTk from standardized MRI sequences (T1, T1GD, T2, FLAIR) and expert-validated tumor segmentations in an independent multicenter cohort. They construct a shared feature space of 1,728 radiomic features across three tumor regions and derive reference-defined semantic states from 611 UPenn cases. They then build an external evidence ledger connecting model outputs to specific radiomic features, enabling deterministic verification of claims expressed as semantic states. They evaluate: (1) cross-cohort transportability of the semantic-state definitions; (2) model-linked provenance via the evidence ledger; (3) deterministic verification performance using a 6,620-claim corruption benchmark; (4) robustness of verification under controlled predictive degradation (varying ROC AUC while tracking verification accuracy); and (5) an LLM-based claim-extraction pilot, where GPT-5.6 Sol generates structured atomic claims from explanations which are then checked by a frozen verifier. MGMT promoter status prediction is used only as a stress test for transportability, not as the main scientific goal.
AI.result: The framework showed substantial agreement of semantic states between cohorts, with median agreement of 0.786 and a weighted kappa of 0.709, though performance varied by feature type (highest for morphologic features at 0.918 and lowest for intensity features at 0.252). The external evidence ledger comprised 1,655 model-linked records for 331 patients, demonstrating scalable provenance tracking. The deterministic verifier achieved 100% exact-set accuracy in a 6,620-claim corruption benchmark, indicating robust detection of any altered or corrupted claims. In a 24-case LLM pilot, GPT-5.6 Sol reproduced all 72 prespecified atomic claims, and the verifier correctly recovered all 24 expected conditions, showing compatibility between LLM-based structuring and symbolic verification. Under controlled model degradation, the ROC AUC dropped from 0.899 to 0.500, but verification accuracy remained at 1.000, demonstrating that verifiability is decoupled from predictive performance. External performance for MGMT status prediction itself was poor (ROC AUC 0.543), underscoring that the framework’s contribution lies in verification, not classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that neuro-semantic verifiability of biomedical AI explanations can be engineered as an independent design objective, separate from and robust to variations in predictive performance. By converting radiomic measurements into structured evidence records and machine-checkable semantic claims, the framework allows deterministic verification of whether explanations are consistent with patient-specific data. LLMs can be used effectively to extract and structure explanatory claims, but final evidence-consistency checks should remain deterministic and symbolically grounded. This suggests a hybrid paradigm where AI-generated narratives are always backed by a verifiable evidence ledger, improving trustworthiness and auditability of clinical AI systems.

title: Explore, Then Commit: Measurement-Efficient Scientific Law Discovery with Language Models
comment: 19 pages, including Supplementary Material S1; code and data included as ancillary files. Preprint
summary: Scientific law discovery requires selecting measurements and converting evidence into a governing equation. We evaluate an explore-then-commit protocol in which a large language model proposes hypotheses, a programmatic planner gathers measurements, and a fresh prompt synthesizes the final law from fixed observations. The protocol combines structured probes, automatic numerical diagnostics, restricted measurement batches, and optional interpreter access. Across 576 NewtonBench trials, we compare eight configurations on 12 physics modules using GPT-4.1-mini and a medium-difficulty GPT-4.1 replication. On medium tasks, interpreter-enabled planners use 8.6 versus 22.5 measurements per trial for GPT-4.1-mini and 8.9 versus 43.0 for GPT-4.1. Their mean magnitude-based root-mean-squared logarithmic error falls from 2.514 to 0.202 and from 0.626 to 0.149, respectively. An additional audit retains incomplete and invalid submissions in a coverage-sensitive analysis. Observed symbolic-accuracy gains are less consistent across modules, and random acquisition is competitive with disagreement scoring. Measurement savings occur in every module, but unequal batch constraints prevent attributing them solely to acquisition quality. These results support the complete protocol as a promising measurement-efficient configuration, while leaving its causal components and generalization beyond noiseless direct-equation tasks unresolved.

AI.tldr: The paper tests a protocol where an LLM explores hypotheses and then commits to a final scientific law, showing it can discover physics equations with far fewer measurements while maintaining or improving accuracy, but causal contributions of components remain unclear.
AI.motivation: Discovering scientific laws usually needs many costly measurements and human insight. With increasingly capable LLMs, there is interest in whether they can guide experiment design and equation discovery efficiently. The authors aim to evaluate a concrete, systematic protocol that integrates LLM hypothesis generation, automated measurements, and final law synthesis, focusing on how to reduce the number of measurements needed while keeping accuracy high.
AI.method: They design an "explore-then-commit" pipeline: (1) an LLM proposes candidate scientific laws; (2) a programmatic planner chooses and executes numerical measurements in batches, guided by structured prompts, diagnostics, and optionally a code interpreter; (3) a fresh LLM prompt, given only the collected data, synthesizes the final governing equation. They instantiate this on NewtonBench, testing 8 protocol variants across 12 physics modules, using GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-4.1 at a medium difficulty level. They vary planner capabilities (with/without interpreter, acquisition strategies like random vs disagreement), batch constraints, and then evaluate numerical and symbolic accuracy plus coverage (including incomplete/invalid runs).
AI.result: On medium-difficulty NewtonBench tasks, planners with interpreter access drastically reduce the needed measurements per trial: from 22.5 to 8.6 for GPT-4.1-mini and from 43.0 to 8.9 for GPT-4.1. Numerical accuracy also improves substantially: magnitude-based RMS logarithmic error drops from 2.514 to 0.202 for GPT-4.1-mini and from 0.626 to 0.149 for GPT-4.1. However, symbolic accuracy improvements are uneven across the 12 modules, and simple random measurement acquisition performs comparably to more sophisticated disagreement-based scoring. An audit including incomplete and invalid outputs yields a coverage-sensitive view but does not overturn the main findings on measurement savings.
AI.conclusion: The full explore-then-commit protocol, especially with interpreter-enabled planners, appears to offer strong measurement efficiency and better numerical accuracy for equation discovery on noiseless Newtonian physics benchmarks. Yet, because batch-size constraints and other design factors are entangled, the authors cannot cleanly attribute gains to any single component, nor do they establish generalization beyond the tested noiseless, direct-equation setting. Further work is needed to isolate causal contributions of the protocol elements and to validate performance in more realistic, noisy scientific environments.

title: Same-Number Citation Swaps: Stress-Testing Jev as a Financial Evidence Judge
comment: counterfactual citation perturbation, evidence attribution verification, financial document question answering, Jev, LLM-as-a-judge, probabilistic source verification, tabular numerical reasoning
summary: Financial reports repeat values across periods, metrics and accounting lines, allowing an LLM-generated calculation to be numerically correct while citing the wrong financial role. We evaluate what probabilistic evidence verification adds beyond number matching using Jev as a source-support verifier for GPT-4.1-mini calculation traces. A signed-number-at-pointer baseline explains most recovery over exact quotation checks. To isolate the remaining role-recognition problem, we hold operands and arithmetic fixed, move citations between same-number cells, and retain controls that express equivalent facts. These contrasts reveal both wrong-role citations that pass and valid alternative citations that are withheld. Explicit column labels improve selected wrong-role decisions while also lowering support for some equivalent evidence. A constructed follow-up on 36 new source pages, labeled by a non-author reviewer, extends this evaluation and exposes the same tradeoff between detecting role errors and retaining valid citations. The contribution is a controlled evaluation that identifies what a probabilistic financial verifier distinguishes when numerical matching is held fixed. For LLM-based financial assistants, it makes numerical correctness, cited-role support and acceptance outcomes separately assessable.

AI.tldr: They study how a probabilistic verifier for financial reports helps check not just that numbers match but that citations refer to the correct financial roles (e.g., the right line item/column), and show it can separate numerical correctness from citation quality and acceptance decisions.
AI.motivation: In financial reports, the same numerical value often appears in different roles (e.g., same amount in different periods, metrics, or line items). An LLM can produce numerically correct calculations while citing the wrong cell, which is problematic for trustworthy, auditable financial assistants. Existing verification focused mostly on whether the numbers match the source, not whether the cited evidence corresponds to the correct financial role. The authors want to understand what additional value a probabilistic source-support verifier brings beyond simple number matching, especially in this role-recognition setting.
AI.method: They use Jev, a probabilistic evidence verifier, to assess the support for GPT‑4.1‑mini’s calculation traces on financial tables. They introduce a signed-number-at-pointer baseline that checks whether the numbers and their signs at specific table positions explain most of Jev’s recovery over exact quotation checks. To isolate the residual problem of recognizing the correct financial role, they construct controlled contrasts by fixing operands and arithmetic and then systematically moving citations between cells that contain the same numbers, while also creating control cases with alternative but semantically equivalent evidence. They test how Jev scores these manipulated citations, analyze wrong-role citations that are erroneously accepted and valid alternatives that are incorrectly rejected, and then replicate the setup on 36 new financial source pages annotated by an independent (non-author) reviewer.
AI.result: The signed-number-at-pointer baseline accounts for most of the performance gain over simple exact-quote matching, showing that much of Jev’s advantage comes from better number localization rather than deeper role understanding. However, even when numerical matching is held constant, Jev exhibits a distinct behavior on role-related contrasts: it sometimes allows wrong-role citations to pass and sometimes withholds support from valid, equivalent citations, revealing a tradeoff between detecting role errors and preserving legitimate alternative evidence. Explicitly including column labels in the verification context improves some wrong-role decisions—Jev is better at spotting certain role mismatches—but simultaneously reduces support for some equivalent evidence. The follow-up experiment on 36 additional pages confirms these patterns: Jev’s sensitivity to role errors increases, but at the cost of rejecting some correct citations.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic financial evidence verification systems like Jev do more than simple number matching but still struggle to reliably distinguish between numerically identical cells that play different financial roles. The paper’s main contribution is a controlled evaluation framework that cleanly separates numerical correctness, role-appropriate citation, and acceptance decisions. For LLM-based financial assistants, this makes it possible to assess and tune numerical accuracy, citation-role correctness, and verifier behavior independently, clarifying what current probabilistic verifiers can and cannot contribute when number matching alone is insufficient.

title: Learning to Outgrow a Theory: Experimental Discovery Beyond the Initial Hypothesis Space
summary: Scientific discovery systems typically optimize experiments within a fixed hypothesis space. This creates a failure mode when all available candidates omit the same missing mechanism: candidate disagreement can collapse even while the model class is systematically wrong. We formulate experimental model-class revision, in which a discovery policy jointly proposes a structural edit and a diagnostic experiment that tests whether that edit is necessary. The method couples a class-level distinguishability objective, in which one shared parameterization must explain all selected experiments, with anytime-valid sequential evidence that triggers structural revision only after the current class is rejected. On 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments, the joint policy reaches 89.5% exact recovery with a budget of 32 real experiments, improving the strongest matched baseline by 10.0 percentage points while requiring fewer executed experiments and candidate fits. The learned revision-experiment pairing transfers across unseen mechanism combinations, held-out but expressible primitives, parameter extrapolation, and shifted experiment costs; when the true mechanism is outside the edit grammar, it detects library insufficiency in 88% of cases with a 5.5% false-support rate. Revision gains also transfer to ODEBench and ODEBase model-library tasks, as well as DiscoverPhysics worlds. These results support a view of scientific discovery in which deciding what mechanisms a theory should make expressible and where to collect evidence are treated as a single sequential decision problem.

AI.tldr: They propose a system that doesn’t just choose experiments within a fixed model class but also learns when and how to revise the model class itself, pairing each proposed structural edit with an experiment designed to test it.
AI.motivation: Most automated scientific discovery methods assume a fixed hypothesis/model class and only optimize which experiments to run or which parameters to fit. If the true mechanism is missing from this class, different candidate models can all agree and still be systematically wrong, making it impossible to detect the missing mechanism from experiments alone. The authors aim to create a framework that can automatically detect when the current model class is insufficient and propose revisions to it, closing this gap in current discovery systems.
AI.method: They formalize “experimental model-class revision,” where a policy jointly proposes (1) a structural edit to the model class (e.g., changing the set of mechanisms a theory can express) and (2) a diagnostic experiment designed to test whether that edit is needed. Technically, they use a class-level distinguishability objective in which a single shared parameterization must explain the outcomes of all chosen experiments. They couple this with anytime-valid sequential testing that only triggers structural revision after rejecting the current class. A learned policy is trained to pair model-class edits with experiments, using a grammar of possible edits and a library of dynamical environments.
AI.result: On 400 held-out controlled dynamical systems, their joint revision–experiment policy achieves 89.5% exact recovery of the ground-truth mechanisms with just 32 real experiments, outperforming the strongest baseline by 10 percentage points while also using fewer experiments and model fits. The learned pairing of edits and experiments generalizes to unseen combinations of mechanisms, to primitives that were held out during training but are still expressible by the grammar, to new parameter ranges, and to settings with different experiment costs. When the true mechanism lies outside the edit grammar, the method detects that the library is insufficient in 88% of cases, with only a 5.5% rate of incorrectly supporting the library. Improvements also transfer to external benchmarks such as ODEBench, ODEBase, and DiscoverPhysics tasks.
AI.conclusion: Treating the choice of what mechanisms a theory can express and where to collect evidence as a single, unified sequential decision problem leads to more robust and data-efficient scientific discovery. Their approach can both improve mechanism recovery when the true dynamics are in the model grammar and reliably flag when the existing mechanism library is inadequate, and it generalizes across different dynamical environments and benchmarks.

title: Agreement Is Not Validity: Cross-Model LLM Consensus in Diagnosing Student Failure Modes in K-12 Math Tutoring Dialogue
comment: Submitted to LAK27 as a short paper. Currently under review
summary: In K-12 mathematics tutoring, student-tutor dialogue provides rich evidence of learners' problem-solving processes and sources of difficulty. Learning analytics research increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs) to extract such information from dialogue for a variety of downstream tasks, including knowledge tracing, behavioral modeling, and diagnosis of student reasoning errors. However, the validity of these model-generated interpretations remains insufficiently understood. In this exploratory study, we examine the validity of LLM classifications of five student failure modes in mathematics tutoring dialogue using an operational diagnostic codebook: uncertainty, misattribution, operator selection, conceptual gap, and procedural slip. Across models, human-LLM agreement was moderate (kappa = .524-.597), while cross-model agreement was substantially higher (kappa = .755-.781; alpha = .769). These findings show that cross-model agreement can create a misleading appearance of correctness, challenging the assumption that consensus among LLMs constitutes evidence of valid learner interpretation. For learning analytics, the implication is clear: scalable labeling is useful only if the inferred constructs are valid, and model consensus cannot substitute for independent evidence of that validity.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how valid large language model (LLM) labels of student failure modes in K-12 math tutoring dialogues are, and shows that high agreement between different LLMs can be misleading and does not guarantee valid interpretation of students’ thinking.
AI.motivation: Learning analytics increasingly uses LLMs to automatically interpret student-tutor dialogue for tasks like knowledge tracing and diagnosis of reasoning errors. This promises scalable labeling but raises an unresolved question: are the inferences LLMs make about students’ difficulties actually valid relative to well-defined diagnostic constructs used by human experts? Moreover, many practitioners assume that if multiple LLMs agree, their conclusions are likely correct, an assumption that has not been empirically scrutinized.
AI.method: The authors conduct an exploratory validation study where multiple LLMs classify segments of K-12 math tutoring dialogue according to an existing operational diagnostic codebook of five student failure modes: uncertainty, misattribution, operator selection, conceptual gap, and procedural slip. They then compare LLM labels to human expert labels to compute human–LLM agreement (using Cohen’s kappa) and also compare agreement among different LLMs themselves (cross-model agreement using kappa and Krippendorff’s alpha).
AI.result: Human–LLM agreement on classifying the five failure modes was only moderate, with Cohen’s kappa ranging from about .524 to .597. In contrast, agreement across different LLMs was substantially higher, with kappa around .755 to .781 and Krippendorff’s alpha of .769. Thus, different LLMs tended to agree strongly with each other even when their classifications only moderately matched human coders using the diagnostic codebook.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that consensus among LLMs can give a false impression of correctness and should not be treated as evidence that the inferred learner states or failure modes are valid. For learning analytics, scalable, LLM-based labeling is beneficial only if the constructs being inferred are empirically validated against independent criteria (e.g., expert-coded data, learning outcomes), and model consensus is not an adequate substitute for such validation.

title: Measuring climate backlash in Twitter and Reddit archives: Lexical definitions, recorded responses and participant turnover
summary: Social media archives are often used to study resistance to climate action, but words, response counters and observed participants do not measure the same social process. We examine four supplied Twitter and Reddit archives by processing all registered files without sampling and applying transparent, non-exclusive lexical rules. The study links frame co-occurrence to source-specific temporal and response models, then separates event-period changes among returning authors from participant turnover. Renewable-energy terms accompany cost-related language on Reddit, yet narrower backlash phrases sharply reduce cross-source contrasts and reverse the sign of the Paris Agreement contrast in submissions. Cross-discourse history does not improve eligible primary-context forecasts. Denial/hoax terms are associated with higher recorded Twitter likes, whereas Reddit response associations depend on frame, outcome and author specification. Around the 2019 global climate strike, returning-author expression and participant turnover both contribute to increased protest-language shares. An archive endpoint prevents the corresponding Climate Twitter migration inference. Most crossed-cluster estimates lack released intervals, and joint author/month response covariance estimates fail, restricting formal inference. These results show how operational definitions, platform-specific response fields and observation boundaries shape what can be claimed about climate backlash. The contribution is an archive-based account of these measurement consequences, rather than a measure of individual opposition, persuasion or advocacy-induced backlash.

AI.tldr: Study of how different ways of measuring climate backlash in social media archives affect research conclusions.
AI.motivation: Researchers often use social media data (Twitter, Reddit) to study resistance to climate action, but common metrics like words, engagement counts, and observed participants may not reflect the same underlying social processes, risking misleading conclusions about climate backlash.
AI.method: Process four full Twitter and Reddit archives without sampling. Apply transparent, non-exclusive lexical dictionaries (frames) to identify climate-related and backlash-related language. Link co-occurring frames to temporal patterns and platform-specific response metrics (likes, comments, etc.). Decompose changes around key climate events (e.g., the 2019 global climate strike) into contributions from returning authors vs. new participant turnover. Test whether cross-platform historical patterns help forecast primary-context responses. Examine how narrowing definitions of backlash (e.g., specific denial/hoax terms) alters measured contrasts between platforms and events. Assess limitations due to missing uncertainty estimates and failed joint covariance estimation for author/month responses.
AI.result: Renewable-energy terms co-occur with cost-related language on Reddit, but using narrower backlash phrases dramatically reduces apparent differences between platforms and even flips the sign of the Paris Agreement contrast in submissions. Including cross-discourse histories does not improve forecasting of primary-context responses. On Twitter, denial/hoax terms correlate with higher like counts; on Reddit, response patterns vary by frame, outcome, and author specification. Around the 2019 global climate strike, both returning authors and new participants drive increases in protest-language usage. Archive endpoints block inference about later migration of climate discourse on Twitter. Many cross-cluster estimates lack confidence intervals, and attempts to estimate joint author/month response covariance fail, limiting formal statistical inference.
AI.conclusion: Measures of climate backlash derived from social media archives are highly sensitive to operational definitions (which words/frames count), platform-specific engagement fields, and observation boundaries. Apparent contrasts between platforms or events can change direction depending on lexical choices. The paper’s main contribution is to document these measurement consequences and methodological constraints, not to quantify true individual-level opposition, persuasion, or backlash to climate advocacy.

title: When Forgetting is not Catastrophic: On the Mechanics of Spurious Forgetting
summary: Knowledge that a language model appears to forget during finetuning often remains stored and can be recovered, a phenomenon called spurious forgetting. Finetuning on new facts can even produce forgetting that undoes itself: recall of the old facts collapses, recovers as training continues on new facts alone, and only then erodes for good. We seek to understand when such forgetting is not catastrophic. A minimal associative memory reproduces these dynamics with three ingredients: keys with shared structure, concentrated new values, and normalization in the network. Finetuning moves all old representations along a common direction, hiding the old facts while preserving their relative geometry; normalization withdraws this shift once the new facts are learned, whereas fact-specific changes accumulate and cause the erosion. Moreover, subtracting the common shift eliminates the collapse in a Transformer trained on synthetic data, and removing a single direction from each weight update restores old facts in a pretrained language model. Forgetting thus combines a shared, reversible loss of access with a slow erosion of individual facts, and only the second is catastrophic. Which one dominates depends on whether the new data move old memories together or apart.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why language models seem to forget old facts during finetuning, showing that much of this forgetting is reversible and caused by a shared shift in representations rather than destruction of information.
AI.motivation: Language models finetuned on new data often show reduced recall of old facts, which is typically interpreted as catastrophic forgetting. However, there are observations of spurious forgetting, where forgotten knowledge can later be recovered. The authors want to understand the mechanisms behind this behavior and identify when forgetting is truly catastrophic versus when it is just a temporary loss of access.
AI.method: The authors build and analyze a minimal associative memory model that can reproduce the observed forgetting and recovery dynamics. They identify conditions under which this happens: shared structure among keys, concentrated new values, and normalization in the network. They then perform experiments with Transformers on synthetic data, manipulating representation shifts by subtracting common directions, and apply an update-projection technique to a pretrained language model to remove a single direction from each weight update.
AI.result: The theoretical model shows that finetuning moves representations of old facts along a shared direction, temporarily hiding them while preserving their relative geometry. Normalization counteracts this shared shift once new facts are learned, revealing old facts again, while fact-specific changes continue to accumulate and eventually erode memories. Empirically, subtracting the common representational shift in Transformers eliminates the collapse in recall, and projecting out a single direction from each finetuning update substantially restores old facts in a pretrained model.
AI.conclusion: Forgetting in finetuned language models consists of two components: a shared, reversible loss of access due to a global shift in representations, and a slower, irreversible erosion of individual memories. Only the latter is truly catastrophic. Which component dominates depends on how the new data move old representations—either together (causing reversible forgetting) or apart (causing permanent loss). This understanding suggests concrete interventions, such as removing shared shift directions from updates, to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.

title: Learning Explainable Representations of Complex Game-playing Strategies
summary: As part of learning to play complex games, human players develop develop abstractions for concepts and strategies of gameplay consistent with game rules to improve their performance. These concepts are applied to explain other players' actions, and to inform their own actions in-game. Understanding other players' strategies is a crucial part of such improvement, but requires time and effort. In this paper, we propose a strategy similar to human cognition for training RL agents to synthesize learned strategies and policies as executable procedures based on sequences of gameplay actions. We present methods to automatically learn such programs to play chess and to solve tasks in a grid-based environment. We show that the learned strategies produce effective actions, and can be learned from gameplay data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method for RL agents to learn human-like, program-style strategies from gameplay sequences, demonstrated in chess and grid-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Humans improve at complex games by forming abstract, rule-consistent concepts and strategies that explain others’ actions and guide their own. Understanding opponents’ strategies is valuable but time-consuming and cognitively demanding. The authors want RL agents to gain similar high-level, interpretable strategic representations that can be learned automatically from data, reducing manual effort and improving generalization.
AI.method: They introduce a training approach for reinforcement learning agents that converts sequences of gameplay actions into explicit, executable procedures (programs). From logged gameplay data, the system infers structured strategies—represented as programs—that capture regularities in how actions are sequenced to achieve goals. These learned procedures are then used as policies for decision making in environments such as chess and a grid-based world.
AI.result: The learned procedural strategies, when executed as policies, lead to effective in-game actions. Experiments in chess and grid-based tasks show that these programmatic strategies can be induced directly from gameplay data and that they perform competently in their respective domains.
AI.conclusion: It is feasible to train RL agents to synthesize human-like, high-level strategies as executable programs from gameplay traces. These learned procedures both play effectively and are derivable automatically from data, suggesting a path toward more interpretable and cognitively inspired RL policies in complex games and tasks.

title: Holdout Best-of-N: Unbiased Evaluation and Its Cost
summary: Reusing the scores that select a Best-of-$N$ winner can overstate its expected reward. We study evaluation from a fixed matrix of $K$ independent scores per candidate for a policy that selects using $J$ fresh scores. A single estimator based only on this matrix is exactly unbiased for expected judge reward under every independent, stable collection of candidate-specific score laws if and only if $J<K$, for every pool size $M\ge N\ge2$. At $J=K-1$, the selector deepens as $K$ grows. For independent Gaussian scores with common variance and fixed $M\ge N\ge2$, the unbiased minimax risk in this regime is of order $σ^2/\sqrt K$, attained by Holdout; allowing bias improves the rate to $σ^2/K$. For two candidates, we derive the minimum-variance unbiased estimator at known variance and the sharp asymptotic unbiased minimax constant $1/(π\sqrt2)$, which Holdout attains without knowing the variance. The cyclic average over subsets and ties can be computed in $O(MK\log M)$ operations. At fixed selector depth, cyclic evaluation of bounded scores has $O(K^{-1})$ risk uniformly in pool size. The impossibility result concerns the fixed matrix: one additional fresh winner score permits unbiased evaluation of the all-$K$ policy.

AI.tldr: The paper studies unbiased evaluation of selection policies that pick the best of several candidates using scores, showing when and how we can correctly estimate expected reward without bias from reused scores.
AI.motivation: In many settings, we select a “Best-of-N” candidate (e.g., best model, best decision) based on multiple noisy scores. A common mistake is to reuse these same scores to estimate the expected reward of the selection policy, which leads to optimistic, biased evaluations. The paper is motivated by the need for principled, unbiased, and efficient evaluation methods that avoid this selection-induced bias while using limited scoring information.
AI.method: The authors formalize a setting with M candidates, each having K independent scores from a candidate-specific distribution, and a selection policy that will in deployment use J fresh scores per candidate to pick a Best-of-N winner. They analyze all estimators that can be built solely from the fixed K×M score matrix. Using theoretical decision-theoretic and minimax risk analysis, they characterize when an exactly unbiased estimator of the policy’s expected reward exists for every collection of independent, stable score laws. They study special cases such as Gaussian scores with common variance, derive optimal rates in K, identify specific estimators (e.g., Holdout and cyclic averaging over subsets/ties), and analyze their risk, variance, and computational complexity. For two-candidate Gaussian problems they explicitly construct the minimum-variance unbiased estimator and compute the sharp asymptotic minimax constants.
AI.result: They prove that a single estimator based only on the fixed K-score matrix is exactly unbiased for the expected reward of the Best-of-N policy under all independent, stable candidate-specific score distributions if and only if the number of deployment scores J is strictly less than K, for all pool sizes M≥N≥2. At J=K−1, as K increases, the selection becomes deeper, and in the Gaussian common-variance case with fixed M≥N≥2 the optimal unbiased minimax risk is of order σ²/√K, achievable by a Holdout scheme; allowing biased estimators improves this rate to σ²/K. For the case of two candidates, they derive the minimum-variance unbiased estimator when the variance is known and identify the sharp asymptotic unbiased minimax constant as 1/(π√2); the Holdout estimator attains this without needing to know the variance. They show that the cyclic average over subsets (handling ties) is computationally feasible in O(MK log M). For fixed selector depth, cyclic evaluation of bounded scores has risk of order O(1/K) uniformly over pool size. They also demonstrate an impossibility: from only the fixed matrix of K scores, no unbiased estimator exists for policies using all K scores for selection, but adding one fresh score for the winner restores unbiased evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Unbiased evaluation of Best-of-N selection policies from a fixed set of scores is possible in a universal sense only when the policy at deployment uses fewer scores (J<K) than are available in the evaluation matrix. In this regime, specific estimators like Holdout and cyclic averaging can achieve near-optimal or optimal minimax risk rates, and can be implemented efficiently. However, if the policy uses all available scores (J=K), then unbiased evaluation based only on the fixed score matrix is impossible; at least one additional fresh winner score is required. The work clarifies the fundamental limits and optimal constructions for unbiased, low-risk evaluation of selection policies under score noise.

title: Towards the Automatic Synthesis of Interpretable Chess Tactics
summary: State-of-the-art reinforcement learning agents are capable of outperforming human experts at games like chess, Go and StarCraft II. These agents do not simply take advantage of their digital hardware in being able to react and calculate faster than humans, but employ better strategies that lead to more victories. Interpreting these strategies would give human players valuable insight into how to improve their play. In this preliminary work, we propose a symbolic sub-policy model for playing chess. Inspired by chess tactics, our model attempts to incorporate domain knowledge to improve interpretability. We adapt patterns learned by an inductive logic programming system called PAL to derive our model. We contribute a divergence metric to evaluate our model against a random baseline, and find a set of tactics that is able to suggest moves of similar playing strength to a human beginner. Finally, we propose a computational evaluation scheme for the model by augmenting an off-the-shelf engine with it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an interpretable, tactic-based symbolic sub-policy model for chess derived from inductive logic programming, and evaluates its move quality and integration with an existing engine.
AI.motivation: Modern reinforcement learning systems achieve superhuman performance in complex games but are opaque, limiting humans’ ability to understand or learn from their strategies. The authors want to bridge this gap by creating chess-playing components whose internal logic is aligned with human chess concepts, particularly tactics, so humans can inspect and learn from them.
AI.method: They use an inductive logic programming system called PAL to learn symbolic patterns that correspond to chess tactics. These patterns are organized into a symbolic sub-policy model that suggests moves based on domain-knowledge-like structures. The authors define a divergence metric comparing the move distributions of this model to a random baseline, and they also propose integrating the sub-policy with an off-the-shelf chess engine to test its effect on play strength.
AI.result: The learned set of symbolic tactics can generate move suggestions whose playing strength is roughly comparable to that of a human beginner. The divergence metric shows that the model produces non-random, tactic-informed move choices, distinguishing it clearly from random move selection.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic, tactic-based sub-policies derived from inductive logic programming can yield interpretable chess move suggestions at beginner-level strength. The work is preliminary, but the proposed divergence metric and the idea of augmenting conventional engines with symbolic models provide a pathway toward more explainable game-playing agents that humans can learn from.

title: Denoising Hierarchical Representations: Joint Continuous Diffusion for Language Modeling
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) hold the promise of order-agnostic, parallel text generation. Recently, continuous diffusion and flow matching models have seen substantial gains, driven by carefully crafted token representations and diffusion/flow spaces. In this work, we introduce Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (H-CDLMs), a simple framework that further improves continuous DLMs with minimal compute and parameter overhead. Drawing on the discrete DLM and continuous image diffusion literature on joint diffusion, we diffuse multiple modalities in parallel. These modalities represent tokens at different semantic granularities: in our instantiation, the tokens themselves and coarser clusters obtained by clustering pretrained token embeddings. We propose a general setup that allows per-modality samplers and schedules to enhance the interplay between modalities. Applied to CoBit, this yields H-CoBit, which delivers large empirical gains across benchmarks. At dataset entropy, H-CoBit improves MAUVE and reaches a generative perplexity (GenPPL) of 49.4 on LM1B and 50.4 on OWT, improving on the baseline by 24.2 and 20.7 points and surpassing even discrete DLMs of comparable size. On GSM8K, it reaches 27.4% accuracy, outperforming prior continuous diffusion and flow-based models. We further apply H-CDLM to the flow matching model FLM, obtaining consistent gains with H-FLM and demonstrating that the framework generalizes across continuous generative paradigms. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/matol-16/HCDLM.git .

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (H-CDLMs), which jointly diffuse token-level and cluster-level semantic representations to improve continuous diffusion-based text generation, achieving better quality and perplexity than prior continuous and even discrete diffusion language models.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion and flow-based language models promise order-agnostic, parallel text generation but still lag behind strong discrete DLMs. Prior gains have come mainly from better token representations and diffusion spaces. The authors aim to further boost performance with minimal computational and parameter cost by better exploiting hierarchical semantic structure during diffusion, inspired by joint diffusion in discrete text and image generation.
AI.method: They introduce H-CDLM, a framework that jointly diffuses multiple modalities corresponding to different semantic granularities of text (e.g., raw tokens and clusters of token embeddings). Each modality has its own diffusion sampler and schedule, and the modalities interact during generation. Concretely, they instantiate this on CoBit to create H-CoBit, where token embeddings are clustered to form coarser semantic tokens that are diffused in parallel with the original tokens. They also instantiate it on a flow matching model (FLM), yielding H-FLM, to demonstrate generality across continuous generative paradigms.
AI.result: On LM1B and OpenWebText at dataset entropy, H-CoBit significantly improves MAUVE and generative perplexity (GenPPL), achieving GenPPL 49.4 on LM1B and 50.4 on OWT—improvements of 24.2 and 20.7 points over the baseline CoBit, and surpassing discrete DLMs of similar size. On GSM8K, H-CoBit reaches 27.4% accuracy, outperforming previous continuous diffusion and flow-based models. Applying the hierarchical framework to FLM (H-FLM) yields consistent performance gains as well, indicating that the approach transfers beyond a single model family.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical joint diffusion over multi-granularity semantic representations (tokens and their clusters) is an effective, lightweight way to enhance continuous diffusion and flow-based language models. The framework provides substantial empirical gains in text quality and perplexity, outperforms prior continuous approaches and even comparable discrete DLMs, and appears broadly applicable across continuous generative modeling paradigms.

title: Matching Object or Relation? Tracing Abstract Reasoning Inside VLMs
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) excel on visual benchmarks but fail systematically on tasks requiring abstract reasoning. Existing benchmarks document this failure but cannot say \emph{why} it happens or which cognitive capability is missing. We close this gap by adopting the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative and developmental psychology and pairing it with a mechanistic analysis of the model's internals. On a parametrically controlled stimulus set evaluated across frontier API models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3), we identify four levers that shift VLMs toward the relational match---capability tier, model scale, the number of objects per scene, and the absence of per-object stimulus noise---together producing a developmental-like trajectory that mirrors the human \emph{relational shift}. Opening up the model, a per-layer representational similarity analysis and a causal mediation analysis reveal that VLM abstract reasoning is implemented by two competing circuits: an early circuit that organises images by their surface object features, and a late circuit that organises them by their abstract relation. Extending the analysis to ARC-AGI-1, we find that ablating the relational heads identified on RMTS degrades performance more than ablating random heads, indicating that the relational circuit is recruited beyond our controlled stimuli. We hope this mechanism-level view serves as a step toward understanding how abstract reasoning is implemented in VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why vision-language models fail at abstract reasoning, using a psychology-inspired task and mechanistic analysis to reveal competing feature-based and relation-based circuits in the models.
AI.motivation: While VLMs perform well on standard visual benchmarks, they systematically fail on tasks that require abstract relational reasoning. Existing benchmarks only show that these failures exist but do not reveal the underlying causes or missing cognitive capabilities. The authors aim to fill this gap by precisely characterizing which internal mechanisms support or hinder abstract reasoning in VLMs.
AI.method: The authors adapt the Relational Match-to-Sample (RMTS) paradigm from comparative and developmental psychology, creating a parametrically controlled visual stimulus set. They evaluate multiple leading API-based VLMs (GPT, Claude, Gemini) and three open-source families (Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, InternVL3) on these tasks. They then perform a mechanistic analysis of model internals using per-layer representational similarity analysis (RSA) and causal mediation analysis to identify circuits that encode either surface object features or abstract relations. They further extend their analysis to a broader reasoning benchmark, ARC-AGI-1, and conduct ablation studies of attention heads identified as relational on RMTS.
AI.result: Behaviorally, the authors find that abstract relational matching performance improves with four factors: overall capability tier of the model, scale (size), scenes containing fewer objects, and the absence of per-object noise, together yielding a developmental-like trajectory akin to human relational shift. Mechanistically, they uncover two competing circuits: an early circuit that represents images via surface features and a late circuit that represents abstract relations. On ARC-AGI-1, ablating the relational attention heads identified on RMTS causes a larger performance drop than ablating random heads, showing that the same relational circuitry supports abstract reasoning beyond the controlled RMTS stimuli.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract reasoning in VLMs is not an emergent black box but can be traced to specific, competing internal circuits—one feature-based and one relation-based—that are differentially engaged across layers. The identified relational circuitry generalizes beyond the specialized RMTS dataset to more complex reasoning tasks like ARC-AGI-1. This mechanism-level account advances understanding of how abstract relational reasoning is implemented in VLMs and provides a foundation for targeted improvements in model design and training.

title: The Missing Minimal Pair: Stereotype Evaluation in LLMs
summary:
A common approach to measuring bias in Large Language Models is to compare the log-likelihoods of two contrastive stereotype sentences. We argue that such single-pair comparisons are often unreliable: simply rewriting the same stereotype with an alternative attribute can yield logically inconsistent preferences. To address this, we propose a dual minimal pair setup that introduces two axes of comparison for robust stereotype evaluation. First, we present a data-augmentation framework that fills critical gaps in existing stereotype datasets by generating paraphrases and alternate attributes. We apply our framework on a set of English, Russian, Spanish and Chinese stereotypes. Second, we introduce two evaluation metrics tailored to the dual minimal pair setup. One of these metrics provides a new perspective on bias by modeling the mutual information (MI) between social groups and stereotyped attributes. This MI-based metric is better suited for aggregation and enables more robust comparisons of stereotype strength across different languages and models.
  Our code is available at https://github.com/stepanat/missing-minimal-pair/.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that common single-pair log-likelihood bias tests for LLMs are unreliable and proposes a dual minimal pair framework with new metrics, including a mutual-information-based one, and a data augmentation pipeline across four languages for more robust stereotype bias evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing bias evaluation in LLMs often relies on comparing log-likelihoods of single pairs of stereotype vs. anti-stereotype sentences. The authors observe that such tests can be logically inconsistent: small rewrites or alternative attributes can flip the model’s apparent bias. There is also a gap in current stereotype datasets, which lack systematic paraphrases and attribute variants, making analyses fragile and hard to compare across languages and models. This motivates a more robust, logically coherent, and aggregatable framework for measuring stereotype bias in LLMs.
AI.method: They introduce a dual minimal pair setup that creates two orthogonal axes of comparison for each stereotype: (1) different paraphrases of the same stereotype and (2) alternate attributes that express the same stereotype. They propose a data-augmentation framework that automatically generates such paraphrases and alternatives, applied to stereotypes in English, Russian, Spanish, and Chinese. For evaluation, they define two new metrics suited to this dual-pair structure, one of which quantifies bias as mutual information between social groups and stereotyped attributes based on model log-likelihoods, facilitating aggregation and cross-language/model comparison.
AI.result: Using their augmented multilingual stereotype datasets and dual minimal pair setup, they demonstrate that single-pair bias measurements are unstable and logically inconsistent, while the proposed metrics, especially the MI-based one, provide more stable, aggregatable estimates of stereotype strength. The approach allows more robust comparisons of how strongly different models and languages encode particular stereotypes.
AI.conclusion: Single contrastive sentence pairs are an unreliable way to measure bias in LLMs because they are sensitive to minor rewrites and attribute choices. A dual minimal pair setup, backed by systematic data augmentation and MI-based evaluation, yields more robust, logically consistent, and comparable measures of stereotype bias across languages and models. This framework can serve as a better standard for future LLM bias evaluation.

title: Where Rules End and Judges Begin: Measuring the Judgment Boundary in Multi-Agent Systems Security
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) engage tools, share memory, and delegate tasks, often encountering adversarial content. Current defenses for MAS are typically evaluated in isolation, focusing on one attack type at a time, which can lead to costly and hard-to-audit outcomes. This study organizes defenses into five principles, implementing them as DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment), which includes a cascade of 28 checks that blocks what it can and refers the rest to a panel of four judges. In independent testing across four domains, attack success rates drop from about 30.0% to approximately 3.0%, with 78% of blocked attacks handled by deterministic checks. Only a quarter of proposals reach the judges in the security-operations domain, illustrating that the rules provide security for attacks violating clear policies, while judges manage those that only misrepresent intent. Both systems have weaknesses, such as a risk-score approval gate that inaccurately approves most attack proposals but few legitimate ones, highlighting the challenges in assessing threats accurately.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates DEFER1, a structured defense framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that combines deterministic checks with residual human-like judgment to significantly reduce multi-domain attack success rates.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems frequently face adversarial content, but existing defenses are typically designed and evaluated against single attack types in isolation. This narrow focus leads to gaps in protection, complex and costly configurations, and systems that are hard to audit or reason about, especially when multiple, diverse threats occur in practice. The authors aim to create a more systematic and principled way to defend MAS, improving robustness and auditability while reducing operational cost.
AI.method: The authors synthesize five high-level defense principles for securing LLM-based multi-agent systems and instantiate them in a concrete framework called DEFER1 (DEterministic-First Enforcement with Residual judgment). DEFER1 implements a cascade of 28 deterministic checks that automatically block clearly policy-violating or high-risk behaviors and then delegates unresolved or ambiguous cases to a panel of four judgment agents acting as residual evaluators. They test this pipeline on multiple attack scenarios across four domains, including a security-operations setting, and measure attack success rates, block rates, and the division of labor between deterministic checks and judgment agents. They also analyze failure modes, such as miscalibrated risk scoring.
AI.result: In independent evaluations spanning four different domains, DEFER1 reduces attack success from about 30% to around 3%. Roughly 78% of the blocked attacks are intercepted by the deterministic rules alone, showing that much of the risk can be handled via structured, auditable checks. In the security-operations domain, only about 25% of proposals escalate to the judgment panel, indicating that deterministic policies effectively handle clear-cut violations while leaving intent-ambiguous cases to residual judgment. The study also reveals weaknesses: for example, a risk-score approval gate incorrectly approves most attack proposals but very few legitimate ones, demonstrating poor calibration and highlighting that certain automated threat assessments remain unreliable.
AI.conclusion: DEFER1 demonstrates that organizing MAS defenses around explicit principles and prioritizing deterministic, rule-based enforcement—augmented by residual LLM-based judgment—can substantially lower attack success rates while improving auditability. Deterministic checks can handle the majority of dangerous cases, but nuanced or deceptive attacks still require flexible judgment, which is itself imperfect and vulnerable to calibration errors. The work underscores both the promise and limitations of layered defenses in MAS, pointing toward the need for better threat assessment mechanisms and continued refinement of combined rule-based and model-based security approaches.

title: AdvSim2Real : Training Web Agents Against Adaptive Prompt Injection in a Web World Model
summary: Web agents complete user requests by reading and acting on pages that third parties write, so an instruction planted on a page can redirect the agent away from the user's goal. The agent cannot simply ignore the page, because the page also holds the values and controls the task requires. Current defenses fine-tune the agent on injections fixed before training, and attackers that adapt to the trained model bypass them. Adversarial training lets the attacker adapt but keeps the tasks fixed, so a task stops teaching once the agent solves it. We introduce AdvSim2Real, which co-evolves a task curriculum, an injection adversary, and the agent inside a frozen web world model. The curriculum is rewarded for tasks the agent solves about half of the time, and the adversary only for a success flip, an injection that turns a judged success into a failure. Training in the simulator makes a 4B agent both more capable and more robust: its completion rises with and without attacks, holds against a frontier-model adversary it never trained against, and its capability gain carries over to a real browser. On 150 web tasks, AdvSim2Real raises completion under this unseen adversary by 33.6\% relative to the base agent.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes AdvSim2Real, a training framework that co-evolves tasks, adversarial prompt injections, and a web agent in a simulated web environment to improve robustness and capability of web agents against prompt injection attacks.
AI.motivation: Web agents that browse and act on third‑party pages are vulnerable to prompt injections embedded in those pages, which can divert them from user goals. Existing defenses are brittle: static fine‑tuning can be bypassed by adaptive attackers, while standard adversarial training uses fixed tasks that stop being useful once solved. There is a need for a training method that jointly adapts tasks and attacks while improving both robustness and capability, and that can transfer from simulation to real browsers.
AI.method: Introduce AdvSim2Real, a framework that co‑evolves three components within a frozen web world model (a simulator of web environments): (1) a task curriculum generator that creates tasks tuned so the agent succeeds about half the time, maintaining learning pressure; (2) an injection adversary that crafts prompt injections and is rewarded only when it flips a judged success into a failure; and (3) the web agent itself, trained within this adversarial, evolving curriculum. Training is done entirely in simulation, then evaluated with a real browser and with stronger, unseen adversarial models.
AI.result: A 4B-parameter web agent trained with AdvSim2Real becomes both more capable and more robust. Its task completion rate increases in both attacked and non‑attacked settings. The robustness generalizes to a frontier‑model adversary not seen during training, and the capability improvements learned in the simulator transfer to a real browser environment. On a benchmark of 150 web tasks under this unseen adversary, task completion improves by 33.6% relative to the untrained base agent.
AI.conclusion: Co‑evolving the task curriculum and an adaptive prompt‑injection adversary inside a simulated web world yields a web agent that is simultaneously more capable and more robust to prompt injection. Simulation‑based training transfers effectively to real‑browser performance and offers a scalable way to harden web agents against evolving attacks, outperforming static fine‑tuning and conventional adversarial training that rely on fixed tasks or fixed attacks.

title: Massive Activation Gating Channel in Large Language Models
summary: Massive activations, a phenomenon in which a small number of hidden channels exhibit exceptionally large magnitudes, are pervasive in large language models (LLMs). However, the mechanism by which a token develops massive activations as it propagates through a pretrained LLM remains poorly understood. In this paper, we find that the emergence of massive activations is controlled by a single channel in the input embedding to a spike feed-forward network (FFN). The position of this channel is fixed for a particular LLM. We name this channel the massive activation gating channel (MAGC). When the value of the MAGC is sufficiently large (or small, depending on the LLM), the output of the spike FFN exhibits massive activations. Examining six LLMs across four model families and different model sizes, we verify the existence and effect of MAGC. We further provide a theoretical explanation of the mechanism by which MAGC induces massive activations. When the value of MAGC is sufficiently large (or small), the output of a spike FFN asymptotically reduces to a quadratic form that mixes a few columns of the down-projection matrix of the FFN. Since these columns exhibit the shape of massive activations, the output therefore exhibits massive activations.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and explains a single special embedding channel—the Massive Activation Gating Channel (MAGC)—that controls when spike FFN layers in LLMs produce massive activations, and shows this mechanism is consistent across several model families, with a theoretical analysis linking large MAGC values to a quadratic form over specific down-projection columns that have massive-activation shapes.
AI.motivation: Massive activations (a few channels having very large magnitudes) are widely observed in large language models, but it is unclear why and how they arise as tokens move through the network. Understanding this mechanism is important for interpretability, stability, and potential mitigation of pathologies in LLMs. The paper aims to pinpoint the structural cause of massive activations and provide a principled theoretical explanation, rather than treating them as mysterious artifacts.
AI.method: The authors empirically probe multiple pretrained LLMs (six models from four families and various sizes) focusing on spike FFN layers. They inspect the input embedding channels to these FFNs and search for a specific channel whose scalar value strongly predicts whether the FFN output exhibits massive activations. They then characterize this channel—the MAGC—and analyze its effect by deriving an asymptotic theoretical approximation for the FFN output when the MAGC value is very large (or very small, depending on model). This analysis shows that the FFN reduces to a quadratic form involving a small subset of down-projection columns. They compare these theoretical predictions with observed activation patterns to validate the mechanism.
AI.result: They find, for each examined LLM, a single, fixed-position channel in the FFN input embedding whose magnitude reliably gates the presence or absence of massive activations at that layer. This Massive Activation Gating Channel (MAGC) is consistent per model and explains when spike FFNs enter a massive-activation regime. Theoretical analysis shows that in the large-magnitude regime for the MAGC, the FFN output can be approximated as a quadratic form involving only a few columns of the down-projection matrix, and those specific columns themselves display the massive-activation shape observed empirically. Thus, the empirical gating behavior is matched by a clear mathematical mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Massive activations in spike FFNs of LLMs are not arbitrary anomalies but are systematically controlled by a single embedding channel, the MAGC, whose position is fixed within each model. When this channel’s value is sufficiently extreme, the network dynamics simplify to a quadratic interaction over a small set of down-projection columns that inherently produce massive activations, thereby explaining both the origin and structure of the phenomenon. This provides a unified, theoretically grounded account of how massive activations emerge in several LLM architectures.

title: IdeaAnchor: Teaching LLMs to Turn Literature into Research Ideas
summary: Scientific research often begins by synthesizing ideas from a set of related papers to identify gaps and formulate new directions. However, training language models to perform this form of literature-grounded ideation remains challenging, as existing approaches based on prompting or feedback lack structured supervision for how papers should be synthesized. We introduce IdeaAnchor, a paradigm for training LLMs to perform research ideation using structured specifications as privileged signals. Each IdeaAnchor instance encodes how each input paper should be synthesized into a successful idea, including their functional roles, relationships, and target synthesis criteria. We build this paradigm by mining instances from published papers, capturing how real ideas emerge from prior literature. We then train models via demonstration, self-distillation, and reinforcement learning, and further enhance generation with retrieval at inference time. Experiments show consistent improvements in ideation quality. Our analysis reveals a functional decomposition: anchor-based training strengthens creative synthesis, retrieval enhances detail elaboration, and combining both yields the best performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IdeaAnchor, a structured training paradigm for LLMs that teaches them to synthesize multiple research papers into novel research ideas using explicit, mined specifications of how prior work is combined.
AI.motivation: Literature-grounded ideation is central to scientific research, but current LLM approaches rely on unstructured prompting or coarse feedback and lack explicit supervision on how to synthesize multiple papers into a coherent, high-quality new idea. This limits models’ ability to mirror how human researchers leverage prior work to identify gaps and propose new directions.
AI.method: The authors introduce IdeaAnchor, where each training instance provides a structured specification that encodes how each input paper contributes to a final research idea: its functional role, inter-paper relationships, and the target synthesis criteria. They mine such instances from existing published papers, effectively reconstructing how real ideas emerged from literature. They then train LLMs using a combination of supervised demonstrations on these anchors, self-distillation to refine model behavior, and reinforcement learning to further optimize ideation quality. At inference time, they augment the model with retrieval to fetch relevant literature that supports more detailed ideation.
AI.result: Across experiments, models trained with IdeaAnchor show consistent improvements in ideation quality compared to baselines that lack structured synthesis supervision. The analysis disentangles the contributions of the components: anchor-based training boosts the model’s capacity for creative synthesis, while retrieval mainly contributes to richer and more detailed elaboration. The combined system outperforms using either component alone.
AI.conclusion: Structured, literature-grounded supervision via IdeaAnchor enables LLMs to better emulate human-like research ideation by teaching them how to functionally decompose and recombine prior work into new ideas. Anchor-based training improves creative synthesis, retrieval helps detail and grounding, and jointly they deliver the strongest ideation performance, demonstrating a promising path toward LLMs that can assist more intelligently in scientific discovery.

title: EIO-Agents: The Missing Semantic Layer for AI Agent Evaluation
summary: AI agents are entering production in increasingly consequential environments without a shared semantic standard for what their evaluations actually mean. Scores, traces, judge outputs, and multi juror findings are increasingly used to justify readiness and release decisions, yet they often do not specify what evidence supports a claim, what that evidence can establish, or how the claim leads to a decision. We introduce EIO-Agents, an open specification for interoperable AI agent evaluation built on two layers. The Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO) provides the semantic layer through typed evidence, versioned behavioral predicates, evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof status, recurrence, and computable derivations for metrics, findings, controls, and PASS, REVIEW, or BLOCK decisions. The Portable Evaluation Record (PER) provides the system of record: a canonical, content addressed representation of one evaluation that preserves the evidence to decision chain and can be re derived, explained, and verified. Scores summarize, juries interpret, and traces record, but none of them define what the evidence means or what it can prove. EIO provides that missing semantic contract, while PER preserves the resulting evaluation as a portable and verifiable system of record. As AI agents assume greater operational responsibility, evaluation must become more than a collection of scores and verdicts; it must become an accountable artifact whose meaning, evidence, limitations, and decisions can be independently checked.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a standard way to formally describe and record AI agent evaluations so their meaning and supporting evidence are clear, auditable, and portable.
AI.motivation: Current AI agent evaluations use scores, traces, and human/jury judgments that lack a shared semantics, making it unclear what evidence supports claims about model readiness or safety and how those claims justify deployment decisions.
AI.method: The authors design EIO-Agents, composed of (1) the Evaluation Intelligence Ontology (EIO), a semantic schema with typed evidence, behavioral predicates, evidence contracts, claims, witness rules, proof statuses, recurrence, and computable derivations; and (2) the Portable Evaluation Record (PER), a canonical, content-addressed format that stores full, re-derivable evaluation records from evidence through to PASS/REVIEW/BLOCK decisions.
AI.result: They define an open, interoperable specification in which evaluations can be expressed as structured claims over evidence, with mechanically checkable derivations to metrics, findings, controls, and deployment decisions, and a portable record format that captures this full chain for verification and re-use across systems.
AI.conclusion: By adopting EIO-Agents, AI evaluations can move from opaque collections of scores and verdicts to accountable, standardized artifacts whose evidential basis, semantics, and decision logic are explicit, inspectable, and independently verifiable.

title: BluffJAX: Adversarial Imperfect Information Games in JAX
