summary: We introduce BluffJAX: an open-source suite of adversarial imperfect information games in JAX. We provide canonical implementations of games designed for high simulation throughputs and parallelization on GPU accelerators. Our suite consists of well-studied benchmarks such as Texas Hold'Em Poker and Kuhn Poker, as well as games that have not been previously studied in reinforcement learning research, such as Bluff, Stud Poker, and Kemps. We hope that implementing a variety of game mechanics and difficulties will introduce new challenges and foster novel research directions in game-theoretic methods for RL. We benchmark the throughput performance and memory usage of our environments in single and multi-GPU settings, demonstrating scaling of up to hundreds of millions of samples per second, and motivating the usage of BluffJAX over related GPU and CPU-based libraries. We benchmark reinforcement learning, tree search, and game-solving algorithms in JAX in order to provide users with baseline results and facilitate future comparisons.

AI.tldr: BluffJAX is an open-source JAX-based suite of adversarial imperfect-information games, designed for high-throughput GPU simulation and benchmarking RL and game-theoretic algorithms.
AI.motivation: Research in reinforcement learning and game theory needs scalable, standardized benchmarks for imperfect-information games, especially ones that fully exploit modern accelerators like GPUs. Existing environments either do not scale well, are CPU-based, or cover only a narrow set of games (like standard poker variants). There is also a lack of diversity in game mechanics and difficulty levels, limiting the exploration of new algorithmic ideas in game-theoretic RL. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a high-performance, GPU-friendly suite of diverse adversarial games with canonical implementations.
AI.method: The authors implement a collection of imperfect-information games in JAX, focusing on designs that enable high simulation throughput and massive parallelization on GPUs and multi-GPU setups. The suite includes classic benchmarks (Texas Hold’em, Kuhn Poker) and introduces additional games (Bluff, Stud Poker, Kemps) that bring new mechanics and difficulty profiles. They carefully engineer the environments to be memory- and compute-efficient on accelerators, then systematically benchmark throughput (samples per second) and memory usage under single- and multi-GPU configurations. They also implement and benchmark various reinforcement learning, tree-search, and game-solving algorithms directly in JAX, establishing baseline performance and results for these games.
AI.result: BluffJAX achieves very high simulation throughput, scaling up to hundreds of millions of environment samples per second in multi-GPU settings, while maintaining efficient memory usage. The benchmarks show that BluffJAX outperforms comparable CPU- and some GPU-based libraries in terms of speed and scalability. Additionally, the authors provide baseline results for several RL, tree search, and game-solving algorithms across the included games, giving concrete performance references for future work.
AI.conclusion: BluffJAX offers a high-performance, GPU-native benchmark suite for adversarial imperfect-information games, broadening the range of available environments beyond traditional poker benchmarks. Its strong scaling properties and provided algorithmic baselines make it a practical and attractive platform for research on reinforcement learning and game-theoretic methods. The authors expect that the diversity of games and the ease of large-scale experimentation will catalyze new research directions and facilitate fair, reproducible comparisons across methods.

title: On the Boundary of Admission Gates: An Injected-Truth Study of Falsification-First Selection in Quantitative Strategy Research
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code and data to reproduce every result: https://github.com/simplify23/quant-trading-agent
summary: Strategy research conflates two problems: finding a profitable rule, and establishing that the finding is not search luck. The latter calls for admission gates -- statistical criteria that must be satisfied before a conclusion is adopted -- yet whether gates work, and at what cost, remains untested. We introduce an injected-truth protocol with a random-admission control that adopts at the same rate as the gate; only if the gate beats this control does it carry information rather than merely raise a threshold. Across synthetic and real-calibrated panels, gates eliminate false discoveries in the weak-signal regime but cut adoption to 1--7%, and add nothing when signals are strong. Most importantly, criteria computed on absolute rather than excess returns silently reject every candidate, including true signals. Keywords: multiple testing, backtest overfitting, strategy admission, injected-truth validation, excess returns, false discovery rate

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes between discovering profitable trading strategies and proving they are not due to chance, proposes an 'injected-truth' validation protocol with random-admission controls, and tests how well different statistical admission criteria work and what they cost in terms of strategy adoption.
AI.motivation: Strategy research often identifies seemingly profitable rules from historical data but struggles to distinguish real opportunities from patterns that arise purely by chance due to intensive search and multiple testing. There is little evidence on whether commonly used statistical 'admission gates' actually help, how much they reduce false discoveries, and what opportunity cost they impose. The paper aims to rigorously evaluate these gates and provide a benchmark to judge whether they deliver information beyond simply tightening acceptance thresholds.
AI.method: The authors develop an injected-truth protocol in which they know which strategies are true signals and which are noise, and pair each statistical admission gate with a random-admission control that approves strategies at the same rate. They conduct experiments on both synthetic panels and data calibrated to real financial returns, comparing the performance, false discovery rates, and adoption rates under various admission criteria, and examining the impact of computing criteria on absolute vs excess returns.
AI.result: The study finds that in weak-signal environments, statistical admission gates can largely eliminate false discoveries but at the cost of reducing strategy adoption to a very low range (1–7%). In strong-signal settings, the gates perform no better than a random-admission control in terms of information content, implying that stringent gates add little value when true signals are strong and plentiful. Furthermore, when admission criteria are based on absolute returns rather than excess returns, every candidate strategy—including genuinely profitable ones—is rejected, often without explicit awareness by researchers.
AI.conclusion: Admission gates can be effective at reducing false discoveries in weak-signal contexts but impose a steep trade-off by severely limiting the number of adopted strategies, and they bring no informational advantage when signals are strong. The injected-truth protocol with random-admission controls provides a principled way to assess whether a gate genuinely contributes information or merely raises the bar. The paper also warns that using absolute-return-based criteria is dangerously overconservative, effectively blocking both spurious and real opportunities, and underscores the importance of focusing on excess returns and properly accounting for multiple testing and backtest overfitting.

title: AgentMemGate: Addressing Speculation Contamination in Conversational Assistant Memory
comment: Accepted at the PALM Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 15 pages, 4 figures
summary: Conversational AI assistants with long-term memory extract facts from user messages into a store consulted in later conversations. A stated plan can enter that store as fact: a user who might move to Seattle may be recorded as already living there. We call this speculation contamination. Final-state memory benchmarks miss this error because they do not probe intermediate state and include few unresolved speculations. We present AgentMemGate, a write-time gate for profile-store memory that classifies extracted statements as speculation, completed event, correction, or other. Speculations remain outside memory, with conditions governing later promotion or deletion. We also contribute a dataset of multi-session conversations in which plans are confirmed, abandoned, or left unresolved. On our 147-conversation held-out set, Mem0 and Graphiti assert unresolved plans as current state for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans. On the core benchmark, AgentMemGate eliminates all observed contamination relative to the identical ungated pipeline (87.5% to zero for the most exposed extraction style) and raises task accuracy from 65% to 95%. On the harder held-out set, gated contamination is 3.4% to 5.7% and task accuracy rises by 9 to 13 percentage points. Our analysis identifies field matching as the main remaining bottleneck: realistic speculations often match no profile field and never reach the gate. We release our datasets, prompts, and evaluation code.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses speculation contamination in long-term conversational AI memory and proposes AgentMemGate, a gate that classifies extracted user statements by status (speculation, completed, correction, other) to prevent unresolved plans from being stored as facts, significantly reducing contamination and improving task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Long-term memory systems for conversational AI often treat user plans or speculations as established facts, leading to incorrect user profiles and downstream errors. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate only final memory states and contain few unresolved plans, so they fail to detect this class of errors. There is a need for mechanisms and datasets that explicitly handle and evaluate speculative or unresolved information over multiple sessions.
AI.method: The authors introduce AgentMemGate, a write-time gating mechanism for profile-store memory. It classifies each extracted statement as speculation, completed event, correction, or other, and then applies rules: speculative items are kept out of the permanent profile until later promotion or deletion conditions are met. They also construct a dataset of multi-session conversations where user plans are eventually confirmed, abandoned, or remain unresolved and evaluate multiple memory extraction systems (Mem0, Graphiti) with and without the gate.
AI.result: On a 147-conversation held-out set, baseline systems Mem0 and Graphiti incorrectly store unresolved plans as current facts for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans. On the core benchmark, adding AgentMemGate to the most vulnerable extraction style reduces contamination from 87.5% to 0% and increases task accuracy from 65% to 95%. On the more challenging held-out set, contamination with gating is reduced to 3.4–5.7%, with task accuracy gains of 9–13 percentage points. The analysis reveals that remaining errors are largely due to field matching failures where speculative content does not map cleanly to existing profile fields and therefore bypasses the gate.
AI.conclusion: AgentMemGate effectively prevents speculation contamination by filtering speculative statements at write time and managing their later promotion or deletion, yielding large improvements in both memory correctness and downstream task accuracy. However, overall reliability is still constrained by upstream field-matching and extraction coverage, suggesting that future work should better connect open-ended user statements to structured profile schemas. The authors provide datasets, prompts, and evaluation code to support further research on long-term conversational memory with explicit treatment of speculation.

title: Evidence Before Sampling: Interpretable Implicit Negative Candidate Discovery for Recommendation
summary: Recommender systems learn from observed user-item interactions, but explicit negative feedback is often unavailable. Since deep learning models require negative signals for training, negative sampling methods typically treat selected unobserved interactions as negatives. However, a missing interaction does not explain why a user is uninterested in an item or whether there is sufficient evidence to label it negative. This is especially important in business recommendation, where negative signals should be interpretable and aligned with business objectives. We formulate implicit negative candidate discovery to identify unobserved interactions supported by observed customer behavior. We encode these patterns as symbolic rules, score them based on support, informativeness, and product relevance, and rank the retained rules by evidence. An LLM then interprets the retained rules using business objectives and domain knowledge; the interpretations are combined with the statistical evidence in the final report. We evaluate our method in an industrial B2B setting and across five public recommendation datasets. Candidate-quality evaluations in the industrial setting and three public datasets show higher precision than the evaluated baselines, while symbolic selection improves downstream test PR-AUC by 12.5% over random selection with four negatives per positive example in the industrial task. Our results show that negative candidate validity can be evaluated separately from downstream recommendation performance. This distinction enables evidence-based, business-aligned, and explainable negative selection, improving both interpretability and model training in sparse, skewed, real-world recommendation settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to discover high-quality, interpretable negative examples for recommender systems by mining symbolic rules from user behavior and then having an LLM explain them in business terms, improving both recommendation performance and explainability.
AI.motivation: Deep recommender systems need negative examples to train, but in implicit-feedback scenarios, explicit negatives are rarely observed. Standard negative sampling treats random unobserved user-item pairs as negatives, which is noisy and uninterpretable, and can misalign with business goals, especially in high‑stakes B2B recommendation. The authors aim to create negative examples that are both statistically well-supported and human/business interpretable, so that model training better reflects real user disinterest and supports decision-making.
AI.method: They formalize an implicit negative candidate discovery task: from observed customer behavior, they mine symbolic rules that indicate items likely to be negative for a given user (e.g., based on co-occurrence, category patterns, or purchase histories). Each rule is scored on support, informativeness, and product relevance. The top-scoring rules are retained and ranked by strength of evidence. A large language model then interprets these rules using business objectives and domain knowledge, producing human-readable explanations. Finally, the system combines statistical scores and LLM-based interpretations into a report that guides negative sampling for recommender training and evaluation.
AI.result: In an industrial B2B recommendation scenario and five public datasets, their negative-candidate discovery method achieves higher precision in candidate-quality evaluations than baseline negative sampling methods on the industrial setting and three public datasets. In the industrial task, using symbolically selected negatives (four per positive) improves downstream recommendation test PR-AUC by 12.5% compared to random negative selection. They also empirically show that assessing the validity of negative candidates can be decoupled from measuring downstream recommender performance.
AI.conclusion: High-quality, interpretable negative candidates can be systematically discovered from implicit feedback by combining symbolic pattern mining with LLM-based interpretation. This yields negatives that are better aligned with business objectives, more explainable, and statistically well-grounded, which in turn improves both the transparency of the recommendation process and the performance of deep recommender models in sparse, skewed real-world settings. The work argues that negative candidate quality should be treated as a distinct, evaluable property rather than being assessed only via end-to-end recommendation metrics.

title: PERSIST: Who-What-When Memory Across Sessions for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue
summary: Modern voice assistants may be shared by multiple users and should be able to answer questions about earlier conversations such as "When did I originally plan to leave?" or adapt their behavior to individual users based on past interactions. This requires more than retrieving a topically similar passage: the assistant must identify the current speaker, recover the relevant past state, and distinguish it from later revisions. We present PERSIST, a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that explicitly models Who, What, and When. PERSIST structures cross-session histories into readable event records and retrieves them with a 3W joint scoring mechanism that combines semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. For real-time full-duplex interaction, PERSIST further reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone, avoiding query-audio re-encoding and reducing retrieval latency from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms. We also introduce SpokenTrace, a diagnostic benchmark that factorizes evaluation along memory tasks and speaker-query types, exposing failures in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking. On SpokenTrace, PERSIST achieves 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy and improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% with BGE-large to 82.10%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PERSIST, a persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that accurately retrieves and reasons over past conversational events by modeling who said what and when, achieving high accuracy and low latency, and is evaluated with a new benchmark, SpokenTrace.
AI.motivation: Existing voice assistants are often used by multiple people across many sessions, but they struggle to correctly answer questions about earlier conversations or personalize behavior based on past interactions. Simple semantic similarity retrieval is insufficient because the system must correctly identify the current speaker, find the relevant past state, and account for revisions over time. There is a need for a structured, efficient memory system that can robustly track and retrieve user-specific conversational history in a way that supports real-time spoken dialogue.
AI.method: The authors propose PERSIST, a persistent memory system for spoken dialogue that explicitly models three key aspects of dialogue history: Who (speaker identity), What (semantic content), and When (temporal state). Dialogue history across sessions is structured into human-readable event records. Retrieval uses a 3W joint scoring mechanism that combines semantic similarity, acoustic speaker identification, and temporal information to select relevant memories and disambiguate revisions. For real-time full-duplex interaction, PERSIST reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue model (dialogue backbone) instead of re-encoding the query audio, which dramatically reduces retrieval latency. They also design SpokenTrace, a benchmark that decomposes evaluation into memory-related tasks and speaker-query types to diagnose specific weaknesses in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal tracking.
AI.result: PERSIST achieves strong performance on the SpokenTrace benchmark, reaching 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy. In terms of retrieval quality, it improves all-support EM@3 from 49.01% when using a strong text embedding baseline (BGE-large) to 82.10%. The system also reduces retrieval latency from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms by reusing backbone representations for full-duplex interaction, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency improvements.
AI.conclusion: By jointly modeling who spoke, what was said, and when it occurred, PERSIST provides a robust persistent memory layer for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue systems. Its structured event records and 3W scoring enable accurate retrieval of past conversational states, including disambiguation of revisions, while its architectural optimizations support low-latency, real-time use. The SpokenTrace benchmark further offers a diagnostic tool to analyze memory, speaker attribution, and temporal reasoning in such systems. Overall, the work shows that explicitly structured, multi-faceted memory is crucial for next-generation voice assistants that must remember and personalize over long-term interactions.

title: How Well Do LLMs Reason with Noisy Evidence? An Active Visual Reasoning Benchmark
summary: Real-world reasoning rarely reduces to static question answering: agents must actively gather information from tools and sensors that are often noisy and unreliable. Yet most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume that environmental feedback is trustworthy, or introduce noise without exposing an explicit, calibrated uncertainty signal, leaving open how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. We introduce VisualNoiseQA, a novel benchmark for active reasoning under noisy visual feedback. A text-only LLM must solve VQA problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, we draw multiple samples and expose an empirical uncertainty signal via self-consistency, enabling the reasoner to probe from different angles and decide what to ask next and when to stop. Our construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, we retain only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable. We evaluate multiple LLM reasoners on 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. VisualNoiseQA thus provides a controlled playground to study how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals for robust reasoning.

AI.tldr: Introduces VisualNoiseQA, a benchmark where an LLM must reason over noisy visual feedback from a VLM treated as a stochastic sensor, using uncertainty signals from multiple samples to decide what to query and when to stop.
AI.motivation: Existing active reasoning benchmarks assume reliable feedback or add noise without explicit uncertainty estimates, so they do not capture how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. Real-world agents, however, must interact with noisy, unreliable tools and sensors, motivating a benchmark that explicitly studies reasoning under uncertain visual evidence.
AI.method: Construct VisualNoiseQA by: (1) using diverse existing VQA datasets and two off-the-shelf noisy VLMs as black-box stochastic sensors; (2) for each text query about an image, drawing multiple response samples from the VLM(s) and using self-consistency across samples to estimate an empirical uncertainty signal; (3) automatically filtering to keep only questions where VLM outputs are inconsistent (noisy) but humans can still solve the item. Then, evaluate text-only LLMs that iteratively query the VLM sensor, leverage the exposed uncertainty signal, adapt their questioning strategy, and decide when to stop and answer. Instances span perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning.
AI.result: A 1,000-instance benchmark is produced that systematically features human-solvable but sensor-noisy VQA questions, across several visual and reasoning domains. Multiple LLM reasoners are evaluated, revealing how well they can use the provided uncertainty signal from noisy VLM sensors to perform robust active reasoning, though specific scores are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: VisualNoiseQA offers a controlled, scalable testbed for investigating LLMs' ability to actively reason under uncertain, noisy visual feedback. By exposing an explicit uncertainty signal derived from multiple VLM samples and requiring iterative querying and stopping decisions, it isolates and evaluates how different LLMs exploit uncertainty for robust reasoning in realistic settings.

title: ST-Bench: A Spatial-Temporal Benchmark for Multi-Agent System Generation on Scientific Research Tasks
summary: The rapid progress of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) has shown that they largely outperform single agents on coding, math, and QA tasks, where executable tests provide a binary success signal. Whether this advantage transfers to real scientific data analysis remains untested. We introduce ST-Bench, a benchmark designed to answer two questions: whether MAS outperform single agents on complex scientific data analysis tasks, and if so, by how much and at what additional cost. ST-Bench contains 100 data science tasks adapted from published Earth science studies across hydrology, agriculture, and wetland methane research, expanded into 2,067 queries grounded in additional published studies and validated by domain experts. Using ST-Bench, we evaluate five recent MAS generation methods under two training protocols, against single-agent baselines on the same GPT-5 backbone. Nine of the ten MAS configurations exceed the cheapest single-agent baseline, with the strongest reaching nearly three times its composite score. This gain is primarily attributable to coverage: trained workflows produce realistic numerical metrics on a larger fraction of queries, while the quality of those metrics, conditional on producing realistic output, is comparable to that of the single-agent baseline. The strongest configuration requires approximately four times the single-agent inference time, whereas a more economical workflow captures the majority of the benefit at less than twice the cost. MAS specialization confers measurable benefit on scientific data analysis, but the benefit is conditional rather than universal.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ST-Bench to rigorously compare LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) with single agents on real scientific data analysis tasks, showing MAS generally achieve higher task coverage and composite scores at increased computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing work shows LLM-based MAS outperform single agents in domains with clear, executable test signals like coding, math, and QA, but it is unknown whether these advantages extend to complex, noisy, real-world scientific data analysis where evaluation is harder. Researchers need a realistic benchmark grounded in published science to quantify if MAS genuinely add value, how large the gains are, and what additional cost they incur.
AI.method: The authors build ST-Bench, a benchmark of 100 Earth science data analysis tasks (hydrology, agriculture, wetland methane), expanded into 2,067 expert-validated queries derived from published studies. They then evaluate five recent MAS generation methods, each under two training protocols (yielding ten MAS configurations), against single-agent baselines that share the same GPT-5 backbone. They compare composite scores, task coverage (fraction of queries with realistic numerical outputs), and conditional quality of those outputs, as well as computational/inference costs.
AI.result: Nine of ten MAS configurations outperform the least expensive single-agent baseline in composite score, with the best MAS achieving nearly three times that baseline’s score. The main source of improvement is increased coverage—MAS successfully produce realistic numerical metrics for more queries—while the accuracy/quality of metrics, given that an answer is produced, is similar between MAS and single agents. The strongest MAS configuration incurs about 4× the inference time of a single agent, while a cheaper MAS workflow achieves most of the accuracy gain at under 2× the cost.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based MAS with specialized workflows offer clear but not universal benefits for real-world scientific data analysis: they substantially improve coverage and composite performance over single agents, at the price of higher computational cost. The benefits arise mainly from solving a larger fraction of tasks rather than from higher per-task accuracy, and practical use requires balancing performance gains against increased inference time.

title: OTel: Open Telco AI Datasets, Benchmarks, and Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026, ED Track, Spotlight
summary: We present Open Telco (OTel), an open telecom AI resource that releases derived telecom datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, together with 30 full-parameter post-trained baselines spanning 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models. The community has already engaged substantially with the resource: as of May 3, 2026, the released models have been downloaded over 16 million times and the project has received 157+ pieces of media coverage worldwide. Building on prior open telecom datasets and benchmarks, OTel provides documented telecom data sources, held-out evaluation partitions, trained embedding models, rerankers, context-grounded LLMs, and safety/abstention data in one unified resource. Each baseline starts from an open-weight model and is post-trained on OTel-derived data using an open training recipe, then evaluated on held-out OTel evaluation partitions. OTel post-training improves performance across all three model families: embedding retrieval reaches 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking reaches 0.947 MRR@10, and language-model correctness reaches 87.8%. We release OTel as a reproducible starting point and invite the community to expand the data, improve embedding and reranking models, and build stronger context-grounded telecom LLMs.

AI.tldr: OTel is an open telecom AI resource providing unified datasets and 30 post-trained baselines for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention, significantly improving model performance and enabling community-driven development of telecom-specialized LLMs.
AI.motivation: There is a need for strong, domain-specialized AI systems in telecommunications, but data, benchmarks, and models are often siloed, proprietary, or inconsistently documented. Existing open telecom datasets are fragmented and do not provide an end-to-end, reproducible pipeline from raw data through models and evaluations. Practitioners lack a common, transparent starting point for building and comparing telecom-focused retrieval and language models, especially for context-grounded question answering and safety-aware deployment.
AI.method: The authors curate and document telecom-related data sources and derive multiple task-specific datasets for retrieval, reranking, instruction tuning, and safety/abstention. They partition the data into held-out evaluation sets and training sets. Starting from open-weight base models, they post-train 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models using open training recipes tailored to the OTel-derived data. Each model family is evaluated on the corresponding OTel held-out partitions using standard IR and QA metrics such as NDCG@10, MRR@10, and correctness for LLM outputs.
AI.result: OTel yields 30 full-parameter post-trained telecom-domain baselines: 10 embedding models, 3 rerankers, and 17 language models. Post-training on OTel data substantially boosts performance versus the base models. Embedding-based retrieval achieves 93.1% NDCG@10, reranking achieves 0.947 MRR@10, and telecom-focused language models reach 87.8% correctness on held-out evaluations. The resource has seen extensive real-world uptake, with over 16 million model downloads and more than 157 media mentions by May 2026, indicating strong community interest and adoption.
AI.conclusion: OTel provides a unified, reproducible, and openly documented telecom AI resource that consolidates data, baselines, and evaluation protocols for retrieval, reranking, and context-grounded LLMs, including safety/abstention. The demonstrated performance gains show that targeted post-training on domain-specific data significantly improves telecom task performance. The authors position OTel as a community foundation and invite further contributions to expand datasets, refine embedding and reranking models, and develop stronger, safety-aware telecom language models built on top of the released baselines and recipes.

title: Quantization Effects on Tool-Failure Recovery Vary Across Prompts and Evaluation Designs
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Small Language Models for Agentic Systems (SLM-Agents). 7 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, plus appendix
summary: Post-training quantization reduces the cost of deploying language-model agents, but its effect on recovery from temporary tool failures can depend on how recovery is evaluated. We compare 8-bit and 4-bit variants of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on twenty deterministic tool-use tasks and five prompts. The 8-bit-4-bit recovery comparison changes direction across prompts and evaluation targets. On tasks that both variants complete without faults under the same prompt, the difference ranges from 0 to +20.2 percentage points for Llama and from -50.0 to +35.0 points for Qwen. Full-pipeline point estimates favor 8-bit Llama under all five prompts, whereas the Qwen comparison changes direction across prompts. The evaluation target can also reverse the result. For Llama under one prompt, scoring each variant only on its own clean-passing tasks favors 4-bit by 17.5 points; scoring the same tasks for both variants gives no difference, while scoring the full pipeline favors 8-bit by 28.3 points. Executor leniency is a third such choice. Rescoring the same logs with strict output parsing, which 8-bit Llama violates far more often than 4-bit Llama under that prompt, turns that +28.3 into -15.0 while leaving Qwen essentially unchanged. These findings show that one prompt, one screened task set, and one scoring policy do not establish a stable conclusion about quantized-agent robustness. Evaluations should compare variants on matched tasks, report full-pipeline success for deployment decisions, state the scoring policy, and quantify uncertainty across tasks rather than injected fault sites.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how post-training quantization (8-bit vs 4-bit) affects language-model agents’ ability to recover from temporary tool failures, and shows that conclusions about robustness are highly sensitive to prompts, task subsets, and scoring policies.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization is widely used to reduce the computational and memory cost of deploying language models, including tool-using agents. However, its impact on robustness—specifically, agents’ ability to recover from transient tool failures—is poorly understood and may be mis-estimated if evaluation design choices bias results. The authors aim to clarify how much evaluation methodology affects perceived robustness differences between quantized variants.
AI.method: They compare 8-bit and 4-bit quantized versions of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 20 deterministic tool-use tasks and 5 prompts. They analyze recovery from temporary tool failures under different evaluation choices: (1) which tasks are included (e.g., only tasks where each variant has at least one clean success vs a shared matched set), (2) what the evaluation target is (per-variant screened set vs shared set vs full-pipeline success), and (3) executor leniency (lenient vs strict output parsing). They compute success-rate differences between 8-bit and 4-bit variants under these different choices and examine how the direction and magnitude of the comparison changes.
AI.result: The relative robustness of 8-bit vs 4-bit quantization changes direction across prompts, models, and evaluation choices. For tasks that both variants can complete cleanly under the same prompt, Llama’s 8-bit–4-bit difference ranges from 0 to +20.2 percentage points; Qwen’s ranges from -50.0 to +35.0 points. Full-pipeline estimates always favor 8-bit Llama across prompts, but for Qwen the favored variant depends on the prompt. For one Llama prompt, scoring each variant on its own clean-passing tasks favors 4-bit by 17.5 points, scoring the same matched tasks yields no difference, and full-pipeline scoring favors 8-bit by 28.3 points. Changing executor leniency (strict parsing) flips that +28.3 advantage for 8-bit to -15.0, largely due to more parsing violations by 8-bit Llama, while Qwen’s comparison is basically unaffected.
AI.conclusion: Apparent robustness differences between 8-bit and 4-bit quantized agents are highly unstable and can reverse solely due to changes in prompts, task-screening criteria, evaluation targets, or executor strictness. Therefore, a single prompt, a filtered task set, or an unspecified scoring policy is insufficient to claim robust superiority of one quantization level. Evaluations should (1) compare variants on matched task sets, (2) report full-pipeline success rates for deployment-relevant decisions, (3) clearly state scoring policies and executor behavior, and (4) quantify uncertainty across tasks rather than over injected fault locations.

title: Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference: What It Costs, What It Buys, and When You Can Tell
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure. Accepted as a poster at the Machine Learning for Systems Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Decomposing long-context inference across cooperating agents bounds the active KV cache per call rather than total evidence, which matters when KV-cache memory binds. Many such systems add a persistent tier storing and recalling reasoning traces, usually validated by an ablation reporting an accuracy gain. We measure both on one three-tier agent architecture. Decomposition delivers: peak KV working set of 14.3 MiB per query against 35.5 and 35.3 MiB for single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. The persistent tier does not: across eight controlled dataset pairs at n=100 per arm it costs +0.368 MiB [+0.167, +0.590] of peak cache and produces no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]). We argue the null is structural: single-question benchmarks supply each item with its own evidence and score it independently, and correctness requires resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. Reaching it took four measurement corrections -- three inflating the apparent benefit, the fourth making an effect that size look resolvable -- none visible in the results table. We give the conditions an agent-memory ablation must satisfy and detection procedures that need no knowledge of the specific defect.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates multi-agent long-context inference architectures with a focus on KV-cache memory usage and the value of a persistent memory tier, finding that decomposition saves KV memory but persistent memory offers no measurable accuracy gain on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Many long-context LLM systems rely on KV-cache memory and sometimes add a persistent memory tier to store and reuse reasoning traces, but evidence for the claimed accuracy benefits of such persistent memory is weak and possibly confounded. The authors want to rigorously measure both the KV-cache savings from decomposed multi-agent setups and the true contribution, if any, of a persistent reasoning memory under realistic constraints.
AI.method: They implement and study a three-tier agent architecture with decomposition and a persistent memory tier, compare it against single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines, and carefully measure peak KV-cache usage and accuracy. They run controlled experiments on eight dataset pairs with n=100 items per arm, apply multiple corrections to the measurement methodology, and perform a detailed ablation of agent memory functions, including proposing structural conditions and defect-detection procedures for valid memory ablations.
AI.result: Decomposing inference across cooperating agents substantially reduces peak KV-cache working set per query (14.3 MiB) compared to single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines (35.5 and 35.3 MiB). In contrast, adding a persistent memory tier increases peak cache usage slightly (+0.368 MiB, with 95% CI [+0.167, +0.590]) and yields no statistically detectable accuracy improvement (accuracy change +0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]) across eight controlled dataset pairs. The authors identify four separate measurement corrections that altered the apparent effect size, three of which had inflated the perceived benefit.
AI.conclusion: Task decomposition across agents is genuinely useful for reducing KV-cache memory, but persistent agent-memory tiers, as commonly evaluated on single-question, independently-scored benchmarks, do not confer measurable accuracy benefits while increasing memory usage. The authors argue this null effect is structural to such benchmarks, where each question comes with its own evidence and traces must be reset, leaving nothing valuable to recall. They conclude that many existing agent-memory ablations are methodologically flawed, and they provide necessary conditions and general detection procedures to ensure future memory-ablation studies are valid and not misled by hidden measurement defects.

title: ThinkFuse: Trajectory-Aware Test-Time Fusion for Small Reasoning Models
summary: Small reasoning models (SRMs) have shown strong performance on complex reasoning tasks by generating extended chain-of-thought trajectories, but they often fail to recover once their reasoning enters an erroneous path. Existing test-time fusion methods rely on local fusion signals to determine when to trigger fusion, which can be misled by transient uncertainty fluctuations and may reinforce unstable reasoning trajectories. We propose ThinkFuse, a training-free test-time fusion framework that selectively intervenes in unreliable reasoning segments. ThinkFuse compares segment-level uncertainty shifts with trajectory-level uncertainty trends to identify unstable reasoning points and fuse auxiliary reasoning paths into the primary model's trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ThinkFuse outperforms baselines on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains across model-family combinations, and remains robust with a smaller primary model. Our analysis shows that ThinkFuse requires fewer fusion triggers and generates fewer tokens, highlighting the efficiency of selective triggering. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/ThinkFuse.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ThinkFuse, a training-free test-time fusion framework that improves small reasoning models by selectively intervening in unstable parts of their chain-of-thought, leading to better and more efficient reasoning on math and knowledge-intensive tasks.
AI.motivation: Small reasoning models perform well on complex reasoning by generating long chain-of-thoughts, but once they go down a wrong reasoning path, they rarely recover. Existing test-time fusion methods, which combine multiple reasoning trajectories, depend on local uncertainty signals to decide when to fuse. These local signals can be noisy or transient, causing fusion to be triggered at the wrong times and potentially amplifying unstable or incorrect reasoning. The authors aim to design a more reliable and efficient way to detect genuinely unstable reasoning segments and intervene only when necessary, without retraining models.
AI.method: The authors propose ThinkFuse, a training-free test-time fusion framework. It segments the chain-of-thought reasoning process and monitors uncertainty at both the segment level and the overall trajectory level. By comparing segment-level uncertainty shifts against the longer-term trajectory-level uncertainty trend, ThinkFuse identifies points where the primary model’s reasoning becomes unstable, rather than just momentarily uncertain. At these identified unstable points, ThinkFuse fuses auxiliary reasoning paths from other trajectories into the primary trajectory, effectively correcting or stabilizing the reasoning process while minimizing interventions and extra computation.
AI.result: Across multiple experiments on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, ThinkFuse consistently outperforms existing fusion baselines. It works across different combinations of model families and remains effective even when the main (primary) model is relatively small. Quantitatively, the method requires fewer fusion triggers and generates fewer total tokens than baselines, indicating that its selective triggering mechanism is more efficient while still delivering better accuracy.
AI.conclusion: ThinkFuse provides an effective and efficient, training-free way to improve small reasoning models at test time by focusing on selective intervention. By using segment-versus-trajectory uncertainty comparisons, it better identifies genuinely unstable reasoning points and fuses auxiliary trajectories only when helpful. This leads to higher performance on complex reasoning tasks, robustness across model families and smaller primary models, and reduced computational overhead due to fewer fusion events and shorter outputs.

title: Attacca: Goal-Directed Control under State Continuity for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
summary: A central capability of embodied agents is to accomplish complex objectives through sequences of interdependent tasks. Yet existing visual goal-conditioned policies underlying these agents are typically evaluated on isolated interactions where the target is already visible, and thus do not capture the conditions that arise during continuous long-horizon task execution. In such settings, each task begins from the state left by the previous one: the agent may end at a different position and orientation, the world may have been modified, and the next interaction target may lie outside the current field of view. As a result, agents relying on such policies may struggle to proceed to the next task when they cannot ground their target in the current observation. To address this challenge, we propose Attacca, a new approach that trains visual goal-conditioned policies on complete search-to-interact trajectories using goal images decoupled from the execution environment. Attacca uses context-decoupled goal sampling to pair each demonstration with a class-compatible masked goal image from another world, removing direct scene and pose correspondence. It learns dense current-view grounding through a target-mask prediction head, providing auxiliary supervision beyond action imitation. We further introduce behavioral-phase conditioning that teaches the policy to distinguish Search, Approach, and Interact stages and adapt its control as execution progresses. We evaluate Attacca on multiple short- and long-horizon embodied tasks in Minecraft. Our method achieves 39.0-47.5% clean success, improving over the strongest baseline by 1.7-2.4x. On long-horizon tasks, it attains 54%, 30%, and 28% completion, yielding up to a 7x improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Attacca, a method for training visual goal-conditioned policies that can handle continuous, long-horizon embodied tasks where goals may be out of view, by learning from decoupled search-to-interact trajectories and phase-aware control.
AI.motivation: Existing visual goal-conditioned policies are usually trained and evaluated in simplified settings where the agent’s goal object is already visible and the environment is not affected by prior actions. This does not reflect realistic, continuous long-horizon scenarios where: (1) each task starts from the resulting state of the previous one, (2) the environment and the agent’s pose can change, and (3) the next target may be outside the current field of view. Under such conditions, conventional policies fail to ground the target and proceed to the next subtask. The authors aim to develop a training approach that enables agents to search for and interact with targets robustly across different worlds and poses, capturing realistic multi-step task execution.
AI.method: The authors propose Attacca, a training framework for visual goal-conditioned policies that operates on entire search-to-interact trajectories and decouples goal images from the execution environment. The key components are: (1) context-decoupled goal sampling, which pairs each demonstration trajectory with a class-compatible but different-world masked goal image, breaking direct correspondence in scene layout and pose; (2) a target-mask prediction head that learns dense grounding of the goal in the current view by predicting the target’s mask, offering auxiliary supervision beyond pure action imitation; and (3) behavioral-phase conditioning, where the policy is explicitly conditioned on discrete execution phases—Search, Approach, and Interact—so the controller can adapt behaviors as the task progresses. The approach is trained on demonstrations and evaluated on embodied tasks in Minecraft.
AI.result: On multiple embodied tasks in Minecraft, including both short- and long-horizon settings, Attacca achieves 39.0–47.5% clean success rate, representing a 1.7–2.4× improvement over the strongest baseline. For challenging long-horizon tasks involving sequences of interdependent subtasks, the method reaches 54%, 30%, and 28% completion rates on different task suites, yielding up to a 7× improvement relative to prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Attacca enables visual goal-conditioned agents to perform more robust continuous long-horizon task execution by training on complete search-to-interact trajectories and decoupling goals from specific environment contexts. Through context-decoupled goal sampling, dense target-mask grounding, and explicit behavioral-phase conditioning, the method overcomes limitations of prior approaches that assume visible targets and static contexts. The empirical results in Minecraft show substantial gains in both success rates and long-horizon task completion, suggesting that this training paradigm is effective for building more capable embodied agents and could generalize to other environments and task families.

title: Isotropic Yet Undecodable: The Sequential Content-Sufficiency Gap in Latent-Predictive Text Representations
summary: We study sequential content sufficiency by investigating whether a representation retains the ordered target information available in its input. An information-theoretic decomposition separates input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. We construct recoverable views where perfect agreement and joint isotropic Gaussianity coexist with zero target information, and establish limits imposed by deterministic canonical anchors. Token log-loss provides a one-sided information-loss bound; a fixed-penalty ridge analysis shows why rank alone cannot determine prediction risk. These results motivate CANOPE, a nonautoregressive framework with ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization. On 40,000 validation sequences, latent-agreement (PL0) and token-grounded (PL2) have nearly identical pooled ranks but reach 13.5% and 98.8% positional Recall@1, respectively, under strong natural corruption when the correct target length is provided. On 3,930 LJSpeech validation utterances, frozen PL2 with a trained MatchaTTS readout yields 21.54% word error rate (WER) on corrupted text, versus 99.22% for frozen PL0, while end-to-end MatchaTTS reaches 10.93%. These results show that geometric regularity alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content or effective downstream access in the text settings studied here.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when sequence representations truly preserve ordered target information, showing that geometric regularity and agreement alone can hide complete loss of target content, and proposes CANOPE, a framework that better preserves sequential content for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Sequential models often produce latent representations that look well-behaved geometrically and match targets under certain views, yet may fail to preserve the actual ordered content needed for downstream tasks, especially under corruption. The authors aim to formally characterize this gap and understand what properties of representations are necessary for reliable recovery of sequential information.
AI.method: They introduce an information-theoretic decomposition of sequential content sufficiency into input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch. They construct counterexample representations (recoverable views) with perfect agreement and Gaussian structure but zero target information, and analyze constraints when deterministic canonical anchors are used. They derive a one-sided information-loss bound from token log-loss and show via a fixed-penalty ridge regression analysis that rank of the representation alone cannot determine prediction risk. Building on these insights, they design CANOPE, a non-autoregressive model with ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization, and evaluate different training objectives (PL0 vs PL2) on synthetic and text-to-speech settings.
AI.result: In controlled experiments on 40,000 corrupted validation sequences, two models (PL0 and PL2) have nearly identical pooled rank statistics but dramatically different positional Recall@1: 13.5% for PL0 vs 98.8% for PL2 when target length is known. On 3,930 LJSpeech utterances with corrupted text, using a frozen CANOPE representation with a MatchaTTS readout, PL2 achieves 21.54% WER while PL0 degrades to 99.22% WER; a fully end-to-end MatchaTTS system reaches 10.93% WER. These results illustrate that some training choices yield representations that are almost useless for content recovery despite good geometric metrics.
AI.conclusion: Sequential representations that appear geometrically regular and even perfectly aligned with certain targets can nonetheless fail to encode recoverable ordered content for downstream tasks. Rank, isotropy, and latent agreement are therefore insufficient indicators of content sufficiency. Canonical-token supervision and appropriately structured non-autoregressive latent canvases, as implemented in CANOPE with PL2 objectives, are crucial for building representations that genuinely preserve sequential information in the studied text and TTS scenarios.

title: OOPMAS: Object-Oriented Multi-Agent Systems for Query-Level Workflow Generation
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown strong performance across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and question answering. However, existing methods for automating MAS design mostly operate at the task level, producing a single fixed workflow per benchmark that is applied uniformly to all queries. This assumption fails under realistic conditions. Query difficulty varies widely within a task, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous task types. We introduce OOPMAS, a training-free framework that generates both the agent set and the coordination workflow at the granularity of individual queries. Agents are represented as object-oriented class definitions with dedicated roles, tools, and persistent state, and workflows are expressed as executable main functions over these agent objects. A dynamic skill library accumulates structured lessons from execution feedback across optimization rounds, enabling in-context improvement without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. On a mixed-task benchmark of queries spanning code, math, and QA, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 18.1 percentage points. A model-swap study across four LLM backbones shows consistent scaling, reaching 92.4% with the strongest model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OOPMAS, a training-free framework that dynamically designs multi-agent systems (agents + workflows) per query, using object-oriented agents and a growing skill library, achieving large accuracy gains on mixed code/math/QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems typically design a single, static workflow for an entire benchmark or task type, applying it uniformly to all queries. This is unrealistic because individual queries can differ greatly in difficulty and structure, and real-world workloads mix heterogeneous tasks. There is a need for a system that can automatically tailor both the selection of agents and their coordination process to each specific query, while also improving over time without expensive training or fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors propose OOPMAS, a training-free framework that: (1) represents each agent as an object-oriented class, with clearly defined roles, tools, and persistent internal state; (2) generates an executable main function per query that specifies how these agents interact (the workflow); and (3) maintains a dynamic skill library that stores structured lessons extracted from execution feedback across optimization rounds. The LLM uses these lessons in-context to refine future agent and workflow generation, enabling iterative improvement without gradient updates or model fine-tuning.
AI.result: On a mixed-task benchmark containing queries from code generation, mathematical reasoning, and question answering, OOPMAS achieves 89.6% accuracy, which is 18.1 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Additionally, when swapping in different LLM backbones, OOPMAS shows consistent performance scaling and reaches 92.4% accuracy with the most capable underlying model.
AI.conclusion: OOPMAS demonstrates that dynamically generating both the agent set and coordination workflow at the level of individual queries, using object-oriented agent definitions and an evolving skill library, can substantially improve the effectiveness of LLM-based multi-agent systems. The framework is training-free yet scales well with stronger backbone models, suggesting a practical path toward adaptive, general-purpose multi-agent orchestration across heterogeneous tasks.

title: Confidence Reasoning Graphs: Structured Confidence Estimation for LLM Agents
summary: When using an LLM agent in a consequential domain, making an informed decision about whether to trust its output or intervene requires calibrated confidence in the agent's success. Confidence estimation for agents is difficult because evidence about success is distributed across heterogeneous, interdependent steps of an agent's trajectory. Practical agentic deployments introduce further challenges: frontier LLMs often provide limited access to internal signals, agent roll-outs are costly, and training data may be unavailable or quickly become outdated. To address these challenges, we introduce Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), an inference-time framework that estimates the probability an agent accomplished its task from a single trajectory, without privileged model access or training data. Rather than compressing an execution into a single holistic judgment, a CRG begins with the claim that the agent accomplished its task, decomposes it into contextualized sub-claims grounded in trajectory evidence, estimates confidence for each terminal claim, and finally aggregates these into an overall confidence estimate. Across three agentic benchmarks, three backbone models, and three agent frameworks, CRGs yield better-calibrated confidence and stronger risk-aware decision making than verbalized, sampling-based, and white-box surrogate baselines. We further find that calibration error alone can be misleading: a white-box surrogate baseline appears well calibrated while providing near-chance discrimination. Ablations attribute CRG's improvements to claim-level confidence estimation and aggregation rather than graph construction alone. Finally, a CRG exposes the claims and trajectory evidence underlying each confidence estimate, enabling it to be audited at decision time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), an inference-time method to estimate how likely an LLM agent successfully completed its task from a single trajectory, improving confidence calibration and decision-making without needing model internals or training data.
AI.motivation: In high-stakes applications, users must decide when to trust an LLM agent’s output or intervene. This requires calibrated confidence estimates of task success, which are hard to obtain because relevant evidence is scattered across many dependent steps of an agent’s trajectory. Existing approaches depend on internal model access, multiple rollouts, or training data that may be expensive, unavailable, or quickly outdated. There is a need for a practical, transparent, and well-calibrated confidence estimation method that works at inference time with only one trajectory and no privileged access.
AI.method: The authors introduce Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), which operate at inference time over a single completed agent trajectory. Starting from the top-level claim that the agent accomplished its task, a CRG decomposes this into contextualized sub-claims tied to specific pieces of trajectory evidence. For each terminal (leaf) claim, the system estimates a probability of correctness, then aggregates these claim-level confidences through the graph structure into an overall probability that the task was successfully completed. CRGs are designed to work without internal LLM signals (black-box models) and without extra training data. The paper evaluates CRGs across multiple benchmarks, LLM backbones, and agent frameworks, and runs ablations to test which components (graph construction vs. claim-level estimation and aggregation) drive performance.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks, three backbone models, and three agent frameworks, CRGs produce better-calibrated confidence estimates and support more effective risk-aware decision policies than several baselines, including verbalized (self-reported) confidence, sampling-based methods, and a white-box surrogate model. The study reveals that focusing only on calibration metrics can be misleading: a white-box surrogate appears well-calibrated yet has near-chance discrimination between success and failure. Ablation experiments show that CRG’s gains primarily come from explicit claim-level confidence estimation and principled aggregation, not just from constructing a reasoning graph.
AI.conclusion: Confidence Reasoning Graphs provide a practical, inference-time framework for estimating an LLM agent’s probability of task success from a single trajectory, without requiring model internals or training data. By decomposing task success into grounded sub-claims, assigning claim-level confidences, and transparently aggregating them, CRGs yield better-calibrated, more discriminative confidence estimates and support improved risk-aware decision making. The structured, auditable nature of CRGs also enables users to inspect and audit the basis for each confidence estimate at decision time.

title: Illusory Pattern Perception Drives Spurious Inference in Large Language Models
summary: Illusory pattern perception is a well-documented human cognitive tendency to infer meaningful relationships in data that is actually random. Such a tendency, often described as "connecting the dots" where none exist, can result in systematic reasoning errors. This paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit such perceptual tendencies, which can lead to systematic errors in downstream applications. To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in LLMs, adapting classic psychological paradigms to three tasks with direct empirical comparison to human behaviors. We find that LLMs frequently exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans. In particular, models tend to over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations, and show increased tendencies to construct causal narratives from ambiguous events. To uncover the mechanism behind these behaviors, we develop a feature interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to analyze internal representations. Our results reveal that holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation are linked to the emergence of illusory perceptions. These findings highlight a previously underexplored cognitive-like illusion that may affect the reliability of LLM reasoning. Code available at https://github.com/NusIoraPrivacy/illusory.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models systematically ‘see’ patterns and causal stories in random or ambiguous data even more than humans do.
AI.motivation: Illusory pattern perception is a known human bias that leads people to detect structure or causality in randomness, causing reasoning errors. As LLMs are increasingly used for decision support and analysis, it is crucial to know whether they exhibit a similar bias, how strong it is relative to humans, and what internal mechanisms produce it, because such illusions could compromise reliability and safety in downstream applications.
AI.method: The authors adapt classic psychological paradigms for studying illusory pattern perception to three LLM evaluation tasks that allow direct behavioral comparison with humans. They analyze how LLMs associate attributes with groups and how they generate causal explanations for ambiguous scenarios. To probe mechanisms, they propose a feature-interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) that is applied to the models’ internal representations, allowing them to link specific representational features to behavioral tendencies toward illusory pattern perception.
AI.result: Empirically, the authors find that LLMs often display stronger illusory pattern perception than humans. Models systematically over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations and are more prone to constructing causal narratives from ambiguous events. Using SAEs, they identify interpretable internal features related to holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation, and demonstrate that these features are associated with the emergence of illusory perceptions in the models’ behavior.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not only subject to human-like illusory pattern perception but can exhibit it more strongly than humans, posing a risk for applications that rely on their judgments or explanations. The study links these illusions to specific internal representational properties—holistic frequency tracking and analytic orientations—via a sparse-autoencoder-based interpretability framework. This reveals a new class of cognitive-like illusions in LLMs and underscores the need to detect, understand, and mitigate such biases to improve the reliability of LLM reasoning in practice.

title: DAEDALUS: Bootstrapping Agent Memory from Self-Generated Tasks
comment: 9 pages (31 including Appendix), 8 figures (11 including Appendix). We release the code and artifacts, including generation and inference traces, at https://github.com/illuin-tech/daedalus
summary: LLM agents often lack the operational knowledge to act reliably in new environments, as they must discover specific tool behaviors or environment conventions on their own. Without memory of past attempts, they repeat the same mistakes across tasks, leading to more task failures and longer trajectories. To address this, agentic systems typically rely on human-written guidelines or on procedural memory built from training tasks and an oracle verifier, both of which require prior knowledge of the environment. We present DAEDALUS, a method for bootstrapping reusable agent memory from self-generated practice without existing tasks or oracle verifiers. DAEDALUS pairs two agents: an explorer that interacts with the environment to generate challenging yet solvable tasks, and a solver that attempts them. A heuristic is derived from each solver failure and accepted only after the solver repeatedly succeeds with that heuristic in context. These outcomes also provide feedback for the explorer to refine the difficulty of future tasks. Accepted heuristics are then consolidated into a memory bank for test-time use. Across AppWorld, $τ^2$-bench, and AutomationBench, DAEDALUS improves mean success rates by up to 15.9 points and pass^5 by up to 2.2x over a no-memory baseline, and is competitive with methods using training tasks, at a lower inference cost than most. We show that performance gains already emerge with a small exploration budget, and that its heuristics also benefit agents from other model families. Our ablations further reveal that solver traces provide the key information needed to derive effective heuristics, while factorizing early discoveries makes exploration more cost-efficient. Beyond memory construction, we find that the tasks generated by DAEDALUS can serve as a proxy for benchmark tasks when ranking models by performance. Code and artifacts: www.github.com/illuin-tech/daedalus.

AI.tldr: DAEDALUS is a method for autonomously building reusable memories (heuristics) for LLM agents through self-generated practice, improving reliability without requiring pre-defined tasks or oracle verifiers.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle in new environments because they must learn tool behaviors and conventions from scratch. Without persistent memory of previous attempts, they repeat mistakes, causing failures and inefficiency. Existing approaches depend on human-written guidelines or training tasks plus oracle verifiers, which assume prior environment knowledge and are costly to obtain. The paper aims to enable agents to acquire reusable operational knowledge autonomously, without these dependencies.
AI.method: DAEDALUS pairs two agents: (1) an explorer that interacts with the environment to generate challenging but solvable tasks, and (2) a solver that attempts to solve them. When the solver fails, the system derives a candidate heuristic from the failure trace. This heuristic is kept only if, when provided in context, the solver repeatedly succeeds on subsequent attempts. Results of these attempts also inform the explorer, which adjusts the difficulty and nature of future tasks. Validated heuristics are consolidated into a memory bank used at test time to guide agents in new tasks. The paper includes ablations to study what information and design choices are important, such as solver traces and factorizing early discoveries.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—AppWorld, τ^2-bench, and AutomationBench—DAEDALUS improves mean success rates by up to 15.9 percentage points and pass@5 by up to 2.2× over an agent without memory. It performs competitively with methods that rely on training tasks and oracle verifiers, while usually having lower inference cost. Benefits emerge even with a small exploration budget, and the learned heuristics transfer to agents based on other model families. Ablation studies show that solver execution traces are crucial for deriving useful heuristics and that factorizing early-found heuristics makes exploration more cost-effective. Additionally, tasks produced during DAEDALUS’s self-practice can approximate benchmark tasks for ranking models by performance.
AI.conclusion: DAEDALUS demonstrates that LLM agents can autonomously bootstrap reusable operational knowledge through self-generated practice, without predefined tasks or oracle supervision. The resulting heuristic memory measurably improves success rates, efficiency, and cross-model transfer, while remaining cost-effective. The method’s task generation process is also useful as a stand-in for formal benchmarks when comparing models. This suggests a promising direction for scalable, environment-agnostic improvement of agentic systems via self-practice and structured memory building.

title: Thin Evidence, Thick Priors: How Language Models Substitute Identity for Missing Financial Facts
comment: 49 pages, 17 figures, 12 tables; Submitted & Accepted to ICAIF'2026
summary: People increasingly ask large language models what to do with their money, yet seldom describe their finances in full. This paper asks what a model does with the gap. Holding finances fixed and changing only who the investor is said to be, we grade the financial evidence in the prompt from eight facts to none and measure how far the recommended equity allocation moves. Across 96,600 prompts to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, built from 100 financial profiles, 138 personas and seven disclosure conditions, the average gap between two personas with identical finances rises from 4.78 percentage points at full disclosure to 10.34 points with no financial facts. A two-way cluster bootstrap counting duplicated prompts once places the ratio at 2.16 (95% interval 1.69 to 2.79), and the rise is already 1.69-fold with a single fact left. Identity explains 5% of within-profile variation in advice at full disclosure and 96% with no disclosure. Household size is the only attribute whose influence grows reliably as evidence is withdrawn. Once standard errors are clustered on the persona, the unit to which identity was assigned, most attribute-specific interactions reported in the conference version lose significance, and gender instead appears as a small standing gap that full disclosure does not close. Stating risk appetite alone brings the swing into the range seen with two to seven generic facts. With no facts, the model's one-line rationale cites incomes, debts and savings it was never told, and these invented finances turn adverse more often for larger households. Inside the network, gender is linearly decodable at every layer, and ablating the gender direction at five layers leaves the aggregate identity swing unchanged. Advisory systems built on such models should be audited at the disclosure levels users actually reach, and judged across the whole identity space rather than one attribute at a time.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how incomplete financial disclosure in prompts to large language models affects investment advice, showing that the less financial detail is provided, the more the model’s recommendations depend on the investor’s stated identity/persona.
AI.motivation: Many people ask language models for personal finance advice but rarely reveal complete financial information. This raises concerns about what models implicitly fill in when key facts are missing, and whether identity-related attributes (e.g., gender, household size) systematically alter recommendations, creating fairness and reliability issues in AI-driven financial advisory systems.
AI.method: The authors construct 96,600 prompts to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using 100 fixed financial profiles crossed with 138 personas (identity descriptions) and seven financial disclosure conditions, ranging from full disclosure of eight financial facts to none. They measure recommended equity allocations across these prompts, quantify variation attributable to identity versus finances, use clustered bootstrap methods and clustered standard errors, analyze attribute-specific interactions (e.g., gender, household size), probe the network for linear decodability of gender across layers, and perform gender-direction ablations at selected layers.
AI.result: As financial disclosure decreases, the effect of persona identity on recommended equity allocation grows substantially: the average difference between two personas with identical finances increases from 4.78 to 10.34 percentage points from full to no disclosure, with a 2.16-fold increase in gap size (95% CI 1.69–2.79). Identity explains only 5% of within-profile variation at full disclosure but 96% with no disclosure. Household size is the only attribute whose influence reliably strengthens as financial evidence is removed. After clustering standard errors on personas, many previously reported attribute-specific interactions lose significance, and gender manifests mainly as a small persistent gap that full disclosure does not eliminate. Disclosing only risk appetite already constrains swings to the range produced by two to seven generic facts. With no facts, the model fabricates incomes, debts, and savings, often more adverse for larger households. Network analysis shows gender is linearly decodable at all layers, but ablating this gender direction at five layers does not reduce the overall identity-based variation in advice.
AI.conclusion: When financial facts are missing, large language models fill gaps using investor identity cues, leading to large, identity-dependent swings in financial advice that do not necessarily vanish with more disclosure and are not fully explained by any single attribute such as gender. Household size plays a particularly sensitive role under missing data, and the model hallucinates financial details in systematically skewed ways. Fair and reliable advisory systems based on such models must therefore be evaluated at realistic levels of user disclosure and across the full space of identities rather than focusing on single attributes or idealized full-information settings.

title: Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce prospective learning, which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to $24.2$ pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when $37$--$98\%$ of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In the 2B setting, where $98\%$ of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at $0.0\%$ success, while adding SRD reaches $60.6\%$ under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new way to train reinforcement learning agents when all trajectories receive similar rewards, by using hindsight from completed trajectories to supervise what the agent should have predicted before acting.
AI.motivation: In many group-relative or sparse-reward settings, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) fails because every rollout in a group can receive the same reward (often all failures).
