When this happens, the scalar reward signal provides almost no information about which behaviors are better or worse, even though the detailed trajectories still contain clues about task requirements and failure modes. The authors are motivated by the question of how to extract useful learning signals from such post-hoc experience, especially when reward contrast is scarce and standard RLVR plateaus at zero success.
AI.method: They propose prospective learning, a framework where post-hoc experience supervises predictions made from the pre-interaction state (the "foresight" view). Their concrete method, Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD), takes completed trajectories and uses the information they reveal (what worked, what failed, what pitfalls to avoid) to train the same policy to have better trajectory-blind predictions in advance. SRD distills privileged hindsight information into the policy’s foresight representations: the agent learns, from the start state, to approximate what would later be known after observing the full trajectory. These foresight predictions are used only as training targets and are not required at inference time. SRD is evaluated on tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, and compared against RLVR and self-distillation baselines.
AI.result: Across 10 tool-use and long-horizon tasks, SRD provides consistent gains over RLVR and self-distillation, with improvements up to 24.2 percentage points in success. The benefit is strongest when reward contrast is minimal: in settings where 37–98% of rollout groups have identical rewards (often all failures), SRD can still extract signal from trajectory details. In the extreme 2B-parameter model case where 98% of groups are all-failure, RLVR alone stagnates at 0.0% success, whereas combining RLVR with SRD achieves 60.6% success under the same rollout budget.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that post-hoc agent experience is valuable not just for evaluation or direct behavior fine-tuning, but also for shaping the agent’s predictive representations before interaction. By distilling hindsight into foresight via SRD, agents can learn from trajectories even when scalar rewards offer no contrast, substantially improving performance in sparse or group-uniform reward regimes.

title: POLAR: Ontology-Guided Risk Prevention for Tool-Calling LLM Agents
summary: LLM tool-use agents operate in dynamic environments where many actions carry operational risk. However, most safety mechanisms react only after errors manifest. Existing pre-emptive approaches either fine-tune the agent on chain-of-thought deliberation or compile natural-language guardrails into runtime checks, but they do so without exposing a structural, auditable verdict. We propose POLAR, a guardrail framework for small tool-calling agents that assesses reversibility through a structured two-layer ontology. POLAR assigns each action a graded reversibility score by deriving a candidate inverse sequence; calls failing a threshold are pruned before execution. Evaluated on $τ^2$-bench across six agent models, POLAR improves mean task reward by 0.11 to 0.18 points on airline for four of six agents, but only eight of eighteen model--domain cells improve overall; retail and stronger agents often regress. POLAR provides an auditable structural check and characterizes its task-utility trade-offs. Reward is not a direct measure of prevented harm.

AI.tldr: Introduces POLAR, a guardrail framework that pre-emptively filters risky tool calls by scoring their reversibility via a structured ontology, modestly improving rewards in some settings and clarifying safety–utility trade-offs.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that call tools often act in dynamic, high-risk environments, yet most safety mechanisms are reactive, intervening only after harmful or irreversible errors occur. Existing proactive methods (like CoT-based fine-tuning or natural-language guardrails compiled into checks) lack a clear, structural, and auditable notion of when an action is too risky to execute. The authors want a principled, inspectable way to decide before execution which actions should be blocked, focusing on reversibility as a key safety signal.
AI.method: They design POLAR, a guardrail framework for relatively small tool-using agents that evaluates each proposed tool call in terms of reversibility using a two-layer ontology. For every candidate action, POLAR attempts to derive a candidate inverse sequence of actions and from that assigns a graded reversibility score. If the score is below a predefined threshold (i.e., the action is deemed insufficiently reversible), the call is pruned before being sent to the environment. They then integrate POLAR with six different agent models and evaluate on the τ^2-bench benchmark across multiple domains (including airline and retail), studying how this pre-execution pruning affects task rewards and documenting the structural decisions POLAR makes.
AI.result: On the τ^2-bench airline domain, for four of six evaluated agent models, POLAR yields a mean task reward improvement between 0.11 and 0.18 points, indicating some benefit from filtering low-reversibility actions. However, when considering all combinations of models and domains (18 cells total), only eight show an overall reward improvement; in the retail domain and for stronger base agents, using POLAR often reduces task reward. This demonstrates that while POLAR can help in some contexts, its impact on utility is mixed and highly context-dependent.
AI.conclusion: POLAR delivers an auditable, structurally grounded guardrail that pre-emptively blocks actions assessed as hard to reverse, explicitly surfacing the safety–utility trade-off rather than hiding it within model weights or opaque heuristics. Its mixed reward outcomes show that improving safety via reversibility-based pruning does not uniformly translate into higher task reward and can sometimes degrade performance, especially for stronger agents or certain domains. The authors emphasize that task reward should not be treated as a direct proxy for harm prevention, and that structured notions like reversibility are valuable both for safety analysis and for transparent governance of LLM tool-use agents.

title: Do I Need the Cloud? Uncertainty-Aware Step-Level Handoff for Small Language Model Agents
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: SLMs for Agentic Systems, Paris, France, 2026
summary: Small language models (SLMs) are attractive as local agent controllers because they reduce remote inference, latency, and deployment footprint, yet structured tool errors can cause an agent step to fail. Existing routers typically select a model once per query. However, agents expose sequential decision points whose difficulty dynamically changes based on intermediate observations. We propose STEPGATE, an uncertainty-aware handoff framework that scores each local SLM action and selectively escalates challenging steps to a stronger model. On a 52-task held-out single-step BFCL-derived test split, the Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B pair attains 82.7% task success with 30.8% escalation, versus 67.3% local-only and 75.4% random escalation (which uses 33.8% escalation). In a separate multi-turn evaluation, STEPGATE achieves 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success using only 30.0% cloud actions, compared with 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, and 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing (strong-only achieves 82.0% trajectory success at 100% cloud actions). These results suggest that step-level escalation recovers a large share of the performance gap to the stronger Qwen2.5-7B backend at a matched cloud-action rate while transmitting fewer tokens remotely. However, our evaluation is limited to one model family, a single stronger backend, and scripted tasks. Furthermore, the test sets are small, multi-turn comparisons rely on paired intervals and statistical tests, and our risk tiers serve as research annotations rather than formal safety guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces STEPGATE, a framework that lets a small local language model handle most agent steps but selectively escalates uncertain or difficult steps to a stronger remote model, improving success while limiting remote calls.
AI.motivation: Small language models are attractive for local agent control due to lower latency, reduced dependence on remote inference, and smaller deployment footprint, but they often fail on difficult, tool-heavy steps. Existing routing approaches choose a model once per entire query, ignoring that agent trajectories have multiple decision points of varying difficulty, leading to either overuse of large models or poor performance. The authors want a finer-grained, step-level mechanism to decide when to rely on a stronger model, based on actual uncertainty at each step.
AI.method: They propose STEPGATE, an uncertainty-aware handoff framework operating at the level of individual agent actions. A local small language model attempts each step, and its action is scored according to an uncertainty or risk metric. If the score indicates the step is challenging or high risk, the action is escalated to a stronger model, otherwise it is executed locally. They evaluate this with the Qwen2.5-1.5B (local) and Qwen2.5-7B (strong) pair on BFCL-derived tasks, comparing against baselines including local-only execution, random escalation, and query-level routing. They also design risk tiers to categorize steps, though these act as research annotations rather than formal safety assurances.
AI.result: On a held-out single-step BFCL-derived test split comprising 52 tasks, the STEPGATE framework using Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B achieves 82.7% task success with 30.8% of steps escalated to the stronger model, outperforming the local-only baseline (67.3% success) and random escalation (75.4% success at 33.8% escalation). In multi-turn evaluations, STEPGATE attains 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success while using only 30.0% cloud actions. This surpasses local-only (48.0% trajectory, 70.5% action), random escalation (60.0% trajectory, 78.2% action), and query-level routing (57.0% trajectory, 77.1% action), and approaches the strong-only model’s 82.0% trajectory success which uses 100% cloud actions. Additionally, STEPGATE reduces the number of tokens transmitted to the remote model compared to strong-only baselines at similar cloud-action rates.
AI.conclusion: Step-level, uncertainty-aware escalation can substantially close the performance gap between small local models and stronger remote models for agentic tasks, while significantly reducing reliance on cloud inference. STEPGATE demonstrates that selectively routing only the most challenging agent steps to a large model recovers much of the stronger model’s performance at a fraction of the remote calls and token transmission. Nonetheless, the current validation is constrained: it uses a single model family with one strong backend, relatively small scripted test sets, and multi-turn evaluations that depend on paired-interval statistics. The proposed risk tiers are exploratory annotations rather than rigorous safety guarantees, so broader validation and more formal safety analysis are needed.

title: Natural Language Questions as an Interface for Knowledge Graphs: QRAKEN Graph Distillation and Semantic Self-Healing
summary: Natural-language access to RDF knowledge graphs is a core Semantic Web ambition. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced Text-to-SPARQL, yet on unfamiliar graphs they often generate valid queries that misrepresent the populated data model. QRAKEN is a training-free, ontology-agnostic neurosymbolic pipeline grounding generation in empirical graph evidence rather than schema expectations. An offline distiller produces TTQL, a compact description of populated multi-hop patterns, conditional frequencies and path-conditioned literal examples, plus a class-property co-occurrence matrix. Online, TTQL guides the LLM, while deterministic syntax, vocabulary and data-model checks provide diagnostics for iterative refinement. On CK25 (First International Text2SPARQL Challenge), under matched-condition recomputation on a QLever snapshot, QRAKEN achieves strict F1 of 0.643 $\pm$ 0.026 with GPT-4.1 mini and 0.652 $\pm$ 0.012 with GPT-5.4: relative gains of 30% and 32% over the strongest recomputed participant, outperforming systems using the same base model family. Ablations identify TTQL patterns as the dominant driver (+0.31 strict F1 over a shape-only baseline); the refinement loop provides a cheap safety net, rejecting triple patterns unsupported by the co-occurrence matrix. Compared with auto-derived SHACL, TTQL yields 64% higher strict F1, supporting the value of empirical patterns beyond schema exposure. With two local 35B 4-bit open-weight models at zero marginal cost, the same pipeline matches the strongest recomputed participant, and TTQL advantages over shape-only and SHACL baselines persist. Results on a single, relatively small benchmark provide an initial empirical signal; monolithic TTQL injection on very open cross-domain graphs remains the main limitation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents QRAKEN, a training-free neurosymbolic pipeline that improves Text-to-SPARQL query generation on unfamiliar RDF graphs by grounding LLM output in empirical graph patterns rather than schemas, achieving substantial F1 gains over prior systems and schema-based baselines on the CK25 benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate syntactically valid SPARQL queries, but on previously unseen or weakly documented RDF graphs they often hallucinate or misinterpret the actual data model, leading to incorrect queries despite formal validity. Existing schema-based approaches (e.g., via SHACL or ontology exposure) do not fully capture the empirical structure of populated graphs and are costly to adapt per-graph. The authors want a lightweight, ontology-agnostic way to align LLM-generated queries with the real content of arbitrary RDF knowledge graphs, improving accuracy and robustness without per-graph training.
AI.method: The authors propose QRAKEN, a two-stage neurosymbolic pipeline. Offline, a distiller component scans the target RDF graph and derives TTQL, a compact, training-free summary of empirical graph structure: multi-hop path patterns, their conditional frequencies, path-conditioned literal examples, and a class–property co-occurrence matrix; they also derive shape-like information. Online, this TTQL representation is injected into the LLM prompt to steer Text-to-SPARQL generation. The system then applies deterministic checks on syntax, vocabulary (URIs, properties, classes), and compatibility with the empirical data model. A refinement loop uses diagnostics to iteratively repair or prune the query, including rejecting triple patterns whose class–property co-occurrences are unsupported by TTQL. Ablation studies contrast full TTQL patterns with shape-only and SHACL-like baselines, and they evaluate with multiple LLMs, including GPT models and local 35B open-weight models.
AI.result: On the CK25 dataset (First International Text2SPARQL Challenge) re-run on a QLever snapshot, QRAKEN with GPT-4.1 mini attains strict F1 = 0.643 ± 0.026 and with GPT-5.4 achieves 0.652 ± 0.012, corresponding to relative improvements of about 30–32% over the strongest recomputed baseline system, even when that system uses the same model family. Ablation shows TTQL multi-hop patterns are the main contributor, adding +0.31 strict F1 over a shape-only baseline. The refinement loop further improves robustness by cheaply discarding triple patterns that are not supported by the class–property co-occurrence matrix. Compared to pipelines using automatically derived SHACL shapes, TTQL-based guidance yields 64% higher strict F1. When substituting GPT with two local 35B 4-bit open-weight models, the same QRAKEN pipeline still matches the strongest recomputed participant, and TTQL’s superiority over shape-only and SHACL-based summarizations remains.
AI.conclusion: QRAKEN demonstrates that training-free empirical graph pattern distillation (TTQL) combined with deterministic neurosymbolic checks can substantially improve Text-to-SPARQL performance of LLMs on unfamiliar RDF graphs, outperforming both state-of-the-art participants and schema-based approaches like SHACL. Empirical multi-hop patterns and co-occurrence statistics provide richer, more actionable guidance than schema exposure alone, and the approach transfers to open-weight models at zero marginal inference cost. However, the current evaluation is limited to a single, relatively small benchmark, and the monolithic TTQL injection strategy does not yet scale cleanly to very large, open-domain graphs, which the authors identify as a key direction for future work.

title: Agentic Semantic Sensing for Resource-Adaptive AI-RAN
summary: Semantic sensing (SemS) acquires task-relevant information rather than reconstructing complete physical information. Existing SemS formulations typically operate open loop: sensing configurations and observation schedules are fixed before inference and cannot respond to evolving task-level evidence. We propose Agentic SemS, a closed-loop framework for AI-enabled radio access networks (AI-RANs) that controls sensing within a communication-feasible profile set. A profile-conditioned causal Transformer updates the semantic belief from streaming observations, while key-value caching enables efficient state updates across profile changes without repeatedly processing the complete history. A semantic utility network estimates the task-level benefit of acquiring the next observation block under each feasible profile after accounting for sensing cost. The resulting continuation utilities jointly support next-profile selection and semantic early exit, adapting sensing configuration and duration to evolving evidence. The expected semantic gain is further related to conditional mutual information, providing a value-of-information interpretation of continued online sensing. Experiments on Widar3.0 with six emulated sensing profiles show that, in comparison with full-sequence High, the resource-efficient Agentic setting reduces normalized cumulative sensing cost by 25.33% while achieving 85.79% Macro-F1. At the same utility checkpoint, semantic early exit provides a further 12.35% cost reduction over adaptive sensing without early exit, with a 0.97-percentage-point Macro-F1 decrease.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Agentic Semantic Sensing (Agentic SemS), a closed-loop sensing framework for AI-enabled radio access networks that adaptively selects sensing configurations and can stop early to save resources while maintaining high task performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional semantic sensing operates in an open-loop manner with fixed sensing configurations and schedules that cannot react to evolving evidence or task needs. This leads to inefficient use of sensing resources in AI-enabled radio access networks, where different sensing profiles may have different costs and benefits. There is a need for a framework that can adaptively control sensing actions based on current belief and utility, trading off task performance and resource cost.
AI.method: The authors introduce Agentic SemS, a closed-loop framework that operates over a set of communication-feasible sensing profiles. A profile-conditioned causal Transformer maintains and updates a semantic belief state from streaming observations, using key-value caching to avoid reprocessing the whole history when profiles change. A semantic utility network predicts the task-level utility of acquiring the next observation block under each available profile, explicitly accounting for sensing cost. These utilities are used both to choose the next sensing profile and to decide on semantic early exit, i.e., when to stop sensing. The expected utility is connected to conditional mutual information to interpret the value of information of continued sensing.
AI.result: On the Widar3.0 dataset with six emulated sensing profiles, the proposed Agentic SemS significantly reduces sensing cost while preserving most performance: compared with a high-cost full-sequence baseline (High), it achieves a 25.33% reduction in normalized cumulative sensing cost with a Macro-F1 of 85.79%. At the same utility threshold, enabling semantic early exit on top of adaptive sensing yields an additional 12.35% cost reduction, with only a 0.97 percentage point drop in Macro-F1.
AI.conclusion: Agentic SemS demonstrates that closed-loop, utility-driven control of semantic sensing profiles and early exit can substantially reduce sensing resource usage with minimal loss in task accuracy. The framework offers a principled, information-theoretic perspective on the value of continued sensing and suggests a practical path for resource-aware semantic sensing in AI-RANs and similar systems.

title: CoDe-LoRA: Mitigating the Orthogonality Dilemma in Continual Learning of LLMs via Knowledge Consolidation and Decoupling
summary: Continual learning (CL) is essential for Large Language Models (LLMs) to sequentially adapt to evolving tasks. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, recent advances implement low-rank adaptation with orthogonal projections (e.g., O-LoRA) to isolate task parameters. However, we reveal that such strict geometric constraints trigger an "Orthogonality Dilemma": rigid parameter isolation impedes the transfer and accumulation of shared representations across semantically related tasks. In this work, we propose a new replay-free method, called Consolidation and Decoupling LoRA (CoDe-LoRA), for CL of LLMs. CoDe-LoRA disentangles the learning process into Consolidating Universal Knowledge and Decoupling Task-Specific Knowledge. To achieve this, CoDe-LoRA leverages an adaptive null space projection mechanism and semantic routing to balance knowledge accumulation with task-specific adaptation. Experimental results across four backbones and three CL benchmarks show that CoDe-LoRA achieves the best average accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/Estrellajer/CoDe-LoRA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoDe-LoRA, a continual learning method for LLMs that improves task performance without replay by better balancing knowledge sharing and task isolation.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning approaches for LLMs use strict orthogonal low-rank adaptations (like O-LoRA) to prevent catastrophic forgetting, but this strong parameter isolation creates an 'Orthogonality Dilemma': it blocks beneficial transfer and accumulation of shared representations across related tasks. The authors aim to design a method that avoids forgetting while still enabling cross-task knowledge sharing.
AI.method: The authors propose Consolidation and Decoupling LoRA (CoDe-LoRA), a replay-free continual learning framework that separates learning into two processes: (1) consolidating universal/shared knowledge and (2) decoupling task-specific knowledge. Technically, CoDe-LoRA employs an adaptive null-space projection mechanism to control how new task parameters are added relative to existing ones, and uses semantic routing to direct inputs through appropriate parameter subspaces, enabling both knowledge accumulation and specialization without replay buffers.
AI.result: Across experiments on four different LLM backbones and three continual learning benchmarks, CoDe-LoRA achieves the highest average accuracy compared to prior CL methods, indicating better retention of past tasks and strong performance on new tasks without using replay.
AI.conclusion: CoDe-LoRA effectively resolves the tension between preventing forgetting and enabling knowledge transfer in continual learning for LLMs. By adaptively managing parameter subspaces and routing based on semantics, it consolidates universal knowledge while isolating task-specific information, leading to superior overall performance in replay-free continual learning settings.

title: DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DHCG, a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems, which adaptively configures agents as a POMDP to improve reasoning performance across tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems can solve complex problems but current dynamic orchestration methods are limited: they support only restricted ways of composing agents, often mis-handle dependencies between agents, and cannot flexibly scale the number and structure of agents during execution. This constrains their ability to adapt to evolving reasoning needs in real time. The authors aim to build a more principled, flexible, and performance-effective way to dynamically configure and coordinate agents.
AI.method: The authors formalize multi-agent system design as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where both the composition and scale of the agent team are decision variables that evolve during reasoning. They introduce DHCG, which uses three modules—Planner, Worker, and Generator—to construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch for each query. At each step, the Planner, guided by execution feedback, creates specialized and complementary roles (nodes) and selectively routes relevant information to them, deciding whether to expand the hierarchy or terminate it. They further propose action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner so that its choices of roles, structure, and routing lead to more effective hierarchical collaboration graphs.
AI.result: On benchmarks for code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning, DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among compared methods. It improves over a strong single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and surpasses existing static and dynamic multi-agent baselines by 2.77–8.02 points. Additional experiments show that the method generalizes across different Planner backbones and also works with unseen Worker models, indicating robustness and modularity.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically building a hierarchical collaboration graph via a POMDP-based Planner is an effective way to orchestrate LLM-based multi-agent systems. DHCG adapts the number, roles, and interactions of agents to evolving reasoning needs, yielding consistent performance gains across tasks and model choices. This validates dynamic, feedback-driven hierarchical orchestration as a promising direction for future MAS design.

title: Toward Alignment Scaling Laws: A Framework and First Preregistered Measurements
comment: 34 pages, 24 figures, 8 tables. Games: https://www.aisafety.fun. Preregistrations: https://osf.io/wda8q, https://osf.io/q2j3y, https://osf.io/8kreb
summary: Whether alignment gets easier or harder as models grow is often argued from isolated findings, as if alignment were one property. We treat it as a family of measurable scaling relations: for each risk category r, the alignment burden needed to hold a fixed safety target is modeled as B_r(N)=a_rN^alpha_r, with N a capability proxy; against a budget proportional to N, scaling helps if alpha_r<1, keeps pace if alpha_r~1, and accumulates alignment debt if alpha_r>1. We give three operationalizations of burden and distinguish observed, audited and true alignment. A toy model, in which corrections consume capability headroom, makes the consequences explicit. We prove that the largest exponent among corrected risks, not an average, sets the long-run regime; that above 1 any policy holding headroom above a floor must grow super-exponentially; that, for burdens that are positive mixtures of power laws, fits on small models underestimate large-scale exponents; and that an audit that uncovers hidden failures without false positives never underestimates true alignment. We propose a pre-registrable protocol and apply reduced versions of it twice. A preregistered reanalysis of public adversarial-training data for Pythia classifiers finds that the compute needed to bring attack success under 10% grows as N^0.60. A preregistered pilot on Qwen2.5 0.5B-72B finds exponents of -0.05 for truthfulness and 0.48 for stated dispositions (both scaling helps under its reduced rule, though local slopes approach 1 at the top; replicated on Qwen3 0.6B-14B), while sycophancy (0.89, or 0.83 with two seeds added at 72B) and a planted backdoor are undetermined: the backdoor is removed quickly when its trigger is known but survives blind safety training at four of five sizes. We release four browser games that play these laws (www.aisafety.fun). We make no claim about which regime holds for current frontier models.

AI.tldr: The paper models AI alignment as multiple measurable scaling laws relating safety burden to model capability, derives theoretical results about how the hardest-to-fix risks dominate long-run behavior, and presents preliminary empirical estimates of alignment scaling exponents on real models.
AI.motivation: Debates about whether alignment becomes easier or harder as AI models scale usually rely on scattered, qualitative observations and implicitly treat alignment as a single property. The authors want a quantitative, operational framework that: (1) breaks alignment into specific risk categories, (2) specifies how the required alignment effort scales with model size for each category, and (3) can be empirically measured and preregistered. This allows more rigorous reasoning about "alignment debt" as models grow.
AI.method: They define, for each risk category r, an alignment burden function B_r(N)=a_r N^{alpha_r}, where N is a proxy for model capability and alpha_r is an exponent indicating how alignment burden scales. They distinguish observed, audited, and true alignment burdens, and introduce three ways to operationalize burden. Using a toy model in which safety corrections consume some of the model’s capability headroom, they mathematically analyze how the exponents alpha_r determine whether alignment gets easier (alpha_r<1), keeps pace (alpha_r≈1), or falls behind (alpha_r>1) under a fixed alignment budget that scales ∝ N. They prove several properties: (i) long-run behavior is governed by the maximum exponent across risks, (ii) if that maximum exceeds 1, maintaining a minimum headroom requires super-exponential policy effort, (iii) mixtures of power laws imply that fitting on small models typically underestimates the true large-scale exponent, and (iv) an ideal audit that detects all failures without false positives cannot underestimate true alignment burden. They then design a preregistrable empirical protocol and run two reduced pilot studies: a reanalysis of adversarial training data for Pythia classifiers, and new experiments on Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models measuring exponents for truthfulness, stated dispositions, sycophancy, and a planted backdoor.
AI.result: The theory shows that the most rapidly growing risk category (largest alpha_r) dominates long-term alignment difficulty, and that alpha_r>1 implies that any policy keeping capability headroom above a floor must grow super-exponentially. It also shows small-scale fits are biased toward underestimating exponents for mixtures of power laws and that perfect audits cannot underestimate true burden. Empirically, their reanalysis of Pythia adversarial-training data suggests that compute required to reduce adversarial attack success below 10% scales as N^{0.60}, implying alignment help from scaling under their budget assumption. In new Qwen2.5 0.5B–72B experiments, they estimate exponents of about -0.05 for truthfulness (alignment improves more than linearly with scale) and 0.48 for stated dispositions, though local slopes near the largest models approach 1. These findings replicate qualitatively on Qwen3 0.6B–14B. Sycophancy shows a higher exponent (~0.89, or ~0.83 with extra seeds at 72B), close to the break-even regime, and the planted backdoor’s exponent is inconclusive: the backdoor is easily removed when the trigger is known but tends to persist under blind safety training in most model sizes. They also release four browser games that illustrate the scaling laws.
AI.conclusion: Alignment should be analyzed as a set of separate scaling laws across risk categories rather than a single dimension. What matters for long-run safety is the worst-scaling risk, not average behavior, and risks with exponents above 1 would create accumulating alignment debt that cannot be sustainably handled by budgets that grow only proportionally with capability. Small-model studies tend to underestimate large-scale alignment difficulty when underlying burdens mix different scaling behaviors, so rigorous, preregistered measurement protocols and strong auditing are crucial. Their pilots suggest that, for some measured behaviors (like basic truthfulness and stated dispositions), alignment may currently benefit from scaling on the tested models, while other behaviors (like sycophancy and backdoor vulnerabilities) remain uncertain or more concerning. They refrain from extrapolating to current frontier systems and instead offer their framework, preliminary exponents, and interactive tools as a foundation for more systematic study of alignment scaling.

title: RA-MoWE: Workflow-Affinity Embeddings for Query Clustering and Agentic Workflow Generation
summary: Agentic workflows enable large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks by coordinating reasoning, tool use, and verification. However, a workflow optimized for an entire task collection can overlook differences in the reasoning strategies that individual queries need, while searching for a new workflow for every query repeats costly optimization. To address this tradeoff, we introduce RA-MoWE, a framework that uses workflow-affinity embeddings to cluster queries and guide the generation of reusable expert workflows. Each embedding records how well a fixed set of reference workflows solves a query, revealing similarities in which reasoning strategies are effective. RA-MoWE uses each cluster's queries and average embedding to initialize and refine a specialized workflow through execution feedback. An embedding encoder predicts these embeddings from query text, allowing new queries to select a generated expert without first executing the reference workflows. On a 300-query test set drawn from four benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and programming, RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points over selecting among the reference workflows, while using 27.7% fewer language-model calls at inference.

AI.tldr: RA-MoWE clusters queries by how well different reasoning workflows solve them, then learns specialized expert workflows per cluster and an encoder that routes new queries to the right expert, improving accuracy and reducing LLM calls.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic workflows for LLMs are either globally optimized for a whole benchmark or re-optimized per query. Global workflows ignore that different queries benefit from different reasoning strategies, while per-query optimization is too expensive. The authors want a scalable way to adapt workflows to query-specific reasoning needs without incurring high optimization cost for every new query.
AI.method: They define workflow-affinity embeddings for each query by running a fixed set of reference workflows and recording how well each one performs. These embeddings capture which reasoning strategies work for which queries. They cluster queries using these embeddings, then for each cluster they initialize and refine a specialized expert workflow with execution feedback. They also train an embedding encoder that predicts workflow-affinity embeddings directly from query text so that, at inference time, new queries can be routed to appropriate expert workflows without executing all reference workflows.
AI.result: On a 300-query test set covering four benchmarks in math, science, and programming, RA-MoWE improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points compared with simply selecting among the original reference workflows, and it achieves this while reducing language-model calls at inference time by 27.7%.
AI.conclusion: Clustering queries by workflow affinity and learning reusable expert workflows, combined with an encoder that routes new queries by text, offers a practical way to adapt agentic LLM workflows to diverse reasoning needs. This approach yields better performance and lower inference cost than relying on a fixed set of workflows alone.

title: SquidAgent: Parallelize Wisely, Coordinate Efficiently
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 37 pages, including appendices
summary: LLM-based agents solve complex multi-step tasks, but sequential execution incurs substantial latency. In principle, parallelizing work across multiple agents should yield near-linear speedups. Yet existing parallel multi-agent systems often run slower than a single-agent baseline. We attribute this gap to two hidden costs that parallel execution incurs but a serial agent avoids. First, there is a re-exploration cost: redundant effort spent by parallel workers reconstructing context that the orchestrator already possesses, such as prior decisions, that would otherwise be inherited implicitly in a serial execution. Second, there is an alignment cost: the overhead required to reconcile inconsistencies across independently generated outputs. We thus derive a principled decision criterion: a layer should be parallelized only when its critical-path cost, plus re-exploration and alignment overheads, is lower than the corresponding serial cost. While this criterion is naturally expressed in wall-clock time, we observe that LLMs are poorly calibrated when asked to estimate task duration. To address this, we instead measure cost in predicted output tokens, which we empirically find LLMs can estimate substantially more reliably than wall-clock time. Building on this token-based criterion, we propose SquidAgent. It estimates all token budgets in a single planning step, forks each worker directly from the orchestrator's session to eliminate re-exploration cost, and replaces post-hoc reconciliation with a pre-generated shared convention block that converts alignment into a bounded upfront cost. A deterministic scheduler then applies the criterion layer by layer. Empirically, SquidAgent achieves a 2.2$\times$ mean throughput improvement and a 2.6$\times$ mean wall-time speedup over Claude Code, and a 2.0$\times$ throughput improvement over the strongest multi-agent baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SquidAgent, a framework to parallelize LLM-based multi-agent systems efficiently by accounting for hidden overheads that usually negate speedups.
AI.motivation: Although LLM-based agents can decompose complex tasks and in principle benefit from parallel execution, existing parallel multi-agent systems often underperform a strong single-agent baseline. The authors aim to understand why naive parallelization fails to deliver expected speedups and to create a principled way to decide when and how to parallelize LLM agents effectively.
AI.method: The authors identify two key hidden costs in parallel multi-agent systems: re-exploration cost (redundant effort as parallel workers reconstruct context already known to the orchestrator) and alignment cost (overhead from reconciling inconsistent outputs). They derive a decision criterion that parallelizes a layer only if its critical-path cost plus these overheads is lower than the serial cost, using predicted output token count as a proxy for cost because LLMs are poor at estimating wall-clock time. Based on this, they design SquidAgent: it does a single planning step to estimate token budgets for all layers, forks workers directly from the orchestrator’s session to avoid re-exploration, and uses a pre-generated shared convention block to bound alignment cost. A deterministic scheduler then applies the token-based criterion layer by layer.
AI.result: SquidAgent is empirically shown to significantly outperform both a strong single-agent baseline (Claude Code) and existing multi-agent baselines. It achieves a 2.2× average throughput improvement and a 2.6× average wall-clock speedup over Claude Code, and a 2.0× throughput improvement over the strongest multi-agent baseline.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for re-exploration and alignment costs is crucial for realizing the benefits of parallelization in LLM-based multi-agent systems. Token-based cost estimation provides a reliable decision signal for scheduling parallel work. SquidAgent, which embeds these ideas in its planning, forking, and alignment strategy, delivers substantial throughput and wall-time gains, demonstrating that principled, overhead-aware parallelization can unlock near-linear speedups in practice.

title: WorkflowOps: Learning Agent Collaboration Priors for Multi-Agent Workflow Orchestration
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed for complex knowledge work, yet their orchestration layers remain largely memoryless: each new task is decomposed, assigned, and executed from scratch with no benefit from prior successful executions. We present WorkflowOps, a multi-agent workflow orchestration framework that learns agent collaboration priors from historical workflows and expands its agent pool on demand to cover new capability requirements. Our approach introduces three coupled mechanisms. First, a transition probability matrix captures pairwise agent collaboration frequencies from past workflows and applies them as soft guidance during DAG workflow construction through intra-layer ordering optimization, probability-thresholded edge suggestion, and transitive reduction for parallelism maximization. Second, a sufficiency-driven agent creation loop detects capability gaps via semantic matching scores, generates specialized agents through an LLM, and simultaneously injects them into the collaboration matrix, so that newly created agents are immediately usable with predicted collaboration priors. Third, a layered semantic matching strategy uses pre-trained sentence embeddings for fast, deterministic capability matching as a first pass, invoking LLM verification only for low-confidence cases, thereby reducing LLM routing calls by over 80\% compared to pure-LLM approaches. Experiments on mixed code, math, and question-answering suites show that WorkflowOps improves end-to-end pass rates over recent workflow-construction baselines, with the largest gains on structured, decomposable tasks where past agent handoff patterns transfer.

AI.tldr: WorkflowOps is a multi-agent orchestration framework that reuses past workflows and dynamically creates new agents to improve task success and reduce LLM routing cost.
AI.motivation: Most multi-agent orchestration layers are memoryless: they recompute task decompositions and agent assignments from scratch, failing to exploit successful past workflows and lacking a systematic way to grow the agent pool when new capabilities are required.
AI.method: WorkflowOps builds a DAG workflow using three coupled mechanisms: (1) a transition probability matrix over agents learned from historical workflows that guides workflow construction via node ordering, edge suggestions, and transitive reduction; (2) a sufficiency-driven loop that detects capability gaps through semantic matching, then uses an LLM to synthesize new specialized agents and directly integrates them into the collaboration matrix; and (3) a layered semantic matching pipeline that first uses sentence-embedding similarity for fast, deterministic routing and then calls an LLM only for low-confidence matches to minimize expensive LLM invocations.
AI.result: On mixed code, math, and QA benchmarks, WorkflowOps achieves higher end-to-end pass rates than recent workflow-construction baselines, with particularly strong improvements on structured, decomposable tasks where collaboration patterns from prior workflows are reusable; it also cuts LLM routing calls by more than 80% compared to approaches that rely solely on LLMs for routing.
AI.conclusion: Learning collaboration priors from historical workflows, automatically expanding the agent pool, and using a layered semantic routing strategy leads to more effective and efficient multi-agent workflow orchestration, especially for structured tasks where past agent handoff patterns generalize.

title: Sherpa: Teaching LLMs to Teach Adaptively
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures. Code and model are available at https://github.com/SALT-NLP/Sherpa
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable problem solvers, but being able to solve a problem is not the same as being able to teach it. Existing approaches to training LLMs as teachers rely on demonstrations, preference data, or predefined pedagogical criteria that specify what good teaching looks like. However, these signals are often not grounded in individual student learning outcomes, where effective teaching strategies can vary substantially across learners. To address this, we introduce Sherpa, a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that instantiates multiple student archetypes with LLMs conditioned on distinct learning preferences and trains a teacher model to adapt its instruction by directly maximizing their learning outcomes. Teacher LLMs trained with Sherpa improve instructed students' performance across all archetypes by an average of 20.5 percentage points. Under MathTutorBench's evaluation, Sherpa raises the overall pedagogy score from 52.5% to 79.2%, indicating better teaching responses. Our human studies show that the trained teacher is preferred over the base model in 79.6% of pairwise comparisons. Together, Sherpa trains LLM teachers to adapt to diverse simulated students and become better aligned with human teachers, paving the road towards AI tutors teaching real students.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Sherpa, a reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to be adaptive teachers by optimizing simulated students’ learning outcomes rather than fixed teaching heuristics.
AI.motivation: Current LLM teaching approaches focus on demonstrations, preferences, or hand-crafted pedagogical rules, which are not personalized and are weakly tied to actual learning gains. Effective teaching depends on individual learner differences, so there is a need for a method that tailors instruction to diverse students and is directly grounded in measurable learning outcomes.
AI.method: The authors instantiate multiple student archetypes as LLM agents, each conditioned on different learning preferences. Using a multi-turn reinforcement learning setup, they train a teacher LLM to interact with these simulated students and adapt its explanations and strategies so as to maximize the students’ performance. Learning signals come from the students’ outcome improvements across turns rather than static labels of what good teaching is.
AI.result: Teacher models trained with Sherpa increase instructed student performance by an average of 20.5 percentage points across all student archetypes. On MathTutorBench, their method boosts the overall pedagogy score from 52.5% to 79.2%. Human evaluators prefer the Sherpa-trained teacher over the base model in 79.6% of pairwise comparisons, indicating both quantitative and qualitative gains in teaching quality.
AI.conclusion: Sherpa demonstrates that LLM teachers can be effectively trained via outcome-based reinforcement learning with diverse simulated students, leading to more adaptive and human-aligned pedagogical behavior. This suggests a promising path toward AI tutors that can better support real students with varied learning styles.

title: Self-Referenced Social Preferences: Cooperation without Observing Others Rewards
summary: Social preferences can promote cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning, but existing approaches often require agents to observe the rewards of their peers. In many real-world interactions, however, an agent can, as humans do, observe others' behavior and outcomes without access to their private reward signals. We introduce self-referenced social preferences, in which each agent learns a model of its own reward, applies it to other agents' observed transitions to assess their outcomes from its own perspective, and feeds these self-referenced assessments into standard social preferences. We study two ways to incorporate these assessments: modifying the learning reward, or using them to weight policy updates. We evaluate the approach on three sequential social dilemmas, Escape Room, Clean Up, and Commons Harvest, which require volunteering, public-good contribution, and resource restraint, respectively. Across all three environments, agents learn cooperative behavior without observing others' rewards, including in settings where independent learners fail to cooperate, and frequently achieve more equitable divisions of jointly produced returns than agents with access to true rewards. The effective integration point depends on the social preference: inequity aversion works best in the reward together with a value look-ahead, whereas a purely benevolent preference benefits from policy-update weighting. Under partial observability, the policy-update approach continues to support cooperation. These results show that explicit access to other agents' reward signals is not necessary for learning cooperative behavior: social preferences can instead be grounded in self-referenced assessments of others' outcomes derived from their observed behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a way for multi‑agent RL agents to become cooperative without needing access to others’ reward signals, by inferring others’ outcomes from a model of their own reward and plugging this into social preference mechanisms.
AI.motivation: In many MARL settings, cooperation is enhanced when agents incorporate social preferences such as inequity aversion or benevolence, but existing methods typically assume that each agent directly observes other agents’ rewards. This is unrealistic in many real-world scenarios, where rewards are private and only behaviors and observable outcomes are visible, as in human interactions. The authors aim to remove this impractical assumption while still enabling the emergence of cooperation and fairness in sequential social dilemmas.
AI.method: Each agent first learns a model of its own reward function from its experience. It then applies this learned reward model to other agents’ observed state–action–next‑state transitions, thereby estimating those agents’ outcome values from its own perspective—these are called self‑referenced social assessments. The paper integrates these assessments into social preference frameworks in two ways: (1) reward shaping—modifying the learning reward to include social terms such as inequity aversion; and (2) policy‑update weighting—using social assessments to weight gradient updates so that policy improvements favor socially beneficial outcomes. The authors test both integration points with different types of social preferences (inequity averse vs. benevolent) and in different observability conditions.
AI.result: On three challenging sequential social dilemma environments (Escape Room, Clean Up, and Commons Harvest), the proposed self‑referenced social preferences lead to robust cooperative policies without direct access to other agents’ true rewards. Agents using the method cooperate in settings where standard independent learners fail. Moreover, in many cases they achieve more equitable distributions of collective returns than agents that do have access to true peer rewards. The experiments also show that the best integration mechanism is preference‑dependent: inequity aversion works best when embedded in the reward along with a value look‑ahead, whereas purely benevolent preferences yield better cooperation when implemented via policy‑update weighting. Under partial observability, the policy‑update weighting variant continues to sustain cooperation.
AI.conclusion: Direct observation of other agents’ reward signals is not necessary for cooperative behavior to emerge in MARL. By learning a self‑reward model and applying it to others’ trajectories, agents can construct self‑referenced assessments of others’ outcomes and use them as the basis for social preferences. When properly integrated—reward shaping for inequity aversion and policy‑update weighting for benevolence—these preferences yield cooperation and fairer outcomes across several social dilemma environments, even under partial observability. This provides a more realistic and flexible foundation for socially aware MARL in settings where rewards are private but behaviors are observable.

title: ShanLiangRen: A Nutrition Agent for Personalized Daily Meal Planning
summary: Dietary nutrition planning plays an important role in chronic disease management and maintaining a healthy body. In applications, it must simultaneously satisfy personalized constraints and reasonable multidimensional nutritional goals. These two aspects often conflict, and user constraints evolve with feedback, resulting in a substantial gap between generic guidelines and executable plans. To bridge this gap, we first propose the personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP). To tackle MDP, we develop a nutrition agent, ShanLiangRen. The system first transforms dietary specifications, nutrient data, user attributes and natural language requirements into an individualized constrained planning instance. It then employs an exact retrieval-augmented generation method to shrink the feasible candidate set from a large scale ingredient and recipe space. Finally, it adopts a refinement guided by Pareto principles, where an LLM iteratively revises candidate plans under deterministic nutrition computation and feedback from constraint verification. The system outputs fully quantified meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes, together with reports on nutrition compliance that show constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment. We have released the system online as a WeChat Program, ShanLiangRen. A demo video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=652OtY5VlGA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ShanLiangRen, a personalized, multiobjective dietary planning agent that generates fully quantified meal plans by combining retrieval-augmented generation, constraint verification, and Pareto-guided refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing dietary guidelines are generic and often hard to translate into executable daily meal plans that respect personal preferences, medical needs, and evolving user constraints. There is a gap between high-level nutritional recommendations and concrete recipes with precise quantities that users can actually follow, especially when multiple nutritional objectives and personal constraints conflict. The authors aim to formalize this challenge and build a system that can generate practical, individualized meal plans with clear nutritional accounting.
AI.method: The authors formalize a personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP). They then design a nutrition agent, ShanLiangRen, that: (1) converts dietary specifications, nutrient databases, user attributes, and natural language requirements into a constrained planning instance; (2) uses an exact retrieval-augmented generation approach to narrow down candidate ingredients and recipes from a large food space; and (3) applies a Pareto-principle-guided refinement loop, where an LLM iteratively revises meal plans using deterministic nutrition calculations and automatic constraint verification until a good trade-off among objectives is found.
AI.result: The implemented system can output complete daily meal plans that list specific ingredients and portion sizes, accompanied by detailed nutrition-compliance reports (constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment). It has been deployed publicly as a WeChat Mini Program called ShanLiangRen, and a demo video is provided, suggesting the approach is practically usable. Quantitative experimental results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The work bridges the gap between abstract nutritional guidelines and concrete, personalized meal plans by introducing the MDP formulation and implementing the ShanLiangRen agent. It demonstrates that combining retrieval-augmented generation, LLM-based refinement, and precise nutrition computation can produce executable, personalized diet plans with transparent nutritional compliance reporting.

title: Textual Environmental Context and Spatial Graphs for LLM-Based Regional SST Forecasting
summary: Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting depends on local temporal persistence, regional spatial dependence, and environmental conditions that evolve with the forecast date. We study how these heterogeneous conditions can be presented to a large language model (LLM) for regional multi-step forecasting without serializing the full SST grid as text. We formulate forecasting as conditional numerical generation: historical SST and anomaly sequences, date-aligned environmental records, and static ocean knowledge form a textual context, while regional spatial state is supplied through continuous graph-derived prefixes. A static graph encodes persistent geographic--climatological relations, and a dynamic graph encodes recent SST correlations and localized tropical-cyclone influence. Two graph neural networks produce a target-node representation that is mapped by a spatial-prefix fusion and injected into the LLM input. On SST forecasting in the South China Sea, the complete configuration achieves the best MAE and $\Rtwo$ among the compared methods over ten forecast steps. Alongside the numerical forecast, a rule-based module matches predicted trends and environmental-factor directions with knowledge entries to return source-linked, post-hoc contextual explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method that combines graph neural networks with large language models to improve multi-step sea surface temperature forecasting in the South China Sea, while also generating textual explanations for forecasts.
AI.motivation: Accurate multi-step sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts are crucial for oceanographic and climate applications, but SST dynamics depend on complex local temporal patterns, spatial dependencies, and changing environmental conditions. Traditional models struggle to incorporate heterogeneous information sources and to provide interpretable explanations. With the rise of LLMs, there is an opportunity to encode rich contextual knowledge and environmental records as text, but directly serializing full SST grids into text is infeasible. The authors are motivated to find a way to harness LLMs for regional SST forecasting without excessive tokenization, while capturing both static and dynamic spatial relationships and improving interpretability.
AI.method: The authors cast SST forecasting as conditional numerical generation by a large language model. Historical SST and anomaly sequences, date-aligned environmental variables, and static ocean knowledge are embedded as a textual context for the LLM. To represent spatial information compactly, they build two graphs over the SST grid: (1) a static graph capturing persistent geographic and climatological relations; and (2) a dynamic graph capturing recent SST correlations and localized impacts from tropical cyclones. Two graph neural networks process these graphs to generate a representation for the target region (node). This representation is integrated into the LLM via a spatial-prefix fusion mechanism, effectively serving as a continuous prefix to the textual prompt. The LLM then generates multi-step SST forecasts numerically. In addition, a rule-based explanation module inspects the predicted SST trends and the directions of relevant environmental factors, then matches them against a knowledge base to produce source-linked, post-hoc textual explanations for the forecasts.
AI.result: On a South China Sea SST forecasting task, the proposed full configuration outperforms alternative methods in terms of mean absolute error (MAE) and R-squared (R^2) metrics across ten forecast steps. The results demonstrate that combining graph-based spatial representations with LLM-based conditional numerical generation can yield more accurate regional SST forecasts than baselines that lack some of these components. The framework also successfully produces contextual textual explanations aligned with the predicted SST trends and environmental indicators, though quantitative evaluation of explanation quality is not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that LLMs, when augmented with graph-derived spatial prefixes and rich textual context, can effectively perform regional, multi-step SST forecasting without needing to serialize full spatial grids as text. Static and dynamic graph neural networks use geographic–climatological relations and recent SST correlations (including tropical cyclone effects) to provide compact and informative spatial state to the LLM. This hybrid GNN–LLM approach achieves superior predictive performance on South China Sea SST forecasts and can be coupled with a rule-based knowledge module to provide post-hoc explanations, showing a promising direction for combining numerical forecasting with interpretable, knowledge-grounded language outputs in geoscience applications.

title: Continuous Memory Machines
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)
summary: Recurrent neural networks typically compress information into a single vector-valued recurrent state, forcing short-term computation and long-term retention to share the same representation. Past extensions alleviate this bottleneck by increasing the memory capacity or separating timescales, but lack the combination of rapid neuron-level processing and longer-term retention found in biology. To that end, we introduce the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), a recurrent architecture with matrix-valued short- and long-term memory states serving distinct functional roles. Building on the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), the CMM's short-term memory tracks recent neural activity, with uniquely parameterized neuron-level models learning to use these activity patterns for computation. A persistent long-term memory stores information for later use, with a Transformer jointly updating both memory stores, providing an expressive bidirectional read--write mechanism such that each store can reorganize its own contents and both read from and write to the other. Across algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks, the CMM outperforms a broad suite of baselines, exhibiting stronger generalization than prior memory-augmented networks while preserving the CTM's interpretable attention patterns. Code is available at https://github.com/SakanaAI/continuous-memory-machines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), a recurrent neural architecture with separate matrix-valued short-term and long-term memories that are jointly updated by a Transformer, achieving better generalization and interpretability than prior memory-augmented networks.
AI.motivation: Standard recurrent neural networks compress all information into a single vector-valued state, forcing the same representation to handle both fast, neuron-level computation and long-term information storage. Existing memory extensions either just increase capacity or separate timescales, but they do not match the biological combination of rapid processing with persistent, structured memory. The paper aims to design a recurrent architecture that better mirrors this separation of roles while remaining expressive and interpretable.
AI.method: The authors propose the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), which maintains two matrix-valued memory states with distinct roles: (1) a short-term memory that tracks recent neural activity, and (2) a persistent long-term memory for information storage. Building on the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), each neuron has a uniquely parameterized model that uses short-term activity patterns for computation. A Transformer module jointly updates both memory matrices, enabling each memory to reorganize its contents and to read from and write to the other using an expressive, bidirectional attention-based mechanism. The architecture is evaluated on algorithmic tasks, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning benchmarks against various baseline memory-augmented networks.
AI.result: Across algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks, the CMM outperforms a broad range of baseline models, including prior memory-augmented architectures. It demonstrates stronger generalization capabilities while keeping interpretable attention patterns similar to those of the Continuous Thought Machine. These results suggest that the explicit separation and interaction of short- and long-term matrix-valued memories yield practical benefits in performance and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The Continuous Memory Machine offers a biologically inspired recurrent architecture that separates rapid neuron-level computation from persistent memory storage via two interacting matrix-valued memories. With a Transformer jointly updating and mediating bidirectional read–write operations between these memories, the model achieves superior performance and generalization on diverse sequence-processing tasks while maintaining interpretable internal mechanisms. This supports the value of structured, interacting memory systems in recurrent neural networks.

title: SIGMA: Self-Improving Alignment Generalization from a Model Spec
summary: LLM agents are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks and of recursively improving themselves on easy-to-verify objectives such as software engineering and mathematics. Since alignment is much harder to verify, this creates a growing risk of capabilities increasing without appropriate safety alignment, especially as capabilities expand to auto-research and cybersecurity. Existing approaches focus on capability self-improvement using verifiable feedback or on alignment training with supervision from stronger models or curated data, creating an external supervision bottleneck for alignment. We ask whether current models can improve their own safety alignment, and propose SIGMA, a data generation and training pipeline enabling alignment self-improvement that generalizes to out-of-distribution settings. Given only a "Model Spec" stating the model's desired behavior, SIGMA leverages a model's reasoning capabilities to strengthen its own safety reasoning. SIGMA first performs spec-guided task synthesis, using the candidate model as a task designer agent to generate diverse alignment dilemma scenarios and convert them into training tasks that stress-test its understanding of the Model Spec. Next, SIGMA conducts self-judged alignment training through supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning with the model itself as the reward model. Despite training only on single-turn chat data, SIGMA improves safety alignment in multi-turn agentic environments (AgentHarm harmfulness decreases from 22.6 to 14.8; Agentic Misalignment decreases from 79.1 to 3.8), outperforms Deliberative Alignment and Constitutional AI baselines, and retains general capability. Analyses show that a Model Spec balancing harmlessness and helpfulness, test-time reasoning for safety deliberation, and high-quality rubrics from SIGMA's task designer agent are crucial for effective self-improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SIGMA, a self-improving safety-alignment pipeline for LLM agents that uses the model’s own reasoning to synthesize alignment dilemmas, judge its behavior, and fine-tune itself, improving safety in agentic settings without external strong supervisors.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are getting better at complex, self-improving tasks in domains where feedback is easy to verify (e.g., coding, math), but alignment is much harder to verify and depends heavily on external human or stronger-model supervision. This creates a supervision bottleneck and a risk that capabilities race ahead of safety alignment, especially as models begin to conduct autonomous research or interact with cybersecurity-relevant systems. The authors want to see whether current models can contribute to improving their own safety alignment using only a written specification of desired behavior, reducing reliance on stronger overseers and enabling scalable safety improvements.
AI.method: The authors propose SIGMA, a pipeline that uses a written “Model Spec” describing desired behavior to guide self-alignment. SIGMA has two main stages: (1) Spec-guided task synthesis, where the candidate model acts as a task designer agent that generates diverse alignment dilemma scenarios tailored to stress-test the Model Spec, and transforms them into labeled training tasks and evaluation items; (2) Self-judged alignment training, where the same model is used as a judge or reward model, applying rubric-based evaluation of candidate responses. This feedback is then used for supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to strengthen the model’s safety reasoning. Although training data are single-turn chats, the evaluation focuses on multi-turn agentic environments to test generalization of the alignment behaviors.
AI.result: Using SIGMA, the authors report substantial improvements in safety metrics for agentic settings: AgentHarm harmfulness scores drop from 22.6 to 14.8, and Agentic Misalignment reduces from 79.1 to 3.8. The method outperforms baselines such as Deliberative Alignment and Constitutional AI while maintaining general capabilities. Ablation-style analyses reveal that several components are particularly important: a Model Spec that carefully trades off harmlessness and helpfulness, explicit test-time safety reasoning, and the quality and diversity of rubrics produced by the task-designer agent.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current LLMs can meaningfully improve their own safety alignment when equipped with a clear behavioral specification and appropriate self-supervision mechanisms. SIGMA offers a scalable approach that alleviates the need for stronger external overseers by turning the model into both task generator and judge. A well-designed Model Spec, structured deliberative reasoning at inference time, and robust rubric-based evaluations are key to successful self-alignment. The improvements generalize beyond the single-turn training setup to multi-turn agentic environments, suggesting that self-guided safety training is a promising direction for future alignment work.

title: Can Agents Work for Everyone? Cross-User Reliability for Mobile GUI Agents in Personalized User Interfaces
summary: Mobile GUI agents increasingly operate on interfaces influenced by users' histories and preferences, but their reliability across different users remains underexplored. We introduce PAIR (Personalized Application-state Instantiation and Rendering), a pipeline for constructing user-conditioned application states that enables controlled evaluation of the same task across different users. We further introduce RePAIR (Reinforcement learning with Personalization-Aware Interaction Rewards), a training approach that learns from cross-user differences in subgoal outcomes to improve reliability across user-conditioned mobile environments. Across six agents, we find substantial variation in task success across users and consistently lower subgoal achievement in user-conditioned UI contexts (6.98 to 15.4 pp). This gap further increases for personal targets drawn from each user's own content (8.77 to 22.0 pp). Failures in these contexts frequently involve selecting another item instead of the intended target, particularly before target exposure. Finally, RePAIR improves user-conditioned SAR (+5.87 pp), all-success (+7.50 pp), and overall Task SR (+9.42 pp) over its supervised fine-tuning parent on unseen users, providing initial evidence that explicitly learning from cross-user variation can improve GUI-agent reliability.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well mobile GUI agents generalize across different users and proposes tools and a training method to make them more reliable in personalized UI contexts.
AI.motivation: Existing mobile GUI agents are typically evaluated on standardized interfaces, but real apps are personalized based on each user’s history and preferences. This personalization changes app state and content, which can affect agent behavior, yet reliability across different users and their personalized environments is underexplored. The authors want a way to systematically test and improve agents when app states and targets vary by user.
AI.method: They introduce PAIR, a pipeline that constructs user-conditioned application states so that the same task can be evaluated across different users’ personalized UIs. They then propose RePAIR, a reinforcement learning approach that uses personalization-aware interaction rewards: it learns from cross-user differences in subgoal outcomes (e.g., whether intermediate steps succeed or fail for different users) to improve robustness across user-conditioned environments. They run evaluations across six mobile GUI agents on various tasks and user-conditioned settings, including tasks where the target is drawn from the user’s own content.
AI.result: They observe large variation in task success rates across users and consistently worse subgoal achievement in user-conditioned contexts, with drops of about 6.98–15.4 percentage points compared to non-personalized contexts. The performance gap is even larger (8.77–22.0 percentage points) when the task targets are items from the user’s own content. Many failures involve the agent selecting the wrong but similar item, particularly before the correct target has been visibly exposed. Using RePAIR for training improves user-conditioned subgoal achievement rate by 5.87 percentage points, all-subgoals success by 7.50 percentage points, and overall task success rate by 9.42 percentage points compared to a supervised fine-tuning baseline on unseen users.
AI.conclusion: Personalization significantly affects mobile GUI agents’ reliability, causing notable performance drops across different users and especially for tasks involving personal content. By explicitly constructing user-conditioned states (PAIR) and leveraging cross-user variation in training rewards (RePAIR), agents can become more robust and reliable in personalized mobile UI environments, as evidenced by improved success metrics on unseen users.

title: Learning from Revision Consequences: Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation for Self-Improving Agents
summary: As agents continuously improve by generating and revising Skills, the process that discovers and refines those Skills becomes a learnable object in its own right. Task-Skills directly act on task execution, whereas Meta-Skills govern how agents discover and improve future Skills; their value therefore emerges through the subsequent search processes they induce. Existing approaches improve Meta-Skills from observed raw Skill-search trajectories and branch outcomes. However, branch performance entangles the effects of the initial discovery state and the Meta-Skill revision that generated the search process, making it difficult to characterize what a particular revision actually changed, and pushing updates toward revisions that benefit from favorable states rather than those that improve the process. We introduce HMED (Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation), a mechanism for constructing Meta-Experience for self-improving agents. HMED revisits the completed event from which a revision originates and re-executes the incumbent and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state, so that the changes associated with the revision can be observed under a shared condition. Each comparison is distilled into a Meta-Experience, a structured record that can be reused by future updates, so that even revisions that are not ultimately retained still contribute a learning signal. Across three interactive agent benchmarks and both open-source and closed-source models, HMED consistently improves Skill discovery performance over strong baselines, shifting Meta-Skill learning beyond branch outcomes toward the consequences of changing the improvement process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HMED, a method to better learn Meta-Skills in self-improving agents by directly comparing old and revised Meta-Skills from the same restored discovery state, and distilling these comparisons into reusable Meta-Experiences.
AI.motivation: Existing methods try to improve Meta-Skills—policies that govern how agents discover and refine Skills—by looking only at raw search trajectories and branch outcomes. This is problematic because observed performance mixes together the quality of the initial discovery state and the effect of the Meta-Skill revision itself, making it hard to understand what a revision actually changed. As a result, updates may favor revisions that started from lucky or favorable states rather than those that genuinely improve the search process. The paper is motivated by the need for a cleaner, more causal way to evaluate and learn from Meta-Skill revisions.
AI.method: The authors introduce Hindsight Meta-Experience Distillation (HMED). When a Meta-Skill revision is proposed, HMED restores the original discovery state from which the revision arose and re-runs both the incumbent and the revised Meta-Skills starting from this same state. This controlled re-execution isolates the impact of the Meta-Skill change.
