Each such comparison is converted into a structured Meta-Experience record that captures how the two Meta-Skills behaved and which performed better. These Meta-Experiences are stored and reused for future updates so that even discarded revisions contribute training signal to the Meta-Skill learning process.
AI.result: On three interactive agent benchmarks and using both open-source and closed-source models, HMED yields consistent improvements in Skill discovery performance compared to strong existing baselines. The results show that evaluating Meta-Skills under shared initial conditions and reusing distilled Meta-Experiences leads to more effective self-improvement of agents.
AI.conclusion: HMED reframes Meta-Skill learning from simply judging search branch outcomes to explicitly assessing the consequences of changing the improvement process itself. By reconstructing the discovery state and comparing incumbent vs. revised Meta-Skills under identical conditions, then distilling these comparisons into reusable Meta-Experiences, the method provides cleaner learning signals and improves Skill discovery in practice across multiple benchmarks and model types.

title: Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality: A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures. Code, policies, evaluation and videos: https://github.com/JordyKieto/puffermoba-dyna
summary: World models are usually judged from the inside: by prediction loss, by the return a policy earns in imagination, or by how convincing their frames look. We judge one from the outside. We learn a structured, multi-agent world model of a complete ten-hero MOBA (206 units, every hero acting every tick, games of up to 6,000 ticks), train a policy only inside it with 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes, and measure that policy in the real game against the opponent the game ships with. The real game never provides a gradient; it provides the policy's own games as training data for the world model, and an online evaluation that selects and anchors the policy. Run as a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop, the policy wins 70.2% of real games as radiant (421 of 600; 95% CI 66.4-73.7) on seeds never used for any decision, up from 0% for dream training alone and 33.7% before the loop. It wins none as dire, and neither does the shipped opponent when it plays itself. Four findings explain the result. Model exploitation is invisible from inside the dream: every unanchored run collapsed within a few updates while no in-dream metric tracked the collapse. A world model that is accurate on its training corpus is badly wrong on the policy's own games, and Dyna repairs it there, which is worth +9.2 points of real win rate with the policy recipe held fixed. Finally, the policy inherits its world model's fidelity profile mechanic by mechanic: the model represents the macro game but not crowd control, cast timing or lethality, and the policy wins by map-wide pressure with almost no coordinated fighting. We release the world model, the dream-PPO harness, a world-model debugger, the evaluation protocol, and every policy and log.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a learned world model for a complex multi-agent MOBA game "from the outside" by how well a policy trained only in imagination performs in the real game, using an asynchronous Dyna loop to close the sim-to-real gap.
AI.motivation: Most work on world models evaluates them using internal metrics such as prediction loss or visual quality, or by performance of policies within the model, which can miss severe model exploitation and miscalibration. The authors want to understand how reliable and useful a world model really is when used as the sole training environment for agents in a complex, multi-agent setting, judged on actual performance in the real game rather than internal metrics.
AI.method: They learn a structured, multi-agent world model of a full ten-hero MOBA game with 206 units and up to 6,000 ticks per game. A policy is trained exclusively inside this model using PPO with 1,400-tick free-running imagined episodes. The real game is used only to generate trajectories for training the world model and to evaluate candidate policies online in a continuous asynchronous Dyna loop: real-game results are used to select and "anchor" policies, while the model is iteratively updated on data from the policy’s real games. They analyze failures such as model exploitation by comparing model accuracy on its training corpus versus on the policy’s own trajectories and inspect how specific mechanics are (mis)represented and reflected in policy behavior.
AI.result: With pure dream (model-only) training, the policy has 0% win rate versus the shipped opponent. After enabling the continuous asynchronous Dyna loop—using real-game play only for data collection and evaluation—the policy reaches a 70.2% win rate as radiant (421/600 games; 95% CI 66.4–73.7) against the built-in opponent on held-out seeds, up from 33.7% before running the loop. It wins 0% as dire, and the shipped opponent also fails to win as dire against itself. They observe that unanchored policies systematically exploit model errors and collapse, that the world model fitted on its original corpus performs poorly on trajectories induced by the trained policy, and that Dyna-style repair of the model on those trajectories adds about +9.2 percentage points in real-game win rate for a fixed policy recipe. They also find a clear correspondence between which mechanics the world model models well and the strategic patterns the policy adopts.
AI.conclusion: External evaluation reveals that internal world-model metrics can be highly misleading: policies can catastrophically exploit model errors while in-model scores look healthy. Closing this gap requires a Dyna-style loop that constantly grounds the model in fresh data from the current policy’s real behavior and anchors policy selection on real-game performance. Even then, the agent only leverages those aspects of the environment that the world model captures with sufficient fidelity, leading to high win rates via macro map pressure but poor handling of micro-mechanics such as crowd control and precise combat. The work underscores the need for outside-the-model evaluation protocols and provides open-source tools and artifacts for studying large-scale world models and imagination-trained agents.

title: Same Feedback, Different Answer: Measuring Run-to-Run Instability in Frontier-Model Customer Feedback Analysis
summary: AI agents are increasingly being programmed to automate knowledge work over large collections of unstructured data. Such automation requires repeatability: when the underlying evidence is unchanged, the agent's categories, priorities, and counts should not shift materially between runs, even if each individual answer appears plausible. We introduce a repeat-run evaluation framework that aligns semantically equivalent categories and focuses on two operating metrics: theme churn, the normalized change in the returned category set, and volume disagreement, the change in counts for categories that persist. We evaluate three recurring customer-feedback tasks across eight frontier models, corpus sizes from 100 to 5,000 records, multiple prompts, and three execution designs: raw generation, taxonomy-free hierarchical decomposition, and a taxonomy-grounded agent (TGA) using persistent themes, subthemes, and record-level predictions. With Claude Opus 4.8 and the 1,000-record corpus fixed, TGA reduces theme churn by 86--88% relative to both raw generation and hierarchical decomposition, while matched-theme volumes have zero disagreement. The taxonomy-grounded agent is more stable than every raw model in the screen, remains more stable at each corpus size, and keeps this advantage when theme matching is made stricter or looser. Although evaluated on customer feedback, the framework targets repeated synthesis of unstructured corpora more broadly, including financial reports, legal documents, incident records, and scientific literature. Overall, these results show that taxonomy grounding produces more consistent and repeatable outputs for recurring knowledge work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a framework to measure and improve the repeatability of AI agents that synthesize large unstructured text corpora, showing that grounding the agent in a stable taxonomy greatly reduces variation between runs.
AI.motivation: AI agents used for recurring knowledge work on unstructured data (e.g., customer feedback, financial and legal documents) must be repeatable: when the underlying evidence is unchanged, the agent should produce stable themes and counts across runs. Current LLM-based workflows, which often rely on free-form generation, can yield plausible but unstable categorizations and volumes, undermining trust and operational use. The authors want a principled way to measure this instability and a design that makes outputs consistent.
AI.method: The authors define a repeat-run evaluation framework with two metrics: (1) theme churn, which measures normalized change in the set of returned categories across runs, and (2) volume disagreement, which measures changes in record counts for categories that persist across runs. They test three types of execution designs on three customer-feedback tasks: (a) raw generation, (b) taxonomy-free hierarchical decomposition, and (c) a taxonomy-grounded agent (TGA) that uses a persistent taxonomy of themes and subthemes plus record-level predictions. They run experiments across eight frontier LLMs, corpus sizes from 100 to 5,000 records, multiple prompts, and different levels of strictness in matching semantically equivalent themes across runs.
AI.result: For a 1,000-record corpus using Claude Opus 4.8, the taxonomy-grounded agent reduces theme churn by 86–88% relative to both raw generation and taxonomy-free hierarchical decomposition, and achieves zero volume disagreement for matched themes. Across all evaluated models and corpus sizes, the TGA remains more stable than raw generation approaches and hierarchical decomposition. This stability advantage persists when the criteria for matching themes across runs are varied to be stricter or looser.
AI.conclusion: Grounding AI agents in a persistent, predefined taxonomy significantly improves the repeatability and stability of their outputs when synthesizing large unstructured text corpora. The proposed evaluation framework (theme churn and volume disagreement) provides a general way to quantify repeat-run reliability. Although demonstrated on customer feedback analysis, the approach is broadly applicable to other domains such as financial, legal, incident, and scientific documents, making taxonomy grounding a strong design principle for recurring knowledge work with LLM-based agents.

title: SpeedrunBench: Challenging LLM Agents with Video Game Speedrunning
summary: Frontier LLM agents have been shown to be capable of solving increasingly complex tasks for which humans have measurable solutions. This begs the pertinent question of whether LLM agents can go beyond what humans have already solved. The ability to develop sophisticated strategies to tackle consequential problems becomes paramount as well-trodden, human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems for which we lack context or enough training data. We study agents' capability of such strategy formation through the communal practice of video game speedrunning. In speedrunning, practitioners compete to find the fastest way to complete a video game under certain conditions, and in so doing uncovering interesting unorthodox play styles that require a thorough understanding and mastery of the underlying game mechanics. We introduce SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well in this benchmark, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit their gained knowledge, and reason across a long-horizon of actions to improve on an increasingly difficult problem: being faster than themselves and everyone else. Our experiments show that while frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games, they remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. These results suggest that SPEEDRUNBENCH is a useful testbed for studying agents' strategy formation capabilities as well as being a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, as there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark using video game speedrunning to evaluate how well frontier LLM agents can form and refine strategies beyond existing human solutions.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents start to tackle complex, real-world-like tasks, it is important to know whether they can not only match but surpass known human strategies, particularly in settings where human solutions are saturated or data is scarce. Speedrunning offers a well-defined, competitive environment where agents must continuously innovate faster strategies, providing a natural testbed for examining strategy formation and long-horizon reasoning beyond merely imitating human play.
AI.method: The authors construct SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark comprising 9 different video games chosen to require strategic planning, mastery of mechanics, and long-horizon reasoning. They evaluate frontier LLM agents as game-playing agents that must iteratively refine their strategies: reflecting on previous runs, exploiting learned knowledge, and attempting to beat their own and human timings under practical compute and interaction budgets. Performance is measured primarily by completion time relative to human world records and baselines.
AI.result: Experiments show that current frontier LLM agents can approach human world-record performance in simpler, short-horizon platformer games but fall notably short on longer and more complex games. Under realistic resource constraints, they struggle to match human experts in these harder settings, revealing clear performance gaps in strategy formation and long-horizon planning.
AI.conclusion: SPEEDRUNBENCH serves as a challenging and saturation-resistant benchmark for assessing LLM agents' abilities to form, refine, and innovate strategies over long horizons. The observed gaps between agents and human world records, especially on complex games, indicate substantial room for improvement in agents’ strategic reasoning, while the nature of speedrunning ensures that new, faster solutions will continue to emerge for rigorous future evaluation.

title: Beyond Corrected Memory: Execution Consistency in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Shared memory coordinates agents' actions, but correct records do not establish that those actions satisfy task requirements. Memory governance and failure diagnosis regulate or inspect recorded information; they do not by themselves establish whether it is sufficient to judge task duties. We define execution consistency through duties governing state use, information handoffs, and final-state agreement, with explicit evidence conditions for judging fulfillment. Our core claim is that identical retained records can correspond to compliant and violating executions under the same task rule. Controlled removal of evidence such as receipt, action dependence, or response validity leaves 82.4% of opposite-label pairs indistinguishable; restoration separates 97.9% of the merged pairs. Natural-log annotations identify the defined violations in actual executions. However, existing logs do not always explicitly represent the execution relationships needed for these judgments. To assess the definition's practical value, we use CAVERT, a framework for consistency diagnosis and recovery, to extract supported relationships from logs and apply these criteria. It consistently outperforms contract-prompted LLM and rule-based baselines in diagnosis across all 12 benchmark-executor settings. Under the same gate and executor limits, it also outperforms rule-guided recovery in all four evaluated environments. These findings identify execution evidence that agent-memory and execution interfaces should preserve for reliable judgment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an evidence-based definition of execution consistency for multi-agent systems and shows that existing shared-memory logs often lack the information required to judge whether agents met their duties. It proposes criteria and a framework (CAVERT) to extract and use execution relationships for better diagnosis and recovery, outperforming LLM- and rule-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Shared memory and correct logs are widely used to coordinate agents and diagnose failures, but they do not guarantee that agents have actually satisfied the underlying task duties. Existing memory governance and failure-diagnosis mechanisms tend to check recorded information rather than whether that information is sufficient to judge compliance, leading to cases where compliant and violating executions look identical in the logs. The authors are motivated to formally define what evidence is needed in execution records to determine if duties have been fulfilled, and to show how to use this definition to improve diagnosis and recovery in agent systems.
AI.method: The authors formalize "execution consistency" in terms of duties governing state use, information handoffs, and final-state agreement, and they define explicit evidence conditions that must be present in logs to judge whether duties were fulfilled. They construct paired executions with opposite labels (compliant vs violating) but identical retained records to demonstrate indistinguishability when key evidence is removed (e.g., receipt confirmation, action dependence, response validity). They then show that restoring this evidence makes most pairs distinguishable. They introduce natural-log annotations that explicitly mark the relationships corresponding to their duty-based violations and use CAVERT, a practical framework, to extract these relationships from real logs. They evaluate CAVERT on 12 benchmark–executor settings for diagnosis and 4 environments for recovery, comparing it to contract-prompted LLM and rule-based baselines under the same resource constraints.
AI.result: When key forms of execution evidence (such as receipt, dependence, and validity markers) are removed, 82.4% of execution pairs that actually differ in compliance become indistinguishable using the remaining records. When this evidence is restored according to their definition, 97.9% of previously merged opposite-label pairs become distinguishable. Using natural-log annotations and the CAVERT framework to recover and apply these relationships, the method consistently outperforms both contract-prompted LLMs and rule-based systems for failure diagnosis across 12 benchmark–executor settings. In recovery tasks across four environments, CAVERT also outperforms rule-guided baselines under the same gate and executor limits.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that correct shared-memory logs alone are insufficient for reliable judgment of whether agents satisfy task duties, because compliant and violating executions can share identical records when critical evidence is missing. A duty- and evidence-based definition of execution consistency clarifies which relationships—state use, handoff, and final-state agreement—must be captured in logs. Their empirical results show that encoding and extracting this execution evidence via CAVERT yields more accurate diagnosis and recovery than LLM- or rule-based approaches that lack such structure. Therefore, agent-memory and execution interfaces should be designed to preserve these key forms of execution evidence to enable trustworthy assessment of multi-agent behavior.

title: DSV-Mem: Evaluating Multimodal Memory in Professional Workflows for MLLM Agents
summary: Conversational MLLM agents are increasingly expected to assist in professional workflows, from AI research and engineering design to product management and business operations. Yet this capability remains underexplored: existing benchmarks largely focus on informal, everyday interactions and personal-life scenarios featuring photographic natural images, isolated static artifacts, and recall-oriented questions. In contrast, professional scenarios often involve structured, information-heavy artifacts that undergo frequent revisions and authority updates, and compositional queries requiring reconciliation of many artifact versions while tracking state precisely. To address these challenges, we introduce DSV-Mem, a benchmark for evaluating Dense Stateful Visual Memory. DSV-Mem comprises expert-reviewed scenarios and 1,000 questions across five user-oriented categories (Current State, Past State, Derived State, Change History, and Conflict/Refusal). A Hartley-inspired criterion favors questions with broader visual-evidence inspection demands. We also introduce a generation harness that produces evaluation suites by decoupling state-transition synthesis from conversation filling. Evaluation over 27 configurations spanning frontier and open-weight models and memory management methods reveals that the strongest baseline scores below 45% on DSV-Mem. Analysis surfaces findings: 1) multimodality and information density both contribute to difficulty, but state evolution, particularly the number of governing updates, is the dominant tested factor. Raw conversation/haystack length, OCR, and arithmetic are not the primary bottlenecks; 2) models often fail to verify user premises against prior state updates before answering; 3) increased reasoning effort and memory management methods yield limited gains, whereas state-aware designs prove more effective. The benchmark and code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DSV-Mem, a benchmark to test how well multimodal conversational agents maintain and reason over dense, evolving visual memory in professional workflows, showing that current models perform poorly and need more state-aware designs.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM benchmarks mostly cover casual, everyday scenarios with simple, static images and recall-oriented questions, which do not reflect demanding professional use cases. Real professional workflows involve dense, structured visual artifacts (e.g., documents, dashboards, designs) that change over time, require tracking multiple versions, and call for precise reasoning about current vs past states, derived information, and conflicting updates. There is a gap in systematically evaluating whether MLLMs can manage and reason over such dense, dynamic visual memories in conversational settings.
AI.method: The authors create DSV-Mem, a benchmark focused on Dense Stateful Visual Memory. It consists of expert-reviewed scenarios and 1,000 questions, grouped into five categories: Current State, Past State, Derived State, Change History, and Conflict/Refusal. They use a Hartley-inspired criterion to favor questions that require broad inspection of visual evidence. They also design a generation harness that separates the process of synthesizing state transitions from populating the conversational context, enabling construction of evaluation suites with controlled state evolution. The benchmark is used to test 27 configurations of multimodal models and memory management strategies, including both frontier and open-weight models, and various reasoning and memory approaches.
AI.result: Across 27 model and memory configurations, the best-performing baseline achieves under 45% accuracy on DSV-Mem, indicating that current systems struggle with dense, evolving visual memory. Detailed analysis shows that: (1) While multimodality and high information density make tasks harder, the main source of difficulty is state evolution, especially the number of governing updates that must be reconciled. In contrast, conversation length, OCR quality, and arithmetic demands are not the primary limitations. (2) Models frequently neglect to check user claims against the accumulated state updates before answering. (3) Simply increasing generic reasoning effort or applying standard memory management techniques yields limited improvements, whereas explicitly state-aware architectures or designs are more effective.
AI.conclusion: DSV-Mem exposes substantial weaknesses in current conversational MLLMs when applied to professional workflows that require dense, stateful visual memory and reasoning over evolving artifacts. The benchmark shows that tracking and reconciling state updates is a central unsolved challenge, and that naive scaling of reasoning or memory is insufficient. Progress will likely require models and systems that are explicitly designed to be state-aware. The authors plan to publicly release the benchmark and code to support further research in this direction.

title: ChartBmkAgent: Harness-Governed Multi-Agent Construction of Chart QA Benchmarks from Sparse Error-Taxonomy Specifications
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance rapidly, while conventional benchmark development lags behind, delaying investigation of newly observed capability gaps. Such investigation requires an expressive task format and an on-demand construction process: information-rich charts make chart question answering (Chart QA) suitable for probing coupled perception and reasoning. Automated Chart QA construction is intended to shorten the benchmark-development cycle by turning identified gaps into targeted samples on demand. Current methods, however, commonly separate target guidance from scratch generation: target-guided systems often require prepared data, charts, or templates, while scratch-generation systems primarily ensure artifact validity, without explicitly controlling whether newly synthesized requirements and content remain aligned with an externally specified diagnostic target. We introduce ChartBmkAgent, which turns an identified capability gap into targeted diagnostic evidence by constructing complete Chart QA samples from sparse error-taxonomy specifications. Throughout construction, a central harness governs specialized agents, requires stage-specific evidence of alignment with the original error category, and records the basis for each acceptance decision. On 300 taxonomy-wide samples, MLLM accuracies ranged from 32.7% to 84.3% with distinct category profiles, showing that generated samples reveal capability differences. Across three source-model comparisons, targeted follow-ups scored 50.0% versus 82.2% on matched controls ($p=8.96\times10^{-6}$); all six cross-model comparisons had the same direction, demonstrating targeted validation and diagnostic-data generation. Multiple evaluator models assessed whether each sample tested its specified error category; 86.4% met this criterion, providing empirical evidence of target preservation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ChartBmkAgent, an agent-based system that can automatically generate targeted Chart QA benchmarks from sparse error-taxonomy descriptions, to quickly probe and diagnose capability gaps in multimodal large language models.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs are improving rapidly, but benchmark development is slow and inflexible, making it hard to quickly investigate newly observed capability gaps. Chart QA is a good vehicle for testing coupled perception and reasoning using information-rich charts, but existing automated benchmark-construction methods either need extensive prepared resources (target-guided) or focus mainly on artifact validity without ensuring that generated data truly targets a specified diagnostic error type. The authors aim to build a system that transforms high-level descriptions of capability gaps directly into concrete, aligned Chart QA samples, shortening the benchmark creation cycle and enabling fine-grained diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors propose ChartBmkAgent, a central harness that orchestrates multiple specialized agent modules to construct full Chart QA samples from sparse error-taxonomy specifications. Starting from a high-level error category (e.g., a particular reasoning or perception failure), agents iteratively design charts, questions, and answers while the harness enforces stage-specific checks for alignment with the original target category. The system requires explicit evidence at each step that the sample still tests the intended error type and logs the justification behind accepting or rejecting intermediate artifacts. They then generate a taxonomy-wide set of 300 samples and run multiple multimodal LLMs and evaluator models on them to assess diagnostic power and target preservation.
AI.result: On the 300 generated Chart QA samples spanning the error taxonomy, different MLLMs achieved accuracies between 32.7% and 84.3%, each showing distinct performance profiles across error categories, indicating that the constructed data exposes meaningful capability differences. In controlled comparisons across three source models, targeted follow-up samples (designed to stress specific error types) led to much lower accuracy (50.0%) than matched control samples (82.2%), with a highly significant p-value (8.96×10−6), and all six cross-model comparisons showed the same direction of effect, evidencing successful targeted validation. Multiple independent evaluator models judged whether each sample truly tested its specified error category; 86.4% of samples were affirmed as correctly targeted, supporting empirical target preservation of the benchmark construction process.
AI.conclusion: ChartBmkAgent can automatically turn high-level error-taxonomy descriptions into targeted Chart QA benchmarks that preserve alignment with specified diagnostic categories. The system reveals fine-grained capability gaps across multimodal LLMs and reliably produces follow-up test items that are measurably harder for models on the intended weaknesses than on matched controls. This demonstrates a practical path to faster, more precise, and on-demand benchmark development for probing perception–reasoning interactions in multimodal models.

title: Test-Time Agent Evolution for Long-Horizon Legal Reasoning
summary: Legal intelligence aims to support reliable decision-making across long-horizon legal processes involving evolving case states and multiple roles. However, real-world legal deployment exhibits substantial case heterogeneity in facts, evidence, and procedural contexts, exposing the limitations of static agent strategies. Moreover, legal reasoning is inherently interdependent across roles and procedural stages, making global reliability fundamentally different from isolated role competence. To address these challenges, we study training-free test-time agent adaptation, where agents continuously exploit deployment-time signals from preceding cases and ongoing interactions without updating model parameters. We propose \method, which introduces \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} to retrieve reusable experience from previous cases, adapt it to the current factual and procedural context, and consolidate accumulated experience for subsequent decision-making. Further, \emph{Rubric-Aligned Collaboration} verifies and revises role-specific actions according to behavioral and procedural requirements, enabling coordinated decision-making across roles and stages. Extensive experiments on J1-EVAL and LegalWorld across five backbone models demonstrate consistent improvements over representative reasoning and agent baselines with reasonable interaction and computational costs. Ablation and case studies further show that the two components provide complementary benefits in experience adaptation and cross-role coordination, improving the reliability and efficiency of long-horizon legal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, test-time adaptation framework for multi-role legal AI agents, improving reliability and coordination in long-horizon legal reasoning by leveraging past cases and structured role collaboration.
AI.motivation: Deployed legal AI systems face high case heterogeneity in facts, evidence, and procedures, which breaks static prompting/agent strategies. Additionally, legal decisions emerge from interdependent actions of multiple roles (e.g., judge, lawyer) across procedural stages, so optimizing each role in isolation does not guarantee globally reliable case outcomes. There is a need for methods that can adapt to varying legal contexts and coordinate multiple roles at test time without expensive retraining.
AI.method: They introduce a framework (\method) with two core components: (1) Test-Time Memory Evolution, which maintains and updates a memory of previous cases. At inference, the system retrieves relevant prior experiences, adapts them to the current case’s factual and procedural context, and then consolidates new experience back into memory for future use—all without changing model weights. (2) Rubric-Aligned Collaboration, which defines behavioral and procedural rubrics for each role and stage, then uses cross-role verification and revision of proposed actions against these rubrics to ensure coordinated, procedurally consistent decisions across the legal workflow.
AI.result: On two benchmarks, J1-EVAL and LegalWorld, and across five different backbone language models, the framework consistently outperforms strong reasoning and multi-agent baselines. It yields better reliability and efficiency for long-horizon legal tasks while keeping interaction and computation overhead reasonable. Ablation experiments verify that both Test-Time Memory Evolution and Rubric-Aligned Collaboration contribute distinct, complementary performance gains, and qualitative case studies illustrate improved experience reuse and cross-role coordination.
AI.conclusion: Training-free test-time adaptation with evolving memory and rubric-based multi-role collaboration can significantly enhance the robustness and coherence of legal AI agents in complex, long-horizon settings. By leveraging prior cases and structured cross-role checks without retraining, the proposed method improves both reliability and efficiency of legal reasoning, suggesting a promising direction for practical deployment of legal intelligence systems.

title: Partially Observable Zero-shot coordination by Predicting Intention of Partner
summary: Zero-shot coordination in embodied settings requires acting while the partner is intermittently out of view, leaving existing methods with ambiguous partner representations and uncertainty over hidden partner states. We propose Predicting Intention of Partner (PIP) to jointly address these challenges. PIP uses a Joint-view VAE to distill richer training-time evidence from the union of both agents' local observations into a partner representation available from local observations alone. Partner-state Belief networks further infer the partner's hidden location and behavioral tendencies from the ego agent's interaction history. We evaluate PIP in Burrito-PO, Overcooked-PO, and a Melting Pot substrate, together with a human evaluation in Burrito-PO. PIP attains the highest mean performance among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. Human evaluation and diagnostic analyses further support coordination with unseen partners and the contributions of both components under partner occlusion.

AI.tldr: They introduce PIP, a method enabling agents to coordinate in partially observable embodied environments by better modeling partner intentions and hidden states, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot coordination.
AI.motivation: In embodied multi-agent settings, partners are often occluded or out of view, making it hard to coordinate, especially in zero-shot scenarios with unseen partners. Existing methods struggle because they rely on ambiguous partner representations and cannot accurately reason about hidden partner states under partial observability.
AI.method: PIP has two main components: (1) a Joint-view Variational Autoencoder (VAE) that, during training, learns a partner representation from the union of both agents' local observations but at test time can be inferred from local observations alone; and (2) Partner-state Belief networks that maintain a belief over the partner’s hidden location and behavioral tendencies based on the ego agent’s interaction history. These are integrated into the agent’s policy for decision-making under occlusion.
AI.result: PIP is evaluated on three partially observable embodied coordination benchmarks: Burrito-PO, Overcooked-PO, and a Melting Pot substrate, plus a human-subject study in Burrito-PO. Across all benchmarks, PIP achieves the highest mean coordination performance with unseen partners compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that explicitly modeling partner intentions via a joint-view representation and maintaining beliefs over hidden partner states substantially improves zero-shot coordination under occlusion. Both components contribute meaningfully to performance gains, as shown by ablations and human evaluation, demonstrating more robust coordination with novel partners in partially observable environments.

title: Which alloy composition,what process parameters? Inferring the recipe from optimized metallic microstructure and texture
summary: The mechanical properties of a metallic alloy are set by its microstructure and texture: the size and shape of its grains and the orientation of their crystals. That structure is in turn set by a recipe, the alloy composition together with the processing parameters. Alloy development runs this chain forwards, tuning the structure until a target property is met. Running it backwards, from an optimized structure to the recipe that would produce it, still relies on expert knowledge. We ask whether this backwards step can be learned. On an in-house dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions across 14 alloys, each with optical micrographs and an X-ray texture measurement, we compare three descriptors of microstructure and texture: conventional grain and texture statistics, a vision embedding from a pretrained image encoder, and a graph neural network on the grain network. Each is paired with prediction heads for two tasks: the alloy composition given the process (Task A), and the process parameters given the composition (Task B). Under 5-fold cross-validation, the conventional descriptors identify the correct alloy for 65% of held-out conditions, against 17% for always guessing the most common alloy, while the learned embeddings stay below 30%. The process parameters are recoverable but noisier: compared with using the composition alone, the microstructure roughly halves the temperature error. Because only a few alloys were cast and only a few press settings were used, both answers are discrete, and heads that pick from these known options, while respecting their order, worked better than heads that predict a free value.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether one can infer alloy composition and processing parameters directly from microstructure and texture data using machine learning, and compares different microstructure descriptors for this inverse design task.
AI.motivation: Alloy properties depend on microstructure and texture, which are controlled by composition and processing. Forward design (from recipe to structure/properties) is standard, but inverse design (from desired microstructure back to recipe) still relies heavily on expert intuition. The authors want to know if this backward mapping can be learned from data, enabling more systematic alloy and process design.
AI.method: Using an in-house dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions across 14 alloys, each with optical micrographs and X-ray texture measurements, the authors construct three kinds of microstructure/texture descriptors: (1) conventional grain and texture statistics, (2) vision embeddings from a pretrained image encoder, and (3) graph neural network embeddings built on the grain network. They attach prediction heads for two supervised tasks: Task A – predict alloy composition given processing conditions and microstructure; Task B – predict process parameters given alloy composition and microstructure. They use 5-fold cross-validation and compare accuracy against baselines, including always guessing the most common alloy. Because both compositions and process settings are discrete in the dataset, they also explore classification-like heads that select from the known options while respecting their ordering, versus continuous regression heads that predict free values.
AI.result: Conventional, hand-crafted grain and texture statistics perform best on predicting alloy composition: they identify the correct alloy for 65% of held-out conditions, substantially above the 17% accuracy of always picking the most common alloy. Learned representations from pretrained vision encoders and graph neural networks perform worse, staying below 30% accuracy. For process parameters, incorporating microstructure information improves predictions relative to using composition alone: adding microstructure roughly halves the error in predicted temperature, although predictions remain noisy. Classification-style ordered heads that choose among the finite set of observed compositions and process settings work better than unconstrained regression heads for this dataset.
AI.conclusion: The backward mapping from microstructure/texture to alloy composition and processing parameters can be partially learned, but current learned embeddings underperform simple, domain-informed microstructure statistics on this small, structured dataset. Microstructure clearly contains usable information about both alloy identity and process settings, significantly improving recovery of composition and reducing error in process parameters such as temperature. However, data limitations (few alloys, few press settings) and the discrete nature of the problem make it more effective to predict among known options than to regress arbitrary values. Overall, conventional descriptors remain strong baselines for inverse microstructure-to-recipe inference, and more data or better-tailored learned representations would be needed to surpass them.

title: LFHE: Local-First Heuristic Evolution for Bounded Local Topology Search in Decentralized Learning with Non-IID Data
summary: Decentralized learning is highly sensitive to communication topology under non-IID data. Adaptive peer-selection methods can exploit local model information, but broader peer discovery may require increasingly large control state, whereas direct spectral optimization typically relies on graph-wide information. We study the intermediate setting of bounded local topology search and propose Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE), a representation-driven rewiring framework whose candidate discovery and scoring use only ego-neighborhood and friend-of-a-friend (FoF) information. The structural score admits an exact interpretation through graph Dirichlet energy: its sum across clients equals twice the representation Dirichlet energy, which under standard linear consensus dynamics governs the instantaneous dissipation of representation disagreement. LFHE combines this state-dependent structural signal with early exploration and degree control, while algebraic connectivity remains an offline graph diagnostic. Under bounded sparse degree, its FoF candidate state remains local rather than expanding toward population-wide peer tracking. Across four image, speech, and text benchmarks, LFHE achieves competitive decentralized learning performance. Matched-protocol controls identify the structural term as the principal empirical topology-selection signal, while comparison with broader peer discovery exposes a trade-off between predictive performance and discovery-state locality. Together, these results motivate state-aware bounded local topology search between pairwise peer selection and globally informed topology optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LFHE, a local-topology-search method for decentralized learning that rewires communication using only ego and friend-of-friend information, achieving competitive performance while keeping state local.
AI.motivation: Decentralized learning under non-IID data is very sensitive to the communication graph. Existing adaptive peer-selection methods either require large, potentially global state for peer discovery or rely on direct spectral optimization using graph-wide information. There is a gap between simple pairwise peer selection and full global topology optimization: a need for methods that can improve topology using only bounded local information and state, preserving scalability and practicality in large networks.
AI.method: The authors introduce Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE), a representation-driven topology rewiring framework. LFHE performs bounded local topology search where each client discovers and evaluates candidate peers using only its ego-neighborhood and friends-of-friends (FoF). It defines a structural score for edges that is exactly related to graph Dirichlet energy, such that the sum of scores across clients equals twice the representation Dirichlet energy, which controls instantaneous dissipation of representation disagreement under linear consensus. LFHE combines this state-dependent structural score with early exploration strategies and degree control, while treating algebraic connectivity as an offline diagnostic. The FoF candidate pool is maintained under bounded sparse degree so that discovery state remains local and does not grow toward global peer tracking.
AI.result: On four benchmarks spanning image, speech, and text tasks, LFHE attains competitive decentralized learning performance compared to stronger or more global topology-optimization baselines. Ablation-style matched-protocol controls show that the structural (Dirichlet-energy-based) term is the main effective signal for topology selection in practice. Comparisons with approaches that perform broader peer discovery highlight a fundamental trade-off: methods that use more global discovery can sometimes yield better predictive performance, but at the cost of much larger, less local discovery state, whereas LFHE maintains locality.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that effective topology adaptation for decentralized learning is possible using only bounded local information and state via representation-aware rewiring. LFHE offers a principled, energy-based structural signal that aligns with consensus dynamics, and in practice provides a good balance between performance and scalability. The results support the value of state-aware bounded local topology search as a middle ground between simple pairwise peer selection and fully global, spectrally optimized communication graphs.

title: Mathematical Proof Assistants for Teaching Logic: The LogiKEy Methodology
summary: We report on an approach to teaching logic to mixed groups of computer science, mathematics, and philosophy students, based on the logico-pluralistic LogiKEy methodology, used for more than a decade in courses, summer schools, and tutorials. LogiKEy uses classical higher-order logic (HOL) as a universal metalogic in which object logics, classical and non-classical alike, are encoded by defining their semantics; through these semantical embeddings a single proof assistant (e.g. Isabelle/HOL), with its automated theorem provers and (counter-)model finders, becomes one environment in which students learn, experiment with, and compare logics. After making the pedagogical case for proof assistants in the logic classroom, we present a graded sequence of classroom examples, each transition motivated by a limitation of the preceding representation, by a need for more explicit modelling resources, or by a new application. A liars-and-truth-tellers puzzle leads from propositional to modal logic; the Wise Men puzzle leads on to dynamic epistemic logic; Boolos's curious inference illustrates what a higher-order meta-logic buys, even for automated proof search; Chisholm's paradox takes the sequence into deontic logic, and from standard to dyadic deontic logic; and Gödel's ontological argument brings it to a research-level metaphysical argument. We then rebut the objection that embedding everything in classical HOL is monism rather than pluralism, reflect on three years of teaching such a course, and sketch the portability of the approach beyond Isabelle.

AI.tldr: The paper presents and evaluates a logic teaching methodology (LogiKEy) that uses higher-order logic embeddings and proof assistants to expose students to multiple logics in one unified framework.
AI.motivation: Teaching logic to mixed cohorts (computer science, mathematics, philosophy) is challenging because of diverse backgrounds, the proliferation of classical and non-classical logics, and the gap between textbook presentations and research-level formal work. The authors want a way to teach logical pluralism in a hands-on, exploratory manner that is both rigorous and engaging, while leveraging modern automated reasoning tools.
AI.method: They use the LogiKEy methodology, which treats classical higher-order logic as a universal metalogic. Different object logics (propositional, modal, dynamic epistemic, deontic, etc.) are semantically embedded in HOL within a single proof assistant (Isabelle/HOL). They design a graded sequence of classroom modules, each motivated by the limits of the previous one or by new modeling needs: starting from propositional logic, moving to modal logic via puzzles, then to dynamic epistemic logic, higher-order reasoning, various deontic logics, and finally a research-level metaphysical argument. They also include reflections on teaching experience and address conceptual objections to the approach.
AI.result: They obtain a coherent, unified teaching environment where students can model, experiment with, and compare multiple logics using one proof assistant and its automated provers/model finders. The sequence of examples (liars-and-truth-tellers, Wise Men, Boolos’s inference, Chisholm’s paradox, Gödel’s ontological argument) demonstrates increasing expressive power and connects basic coursework to current research. Over several years of teaching, the approach proves workable and pedagogically valuable across student backgrounds.
AI.conclusion: Using HOL-based semantic embeddings in a proof assistant is an effective way to support logically pluralistic teaching: it avoids commitment to a single object logic while providing a common rigorous framework. The graded example sequence both motivates successively richer logics and showcases the capabilities of automated reasoning tools. The method is portable beyond Isabelle/HOL and offers a scalable template for teaching logic to heterogeneous student groups.

title: Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments?
summary: Learning from experience is essential for LLM agents to adapt to unfamiliar and dynmaic environments. Evaluating this ability is therefore important for understanding how effectively agents acquire and use new knowledge. Existing benchmarks have sought to evaluate this ability, but they primarily evaluate tasks whose rules are provided in the instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it difficult to distinguish learning from interactions from reasoning with existing knowledge. To address this, we introduce Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of newly designed text-based games, whose rules are novel or counterintuitive, requiring agents to acquire knowledge through interaction rather than rely solely on pretrained knowledge. These games provide reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, enabling controlled evaluation of learning across repeated attempts. We also vary game instances to test whether agents can apply what they have learned to new situations. Therefore, we evaluate how backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses affect agents' learning ability, revealing three findings: (1) Experience retention: Retaining complete records of actions and feedback can support more effective learning than summarizing these experiences into rules or strategies. (2) Human agent gap: Top-performing human players achieve higher peak scores than the evaluated agents. Human explore more varied strategies, and repeat actions less. (3) Harness matters: With the backbone fixed, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost. Together, these findings provide insights into how LLM agents learn from experience and suggest directions for future work to improve their learning ability. Project website: https://liushiliushi.github.io/learn2play-bench-website/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of novel text-based games designed to evaluate how well LLM agents learn from interaction rather than pretrained knowledge, and reports empirical findings about experience retention, human–agent gaps, and the importance of agent harness design.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM agents’ learning abilities mostly involve tasks whose rules are either explicitly given in instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it hard to isolate genuine learning from interaction. The authors want a benchmark where agents must truly acquire new, often counterintuitive rules through trial and error, with reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, to better understand and compare how different models and agent frameworks learn from experience.
AI.method: The authors design Learn2Play Bench, a suite of novel text-based games whose rules are unknown, non-obvious, or counterintuitive to existing LLMs. The games give structured, repeatable feedback and automatic scoring and can be instantiated in varied configurations to test transfer of learned strategies. They then evaluate multiple systems: different backbone models, self-evolving (self-improvement) methods, and different agent harnesses that manage memory and interaction. They compare approaches that store full interaction histories versus those that summarize experiences into rules/strategies, and they benchmark LLM agents against human players on game performance and behavioral patterns.
AI.result: Empirical experiments show: (1) Agents that retain complete records of past actions and feedback generally learn more effectively than those relying on condensed summaries of experience. (2) Skilled human players reach higher peak scores than all evaluated agents, exploring a broader set of strategies and repeating ineffective actions less. (3) The agent harness has a substantial impact: with the same backbone model, alternative harness designs can simultaneously improve performance and reduce estimated inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Learn2Play Bench offers a controlled, automatic, and interaction-focused way to evaluate how LLM agents learn from experience in novel environments. The results indicate that rich experience retention, better exploration strategies (as seen in humans), and careful harness design are all critical to improving agents’ learning capabilities. The benchmark and findings highlight key directions for future work on memory, exploration, and agent architecture to close the gap between current LLM agents and human learners.

title: Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN): Resource-Aware Hybrid Vision-Language Fusion via Trainable Entanglement
summary: Multimodal vision-language systems typically fuse image and text embeddings through classical operators such as concatenation, attention, bilinear pooling, or tensor interactions. We propose Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN), a hybrid quantum-classical framework that introduces parameterized entanglement as a structured inductive bias for multimodal fusion. Pretrained visual and textual features are projected into compact latent spaces, encoded as angle-parameterized quantum states, processed through intra-modal and paired cross-modal entangling circuits, and measured to produce fused representations for retrieval. Under matched parameter budgets and identical frozen CLIP backbones, QEMFN outperforms classical fusion baselines on COCO-5k and Flickr30k, including multilayer perceptron, tensor fusion, FiLM, cross-attention, compact transformer, and a dequantized paired-topology analogue. An ablation suite isolates the quantum module's contribution from the surrounding classical projections, and quantum-centric analyses report Meyer-Wallach entangling capability, expressibility, gradient variance against barren-plateau bounds, and entropy-performance correlation under controls for training progress alongside an intervention study on the entangling component. QEMFN is executed under shot-based estimation, a noise-modeled fake backend, and a real superconducting device with zero-noise extrapolation. This work does not claim quantum computational advantage; the contribution is the framework together with a controlled empirical and quantum-centric evaluation that positions trainable entanglement as an interpretable, hardware-executable fusion mechanism at scales accessible on contemporary devices.

AI.tldr: They introduce a quantum-inspired fusion module for vision–language models and show it outperforms several classical fusion baselines under controlled conditions, while carefully analyzing its quantum properties rather than claiming quantum speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal fusion in vision–language systems mostly relies on standard classical operators (concatenation, attention, tensor fusion, etc.) that are not inherently structured to capture complex cross-modal correlations, and there is growing interest in whether quantum mechanisms like entanglement can provide new inductive biases for such tasks. The paper aims to design and rigorously evaluate a practically executable quantum-classical fusion framework that uses entanglement in a controlled, interpretable way, without resorting to vague claims of quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors propose Quantum Entangled Multimodal Fusion Networks (QEMFN), where visual and textual embeddings (from frozen CLIP backbones) are first projected into low-dimensional latent spaces, then encoded as angle-parameterized quantum states. These states are processed by intra-modal and paired cross-modal entangling quantum circuits. The circuits are measured to yield fused representations used for retrieval. They compare QEMFN against multiple classical fusion baselines under matched parameter counts, perform ablations to separate the impact of the quantum module from classical projections, and conduct quantum-centric analyses of the circuits, including measuring entanglement (Meyer–Wallach), expressibility, gradient variance vs. barren plateau expectations, and entropy–performance correlations, plus an intervention on the entangling component. Implementation spans shot-based sampling, simulated noisy backends, and real superconducting hardware with zero-noise extrapolation.
AI.result: On COCO-5k and Flickr30k retrieval benchmarks, QEMFN consistently outperforms a range of classical fusion baselines (MLP, tensor fusion, FiLM, cross-attention, compact transformer, and a dequantized paired-topology counterpart) when controlling for parameter budget and backbone. Ablations confirm that gains stem from the quantum entangling module rather than just the surrounding classical parts. Quantum-analytic metrics show that the circuits achieve meaningful entanglement and expressibility, maintain trainable gradients without severe barren plateaus, and exhibit a measurable correlation between entropy-related properties and retrieval performance.
AI.conclusion: Trainable quantum entanglement can act as a useful inductive bias for multimodal fusion in vision–language models and is feasible to implement on current quantum hardware for small problem sizes. While the approach does not yet provide quantum computational advantage, QEMFN demonstrates that quantum circuits can serve as interpretable, hardware-executable fusion mechanisms that outperform several carefully controlled classical baselines and can be systematically probed with quantum-specific diagnostics. This establishes a concrete, empirically validated framework for quantum-enhanced multimodal representation learning and sets the stage for future scaling and exploration.

title: Confidence-Ordering Reversal under Contextual Priors in Neural Decoding
summary: Contextual priors improve neural-to-language decoding by reshaping candidate scores. However, confidence is read from the same reshaped scores, so the errors a prior leaves behind can become more confident with no change in accuracy to reveal it. We study how a prior shapes confidence in speech retrieval on MEG-MASC and MOUS using local decoding scores, a contextual prior combined by additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence. Among initially incorrect predictions, we find a confidence-ordering reversal: a larger margin makes a repair more likely when the correct candidate starts near the top of the local ranking, but less likely when it starts lower. On MEG-MASC, pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87, yet AUROC separating repairs from residual errors falls from 0.70 at initial ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50. Errors starting beyond rank 20, inside the reversed region, make up 46.6% of all post-fusion errors. We propose a score-level account: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, limiting its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. A causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted. Under a word-level LM prior, it keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence. Reading local and prior scores separately improves selective decoding: the decoder answers on 74.5% of windows instead of 56.7%, while 92% of output sets still contain the correct candidate. Confidence after contextual fusion should retain the local and contextual evidence behind each prediction, not just the fused scores. Project website: https://confidencereversal.github.io/; Code: https://github.com/AmadeusFake/NeuDecodingConfReversal

AI.tldr: The paper studies how contextual priors used in neural decoding can distort confidence estimates, revealing a confidence-ordering reversal phenomenon and proposing ways to better separate confidence and accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural-to-language decoding systems often use contextual priors (e.g., language models) via shallow fusion to improve accuracy. However, confidence estimates are usually derived from the same fused scores. This entanglement can make remaining errors look more confident without changing overall accuracy, which is problematic for applications that rely on calibrated confidence for decision-making and selective prediction. The authors want to understand and characterize how contextual priors shape confidence, and to identify failure modes and better ways to use confidence in neural decoding.
AI.method: They analyze speech retrieval performance on MEG-MASC and MOUS datasets using three components: local decoding scores, a contextual prior combined via additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as a confidence proxy. They examine how fusion affects confidence on initially incorrect predictions, stratified by the initial rank of the correct candidate in the local ranking. They quantify performance using AUROC for correctness and for distinguishing repaired errors from residual errors at different rank ranges. They propose a score-level explanation based on how much deficit the correct candidate must overcome during fusion to be repaired, versus how residual errors can amass large margins between two incorrect candidates. They also perform a causal intervention by varying the fusion weight to observe how the confidence-ordering reversal region shifts with depth. Finally, they demonstrate a selective decoding scheme that reads local and prior scores separately rather than relying only on fused scores.
AI.result: They discover a confidence-ordering reversal among initially incorrect predictions: a larger fused margin is associated with a higher probability of repair when the correct candidate initially ranks near the top, but with a lower probability of repair when it starts lower in the local ranking. On MEG-MASC, overall correctness AUROC remains high (0.87), yet AUROC for separating repairs from residual errors drops sharply from 0.70 for items with initial ranks 2–3 to 0.39 for ranks 21–50. Errors whose correct candidate starts beyond rank 20 account for 46.6% of post-fusion errors and fall into the reversed region. The proposed score-level account explains how corrected items are constrained to have smaller final margins, while residual errors can attain large margins between incorrect candidates. Manipulating the fusion weight moves the reversal region deeper in the ranking, confirming the explanation; under a word-level LM prior, the reversal continues to move even after accuracy gains plateau, indicating that tuning for accuracy alone does not ensure stable confidence behavior. Using separate access to local and prior scores in selective decoding allows the system to answer on 74.5% of windows instead of 56.7%, while still including the correct candidate in 92% of output sets.
AI.conclusion: Contextual priors via shallow fusion can substantially distort confidence signals, producing a confidence-ordering reversal where the most confident fused predictions are not the most likely to be correct among initially incorrect items, especially when the true candidate begins at lower ranks. Overall correctness metrics such as AUROC conceal this failure mode. Confidence estimation should not be based solely on fused scores; instead, systems should preserve and exploit both local and contextual score components to obtain better-calibrated confidence and more effective selective decoding. Fusion weights tuned for accuracy alone are insufficient to guarantee sound confidence behavior, so confidence considerations must be explicitly incorporated into decoding design.

title: OSFP4: Joint Optimization of Diagonal Smoothing and Block Scales for NVFP4 Quantization
summary: NVFP4 is an attractive datatype for large language model (LLM) inference, offering compact storage and native tensor-core acceleration. However, preserving accuracy using NVFP4 requires careful quantization. In this work we develop a novel quantization scheme called Optimized Smoothing and Scaling for NVFP4 (OSFP4). For each linear projection it uses a diagonal smoothing matrix whose entries are optimized to minimize the squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4, taking into account the rounding procedure that is used (either round-to-nearest, or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation). This requires performing joint optimization on the smoothing entries as well as the block scales, which is facilitated by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one. Experiments show that OSFP4 achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated competitors in the corresponding quantization settings, while retaining approximately 94-97\% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on the measured workloads. Our code is available in https://github.com/neriahbd/OSFP4

AI.tldr: Proposes OSFP4, a quantization scheme for NVFP4 that improves LLM inference accuracy while keeping near-vendor throughput.
AI.motivation: NVFP4 is a compact, tensor-core-accelerated datatype promising efficient LLM inference, but naive quantization to NVFP4 harms accuracy. There is a need for a principled quantization method that preserves accuracy without sacrificing the performance benefits of NVFP4.
AI.method: Introduce OSFP4, which assigns each linear projection a diagonal smoothing matrix whose entries are optimized to minimize squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4. The optimization jointly tunes smoothing entries and block scales, explicitly modeling the rounding procedure (round-to-nearest or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation). To make this tractable, the authors analyze a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer as a proxy for the deterministic NVFP4 quantizer.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that OSFP4 yields the best average accuracy among compared quantization schemes in the tested NVFP4 settings, while maintaining roughly 94–97% of the vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on benchmark workloads.
AI.conclusion: OSFP4 is an effective quantization strategy for NVFP4 that significantly improves accuracy for LLM inference with minimal throughput loss, making NVFP4 more practical for high-performance deployment. Open-source code is provided for reproducibility and adoption.

title: Sensor-Language-Action Models
summary: Sensors are useful not only for understanding the world but also for deciding what to do next. Existing sensor models however largely stop at perception: they recognize states or predict outcomes, leaving actions modeled separately through task-specific and often closed label spaces. We introduce Sensor-Language-Action (SLA) modeling, a framework that connects multimodal sensor observations, natural language, and actions within a unified model. SLA uses language as a semantic interface between sensing and acting, allowing heterogeneous actions to be represented, predicted, and explained while remaining grounded in the underlying sensor evidence. We build a large-scale SLA benchmark consisting of datasets that span more than 116,000 individuals, 79 sensor modalities, and 60 action groups, together with a multi-faceted captioning pipeline that aligns user context, sensor dynamics, and action evidence. Building on this framework, we present OpenSLA, a unified SLA model for hierarchical action prediction, state understanding, and action explanation. Extensive experiments on real-world tasks in clinical prediction, operating rooms, and metabolic health verify its superior performance over the state-of-the-art. OpenSLA also demonstrates intriguing capabilities including language-guided evidence grounding and zero-shot generalization to unseen actions and cohorts.

AI.tldr: They propose a unified model and benchmark that link multimodal sensor data, natural language, and actions, enabling better prediction and explanation of actions from sensor evidence.
AI.motivation: Current sensor models mostly focus on perception—recognizing states or predicting outcomes—while actions are modeled separately with closed, task-specific label spaces. This separation limits generalization, interpretability, and the ability to flexibly handle heterogeneous actions informed by sensor data. The authors want a framework where sensors, language, and actions are jointly modeled so actions can be predicted and explained in a more general, open-ended way.
AI.method: They define Sensor-Language-Action (SLA) modeling, which uses natural language as a semantic interface between sensor observations and actions. They construct a large-scale SLA benchmark that brings together datasets covering over 116,000 individuals, 79 sensor modalities, and 60 action groups, and design a captioning pipeline to align user context, sensor dynamics, and action evidence in language form. On top of this, they develop OpenSLA, a unified model capable of hierarchical action prediction, state understanding, and action explanation, integrating multimodal sensor inputs with language representations of states and actions.
AI.result: On real-world tasks in clinical prediction, operating rooms, and metabolic health, OpenSLA outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. It also shows additional abilities such as grounding language descriptions in sensor evidence and performing zero-shot generalization to previously unseen actions and populations.
AI.conclusion: A unified Sensor-Language-Action framework that leverages language as the bridge between sensing and acting yields a powerful and general model for predicting and explaining actions from multimodal sensor data. The extensive benchmark and the OpenSLA model demonstrate improved performance, interpretability, and generalization, suggesting that SLA modeling is a promising direction for real-world sensor-based decision-making systems.

title: LeanPlan: Optimal Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics and Admissibility Proofs
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) can generate heuristic functions that guide search to achieve state-of-the-art performance in satisficing planning, where any plan is acceptable. However, these heuristics are not guaranteed to be admissible and can lead to suboptimal plans. We introduce LeanPlan, the first planning system that finds optimal plans with LLM-generated heuristics whose admissibility is machine-checked. Given a domain description and training tasks, an agentic loop uses planner feedback to iteratively improve a reusable domain-specific heuristic, its admissibility proof and the required domain assumptions. LeanPlan implements the heuristic, its proof and an efficient planner with machine-checked grounding and search in Lean 4. We evaluate LeanPlan on ten domains from the International Planning Competition and three new domains, using test tasks with up to 57 times as many objects as the training tasks. With GPT-5.6 Sol in the agentic loop, we successfully generate heuristics and admissibility proofs for all these domains. With the resulting heuristics, LeanPlan usually expands fewer states than the state-of-the-art Scorpion planner and solves more tasks overall.

AI.tldr: LeanPlan is a planning system that uses LLM-generated heuristics whose admissibility is formally verified to guarantee optimal plans.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-generated heuristics for planning achieve strong performance in satisficing planning but lack admissibility guarantees, so they can yield suboptimal plans when optimality is required. There is a need for a method that combines the empirical strength of LLM-designed heuristics with formal guarantees of optimality.
AI.method: LeanPlan uses an agentic loop with an LLM that, given a planning domain description and training tasks, iteratively proposes a reusable, domain-specific heuristic, a corresponding admissibility proof, and necessary domain assumptions. These are refined based on feedback from a planner. The final heuristic, proof, and an optimal planner with machine-checked grounding and search are implemented in the Lean 4 theorem prover, which mechanically checks admissibility and correctness.
AI.result: On ten International Planning Competition domains and three newly introduced domains, with test tasks that scale up to 57x more objects than training tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol successfully generates both heuristics and admissibility proofs for all domains. Using these heuristics, LeanPlan typically expands fewer states than the state-of-the-art optimal planner Scorpion and solves more tasks overall.
AI.conclusion: Formally verified LLM-generated heuristics are feasible and effective: LeanPlan can automatically synthesize admissible, domain-specific heuristics with machine-checked proofs, enabling optimal planning that is both efficient and more scalable than a leading existing planner on the tested domains.

title: MASC: A Multi-Agent Self-Calibration Framework with Latent Construct Alignment for Consistent Client Role-Playing in Psychological Counseling
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate clients for counselor training and psychological counseling research, but reliable simulation requires clients to remain psychologically coherent across extended interactions. Existing role-playing methods largely rely on static profile prompts and may exhibit persona drift, unrealistic cooperativeness, or inconsistent psychological states, communicative actions, and emotions. Existing evaluations also lack a unified testbed for both stable client characteristics and evolving psychological dynamics. We propose MASC, a Multi-Agent Self-Calibration framework with latent construct alignment for consistent client role-playing in psychological counseling. MASC combines construct-guided generation, collaborative refinement, consistency verification, and memory-based revision in a closed calibration loop that detects and corrects inconsistencies as dialogue unfolds. We further introduce CRPC-Bench, a benchmark covering session-level profile information and Big-Five personality traits, as well as turn-level psychological state, communicative action, and emotion expression. CRPC-Bench contains 38 motivational interviewing client profiles augmented with personality and emotion annotations. Experiments show that MASC outperforms existing methods across profile, personality, receptivity, and turn-level consistency, with the heterogeneous configuration achieving the strongest overall performance. MASC and CRPC-Bench provide a unified foundation for developing and evaluating psychologically coherent client simulations for AI-assisted counseling research and training.

AI.tldr: They propose a framework (MASC) and a benchmark (CRPC-Bench) to make and test psychologically coherent LLM-based client simulations for counseling dialogues.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based client simulators for counseling suffer from persona drift, overly cooperative behavior, and inconsistencies in psychological states, actions, and emotions. Moreover, there is no unified evaluation setup that jointly assesses stable traits (profile, personality) and evolving dynamics (momentary state, communicative moves, emotions). This hinders reliable use of LLMs in counselor training and psychological counseling research.
AI.method: They introduce MASC, a Multi-Agent Self-Calibration framework. It runs LLM agents in a closed calibration loop that (1) generates client responses guided by latent psychological constructs, (2) has agents collaboratively refine those responses, (3) verifies consistency against profile, personality, and dynamic states, and (4) uses memory-based revision to correct detected inconsistencies as the dialogue progresses. They also build CRPC-Bench, a benchmark with 38 motivational interviewing client profiles annotated with Big-Five traits, session-level info, and turn-level labels for psychological state, communicative action, and emotion expression to evaluate consistency across multiple dimensions.
AI.result: In experiments comparing different role-playing strategies, MASC achieves better consistency than baselines on client profile fidelity, Big-Five personality adherence, receptivity to counseling, and turn-level coherence of state, action, and emotion. Among MASC variants, a heterogeneous multi-agent configuration yields the best overall performance.
AI.conclusion: MASC enables more stable and psychologically coherent LLM client simulations over extended counseling dialogues, and CRPC-Bench offers a standardized way to evaluate such simulators across both stable traits and evolving dynamics. Together, they provide a foundational toolkit for AI-assisted counseling research and counselor training that requires realistic, consistent virtual clients.

title: zkLLMPoT: Efficient Zero Knowledge Proof of Training for Large Language Models
