summary: Auditing the claimed outcomes of large language model (LLM) training is challenging when model weights and training data are private, while cryptographically proving the full training process is prohibitively expensive at Transformer scale. We present zkLLMPoT, a zero-knowledge framework that certifies auditor-defined properties of a trained checkpoint through forward evaluation rather than verification of its optimization trajectory. zkLLMPoT includes 2 phases: 1) The trainer fixes the architecture and the model weights are committed. Then the auditor selects challenge sequences, preventing the trainer from modifying the checkpoint in response to the audit data. 2) Then the trainer proves the objective value attained by the committed model on those sequences. This formulation makes the certification cost independent of the number of training iterations, without revealing model weights or requiring access to private training data. We build on sumcheck- and lookup-based arguments to certify Transformer computations, while supporting next-token loss and task-specific audit objectives. Across four model families, operator-level benchmarks yield proving times of 41-59 seconds for 1.1-1.5B-parameter models and 131 seconds at 13B for the covered operators, with verification below half a second at a sequence length of 512.

AI.tldr: Proposes zkLLMPoT, a zero-knowledge framework to certify properties of trained LLM checkpoints via forward evaluation instead of proving the full training process.
AI.motivation: Auditing claimed outcomes of LLM training is difficult when weights and data are private, and fully cryptographic proofs of the entire training trajectory are computationally infeasible at Transformer scale. There is a need for a practical way for auditors to verify properties of trained models without accessing proprietary weights or training data, and without incurring costs that scale with the number of training iterations.
AI.method: Introduce zkLLMPoT, a two-phase zero-knowledge protocol: (1) the trainer fixes the model architecture and commits to the model weights; the auditor then chooses challenge input sequences, which prevents the trainer from adapting the model to the audit. (2) The trainer proves in zero-knowledge the objective values (e.g., next-token loss or task-specific metrics) that the committed model achieves on these sequences. The system uses sumcheck- and lookup-based cryptographic arguments tailored to certify Transformer forward computations efficiently.
AI.result: They implement operator-level benchmarks across four LLM families. For models with 1.1–1.5B parameters, proving times are 41–59 seconds for the covered operators, and 131 seconds for a 13B-parameter model, with verification taking under 0.5 seconds at sequence length 512. These timings demonstrate practicality of their approach for non-trivial model sizes, with verification remaining very fast.
AI.conclusion: Forward-evaluation-based zero-knowledge proofs can certify auditor-defined properties of large Transformer models without revealing model weights or relying on access to private training data, and with costs that do not grow with the length of the training process. zkLLMPoT shows that sumcheck- and lookup-based arguments can make such certification practical for billion-parameter LLMs, enabling more trustworthy auditing of proprietary models.

title: The Standardization Trap: Certifying Joint Label Processing in Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Linear regression and kernel smoothing offer tractable explanations of in-context learning: in both, the features determine the weight assigned to each context label. However, whether this fixed-weight account describes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) remains unclear. Testing this account using derivatives runs into a standardization trap: public TFM packages standardize the labels before the model sees them, yet ordinary derivatives also reflect behavior outside the set of standardized labels, making a model appear nonlinear even when every prediction it makes agrees with a fixed-weight map. We propose two certificates that depend only on predictions at standardized labels and can reject two distinct explanations: fixed-weight prediction and sums of independent nonlinear label transformations. Across the five public TFMs that we evaluate, our certificates show that changing one context label alters how other labels influence the prediction, a behavior we call joint processing. We further find that joint processing emerges with training and that attention scores carry most of the measured interaction. Together, these findings motivate TFM explanations that account for how context labels change the influence of individual examples.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether tabular foundation models behave like simple fixed-weight regressors in in-context learning and shows they do not.
AI.motivation: Existing explanations of in-context learning in terms of linear regression or kernel smoothing assume that each context label affects predictions through fixed weights determined only by features, but it is unclear if this matches the behavior of practical tabular foundation models whose implementations standardize labels internally.
AI.method: The authors identify a “standardization trap” whereby derivatives misleadingly suggest nonlinearity in models that only see standardized labels. They design two prediction-based certificates that only use model outputs on standardized labels to test and potentially falsify two hypotheses: (1) predictions come from a fixed-weight map from labels to outputs; and (2) predictions are sums of independent nonlinear transformations of each label. They apply these certificates to five public tabular foundation models and analyze the role of attention scores.
AI.result: Across all evaluated TFMs, the certificates reject both fixed-weight prediction and independent nonlinear label transformation explanations. Empirically, changing one context label modifies how other labels influence the prediction, a phenomenon the authors call joint processing, and this joint processing grows during training. Attention mechanisms account for most of the measured interaction effects.
AI.conclusion: Tabular foundation models for in-context learning cannot be adequately described by fixed-weight or independent-label nonlinear explanations. Instead, they exhibit joint processing, where context labels interact to shape each other’s influence on predictions, with attention playing a central role. This calls for new theoretical accounts of in-context learning in TFMs that explicitly model these label interactions.

title: SCOPE: Certified Theorem Proving with a Language Model as the Policy Planner
summary: In proof assistants such as Lean, a generated proof must pass machine compilation checks, so evaluation needs no human scoring. Direct generation fails on multi-step numeric propositions: a proof is valid only if every content integer is correct, so the pass rate is bounded by the k-th power of the per-integer accuracy. Controlled corruption across 2,617 reference proofs confirms this power law. SCOPE (State-Conditioned Operator Planning and Execution) enforces the natural division of labor: the model plans over an operator vocabulary, a symbolic engine executes the numerics, and a compiler renders the proof. On a 218-problem suite it certifies 191/218 (87.6%) with a 135M backbone; the 7B DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL certifies 18/218 at 27.5 times the tokens and 37.5 times the wall-clock, and DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B certifies zero on a bidirectional dual suite. Multi-step thinking costs 6.12 discrete decision actions per problem and produces no natural-language thinking text. Replacing the lagged engine state in the decision frame with the current one lifts the pass rate from 117/218 to 191/218, while up-weighting the chain-end loss hurts. On the public Lean-Workbook library, 2,132 of 3,536 gradeable admissible problems certify (60.29%) with zero regression on the main suite. All readings come from a version-frozen review with independent rechecks and reverse verification. Restricting free generation and keeping decision-time information visible is a more direct route than enlarging the model.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a combinatorial failure mode of direct proof generation in Lean for multi-step numeric problems and proposes SCOPE, a planning-plus-symbolic-execution framework that sharply improves proof certification rates without scaling model size.
AI.motivation: Directly generating full formal proofs in systems like Lean struggles especially on multi-step numeric propositions because every numeric literal must be correct; a single mistake invalidates the whole proof. This leads to a power-law decay in success as the number of numeric steps grows, making naive model scaling or generic chain-of-thought insufficient. The authors aim to understand and quantify this failure mode and to design an architecture that separates symbolic planning from numeric execution so that proofs can be reliably certified while keeping models small and inference efficient.
AI.method: The authors first analyze the combinatorial reliability issue by controlled corruption of 2,617 reference Lean proofs, empirically confirming that proof pass rate follows a k-th power law in per-integer accuracy. They then introduce SCOPE (State-Conditioned Operator Planning and Execution), in which a language model plans over a discrete vocabulary of proof operators conditioned on the proof state, a separate symbolic engine executes the numeric and logical operations, and a compiler assembles the final Lean proof. They perform ablations on aspects such as the engine state used in the decision frame and loss weighting on chain-end decisions. SCOPE is evaluated on a 218-problem suite, on a bidirectional dual suite, and on the Lean-Workbook library, with careful version-freezing, independent rechecks, and reverse verification to ensure robustness of reported results.
AI.result: With a 135M-parameter backbone, SCOPE certifies 191 out of 218 problems (87.6%) on the main suite, outperforming much larger baselines: DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL-7B certifies only 18/218 while using 27.5× more tokens and 37.5× more wall-clock time, and DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B certifies none on a harder bidirectional dual suite. SCOPE’s multi-step reasoning uses about 6.12 discrete decision actions per problem and does not emit natural-language chain-of-thought. An architectural change—feeding the current instead of lagged engine state into the decision frames—improves certification from 117/218 to 191/218, whereas emphasizing chain-end loss degrades performance. On the broader Lean-Workbook benchmark, SCOPE certifies 2,132 of 3,536 gradeable admissible problems (60.29%) without regressing on main-suite performance.
AI.conclusion: The work concludes that the reliability barrier for multi-step numeric formal proofs stems from a fundamental combinatorial effect: error probability compounds over many required-correct integers. This makes unconstrained free generation increasingly brittle as problem complexity grows. SCOPE shows that constraining generation to operator-level planning, delegating numerics to a symbolic engine, and preserving rich decision-time state can dramatically improve proof certification without enlarging the underlying model. The findings suggest that architectural and inference-time control—rather than ever-larger models or heavier chain-of-thought generation—offer a more direct and efficient route to scalable formal reasoning in proof assistants like Lean.

title: MedZERO: Self-Evolving Agents for Open-Ended Medical Reasoning Through Controlled Knowledge Accumulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in medical question answering and clinical reasoning, yet their improvement remains constrained by static parametric knowledge and costly expert supervision. Self-evolving agents offer a promising alternative by enabling models to improve through iterative task generation and problem-solving. However, most existing self-evolving methods are designed for easily verifiable domains such as mathematics and coding, where solutions can be checked by exact answers or executable programs. Medical reasoning is fundamentally different: it is open-ended, knowledge-intensive, and often only partially verifiable. We present MedZERO, a self-evolving framework for open-ended medical reasoning. MedZERO couples an Examiner that generates frontier medical question-option pairs with a Reasoner that solves them through evidence-grounded multi-turn reasoning with external knowledge tools. To support reliable, continual improvement, MedZERO adopts controlled knowledge accumulation, which maintains temporary exploratory knowledge and curated persistent knowledge in reasoning. We evaluate MedZERO on five public medical reasoning benchmarks using 4B- and 8B-scale base models under open-ended evaluation. Across all settings, MedZERO consistently outperforms the underlying base models and prior self-evolving baselines, achieving up to 13.7 average accuracy-point gains over the next-best self-evolving baseline.

AI.tldr: MedZERO is a self-evolving framework that improves medical reasoning of LLMs by iteratively generating medical questions and solving them with evidence-grounded reasoning, outperforming base models and prior self-evolving methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs for medical QA and clinical reasoning are limited by fixed parametric knowledge and the high cost of expert-labelled supervision. While self-evolving agents can improve models without extensive human labels, current approaches mostly work in domains with easily verifiable answers (math, coding) and are not suited for open-ended, partially verifiable medical reasoning. There is a need for a self-improving framework tailored to the complexity and verification challenges of medical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose MedZERO, a self-evolving framework composed of two main components: (1) an Examiner that automatically generates frontier medical question-option pairs, expanding the task space; and (2) a Reasoner that answers these questions using multi-turn, evidence-grounded reasoning with external knowledge tools (e.g., knowledge bases or retrieval systems). MedZERO introduces controlled knowledge accumulation, separating temporary exploratory knowledge from curated persistent knowledge, so that the system can learn from successful reasoning patterns and trustworthy information while avoiding uncontrolled drift from unreliable or exploratory content.
AI.result: MedZERO is evaluated on five public medical reasoning benchmarks using 4B and 8B base models under open-ended evaluation protocols. In all tested settings, MedZERO improves performance over the underlying base models and previous self-evolving methods, with reported gains up to 13.7 average accuracy points over the strongest prior self-evolving baseline.
AI.conclusion: A tailored self-evolving framework can effectively enhance open-ended medical reasoning in LLMs without relying solely on expensive expert supervision. By combining automatic frontier-question generation, evidence-grounded multi-turn reasoning, and controlled knowledge accumulation, MedZERO enables reliable, continual performance gains in medical reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating that self-evolution is feasible even in partially verifiable, knowledge-intensive domains.

title: An AI-Assisted Formalization of the Poincaré Conjecture
summary: We present an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization of the Poincaré conjecture. The project began with limited reusable formal infrastructure for the geometric analysis behind the proof. To organize this work, we combined a proof blueprint prepared by mathematicians with explicit milestone statements. These milestones enabled parallel agent work and gave mathematicians clear points to locate blockers and provide effective mathematical guidance. Our analysis identifies the human interventions and organizational choices behind this workflow. The project provides a starting point toward reusable infrastructure for future formalization projects; such infrastructure, once developed, could eventually reduce the cost of verifying mathematical results in geometric analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper reports an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization project of the Poincaré conjecture, focusing on how structured milestones and human-AI collaboration enabled progress and created reusable infrastructure for future geometric analysis formalizations.
AI.motivation: Formalizing deep mathematical results like the Poincaré conjecture in proof assistants is extremely costly, especially in areas like geometric analysis where reusable formal libraries are scarce. The authors want to understand and improve the human and organizational workflow needed to carry out such large formalization projects, with the goal of making future verifications cheaper and more scalable.
AI.method: They use a structured workflow that combines a detailed, human-written proof blueprint with a system of explicit milestone statements. These milestones decompose the overall proof into manageable units that can be tackled in parallel by multiple agents (human mathematicians and AI tools), while also serving as diagnostic points where mathematicians can detect blockers and inject targeted guidance or new theory into the formalization effort. They then analyze the pattern of human interventions and organizational decisions that shaped this process.
AI.result: They obtained a Lean 4 formalization of the Poincaré conjecture supported by newly built infrastructure in geometric analysis. The milestone-based organization allowed parallel progress by multiple agents and made it easier to identify and resolve bottlenecks. Their analysis distills where human expertise was crucial and how organizational choices impacted efficiency and success.
AI.conclusion: The project demonstrates that a milestone-driven, AI-assisted workflow can make it feasible to formalize very deep theorems in geometric analysis even when initial library support is limited. The resulting infrastructure forms a base for more reusable libraries, and with further development such methods could substantially reduce the cost of verifying complex mathematical results in this and related fields.

title: MoF: Preference-Aware Mixture Modeling for Black-Box LLM Personalization
summary: Proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks, yet aligning their outputs with diverse user preferences remains challenging. Existing personalization approaches for black-box LLMs often rely on user-specific scoring heads, causing the number of personalized parameters to grow linearly with the number of users and requiring additional adaptation for unseen users. To address these limitations, we propose Mixture-of-Facets (MoF), a scalable personalization framework for black-box LLMs that models user preferences as compositions of shared latent preference facets rather than dedicated user-specific parameters. MoF performs personalization through history-conditioned routing over shared facet heads, enabling personalization for users unseen during training without additional parameter updates. Across diverse personalization tasks, MoF delivers stronger personalization performance while maintaining a more scalable and parameter-efficient design than prior approaches. Additional analysis indicates strong generalization to unseen users.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mixture-of-Facets (MoF), a scalable and parameter-efficient framework to personalize black-box large language models by modeling user preferences as combinations of shared latent facets rather than user-specific parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing personalization methods for proprietary, black-box LLMs typically use user-specific scoring heads, which scale linearly with the number of users and cannot directly handle unseen users without extra adaptation. There is a need for a more scalable, parameter-efficient approach that generalizes to new users while still capturing diverse user preferences.
AI.method: The authors propose Mixture-of-Facets (MoF), which represents user preferences as compositions over a set of shared latent preference facets. Instead of per-user heads, MoF uses shared facet heads and performs history-conditioned routing: a routing mechanism looks at a user’s interaction history and determines how to mix or weight these facets to generate personalized outputs. This design allows reusing the same facet heads across many users, including those not present during training, without further parameter updates.
AI.result: On multiple and diverse personalization tasks, MoF outperforms previous black-box LLM personalization approaches in personalization quality, while using fewer additional parameters and exhibiting better scalability in the number of users. Empirical analysis further shows that MoF generalizes well to users that were unseen during training.
AI.conclusion: Modeling user preferences as mixtures of shared latent facets and using history-conditioned routing is an effective and scalable way to personalize black-box LLMs. Mixture-of-Facets achieves stronger personalization, better parameter efficiency, and good generalization to unseen users compared to prior user-specific head approaches.

title: Explainable Failure Prediction and Prevention in Maritime
summary: Maritime systems operate in highly dynamic environments where unexpected equipment failures can compromise safety, reliability, and operational efficiency. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, digital twins, and predictive maintenance enable proactive failure prediction and prevention. However, ensuring trustworthy and explainable decision-making remains a major challenge in safety-critical maritime applications. This chapter reviews key AI technologies required for explainable failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems and presents a conceptual architecture capable of supporting autonomous or human-in-the-loop corrective actions. This architecture integrates data acquisition, time-series forecasting, anomaly detection, risk assessment, decision-making, and explainable AI into a closed-loop framework. With reference to the architectural components, a review and discussion of relevant maritime studies is performed, outlining their methods, advantages, and limitations. Furthermore, it highlights current challenges, including uncertainty and robustness, model generalization, explainability, limited availability of maritime datasets, and operational deployment, and identifies future research directions toward trustworthy AI-assisted maritime decision-making.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews AI technologies and proposes an architecture for explainable, trustworthy failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems, discussing current methods, gaps, and future research needs.
AI.motivation: Maritime systems operate in dynamic, safety-critical environments where unexpected equipment failures threaten safety, reliability, and efficiency. While AI, machine learning, digital twins, and predictive maintenance offer proactive failure prediction capabilities, there is a critical need to ensure that such AI-based decisions are trustworthy and explainable to be usable in real-world maritime operations.
AI.method: The chapter conducts a structured review of AI technologies relevant to maritime failure prediction and prevention, focusing on explainability and trustworthiness. It proposes a conceptual closed-loop architecture that integrates data acquisition, time-series forecasting, anomaly detection, risk assessment, decision-making, and explainable AI. Using these architectural components as a lens, it surveys and compares existing maritime studies, describing their methods, strengths, and limitations.
AI.result: The work yields: (1) a conceptual architecture for explainable, AI-driven failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems; (2) a synthesized overview of existing maritime applications mapped to this architecture; and (3) a critical analysis of their advantages and shortcomings in terms of uncertainty handling, robustness, generalization, explainability, data availability, and deployability.
AI.conclusion: The chapter concludes that although AI shows strong potential for predictive maintenance and failure prevention in maritime systems, current solutions face significant challenges related to uncertainty quantification, robustness, generalization across vessels and conditions, explainability, data scarcity, and real-world deployment. It calls for focused research on trustworthy and explainable AI methods, better datasets, and practical integration of autonomous and human-in-the-loop decision-making to enable safe and reliable AI-assisted maritime operations.

title: Transect: Retaining Observability for Long-Horizon LLM Agent Evaluations
summary: Frontier AI evaluations increasingly use open-ended, agentic, long-horizon tasks whose transcripts can span hundreds of pages of outputs and actions from complex multi-agent networks. The observability envelop-the range of what evaluators can reliably infer about an agent's behaviours-is therefore narrowing. Language model assistants can help classify and interpret agent behaviour but also afford human evaluators significant analytical degrees of freedom, threatening the reproducibility and auditability of language-model-based transcript analysis. Transect is an open source package built on Inspect Scout to help evaluators understand how a long agent run unfolded, identify behaviour worth investigating, and check interpretations against the transcript. Users specify task context and behavioural vocabulary in a reusable evaluation-family configuration, with judge models and analysis settings supplied separately. Transect's navigable reports align recorded events, token use, sub-agent activity, and model-generated behavioural labels on a common turn-based timeline. Reviewers can quickly grasp a run's narrative, trace any label or event to its source turns, and export the underlying data tables for cross-run analysis. We demonstrate the workflow on an AI R&D evaluation that generated almost 13 million tokens, dividing the agents' work into behavioural phases aligned with research-skill classifications, sub-agent delegations and interactions, and token use. The combined view shows a focus on operational work and manuscript production, with little evidence of a sustained hypothesis generation stage-arguably a necessary component for high-quality scientific outputs. Transect's flexible, customisable transcript-analysis pipeline will enable evaluators to keep pace with longer, more complex, more frequent AI evaluations while supporting scientific rigour, transparency, and reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Transect is an open-source tool for systematically analyzing long, complex AI agent transcripts to improve transparency and reproducibility in evaluations.
AI.motivation: As frontier AI evaluations rely on long, open-ended agentic tasks, transcripts become massive and complex, making it hard for human evaluators to reliably understand behavior. Language models can help interpret these logs but introduce subjective analytical choices that threaten reproducibility and auditability. There is a need for structured, transparent, and reusable ways to analyze and compare such agent runs.
AI.method: The authors build Transect, an open-source package on top of Inspect Scout. Evaluators define an “evaluation-family” configuration that captures task context and a reusable behavioral vocabulary, while judge models and analysis settings are plugged in separately. Transect produces navigable reports that align multiple streams of information—events, token usage, sub-agent activity, and model-generated behavioral labels—onto a unified, turn-based timeline. It supports inspection of narrative flow, tracing labels to specific turns, and exporting data tables for quantitative, cross-run analysis.
AI.result: Using an AI R&D evaluation run with ~13 million tokens, Transect partitions the agents’ work into behavior phases keyed to research-skill categories, sub-agent interactions, and token expenditure. The analysis reveals that the agents concentrated on operational tasks and manuscript drafting, with minimal evidence of a persistent hypothesis-generation phase, suggesting a qualitative gap in research-like reasoning despite large-scale activity.
AI.conclusion: Transect offers a flexible, configurable pipeline for transcript analysis that scales to long, complex, multi-agent evaluations. By standardizing how behaviors are labeled, visualized, and traced back to source turns, it helps evaluators keep up with increasingly demanding AI evaluations while enhancing scientific rigor, transparency, and reproducibility in behavior assessments.

title: EMHO: EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization via Experience Traces
summary: Improving embodied agents often focuses on optimizing the underlying model through training, while the surrounding agent harness that controls planning, context, and tool use is typically engineered. We ask whether this harness can instead improve itself directly from experience traces under sparse environmental feedback. We propose EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization (EMHO), a self-evolving framework that keeps the embodied model frozen and iteratively revises its harness by analyzing execution trajectories and prior harness history. EMHO optimizes beyond skills or recovery prompts, modifying how the agent monitors progress, uses vision tools, grounds observations, and responds to failures. To support multiple subtasks with a single harness, we introduce EMHO-Merge, which addresses trade-offs in jointly optimizing a single shared harness across subtasks by using episode-level gains and losses to guide evidence-supported refinement of when and how revised behaviors are applied. We evaluate EMHO on EmbodiedBench across navigation and manipulation tasks, and EMHO consistently improves task success for both Qwen 9B and 27B models. Qualitative analysis shows that EMHO goes beyond recovering from failures and unproductive actions to reshape how the embodied agent interprets and interacts with its environment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EMHO, a framework that lets an embodied agent’s control harness (planning, monitoring, tool use logic) automatically improve itself from past execution traces, without retraining the underlying model, leading to consistent performance gains across navigation and manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Most work on embodied agents improves performance by training or scaling the underlying model, while the logic around it—the harness that plans, manages tools, monitors progress, and handles failures—is manually engineered and static. This harness is crucial to real-world performance but expensive to design and adapt, especially under sparse feedback and across varied subtasks. The authors are motivated to find a way for the harness itself to learn and evolve from experience, reusing existing frozen models yet still improving task success and general behavior across multiple embodied tasks.
AI.method: They propose EMbodied Agent Harness Optimization (EMHO), which keeps the base embodied model fixed and instead iteratively revises the surrounding harness based on execution trajectories and the history of prior harness versions. EMHO analyzes where and why episodes succeed or fail, then edits harness behaviors beyond just adding recovery prompts—for example, changing how the agent monitors task progress, invokes vision tools, grounds observations, and reacts to failure states. To support multiple subtasks with a single shared harness, they introduce EMHO-Merge, which uses episode-level performance gains and losses to reason about trade-offs between subtasks and to selectively merge or gate revised behaviors so that improvements for one subtask do not unduly harm others.
AI.result: On the EmbodiedBench benchmark covering navigation and manipulation tasks, EMHO consistently improves task success rates when wrapped around frozen Qwen 9B and 27B models. The method yields measurable quantitative gains and, via qualitative analysis, shows richer, more robust behaviors in how agents interpret sensory input, structure their plans, and recover from unproductive action sequences.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that significant improvements to embodied agents can come from self-evolving the control harness rather than retraining the underlying model. EMHO demonstrates that harnesses can be autonomously refined using sparse environmental feedback and trajectory analysis, leading to better monitoring, tool use, grounding, and failure handling. EMHO-Merge further shows that a single, adaptively optimized harness can successfully support multiple subtasks by carefully managing cross-task trade-offs. Overall, harness-level self-optimization is a promising, model-agnostic path to more capable and adaptive embodied agents.

title: AssemState: Manual and Physical-State-Guided Reasoning for Zero-shot Furniture Assembly
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding, but precise 3D spatial reasoning integrated with physical environment remains difficult. Furniture assembly requires not only recovering step-level operations from diagrammatic manuals, but also translating semantic attachment relations into 6D pose updates that enable parts to physically interact with the environment and previously assembled components. To study this problem, we propose AssemState, a zero-shot framework for manual and physical-state-guided furniture assembly. It firstly employs anchor-guided boundary assembly states to decompose manual pages into single-part operations and recover an assembly-tree. Then, it uses iterative after-state feedback refinement to guide successive (SE(3)) updates and corrections, and validates their physical plausibility through simulation-based release tests. Experiments show that compared with the strongest prior baseline, AssemState improves F1 from 38.58\% to 62.80\% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24\% to 53.92\% for assembly-tree recovery. On 243 independently evaluated part-level operations, our proposed iterative refinement improves judge-accepted operations from 0 to 5.3\% and reduces mean Chamfer distance from 5.4111 to 1.7744. However, visually plausible candidate poses may still suffer from collision, floating, mirror-orientation errors, incomplete seating, and wrong-side attachment. These results show that AssemState improves operation-structure recovery and selected local pose metrics, while MLLMs remain limited for spatial relationship reasoning.

AI.tldr: AssemState is a zero-shot framework that uses manuals and physical-state feedback to infer both the correct assembly sequence and 3D poses for furniture parts, significantly improving assembly structure recovery and some pose metrics, but still revealing core limits of current MLLMs in fine-grained spatial reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal large language models can interpret images and text but struggle with precise 3D spatial reasoning, especially when physical feasibility matters. Furniture assembly from manuals is a challenging benchmark because it requires understanding diagrams, inferring an ordered sequence of operations, and computing physically valid 6D poses for parts so they interact correctly with other components and the environment. Existing methods underperform in recovering accurate assembly trees and reliable part poses, indicating a gap between high-level visual understanding and grounded physical reasoning that this work aims to address.
AI.method: The authors propose AssemState, a zero-shot framework guided by both the assembly manual and physical state. First, they introduce anchor-guided boundary assembly states to segment manual pages into single-part operations and reconstruct an assembly tree that captures operation order and part relationships. Second, they perform iterative after-state feedback refinement, where predicted SE(3) pose updates for parts are repeatedly corrected based on feedback from simulated physical interactions and release tests that check for physical plausibility. This loop refines part poses and eliminates obviously invalid configurations while remaining zero-shot with respect to specific furniture types.
AI.result: On assembly-tree recovery, AssemState outperforms the strongest prior baseline by a large margin, improving F1 from 38.58% to 62.80% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24% to 53.92%. On 243 separately evaluated part-level assembly operations, the iterative refinement procedure increases the proportion of operations accepted by human judges from 0% to 5.3% and reduces the mean Chamfer distance between predicted and ground-truth configurations from 5.4111 to 1.7744. Despite these gains, qualitative analysis shows that candidate poses can still exhibit serious physical errors such as collisions, floating parts, mirrored orientations, incomplete seating, and incorrect attachment sides.
AI.conclusion: AssemState substantially advances automatic recovery of assembly structures and improves local 3D pose predictions for furniture assembly by integrating manual understanding with simulation-based physical feedback. Nonetheless, persistent issues in fine-grained spatial plausibility demonstrate that current MLLMs, even with such frameworks, are still limited in robust 3D spatial relationship reasoning and physically grounded manipulation planning.

title: Cylindrical Geodesic Flow Matching for Quasiperiodic Physiological Signal Transformation
summary: Paired translation between quasiperiodic physiological waveforms (i.e., recovering a target oscillatory signal from the source) is central to the interpretation of cardiovascular signals derived from wearables placed at different body locations. This source-to-target mapping in these problems carries inherent geometric structure: the phase wraps around the cycle and must be treated as a circular variable, the amplitude remains strictly positive, and the beat-to-beat alignment can drift unpredictably across cycles and subjects. While deep neural networks have been used for phase estimation and complex-valued signal modeling, prior work does not explicitly learn phase transport between paired signals. Consequently, neither endpoint-supervised regression nor the standard affine path used in flow matching accounts for this phase--amplitude structure. We introduce \emph{cylindrical geodesic flow matching} for paired cardiovascular waveform translation. We show that the standard affine path used in flow matching distorts intermediate amplitude and instantaneous frequency when interpolating between quasiperiodic signals; replacing it with a closed-form geodesic on the phase--amplitude cylinder eliminates these artifacts and converts each training pair into dense, geometry-consistent velocity supervision. On zero-shot photoplethysmography and limited-support seismocardiography adaptation benchmarks, our method consistently outperforms interpolation baselines and matches or exceeds direct supervised prediction, reducing Hilbert Transform, $L_2$, and Dynamic Time Warping distance by up to ${\sim}15\%$ over the strongest competing baseline. These results suggest that bridge geometry is a critical inductive bias for flow matching on oscillatory signal translation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new geometric flow-matching method to translate one quasiperiodic cardiovascular waveform into another, improving alignment and accuracy by respecting phase and amplitude structure.
AI.motivation: Translating physiological waveforms between different sensor locations (e.g., various wearables) is important for interpreting cardiovascular signals. Existing deep learning and flow-matching methods fail to explicitly model phase transport and the cylindrical geometry (circular phase, positive amplitude), causing distortions when interpolating between oscillatory signals.
AI.method: The authors introduce cylindrical geodesic flow matching, which replaces the standard affine interpolation path in flow matching with a closed-form geodesic path defined on a phase–amplitude cylinder. This path respects circular phase, positive amplitude, and quasiperiodic alignment. Each paired source–target signal provides dense supervision of geometry-consistent velocities along this cylindrical geodesic bridge during training.
AI.result: On zero-shot photoplethysmography and limited-support seismocardiography adaptation tasks, the proposed method outperforms interpolation-based baselines and performs on par with or better than direct supervised prediction. It achieves up to about 15% reduction in Hilbert Transform distance, L2 error, and Dynamic Time Warping distance compared with the strongest competing baseline.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating the correct cylindrical bridge geometry into flow matching is an effective inductive bias for oscillatory signal translation. Modeling phase–amplitude structure via geodesic paths significantly improves cardiovascular waveform translation between sensors and can reduce common distortion artifacts in intermediate signals.

title: How Much Evidence Should a Coding Agent's Self-Correction Carry? Adaptive Dirichlet Evidence for Self-Distillation
summary: Execution feedback lets coding agents revise programs and learn from their own corrections. A correction's learning weight should reflect both the transitions supported by its executions and the amount of evidence behind that support. We introduce Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD), which represents these quantities separately. Normalized execution relevance determines relative transition support and an effective pseudo-count mass; a Dirichlet posterior then produces an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. Under a symmetric prior, changing mass preserves category ordering, and effective mass yields a supervised coefficient bounded by its matched fixed-mass counterpart. Across four model-domain history sweeps, increasing visible observations from one to eight reduces future-outcome NLL by 55.0-59.3%. At eight observations, effective mass achieves lower NLL than fixed mass in all four comparisons. In the primary matched DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with the largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance. After one correction-learning round, DeepSeek/CodeARC all-tests Pass@1 increases from 15.0% to 20.4%, with a paired 95% source-bootstrap interval of [+2.8, +8.0] percentage points. The twelve-setting downstream evaluation establishes the model-domain scope of this update. These results show how separating evidence support from evidence mass changes probability estimation and correction learning in coding agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD), a method for improving how coding agents learn from execution-based corrections by separating evidence support from evidence mass, leading to better probability estimation and correction learning.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agents learn from execution feedback but typically conflate how strongly a correction is supported by executions with how much evidence underlies that support. This can miscalibrate learning weights for corrections, harming probability estimation and downstream performance. The authors aim to create a principled way to weight corrections that accounts for both transition support and uncertainty about that support.
AI.method: They introduce EESD, which factorizes learning weight into: (1) normalized execution relevance, capturing relative support for transitions, and (2) an effective pseudo-count mass that reflects the amount of evidence. They then place a Dirichlet prior over categories and compute a posterior that yields uncertainty-penalized weights used in KL-anchored self-distillation for correction learning. Under symmetric priors, they analyze how changing effective mass affects category ordering and bounds the resulting supervised learning coefficient compared with a fixed-mass baseline. They run multi-setting experiments over model-domain history sweeps and downstream coding benchmarks (e.g., DeepSeek with RunBugRun and CodeARC).
AI.result: Across four history-sweep setups, increasing the number of visible execution observations from 1 to 8 cuts future-outcome negative log-likelihood (NLL) by roughly 55–59%. With 8 observations, the effective-mass version consistently achieves lower NLL than a fixed-mass counterpart. In the primary DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, the argmax predictions of effective-mass and fixed-mass models match on all 3,000 examples, but EESD yields substantial NLL improvements, especially when relevance is highly concentrated. On the downstream DeepSeek/CodeARC benchmark, one round of correction learning raises all-tests Pass@1 from 15.0% to 20.4%, with a paired 95% bootstrap interval of about +2.8 to +8.0 percentage points. A broader 12-setting evaluation supports the generality of the gains across model-domain pairs.
AI.conclusion: Separating evidence support from evidence mass allows more calibrated uncertainty-aware learning from execution feedback in coding agents. EESD changes probability estimation behavior without necessarily altering argmax predictions, yet leads to better NLL and significant improvements in downstream coding performance. The approach offers a principled Bayesian-inspired framework for weighting corrections and appears robust across multiple models, domains, and evaluation settings.

title: AnyBottle: A Recipe to Only Keep the Concepts You Really Need
summary: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make predictions inspectable and intervenable by routing them through human-interpretable concepts, but originally required concept annotations. Annotation-free variants remove this requirement, but typically use large concept vocabularies, static at both training and inference, producing bottlenecks larger than any task or prediction needs and harder to inspect. We propose AnyBottle, a single recipe for building compact, task-specific CBMs. AnyBottle assumes only a frozen backbone and an unsupervised concept pool, such as a sparse autoencoder. A black-box teacher trained on the same backbone then guides selection: each round adds the concept that best explains the bottleneck's current failures, with candidates restricted to regions of teacher/student disagreement. Trained with nested dropout over this selection order, the final bottleneck predicts accurately from any concept prefix, so inference spends fewer concepts on inputs it is confident about early and more on hard ones. Since no stage is modality-specific, a new domain and task requires swapping only the backbone and concept pool. Across six vision and two text datasets and two teacher paradigms, AnyBottle yields bottlenecks with fewer concepts and higher concept consistency than annotation-free baselines, while staying close to the black-box reference. Overall, AnyBottle shows that going annotation-free need not mean going large: a small, discovered vocabulary can be as expressive as a much larger, fixed one.

AI.tldr: AnyBottle is an annotation-free, compact, task-specific concept bottleneck model that selects a small but expressive concept set guided by a black-box teacher and supports adaptive, confidence-based concept usage at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing annotation-free concept bottleneck models rely on large, static concept vocabularies, which are inefficient, hard to inspect, and not tailored to individual tasks or examples. There is a need for a method that can retain interpretability and intervention benefits of CBMs while being compact, adaptive, and annotation-free, and easily transferable across modalities and domains.
AI.method: AnyBottle assumes a frozen backbone and an unsupervised concept pool (e.g., from a sparse autoencoder). A black-box teacher, trained on the same backbone, guides iterative concept selection: in each round it chooses the concept that best explains the current bottleneck’s errors, focusing only on regions where teacher and student disagree. The concepts are ordered by this selection, and the CBM is trained with nested dropout so that it learns to predict accurately using any prefix of this ordered concept list, enabling early-exit behavior based on confidence. The approach is modality-agnostic, requiring only swapping in an appropriate backbone and concept pool for new domains.
AI.result: On six vision and two text datasets and with two types of teachers, AnyBottle produces concept bottlenecks that use significantly fewer concepts while achieving higher concept consistency compared to existing annotation-free baselines, and maintains predictive performance close to a black-box reference model.
AI.conclusion: Annotation-free concept bottleneck models do not need large, static concept vocabularies to be expressive. By selecting a small, task-specific concept set guided by a teacher model and training for prefix robustness, AnyBottle yields compact, interpretable, and adaptive bottlenecks that match or nearly match black-box performance across modalities while improving inspectability and efficiency.

title: Adaptive Power Sampling for LLM Reasoning
summary: Sequence-level power sampling has recently emerged as a training-free approach to reasoning by sampling from a sharpened output distribution of a base large language model (LLM). Nevertheless, existing methods typically sharpen the base model distribution uniformly across queries, overlooking variations in query difficulty and in how well the base model already handles each query. The goal of this work is to equip power sampling with query adaptivity. Theoretically, we show that the benefits of further sharpening are determined by the self-reward gap between correct and incorrect responses. Based on this insight, we propose \emph{Adaptive Power Sampling} (APS), which adjusts the sharpening exponent on a per-query basis at test time using the relationship between answer agreement and the model's self-reward. Experiments across diverse reasoning tasks, including MATH500, HumanEval, and GPQA, show that APS consistently outperforms power sampling with a fixed sharpening exponent, without additional training.

AI.tldr: They propose Adaptive Power Sampling (APS), a training-free, query-adaptive way to sharpen an LLM’s output distribution for reasoning tasks, improving over fixed power sampling.
AI.motivation: Existing sequence-level power sampling methods sharpen an LLM’s output distribution with a fixed exponent for all queries. This ignores that different queries have different difficulty and that the base model is more or less confident/capable on each one. The authors want a method that adapts sharpening strength per query to exploit cases where more sharpening helps and avoid over-sharpening where it hurts.
AI.method: They first provide a theoretical analysis showing that whether additional sharpening is beneficial depends on the self-reward gap between correct and incorrect responses. Leveraging this, they design Adaptive Power Sampling (APS), which at test time adjusts the sharpening exponent for each query separately, guided by the observed relationship between answer agreement (how candidate answers align) and the model’s self-reward scores. APS is training-free and operates purely at inference by modifying the sampling process.
AI.result: On several reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, HumanEval, GPQA), APS consistently outperforms standard power sampling that uses a single global sharpening exponent, while requiring no extra training of the base LLM. This suggests better reasoning performance simply through smarter, adaptive sampling.
AI.conclusion: Query adaptivity is important for making power sampling effective across diverse reasoning tasks. By tying the degree of distribution sharpening to a theoretically motivated self-reward gap and implementing this as Adaptive Power Sampling, the authors achieve superior reasoning performance over fixed-exponent power sampling without incurring training costs.

title: MINDSET: Energy-based Schema Evolution for Long Conversational Agent Memory
summary: Long conversational agents have become essential in our daily lives. They must remember what was said long back in order to help us efficiently complete a task without needing the user to repeat instructions and context repeatedly. However, the main issue is that instructions and context change over time and so the agents must be able to adapt accordingly. A useful memory system should preserve both current and historical states, distinguish stale information from active knowledge, retrieve evidence appropriate to the query and avoid repeatedly invoking a large language model to rewrite prior interactions. We introduce MINDSET, a memory controller that stores a conversation as immutable episodes and organizes them into versioned schemas through minimum-energy state transitions. Each incoming episode may reinforce, supersede, split or create a schema. The transition decision balances representation distortion, contradiction, historical damage, fragmentation and internal inconsistency, while hysteresis prevents isolated contradictions from prematurely rewriting stable memory. We evaluate MINDSET against 5 memory systems on a reproducible sample of 850 questions (700 LoCoMo + 150 MemoryAgentBench). MINDSET obtains the highest observed LoCoMo answer F1 while significantly improving retrieval ranking (Recall@8, MRR and nDCG@8) over the second best method LightMem (p<0.01 after Holm correction). It obtains the highest observed scores on MemoryAgentBench although the relative difference is low. Ablations identify controlled fragmentation and schema-aware assignment as the largest contributors to answer quality. Additionally, a 700-question cross-model evaluation with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B supported model independence. These results show that long-term memory can be better handled as constrained state management rather than continual summarization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MINDSET, a memory controller for conversational agents that models long‑term memory as constrained state management over immutable conversation episodes, achieving better QA accuracy and retrieval than existing memory systems.
AI.motivation: Conversational agents need robust long‑term memory so users are not forced to repeat instructions or context. Existing approaches often rely on continual summarization or frequent LLM rewriting of past interactions, which struggles when user preferences and instructions evolve over time. They also have difficulty distinguishing stale information from currently valid knowledge, managing contradictions, and retrieving the right evidence efficiently. The paper aims to design a memory system that preserves historical states, adapts to changes, and retrieves appropriate evidence without expensive constant rewriting.
AI.method: The authors introduce MINDSET, a memory controller that stores each conversational turn as immutable episodes. These episodes are organized into versioned schemas that represent different states of the user or task. For every new episode, the system chooses a transition type—reinforce, supersede, split, or create a schema—based on a minimum‑energy objective that trades off representation distortion, contradictions, historical damage, fragmentation, and internal inconsistency. A hysteresis mechanism prevents isolated contradictions from destabilizing well‑established memories. The system is evaluated against five baseline memory systems on two benchmarks (LoCoMo and MemoryAgentBench), using both answer quality metrics (F1) and retrieval metrics (Recall@8, MRR, nDCG@8), along with ablation studies and cross‑model tests with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B.
AI.result: On 850 benchmark questions (700 LoCoMo + 150 MemoryAgentBench), MINDSET achieves the highest answer F1 on LoCoMo and significantly better retrieval metrics (Recall@8, MRR, nDCG@8) than the second‑best method, LightMem, with statistical significance (p<0.01 after Holm correction). It also attains the highest scores on MemoryAgentBench, though with smaller margins. Ablation experiments show that controlled fragmentation and schema‑aware assignment are the main drivers of answer quality. A 700‑question cross‑model evaluation with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B indicates that the benefits of MINDSET are not specific to a single LLM.
AI.conclusion: Treating long‑term memory for conversational agents as constrained state management over versioned schemas, rather than as continual summarization with frequent rewriting, leads to better handling of evolving user information and improved QA and retrieval performance. MINDSET’s design—immutable episodes, minimum‑energy transitions, and hysteresis—provides a more stable yet adaptable memory representation that generalizes across different LLM backends.

title: Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness
summary: Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer's feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Code is coming soon.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Recursive Game Creator, a multi-agent, experience-oriented framework that iteratively turns rough game prototypes into more enjoyable, high-quality games through automated design, building, playtesting, and review.
AI.motivation: Existing game design agents can produce syntactically correct and playable games, but they often fail to ensure that these games are engaging or enjoyable for players. Traditional evaluation relies on slow GUI-based playtesting and simple correctness checks, which are insufficient to capture player experience or support iterative improvement toward fun and quality. The authors aim to close the gap between program correctness and player enjoyment with a more holistic, experience-driven development loop.
AI.method: The authors propose Recursive Game Creator, which structures development around four specialized components that interact in a recursive loop. (1) The Designer converts high-level user instructions and Reviewer feedback into detailed design plans. (2) The Builder implements these plans as concrete game candidates. (3) The coding-native Player interacts with games via programmatic interfaces, creating reusable gameplay policies to generate rich and diverse trajectories more efficiently than manual or GUI-based play. (4) The Reviewer evaluates games using trajectory-based metrics that infer player preferences, combining these with visual cues and explicit textual preference criteria. After comparing candidate versions, the Reviewer selects the better one and generates improvement feedback, which feeds back to the Designer to start the next iteration.
AI.result: On GameCraft-Bench, Recursive Game Creator reaches a state-of-the-art overall score of 77.89. On GameASG-Bench, it attains a strict task success rate of 53.2%, which is a 34.1% improvement over a baseline using the same base model, and achieves the highest runtime-check pass rate (93.4%) among all compared methods. Additionally, a human user study indicates that games generated by this framework lead to longer playtimes and higher user ratings, suggesting improved entertainment value.
AI.conclusion: Recursive Game Creator demonstrates that structuring game generation as a recursive, multi-agent process centered on player experience can substantially improve both objective benchmarks and subjective enjoyment of generated games. By combining automated design, implementation, programmatic playtesting, and trajectory-based review, the framework moves beyond mere correctness toward more engaging gameplay, setting a new state-of-the-art on standard benchmarks and showing promising results in user studies.

title: Parallel Predictive World Models for Accurate and Efficient Long-Horizon Planning
summary: Long-horizon world-model planning typically relies on autoregressive rollouts, where predicted states are repeatedly fed back into the model. This preserves temporal structure but creates a horizon-length sequential path and exposes later predictions to recursive decoded-state feedback. We introduce Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), which predict a finite-horizon trajectory in parallel while retaining causal interaction among future representations. Each horizon is conditioned on its causal action prefix, and future representations interact before decoding, separating temporal causality from state-by-state output recursion. We formalize this distinction by viewing autoregressive rollout as a causal trajectory map and identifying the decoded-state feedback pathway removed by PPWM. Across four visual-control tasks, PPWM achieves the lowest long-horizon prediction error and the highest Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) simulator success among the evaluated predictive interfaces. Meanwhile, PPWM achieves more than a 3$\times$ average CEM planning speedup over the autoregressive LeWM baseline. These results suggest that accurate and efficient long-horizon world-model planning does not require state-by-state autoregression, but can instead be achieved through parallel causal trajectory prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), a non-autoregressive yet causally structured way to predict future trajectories for long-horizon planning, achieving lower long-horizon error and faster planning than autoregressive world models.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive world-model rollouts for long-horizon planning suffer from two main issues: (1) they create a sequential computation path whose length grows with the horizon, slowing down planning, and (2) they repeatedly feed back decoded predicted states, causing error accumulation and compounding model mistakes. The authors want a predictive interface that keeps temporal causality but avoids slow, error-prone state-by-state autoregression.
AI.method: The authors introduce Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), which predict a fixed-length future trajectory in parallel rather than step-by-step. Each future step’s representation is conditioned only on the causal sequence of actions (the action prefix), while all future latent representations are allowed to interact with each other before being decoded into states. They formalize the usual autoregressive rollout as a causal trajectory map and identify the feedback path from decoded states back into the model that PPWM removes. They then plug PPWM into Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) planners and benchmark it on several visual-control tasks against autoregressive world-model baselines, including LeWM.
AI.result: On four visual-control benchmarks, PPWM achieves (1) the lowest long-horizon prediction error and (2) the highest CEM-based planning success rate among tested predictive interfaces. Additionally, PPWM yields more than a 3× average speedup in CEM planning compared to an autoregressive LeWM baseline, thanks to its parallel trajectory prediction that shortens the effective sequential path.
AI.conclusion: State-by-state autoregressive rollouts are not strictly necessary for accurate, temporally causal long-horizon world-model planning. By decoupling temporal causality from state-wise autoregressive decoding and instead predicting future trajectories in parallel with causal action conditioning, PPWM can improve both accuracy and efficiency of planning algorithms such as CEM.

title: ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding
summary: As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important. Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors. To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents. Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence. We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide the diagnosis and improvement of this capability.

AI.tldr: Introduces ParanoiaEval, a benchmark to systematically evaluate how coding agents treat software-engineering risks, and shows current agents often mis-handle risk treatment regardless of capability.
AI.motivation: As coding agents are increasingly used autonomously in real-world software development, it becomes important to know whether the ways they handle risks—such as avoiding risky changes, mitigating issues, transferring responsibility, or accepting risks—are appropriate. Existing evaluations look at related behaviors (e.g., safety, reliability) from isolated angles and lack a unified, risk-management-grounded framework. The paper aims to fill this gap by creating a systematic way to assess risk-treatment decisions in coding agents, rather than just their task success or raw capabilities.
AI.method: The authors adopt the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance (ATMA) framework from software engineering risk management and adapt it to coding-agent scenarios. They construct ParanoiaEval, a benchmark of 200 pairs of repository-level coding tasks, where each pair is identical except for specific, controlled evidence that should drive a distinct risk-treatment decision. They define metrics for (1) risk-treatment violations (e.g., taking or refusing actions contrary to what the evidence warrants) and (2) evidence responsiveness (the degree to which the agent’s choices change appropriately with the provided evidence). Evaluation uses an "agentic" judge model calibrated against humans for reliability. They then run large-scale experiments on 8 representative coding-agent models/configurations, and complement this with a post-hoc human user study to measure developer experience impacts.
AI.result: Experiments show that unnecessary or inappropriate risk treatments are common: depending on the model and configuration, 11.2%–58.7% of runs apply risk treatment even when evidence indicates it is not needed. Performance and risk treatment are decoupled: models with stronger coding or task-solving capabilities do not consistently make better risk-treatment decisions. Violations of appropriate treatment significantly worsen developers’ subjective experience. Additionally, agents display recognizable, systematic patterns in how they treat risk that align with known phenomena in human risk management (e.g., over-avoidance, inconsistent acceptance), indicating these behaviors are structured rather than random errors.
AI.conclusion: ParanoiaEval provides the first unified, risk-management-based benchmark for evaluating how coding agents treat software risks, highlighting risk treatment as a distinct capability dimension, separate from raw task competence. Current agents frequently mis-handle when and how to treat risks, often over- or under-reacting to evidence, which negatively affects developer experience. The systematic nature of their patterns suggests that established human risk-management knowledge can inform targeted diagnosis and improvement of these capabilities in future coding agents.

title: Coupled but Late: Turn-Taking Between Full-Duplex Speech Models in Unscripted Dialogue
summary: Full-duplex speech models are trained to converse with a person, but they are increasingly made to converse with each other, in self-play data generation, agent societies, and model-based evaluation. In that loop no human absorbs a timing error: each model's turn-taking is the other's input. We ask what timing the loop settles into. Two PersonaPlex-7B instances exchange audio tokens on a shared clock in unscripted conversation, and one floor-transfer rule is applied to them and to Switchboard. Their timing is coupled: re-pairing speakers across conversations destroys it. But the floor changes hands late, at a median of 400-560 ms against 137 ms for humans, and the last 120 ms of the partner's turn, where human projection places a tenth of its transfers, holds 1% of theirs. Delaying one direction of the channel shifts the response one-for-one and leaves the run-up to it empty, consistent with a reactive wait after the perceived end rather than the turn-end projection human timing requires.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how two full-duplex speech models time their turns when conversing with each other, finding that their turn-taking is tightly coupled but much slower and more passive than human timing.
AI.motivation: As speech models are increasingly used to converse not only with humans but also with each other—for self-play training, multi-agent simulations, and model-based evaluation—there is a need to understand the temporal dynamics of their interaction. Unlike human–machine setups, when two models talk to each other, any timing errors are no longer absorbed by a human partner; instead, each model’s timing behavior directly shapes the other’s input. The authors want to know what kind of conversational timing regime such closed loops naturally settle into, and how that compares to human turn-taking patterns.
AI.method: The authors run unscripted, full-duplex audio conversations between two instances of PersonaPlex-7B, exchanging audio tokens on a shared clock. They apply the same floor-transfer (turn-taking) rule to both these model–model conversations and a human conversational corpus (Switchboard) to make timing comparisons. They analyze coupling by re-pairing speakers across conversations to see if timing dependencies are destroyed. They also manipulate timing by artificially delaying one direction of the audio channel and observe how response timing shifts, especially in the period just before a model’s reply begins.
AI.result: They find that the models’ turn timings are strongly coupled—when a given pair converses, their timing depends on each other, and this structure is lost if they are re-paired across different conversations. However, compared with humans, the models transfer the floor much later: median floor-transfer times are around 400–560 ms versus about 137 ms in human Switchboard conversations. Humans frequently initiate their next turn in the final ~120 ms of the partner’s speech, but the models do this only about 1% of the time, showing very little anticipatory overlap. When one direction of the channel is delayed, the model’s response onset shifts almost exactly by the same amount, and the period before that onset remains essentially empty, indicating that the model waits reactively until it perceives an end rather than projecting turn ends in advance.
AI.conclusion: Model–model speech interactions exhibit tightly coupled but non-human-like timing: the systems wait reactively for perceived silence rather than using human-style turn-end projection. This leads to substantially longer gaps between turns and almost no anticipatory starts. Such timing behavior may be acceptable or even invisible when talking to patient humans but becomes structurally important in closed conversational loops, multi-agent systems, and evaluation pipelines. The findings imply that to achieve human-like, efficient spoken dialogue—especially in multi-agent settings—future work must explicitly model and train for predictive turn-taking behavior rather than relying on simple reactive floor-transfer rules.

title: ScienceClaw: Benchmarking Continual Self-Evolution of AI-for-Science Agents Across the Natural and Social Sciences
summary: Large language model agents are accelerating scientific automation, yet verified executions rarely become persistent program-level improvements, and existing evaluations do not examine this process across sequential tasks in both the natural and social sciences. We formalize ScienceClaw as fixed-parameter program self-evolution that unifies task solving, scientific verification, and program updates. ScienceClaw-Eval spans 23 disciplines and measures scientific correctness, evolutionary gain, retention, cross-dataset transfer, and evolution cost through sequential streams and independent reset evaluation. Our framework repairs executable workflows through multi-turn interaction, converts re-execution-verified failure--success trajectories into linked Skill and Operator candidates, and retains an update only when source-task replay reproduces the repair and independent scientific tasks improve. Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/ScienceClaw.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ScienceClaw, a framework for self-evolving scientific code using large language model agents, along with a benchmark (ScienceClaw-Eval) spanning 23 disciplines to evaluate how verified fixes can be retained as persistent program improvements.
AI.motivation: Although LLM agents can autonomously run and fix scientific workflows, their successful executions are usually one-off and do not accumulate as reusable program-level improvements. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not test this kind of sequential self-improvement across multiple scientific domains. The authors aim to formalize and systematically evaluate how LLM-driven scientific automation can continuously evolve its own codebase while preserving scientific correctness.
AI.method: They formalize ScienceClaw as a fixed-parameter program self-evolution framework that unifies three steps: solving tasks, verifying the scientific correctness of the solution via re-execution, and updating the underlying program only when changes are validated. They construct ScienceClaw-Eval, a benchmark covering 23 disciplines with sequential task streams and independent reset evaluations. The system repairs executable workflows via multi-turn interaction with an LLM agent, logs failure-to-success trajectories that are re-execution-verified, converts these into reusable Skills and Operators, and accepts an update only if (1) replay on the source task reproduces the repair and (2) performance improves on independent scientific tasks.
AI.result: ScienceClaw-Eval reports metrics such as scientific correctness, evolutionary gain (how much the program improves over time), retention of useful updates, cross-dataset transfer of learned skills, and the cost of evolution. Empirically, the framework can repair broken workflows and extract reusable Skills/Operators that improve performance on later tasks while enforcing strict verification and replay criteria.
AI.conclusion: The work provides both a formal definition and a practical benchmark for LLM-driven self-evolving scientific workflows. By tightly coupling verification, replay, and cross-task evaluation, ScienceClaw offers a more rigorous path for turning individual successful LLM interventions into persistent, reusable program improvements across diverse scientific domains.

title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://nanomuse.cn ; Code: https://github.com/nano-muse/nanoMuse
summary: Assistants from 2011 answered and waited, and agents from 2023 did a task and stopped. In September 2026 Meta's Muse showed an agent for one person, with accounts, devices, memory and a conversation that lasts, closed, in a vendor's cloud, in one country. Such an agent is expected to act on a person's accounts and devices, remember them across weeks, speak first when it is worth it, and answer for what it did. It is a kind of software, not a model, and until now had no open counterpart. This report defines the personal agent in five questions and three horizons. It reads how Muse is built from Meta's public record and a copy of its production prompt, each statement marked by its source. It then presents nanoMuse, the open-source counterpart under the GPL-3.0, one agent on every device a person owns, with hands on the phone's screen and the computer's. They share one conversation over a relay anyone can run; every action goes through a Sentinel, memory is files the person can read, and the model is their choice. Its size and cost are given as estimates. What is open, memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the hands and an open model for them, is set out as a roadmap.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces nanoMuse, an open-source, device-local personal agent architecture inspired by Meta’s proprietary Muse agent, and outlines its design, capabilities, cost, and roadmap.
AI.motivation: Proprietary personal agent systems like Meta’s Muse can act across a user’s accounts and devices with persistent memory but are closed, cloud-bound, and controlled by a single vendor, leaving no open, user-controlled alternative. The paper aims to define what a modern personal agent is and to provide an open implementation that users can own, inspect, and self-host across their devices.
AI.method: The authors first analyze and reverse-engineer the concept and architecture of Meta’s Muse from public material and a production prompt, organizing their definition into five key questions and three future horizons.
