They then design nanoMuse as an open GPL-licensed system: one agent per device, linked via a relay, with a shared conversation state, explicit ‘hands’ for acting on phone and computer screens, a Sentinel component that mediates all actions, file-based user-readable memory with provenance, and pluggable language models chosen by the user. They estimate resource requirements and costs, and sketch tooling such as an evaluation suite for the agent’s ‘hands.’
AI.result: The paper specifies a concrete architecture and implementation plan for nanoMuse, including how agents coordinate across devices, how actions are mediated and logged, how memory is represented as readable files with provenance, and how users can swap underlying models. It provides initial size and cost estimates and describes infrastructure such as a user-run relay and Sentinel. It also produces a structured definition of ‘personal agent’ derived from the Muse case study.
AI.conclusion: Personal agents should be treated as user-owned software systems rather than proprietary model endpoints: they must span multiple devices, act autonomously within user-authorized boundaries, maintain long-lived, inspectable memory, and remain accountable for their actions. nanoMuse demonstrates that such an architecture can be realized in an open, self-hostable, and model-agnostic way, and the authors propose future work on open memory with provenance, a standardized evaluation suite for action capabilities, and dedicated open models optimized for agent ‘hands’ to complete the open ecosystem.

title: WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly advancing scientific and engineering problem solving, with physics simulation emerging as a challenging yet practical testbed for reproducing complex physical phenomena with application in embodied AI, games and films. As the workhorse of such simulation, a solver computes how the state of a dynamic system evolves over time. Building such solvers requires physical understanding to identify appropriate models, mathematical reasoning to formulate the underlying dynamics, and software engineering to implement them as executable code, yet this capability of LLM agents remains underexplored. To this end, we introduce WorldSolver, a benchmark of 168 simulation tasks derived from physical phenomena in 61 classic computer graphics papers, spanning 7 physical domains. Each task contains a code scaffold that provides a fixed simulation environment for the scene, with the solver implementation left for the agent to complete. Specifically, we evaluate them along three dimensions: Execution Checks for successful execution, Visual Fidelity for reproducing the intended dynamic behavior in the rendered simulation, and Physical Plausibility for physics-grounded verification of the generated dynamics. Experiments on frontier agents reveal that producing executable solvers is difficult itself, and satisfying visual and physical correctness is even harder. GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5 perform comparatively better than the other evaluated agents, yet achieve overall scores of only 48.7% and 46.7%, respectively. WorldSolver is an early step toward agentic solver generation, and we hope it helps drive progress toward agents that can faithfully simulate the dynamic physical world. Code is available at https://github.com/sirujiang/WorldSolver.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WorldSolver, a benchmark to test LLM-based agents on generating physics solvers that simulate complex physical phenomena from classic graphics papers.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents are being used for scientific and engineering tasks, but their ability to design and implement physics simulation solvers—requiring physical insight, mathematical formulation, and coding skill—is underexplored. There is a need for a systematic benchmark to measure and improve this capability.
AI.method: The authors construct WorldSolver, a benchmark of 168 simulation tasks drawn from 61 classic computer graphics papers across 7 physical domains. Each task provides a fixed simulation environment as a code scaffold, leaving the core solver implementation for the agent to write. They assess agents using three metrics: (1) Execution Checks (does the code run), (2) Visual Fidelity (does the rendered simulation match intended behavior), and (3) Physical Plausibility (are the dynamics physically sound). Multiple state-of-the-art LLM agents are evaluated on this suite.
AI.result: Frontier LLM agents struggle with the tasks: many fail even at producing executable code, and achieving both visually correct and physically plausible simulations is even more difficult. The best-performing agents, GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, reach only 48.7% and 46.7% overall scores, respectively.
AI.conclusion: WorldSolver exposes a large performance gap between current LLM agents and the goal of automated solver generation for physics simulation. The benchmark is positioned as an early but important step toward agents that can reliably design and implement physically faithful dynamic simulations, aiming to stimulate future research in this direction.

title: Does an Agent's History Tell You When Compaction Will Hurt? A Modest, Bounded Effect on the TRACE Paired-Replay Corpus
comment: Accepted at the IAB Workshop (Interpreting Agent Behavior) at NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 20 pages
summary: Many long-horizon agents compact their context on a global rule, usually a token budget, blind to what the agent was doing. We ask whether the agent's recent behaviour predicts when a compaction will hurt. TRACE's public corpus of 590 harness-triggered AppWorld compaction boundaries replays each boundary from a re-executed prefix state under the pre-compaction context and under the summary, and records the burden of the next actions: calls that error or repeat a call already made. We find that pre-boundary history predicts post-compaction harm only weakly. An internally prespecified contrast by prefix placement is a wide null, and the naive "has-written" label behind it turns out to measure trajectory phase. The best extension-protocol trigger reaches held-out AUROC 0.66 (0.64 on the replicate's own label) against a same-boundary replicate of 0.72; the best frozen, interpretable trigger avoids 21% of harmful (positive-burden) boundaries while keeping 84% of compaction opportunities, and exceeds the random-rule expectation on count but not on burden mass (a post hoc comparison). Whether the best trigger beats a token-budget rule at matched retention cannot be evaluated on the release. We state what corpora should ship to answer it.

AI.tldr: Study on when context compaction in long-horizon agents causes harm, and how well pre-compaction behavior predicts that harm.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agents must periodically compact or summarize their context due to token limits, but current policies trigger compaction based on global rules like token budgets, ignoring what the agent is actually doing. This may cause harmful compactions that lead to errors or redundant actions. The authors want to know whether agents’ recent behavior can predict when compaction will be harmful, enabling smarter, behavior-aware triggers.
AI.method: They construct TRACE, a public corpus of 590 compaction boundaries collected from harness-triggered AppWorld runs. For each boundary, they re-execute from a saved prefix state twice: once with the full pre-compaction context and once with the compacted summary. They then measure the "burden" of the subsequent actions, defined as calls that error or repeat previously made calls. They analyze how well various labels and triggers derived from pre-boundary history predict post-compaction harm, including an internally prespecified contrast based on prefix placement, naive "has-written" labels, and more sophisticated extension-protocol triggers. They evaluate triggers using AUROC and coverage metrics and compare to random rules and replicate performance.
AI.result: Pre-compaction history is only weakly predictive of post-compaction harm. The prespecified contrast based on prefix placement yields a wide null result, and the naive "has-written" label is revealed to mostly capture trajectory phase instead of true risk. The best learned extension-protocol trigger attains an AUROC of 0.66 on held-out data (0.64 on the replicate’s own label), which is notably worse than a same-boundary replicate AUROC of 0.72, indicating limited predictability. The best simple, frozen, interpretable trigger can avoid 21% of harmful boundaries while preserving 84% of compaction opportunities, doing better than random selection in terms of boundary count but not in total burden mass reduced (per a post hoc analysis).
AI.conclusion: Behavior-aware compaction triggers can identify and avoid some harmful compaction events, but the signal in pre-compaction behavior is weak, and current triggers only modestly outperform naive baselines. The work provides TRACE, a reusable corpus and evaluation framework, and specifies what additional data future corpora should include so that researchers can properly compare behavior-aware triggers to standard token-budget rules at matched retention. Overall, smarter compaction triggers are promising but not yet clearly superior to simple global rules with the currently available data.

title: VeriFine: Scaling Verification for Self-Improvement in Embodied Reasoning
summary: Self-improving policies continually expose new failure patterns, changing what their judges must be able to verify. However, current fixed judges constrain both optimization feedback and the discovery of useful training examples, limiting further self-improvement. This challenge is even more acute in embodied reasoning, where reliable evaluation must account for spatial grounding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making. We introduce VeriFine, an agent harness framework that scales verification through the co-evolution of the policy, training curriculum, and judge. The Policy Improvement Loop uses a rubric judge to diagnose recurring failures, construct an adaptive curriculum, and optimize the policy. When progress plateaus and verification becomes a bottleneck, the Judge Improvement Loop selectively queries human guidance on informative failure cases and refines the judge through coactive calibration, in which humans and agents resolve disagreements and converge toward the objective rubric of physical reasoning. The revised judge then guides the next stage of data selection and policy optimization. Experiments on driving and robot navigation tasks demonstrate continuous self-improvement in both policy and judge capability across reinforcement and supervised fine-tuning. These results show how scaling verification supports continuous self-improvement as policy failure patterns evolve.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VeriFine, a framework where both the policy and its judge co-evolve, enabling continuous self-improvement by scaling verification as failure patterns change.
AI.motivation: Fixed evaluation judges limit the ability of self-improving agents to find and learn from new failure modes, especially in embodied reasoning tasks that require spatial grounding, causal reasoning, and safety. As policies improve, their failure patterns shift, but static judges cannot keep up, creating a verification bottleneck that slows or stops further improvement.
AI.method: VeriFine introduces an agent harness with two intertwined loops: (1) a Policy Improvement Loop that uses a rubric-based judge to diagnose recurring failures, build an adaptive training curriculum from these failures, and optimize the policy via reinforcement or supervised learning; and (2) a Judge Improvement Loop that, when policy progress stalls due to verification limits, selects informative failure cases, queries humans, and refines the judge through coactive calibration, where humans and agents resolve disagreements to better align the judge with an intended rubric of physical reasoning. The updated judge then drives the next cycle of data selection and policy optimization.
AI.result: On driving and robot navigation benchmarks, VeriFine achieves continuous improvement of both the control policy and the evaluation judge. Experiments show that as the system iterates, the policy handles increasingly complex scenarios and the judge becomes more capable at detecting nuanced, safety-relevant errors across both reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning regimes.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving the policy and its evaluation judge, rather than keeping the judge fixed, allows verification capacity to scale with policy capability. This enables ongoing discovery and correction of new failure patterns, particularly in embodied reasoning tasks, demonstrating that improved verification is a key lever for sustained self-improvement in learning-based agents.

title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can solve many narrow tasks, but querying them separately for millions of related instances can be prohibitively expensive. Can LLM agents autonomously create cheaper solutions for such workloads? We call this ability "bottling": the ability to turn general capabilities into task-specific solutions that balance answer quality and amortised cost. We introduce BOTTLED, a benchmark in which agents receive an entire unlabelled workload and must complete it under fixed time, compute and LLM API budgets. Agents choose their own approach, such as training a small model or writing a reusable program. Across ten models and three tasks, we find that strong zero-shot task performance does not reliably translate into strong bottling capabilities. Models with similar zero-shot scores can differ substantially after bottling, and 48 of 60 bottling runs score below the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of their model's zero-shot performance. Moreover, 31 of 60 runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same token budget. Nevertheless, bottling can yield substantial savings: on query-product relevance classification, Opus 5 retains about 82% of its zero-shot macro-F1 at roughly 657 times lower reported cost. Bottling is also competitive with Jev, a "system one" model built especially for cheap, repetitive inference: Opus 5 on the same task recovers about 94% of Jev's macro-F1 at a quarter of Jev's projected full-workload cost. BOTTLED provides a basis for evaluating and improving agents' ability to invest limited resources in reusable solutions for large, repetitive workloads.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BOTTLED, a benchmark for testing whether LLM agents can “bottle” their general capabilities into cheaper, task-specific solutions for large workloads under strict budget constraints, showing that strong zero-shot performance does not necessarily imply strong bottling ability, but that effective bottling can still yield large cost savings with modest quality loss.
AI.motivation: Although large language models can perform well on many tasks, using them directly for millions of similar queries is often too expensive. There is a need to understand whether LLM agents can autonomously design and build cheaper, reusable solutions—such as distilled small models or programs—that maintain acceptable quality while drastically reducing amortized cost. Existing evaluations mostly focus on single-query or few-shot settings and do not systematically measure this “bottling” ability across workloads, time, and compute budgets.
AI.method: The authors define “bottling” as turning general LLM capabilities into task-specific, reusable solutions that trade off answer quality against per-instance cost. They propose BOTTLED, a benchmark where an agent is given an entire unlabelled workload plus fixed budgets of time, compute, and LLM API calls. The agent must decide how to use these resources—e.g., by training a smaller model, performing distillation, writing reusable code, or other strategies—and then process the workload. They run experiments across three tasks and ten different LLMs, comparing each model’s performance after bottling against (1) its own zero-shot performance and (2) strong small-model distillation baselines under the same token budget. They analyze how much performance is retained after bottling and the extent of cost savings achieved.
AI.result: Empirically, high zero-shot task performance does not consistently translate into strong bottling performance. Models with similar zero-shot scores can diverge significantly after bottling. In 48 out of 60 experimental runs, the bottling process yields scores below the lower bound of the model’s own 95% confidence interval for zero-shot performance, indicating substantial degradation. Additionally, in 31 out of 60 runs, the agents underperform a stronger of two small-model distillation baselines that use the same token budget. However, when bottling works well, it can produce large cost savings with relatively modest quality loss. For example, on a query–product relevance classification task, the Opus 5 model retains about 82% of its zero-shot macro-F1 while reducing the reported cost by roughly a factor of 657. Opus 5’s bottled solution also recovers about 94% of the macro-F1 of Jev—a purpose-built, cheap “system one” model—at only about one-quarter of Jev’s projected full-workload cost.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that strong zero-shot performance alone is not a reliable indicator of an LLM’s ability to “bottle” its capabilities into efficient task-specific solutions for large workloads. Current agents often fail to match even simple distillation baselines under equivalent budgets, revealing a substantial gap between general competence and effective resource investment strategies. Nevertheless, successful bottling can dramatically reduce inference costs while maintaining most of the original performance and can even approach or surpass specialized cheap models on some tasks. BOTTLED thus offers a framework to rigorously evaluate and improve agents’ capacity to design reusable, low-cost solutions for large-scale, repetitive inference scenarios.
